paras.en: [[1:22|Pharao therefore charged all his people, saying: Whatsoever shall be born of the male sex, ye shall cast into the river: whatsoever of the female, ye shall save alive|Præcepit ergo Pharao omni populo suo, dicens: Quidquid masculini sexus natum fuerit, in flumen projicite; quidquid feminini, reservate]]. The people of Pharao are the demons, subject to their prince; and also all the wicked, heretics, schismatics and unbelievers, all of whom the devil commands and urges to cast the males into the river, that is, to persecute and destroy those who are truly catholic, just and spiritual, overwhelming them with the disquiet of tribulations, the onset of temptations, and the flood and abundance of vices; but to keep the females, that is, to cherish and preserve in evil those who, like women, are unstable, soft and weak in resisting temptations and vices.

2.title: Elucidatio litteralis capituli secundi: Egressus est post hæc vir de domo Levi
2.title_en: Literal explanation of the second chapter: “After this there went a man of the house of Levi”

paras.t: Consequenter Moyses quasi de alio loquens, sui ipsius nativitatem, educationem, provectum, eventum et gesta describit. Sic quippe auctores Scripturæ, de se ipsis quasi de aliis frequenter loquuntur.
paras.en: Next Moses, as though speaking of another, describes his own birth, upbringing, advancement, fortunes and deeds. For the authors of Scripture often speak of themselves as though of others.

paras.t: Egressus est post hæc vir de domo Levi, et accepit uxorem stirpis suæ. Si quod ait, Post hæc, intelligitur de omnibus de quibus facta est mentio in præcedenti capitulo, tunc egressus hujus viri, non potest intelligi de ejus nativitate ; neque quod ait, Accepit uxorem, accipi potest de sumptione mulieris illius in matrimonium : quoniam vir iste, diu natus fuit ante præfatum Pharaonis præceptum de submersione parvulorum ; similiter ante præceptum illud duxit feminam illam conjugem. Imo et ante illud præceptum genuit ex eadem Aaron et Mariam. Siquidem Aaron fuit triennio senior Moyse ; et si ante nativitatem Aaron emanasset illud præceptum, Aaron fuisset submersus. Maria vero soror Moysis et Aaron, fuit per tempus notabile eis senior, ut in isto dicetur capitulo. Si itaque quod dicitur, Post hæc, intelligatur de omnibus illis, sic exponetur particula ista, Egressus est : id est, ad certum actum et determinatam prolificationem processit, atque de loco et actu orationis, ad locum et actum generationis progressus est post hæc, quæ præcedenti narrantur capitulo, vir de domo Levi, id est de semine et familia Levi patriarchæ. Fuit namque vir iste Amram filius Caath filii Levi, ut infra patebit ; et accepit uxorem stirpis suæ, id est, maritali affectu atque amplexu illam accessit, quæ uxor fuit etiam de progenie Levi. Fuit enim (ut infra habetur) Jochabed patruelis istius Amram. Porro si quod ait, Post hæc, referatur solum ad aliqua in præcedenti capitulo scripta, puta ad ingressum Jacob filiorumque ejus in Ægyptum, ad exsistentiam quoque diuturnam, quamvis non totalem, ipsius Joseph in Ægypto, sic egressus viri hujus accipi possit de nativitate ejus ; et acceptio suæ uxoris, de acceptione in conjugem.
paras.en: [[2:1|After this there went a man of the house of Levi; and took a wife of his own kindred.|Egressus est post hæc vir de domo Levi, et accepit uxorem stirpis suæ]] If what he says, [[2:1|After this|Post hæc]], is understood of all the things mentioned in the preceding chapter, then the going out of this man cannot be understood of his birth; nor can what he says, [[2:1|took a wife|Accepit uxorem]], be taken of his taking that woman in marriage: for this man was born long before the aforesaid command of Pharao about the drowning of the little ones; likewise he married that woman before that command. Indeed, even before that command he begot of her Aaron and Mary. For Aaron was three years older than Moses; and if that command had gone out before the birth of Aaron, Aaron would have been drowned. And Mary, the sister of Moses and Aaron, was older than they by a considerable time, as will be said in this chapter. If, then, what is said, [[2:1|After this|Post hæc]], is understood of all those things, this phrase, [[2:1|there went|Egressus est]], will be explained thus: that is, he went forth to a certain act and a determined begetting of offspring, and passed from the place and act of prayer to the place and act of generation, after these things which are narrated in the preceding chapter, [[2:1|a man of the house of Levi|vir de domo Levi]], that is, of the seed and family of the patriarch Levi. For this man was Amram, the son of Caath the son of Levi, as will appear below; [[2:1|and took a wife of his own kindred|et accepit uxorem stirpis suæ]], that is, he went in to her with a husband's affection and embrace, a wife who was also of the progeny of Levi. For (as is found below) Jochabed was this Amram's aunt by the father's side [Latin *patruelis*, the word of the Vulgate at 6:20]. But if what he says, [[2:1|After this|Post hæc]], is referred only to some of the things written in the preceding chapter, for instance to the entry of Jacob and his sons into Egypt, and also to the long, though not total, presence of Joseph himself in Egypt, then the going out of this man may be taken of his birth, and the taking of his wife, of taking her in marriage.

paras.t: Quæ concepit et peperit filium, scilicet Moysen. Magister in historiis, aliique communiter ex Josepho referunt, quod post exitum præfati præcepti de parvulorum submersione, Amram iste ab uxore sua abstinuit, malens non generare, quam infantulos mox necandos procreare. Et creditur Deum devote orasse, ut succurreret populo suo tam inhumane oppresso ; tuncque in somno apparuit ei Dominus, admonens ut secure uxorem cognosceret, quia generaturus esset ex ea filium liberaturum filios Israel, de cujus filii ortu formidarent Ægyptii. De sacerdotio quoque Aaron filii sui prædixit ei. Quibus auditis, cognovit uxorem. Et videns eum elegantem : fuit equidem Moyses puer valde formosus et magnus ; dicuntque aliqui quod natus mox matri suæ arrisit ; abscondit eum tribus mensibus. Infra quos occulte alunt eum. Sed mirum videtur, qualiter potuit puerum tamdiu celare, quia ex uteri sui tumore patuit cunctis intuentibus quod concepit, similiter ex uteri sui depressione patuit eam jam peperisse ; in partu quoque videtur instar parientium clamitasse, nec habuit testem, puerum natum esse submersum. Ad ista quidam respondent, quod quædam sunt feminæ ita dispositæ, quod earum impregnatio parum appareat, et quod sine dolore vehementi parere solent. Et talem dicunt istam fuisse.
paras.en: [[2:2|And she conceived, and bore a son|Quæ concepit et peperit filium]], namely Moses. The Master in the Histories [that is, Peter Comestor in his *Historia Scholastica*] and others commonly relate from Josephus that after the going out of the aforesaid command about the drowning of the little ones, this Amram abstained from his wife, preferring not to beget rather than to beget infants soon to be slain. And he is believed to have prayed devoutly to God to succour His people, so inhumanly oppressed; and then the Lord appeared to him in sleep, admonishing him to know his wife without fear, because he would beget of her a son who would deliver the children of Israel, a son at whose birth the Egyptians would tremble. He also foretold to him the priesthood of his son Aaron. Having heard this, he knew his wife. [[2:2|and seeing him a goodly child|Et videns eum elegantem]]: for Moses was indeed a very beautiful and large child; and some say that as soon as he was born he smiled at his mother; [[2:2|hid him three months|abscondit eum tribus mensibus]]. During these they nourish him in secret. But it seems a wonder how she could hide the child so long, since from the swelling of her womb it was plain to all who looked on her that she had conceived, and likewise from its going down it was plain that she had now given birth; in childbirth too she would seem to have cried out like women in labour; nor had she a witness that the child born had been drowned. To this some answer that certain women are so made that their pregnancy shows little, and that they usually give birth without violent pain; and they say that she was such a one.

paras.t: Quumque jam celare non posset diutius puerum adhuc viventem. Paulatim quippe res cœpit erumpere et patere. Aliqui quoque dicunt, quod ex præcepto regis, Ægyptii statutis diebus scrutabantur habitacula Hebræorum, an eis esset puer absconditus : quod ad minus semel fecerunt (ut dicitur) infra tres menses. Sumpsit fiscellam scirpeam, et linivit eam bitumine ac pice ; posuitque intus infantulum, et exposuit eum in carecto ripæ fluminis, stante procul sorore ejus, et considerante eventum rei. Fiscella scirpea est vasculum rotundum instar alveoli, factum de scirpis, id est de juncis. Quod linitum fuit bitumine et pice, ne aqua Nili illud intraret. Fecit quoque illud de juncis, qui sunt levis, aqueæ, aereæque naturæ, ut super aquas posset natare. Posuit etiam vasculum illud juxta ripam, in loco ubi solent crescere carices, quæ sunt herbæ acutæ, ut ensis, ita quod manum secant prementis. Unde locus ille vocatur carectum. Non enim posuit fiscellam illam remote a ripa, ne vi aquæ abduceretur longe a terra.
paras.en: [[2:3|And when she could hide him no longer|Quumque jam celare non posset]], the child being still alive. For little by little the matter began to break out and come to light. Some also say that by the king's command the Egyptians searched the dwellings of the Hebrews on set days, to see whether they had a child hidden; which (it is said) they did at least once within the three months. [[2:3|she took a basket made of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and pitch: and put the little babe therein, and laid him in the sedges by the river's brink|Sumpsit fiscellam scirpeam, et linivit eam bitumine ac pice ; posuitque intus infantulum, et exposuit eum in carecto ripæ fluminis]], [[2:4|His sister standing afar off, and taking notice what would be done.|stante procul sorore ejus, et considerante eventum rei]] A *fiscella scirpea* is a little round vessel like a small trough, made of *scirpi*, that is, of rushes. It was daubed with slime and pitch so that the water of the Nile should not get into it. She made it of rushes, too, which are of a light, watery and airy nature, so that it could float on the waters. She also put that little vessel next to the bank, in a place where *carices* [sedges] usually grow, which are plants sharp as a sword, so that they cut the hand of one who presses them; hence that place is called *carectum* [a bed of sedges, “the sedges” of the Douay-Rheims]. For she did not put the basket far from the bank, lest the force of the water should carry it far from land.

paras.t: Ecce autem descendebat filia Pharaonis, ut lavaretur in flumine. Exivit namque de palatio et civitate regali, quæ erat in situ altiori quam Nilus. Ideo dicitur descendisse ut in flumine lavaretur. Nec puto quod instar natantium voluerit se nudam lavare in aqua, sed pro refrigerio atque solatio pedes et partes eis vicinas. Et secundum Josephum, lusit circa littus. Verumtamen consuetudines juxta diversitatem locorum et temporum ac hominum variantur. Et puellæ ejus gradiebantur per crepidinem alvei, id est, pedisequæ ejus juxta ripam Nili deambulabant. Quæ cum vidisset fiscellam in papyrione, id est in parte et loco Nili, in quo crescit papyrus, id est juncus sic appellatus, misit unam e famulabus suis, ut afferret sibi fiscellam. Ex quo constat, quod aqua non erat profunda usque ad locum illum. Et allatam fiscellam aperiens filia Pharaonis, cernensque in ea parvulum vagientem, miserta ejus, ait : De infantibus Hebræorum est hic infans. Hoc enim faciliter conjicere potuit, quia patris sui cognovit præceptum de infantulis illis mergendis.
paras.en: [[2:5|And behold the daughter of Pharao came down to wash herself in the river|Ecce autem descendebat filia Pharaonis, ut lavaretur in flumine]]. For she went out from the palace and the royal city, which stood on higher ground than the Nile; therefore she is said to have come down to wash herself in the river. Nor do I think that she meant to wash herself naked in the water like swimmers, but her feet and the parts near them, for refreshment and comfort. And according to Josephus, she was playing by the shore. Yet customs vary with the difference of places, times and men. [[2:5|and her maids walked by the river's brink|Et puellæ ejus gradiebantur per crepidinem alvei]], that is, her waiting-women were walking along the bank of the Nile. [[2:5|And when she saw the basket in the sedges|Quæ cum vidisset fiscellam in papyrione]], that is, in the part and place of the Nile where papyrus grows, that is, the rush so called [Latin *papyrio*, a bed of papyrus, where the Douay-Rheims has “the sedges”], [[2:5|she sent one of her maids|misit unam e famulabus suis]] to bring her the basket. From this it is clear that the water was not deep as far as that place. [[2:5|and when it was brought|Et allatam]], the basket, Pharao's daughter [[2:6|opened it|aperiens]], [[2:6|and seeing within it an infant crying, having compassion on it, she said|cernensque in ea parvulum vagientem, miserta ejus, ait]]: [[2:6|This is one of the babes of the Hebrews|De infantibus Hebræorum est hic]], this infant. For she could easily guess this, because she knew her father's command about drowning those infants.

paras.t: Cui soror pueri, puta Maria, quæ jam juvencula erat : Vis, inquit, ut vadam, et vocem tibi mulierem Hebræam, quæ nutrire possit infantulum? Respondit : Vade, id est, fac ita. Circa quod quæri potest, cur filia regis non ordinavit, ut ille puerulus a muliere Ægyptia nutriretur. Cujus ratio paulo post exprimetur.
paras.en: [[2:7|And the child's sister said to her|Cui soror pueri]], namely Mary, who was already a young girl: [[2:7|Shall I go, and call to thee a Hebrew woman, to nurse the babe?|Vis, inquit, ut vadam, et vocem tibi mulierem Hebræam, quæ nutrire possit infantulum?]] [[2:8|She answered: Go|Respondit : Vade]], that is, do so. On this it may be asked why the king's daughter did not arrange for that little boy to be nursed by an Egyptian woman. The reason for this will be given a little further on.

paras.t: Perrexit puella, et vocavit matrem ejus, scilicet pueri, imo et suam, quam tamen adduxit quasi alienam, nec indicavit quod mater esset illius infantuli. Ad quam locuta filia Pharaonis : Accipe, ait, puerum istum, et nutri mihi, id est ad commodum atque solatium meum. Ego dabo tibi mercedem tuam, quam postulaveris a me, et quam te mereri putavero. Verumtamen mater Moysis in illo casu aliunde, videlicet jure naturali ac divino, tenebatur proprium nutrire infantem ; nec videtur in hoc mercedem meruisse humanam, nisi secundum æstimationem filiæ Pharaonis. Suscepit mulier et nutrivit puerum ; adultumque, utpote ablactatum et rationis capacem, tradidit filiæ Pharaonis. Non dicitur quod postulavit mercedem a filia Pharaonis pro pueri nutritione : forsitan tamen postulavit, ut minus putaretur mater infantuli ; et forsan non postulavit, sciens se matrem infantis, et volens complacere reginæ.
paras.en: [[2:8|The maid went and called her mother|Perrexit puella, et vocavit matrem ejus]], that is, the child's mother, and indeed her own; yet she brought her as though a stranger, and did not reveal that she was that infant's mother. [[2:9|And Pharao's daughter said to her: Take this child, and nurse him for me|Ad quam locuta filia Pharaonis : Accipe, ait, puerum istum, et nutri mihi]], that is, for my advantage and comfort. [[2:9|I will give thee thy wages|Ego dabo tibi mercedem tuam]], whatever thou shalt ask of me and I shall think thou hast earned. Yet in that case the mother of Moses was bound on other grounds, namely by natural and divine law, to nurse her own infant; nor does she seem to have earned a human wage in this, except in the estimation of Pharao's daughter. [[2:9|The woman took and nursed the child|Suscepit mulier et nutrivit puerum]]: [[2:9|and when he was grown up|adultumque]], that is, weaned and capable of reason, [[2:9|she delivered him to Pharao's daughter|tradidit filiæ Pharaonis]]. It is not said that she asked a wage of Pharao's daughter for nursing the child: perhaps she did ask, so as to be the less thought the infant's mother; and perhaps she did not ask, knowing herself the infant's mother and wishing to please the queen.

paras.t: Quem illa adoptavit in locum filii. Nam creditur tunc non habuisse alium filium. Ex quo innotescit etiam, quod ille infantulus erat miro modo pulcher, gratiosus, amabilis, in tantum quod pagana regis filia sic accendebatur amore pueruli. Vocavitque nomen ejus Moyses, dicens : Quia de aqua tuli eum, ideo voco eum hoc nomine. MOYS quippe in Ægyptio idiomate, dicitur aqua ; IS, salvatus : sicque Moyses interpretatur, salvatus de aqua.
paras.en: [[2:10|And she adopted him for a son|Quem illa adoptavit in locum filii]]. For she is believed to have had no other son then. From this it also becomes known that that infant was wonderfully beautiful, graceful and lovable, so much so that the king's pagan daughter was thus kindled with love for the little boy. [[2:10|and called him Moses, saying|Vocavitque nomen ejus Moyses, dicens]]: [[2:10|Because I took him out of the water|Quia de aqua tuli eum]], therefore I call him by this name. For in the Egyptian tongue *Moys* means water, and *is*, saved: and so Moses is interpreted, saved from the water.

paras.t: Hanc de se ipso historiam Moyses multum breviter scripsit, quam Josephus plenius recitat, dicens : Metuens Amram ne captus incideret iram regis, propter occultationem videlicet Moysis, et ne simul cum puerulo deperiret, providentiamque Dei excluderet, quia videlicet audivit a Deo, quod puer ille esset liberaturus Israeliticum populum, præparavit vas rotundum, in quo infans spatiose jaceret. Itaque infantem ibi positum, et in flumine collocatum, Deo commisit. Thermuthis autem filia regis circa littus fluminis ludens, et vas illud conspiciens, jussit sibi afferri. In quo videns infantem, gavisa est valde propter magnitudinem et pulchritudinem pueri, præcepitque adduci mulierem Ægyptiam, quæ daret infanti mamillam. Quo renuente ubera mulieris Ægyptiæ, atque hoc idem in multis mulieribus Ægyptiis faciente, Maria adstans, dixit : Frustra, o regina, has mulieres ad nutrimentum vocas infantis, quæ nullam cognationem habent ad eum. Si autem aliquam Hebræarum adduci præceperis, puto quod ubera ejus accedet. Quod † tamen rationabiliter dictum credens regina, jussit adduci Hebræam. Sicque adducta matre pueruli, ubera ejus infans grate accepit ; commisitque filia regis mulieri Hebrææ, ut puerum cum omni diligentia enutriret. Talem etenim fecit Deus puerum illum, ut dignus haberetur educatione et cura etiam ab illis, qui timore ejus decreverunt interimere totum genus Hebræorum virorum.
paras.en: This story of himself Moses wrote very briefly; Josephus relates it more fully, saying: Amram, fearing that he would be caught and fall under the king's anger (for hiding Moses, that is), and that he would perish together with the little boy and shut out the providence of God (since he had heard from God that that child would deliver the Israelite people), prepared a round vessel in which the infant could lie at ease. And so, having put the infant there and set it in the river, he committed it to God. Now Thermuthis, the king's daughter, playing by the bank of the river and catching sight of that vessel, ordered it brought to her. Seeing the infant in it, she rejoiced greatly at the size and beauty of the child, and ordered an Egyptian woman to be brought to give the infant the breast. When he refused the breasts of the Egyptian woman, and did the same with many Egyptian women, Mary, standing by, said: In vain, O queen, dost thou call these women to nurse the infant, who have no kinship with him. But if thou order one of the Hebrew women to be brought, I think he will take to her breasts. The queen, believing this to be reasonably said, ordered a Hebrew woman to be brought. And so, the little boy's mother being brought, the infant gladly took her breasts; and the king's daughter entrusted the boy to the Hebrew woman, to bring him up with all care. For God made that child such that he was held worthy of upbringing and care even by those who, for fear of him, had decided to destroy the whole race of Hebrew males.

paras.t: Insuper Josephus refert : Filia Pharaonis adultum Moysen coram patre suo adduxit, qui suam coronam imposuit capiti Moysis. Moyses vero videns in ea simulacrum sculptum, projecit eam cum indignatione in terram, ac fregit. Quod cernens quidam sacerdotum Heliopoleos valde commotus, videlicet ille scriba, qui prædixit unum de Hebræis nasciturum qui vastaret Ægyptum, dixit : Hic est puer quem ex oraculo deorum audivimus oppressurum Ægyptum. Statimque voluit irruere in Moysen, dicens : Occidatur, ut de cetero careamus timore. Porro filia regis totis viribus se objecit, et filium suum adoptivum defendit. Nam et unus sapientium adstans, dixit puerum hoc ex puerili ignorantia commisisse : quod ut certius fieret, fecit prunas ardentes afferri, et puero præsentari, qui more puerorum unam ori suo apposuit, et inde linguæ suæ extremitatem combussit, unde (ut ferunt Hebræi) impeditioris linguæ effectus est.
paras.en: Josephus further relates: Pharao's daughter brought Moses, when he was grown, before her father, who put his own crown on Moses' head. But Moses, seeing a carved image on it, threw it to the ground in indignation and broke it. Seeing this, one of the priests of Heliopolis, greatly moved (namely that scribe who had foretold that one of the Hebrews would be born who would lay Egypt waste), said: This is the child who, as we heard from the oracle of the gods, will crush Egypt. And at once he wished to rush upon Moses, saying: Let him be killed, so that we may be free of fear from now on. But the king's daughter threw herself in the way with all her strength, and defended her adopted son. For one of the wise men standing by also said that the child had done this out of a child's ignorance; and to make this more certain, he had burning coals brought and set before the child, who, as children do, put one to his mouth, and so burnt the tip of his tongue; whence (as the Hebrews say) he became slower of tongue.

paras.t: Denique, ut Josephus scribit, tantæ pulchritudinis exstitit Moyses, quod nullus erat tantæ severitatis, quin ejus delectabatur adspectu. Multi quoque dum eum per plateam cernerent ferri, postpositis occupationibus suis, festinabant post eum. Insuper narrat, et tangitur in Glossa, pleniusque in Scholastica habetur historia, quod Ægyptii perrecturi ad prælium contra Æthiopes, ex oraculo suorum deorum virum Hebræum, videlicet Moysen, præfecerunt exercitui suo. Itaque Moyses vallatus Ægyptiis, vicit Æthiopes. Quumque urbem Saba nomine, diutius obsideret, filia regis Æthiopum injectis oculis suis in Moysen, eum dilexit, atque ex condicto tradidit ei urbem, ut eam duceret conjugem : duxitque eam, et hæc est uxor ejus Æthiopissa, propter quam Aaron et Maria contra eum jurgati leguntur, ut in Numeris scribitur, et Deo præstante exponetur ibidem.
paras.en: Moreover, as Josephus writes, Moses was of such beauty that no one was so stern as not to delight in the sight of him. Many too, when they saw him carried through the street, left their occupations and hurried after him. He also relates (and it is touched on in the Gloss, and found more fully in the Scholastic History) that the Egyptians, about to go to battle against the Ethiopians, by an oracle of their gods set a Hebrew man, namely Moses, over their army. And so Moses, surrounded by Egyptians, conquered the Ethiopians. And when he had been besieging a city named Saba for a long time, the daughter of the king of the Ethiopians cast her eyes on Moses and loved him, and by agreement handed the city over to him on condition that he should marry her: and he married her, and this is his Ethiopian wife, on whose account Aaron and Mary are read to have quarrelled with him, as is written in Numbers[[Num 12:1||]], and will be explained there, God granting.

paras.t: In diebus illis postquam creverat Moyses, egressus est ad fratres suos, id est Hebræos visitans in terra Gessen, qui fratres ejus dicuntur ex genere, dilexitque illos præcipue, tam naturali quam infusa dilectione, et frequenter condoluit eis in tantis eorum angustiis : et forsan specialiter visitavit quosdam suos cognatos, qui fratres ejus fuerunt consanguinitate : videlicet afflictionem eorum oculo corporali, et mentis compassione, et virum Ægyptium, percutientem quemdam de Hebræis fratribus suis. Quumque circumspexisset hac atque illac, et nullum adesse vidisset, percussum Ægyptium abscondit sabulo. Ægyptius ille fuit unus præpositorum, quos Pharao præfecit Hebræis ad sollicitandum opus eorum, quem Moyses vir fortis et bellicosus, secundum Josephum, interfecit.
paras.en: [[2:11|In those days, after Moses was grown up, he went out to his brethren|In diebus illis postquam creverat Moyses, egressus est ad fratres suos]], that is, visiting the Hebrews in the land of Gessen, who are called his brethren by race; and he loved them especially, with a love both natural and infused, and often grieved with them in their so great distress; and perhaps he especially visited certain kinsmen of his, who were his brethren by blood: [[2:11|and saw their affliction|videlicet afflictionem eorum]] with the bodily eye and with compassion of mind, [[2:11|and an Egyptian striking one of the Hebrews, his brethren|et virum Ægyptium, percutientem quemdam de Hebræis fratribus suis]][[Acts 7:24||]] [the margin note here is unreadable; Stephen tells of this deed in Acts 7:24]. [[2:12|And when he had looked about this way and that way, and saw no one there, he slew the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.|Quumque circumspexisset hac atque illac, et nullum adesse vidisset, percussum Ægyptium abscondit sabulo]] That Egyptian was one of the overseers whom Pharao set over the Hebrews to press on their work; and Moses, a strong and warlike man, killed him, according to Josephus.

paras.t: Circa quod quæritur, qua auctoritate hoc Moyses fecerit, et an sine peccato hoc egit. Ad quod aliqui responderunt, quod in hoc facto peccavit mortaliter, quia non fuit legitimus judex illius Ægyptii, manumque misit in messem alienam, et usurpatum commisit judicium, puniendo non sibi subjectum. Et isti nituntur auctoritate Augustini, dicentis : Moyses tunc nullam adhuc legitimam potestatem gerebat, nec divinitus acceptam, nec humana societate ordinatam. Primo quoque de Civitate Dei testatur : Non licet privata potestate occidere hominem. Itemque ubi dictum est, Non occides : Hic, inquit, fiunt quædam exceptiones, videlicet sine divina auctoritate, aut data lege, vel expressa jussione. Unde in secunda secundæ, quæstione 60. loquitur Thomas : Augustinus in quæstionibus Exodi dicit, homicidium illud in se vitiosum fuisse, magnum tamen fertilitatis indicium exstitisse, puta virtutis qua liberaturus fuit populum Dei. Verumtamen si verba Augustini plene pensentur, non videtur sic absolute sensisse. Nam et in Glossa ex verbis Augustini inducitur : De hoc Moysis facto satis disputavimus in libro de Vita Patriarcharum, quem scripsimus contra Faustum, utrum Moyses laudabili indole illud fecit, quemadmodum terra ante productionem utilium seminum laudatur de fertilitate infructuosarum herbarum, an ipsum factum justificandum sit. Quod ideo non videtur, quia nullam adhuc legitimam potestatem gerebat. Deinde subjungit : Et tamen sicut Stephanus ait in Actibus Apostolorum putabat intelligere fratres suos, quod per eum Deus daret illis salutem : ut per hoc testimonium videatur Moyses jam divinitus admonitus, quod Scriptura eo loco tacet, ut scilicet facere illud auderet. Ex quibus Augustini verbis ostenditur quod senserit ipse. Hinc ait et Thomas : Dici potest quod Moyses occidit Ægyptium inspiratione divina. Vel sicut Ambrosius in libro de Officiis videtur innuere, Moyses fecit hoc defendendo Hebræum cum moderamine inculpatæ tutelæ. Ait namque Ambrosius : Qui a socio non repellit injuriam quando potest, tam est in culpa, ut ille qui injuriatur. Et ponit exemplum de Moyse. Reor itaque absolute tenendum, quod Moyses fecit hoc ex virtute, non ex vitiosa radice. Sicque ex revelatione divina cognovit se præordinatum a Deo in liberatorem populi sui.
paras.en: On this it is asked by what authority Moses did this, and whether he did it without sin. To this some have answered that in this deed he sinned mortally, because he was not the lawful judge of that Egyptian, and put his hand to another man's harvest, and committed a usurped judgment, punishing one not subject to him. And these rely on the authority of Augustine, who says: Moses as yet bore no lawful power, neither received from God nor ordained by human society. In the first book of the City of God, too, he testifies: It is not lawful to kill a man by private authority. And again, where it is said, [[Ex 20:13|Thou shalt not kill|Non occides]]: Here, he says, certain exceptions are made, namely [it holds] where there is no divine authority, or law given, or express command. Hence Thomas says in the Secunda Secundæ, question 60: Augustine says in the Questions on Exodus that that killing was faulty in itself, yet was a great sign of fruitfulness, that is, of the virtue by which he was to deliver the people of God. Yet if Augustine's words are weighed fully, he does not seem to have held this so absolutely. For in the Gloss too this is brought in from Augustine's words: We have discussed this deed of Moses enough in the book on the Life of the Patriarchs which we wrote against Faustus, whether Moses did it from a praiseworthy disposition, as land is praised, before it brings forth useful seeds, for the fruitfulness of its useless weeds, or whether the deed itself is to be justified. Which it does not seem to be, since he as yet bore no lawful power. Then he adds: And yet, as Stephen says in the Acts of the Apostles, [[Acts 7:25|he thought that his brethren understood that God by his hand would save them|putabat intelligere fratres suos, quod per eum Deus daret illis salutem]] [the margin note here is unreadable; the words are Stephen's in Acts 7:25]: so that by this testimony Moses seems to have been already admonished by God, of which Scripture is silent in that place, so that he should dare to do it. From these words of Augustine it is shown what he himself thought. Hence Thomas also says: It can be said that Moses killed the Egyptian by divine inspiration. Or, as Ambrose seems to hint in the book On Duties, Moses did this in defending the Hebrew, within the bounds of blameless defence [*cum moderamine inculpatæ tutelæ*: the technical term for lawful defence, which uses no more force than is needed to ward off the attack]. For Ambrose says: He who does not ward off injury from his fellow when he can is as much at fault as he who does the injury. And he gives the example of Moses. I think, then, that it must be held absolutely that Moses did this out of virtue, not from a faulty root. And so by divine revelation he knew that he was foreordained by God as the deliverer of his people.

paras.t: Sed tunc rursus inquiritur, qua æquitate occidit Ægyptium pro sola percussione læsiva, non interfectiva, quam Ægyptius ille infligebat Hebræo. Videtur quidem in hoc modum excessisse justæ vindictæ, quum secundum legem talionis, par læsio fuerit rependenda, juxta illud : Vulnus pro vulnere, dentem pro dente, oculum pro oculo. Ad hoc Lyra respondet, recitando fabulam Judæorum, dicentium quod Hebræus ille habuit valde formosam uxorem, quam Ægyptius concupiscens, fecit Hebræum valde mane exire ad opus : quo egresso, rediit, et ejus conjugem constupravit ; quo cognito, increpavit eum Hebræus. Cui indignans Ægyptius, percussit eumdem. Quod quum Moyses ex relatione Hebræi novisset, occidit Ægyptium, non pro sola et simplici percussione illata Hebræo, sed et pro adulteratione suæ uxoris. Verumtamen contra hoc asserit Rabbi Paulus : Non est necessarium dicere, quod Moyses interficiendo Ægyptium, percussit ut judex, sed potius ut pars. Ex debito enim caritatis quilibet tenetur repellere injuriam a proximo, si potest. Et quia Moyses non poterat hoc facere per aliquam percussionem, nisi Ægyptius moreretur : immineret enim periculum mortis Moysi, si Ægyptius de sua percussione conqueretur regi : idcirco oportuit ut Moyses eum occideret. Ideo non oportet ad hoc adulterium allegare Ægyptii, de quo nulla fit mentio in Scriptura. Hæc Rabbi Paulus. Cujus verba non videntur satis perita, quia (ut tactum est) communiter dicunt doctores, nulli licere alium judicare atque occidere, nisi constitutus sit ejus judex legitimus. Et quamvis pars communitatis ex caritate teneatur a proximo suo injuriam pro posse repellere, non tamen sic, ut alium lædat aut puniat, nisi (ut dictum est) cum moderamine inculpatæ tutelæ. Nec licet privatæ personæ occidere injuriantem alteri, ne injurians ille conqueratur superiori contra privatam personam, et ex hoc privatæ personæ periculum mortis instet, quia non debet quisquam peccare propter vitandum malum pœnæ. Nec etiam Moysi imminebat necessario periculum mortis ex querela Ægyptii. Potuisset enim vulnerato Ægyptio fugere, et fugiendo manum regis evadere, sicut et postea fecit.
paras.en: But then it is asked again with what equity he killed the Egyptian for a mere blow, one that hurt but did not kill, which that Egyptian was dealing the Hebrew. In this he seems indeed to have gone beyond the measure of just punishment, since by the law of retaliation like injury was to be repaid, according to that saying: [[Ex 21:25|wound for wound|Vulnus pro vulnere]], [[Ex 21:24|tooth for tooth|dentem pro dente]], [[Ex 21:24|Eye for eye|oculum pro oculo]]. To this Lyra answers by recounting a tale of the Jews, who say that that Hebrew had a very beautiful wife, whom the Egyptian lusted after; and he made the Hebrew go out to work very early in the morning, and when he had gone out, came back and violated his wife; on learning of it the Hebrew rebuked him, and the Egyptian, angered, struck him. When Moses learned this from the Hebrew's account, he killed the Egyptian, not only for the mere blow given to the Hebrew, but also for the defiling of his wife. Against this, however, Rabbi Paul [that is, Paul of Burgos, a convert from Judaism, whose Additions go with Lyra's commentary] asserts: It is not necessary to say that Moses, in killing the Egyptian, struck as a judge, but rather as a party. For by the debt of charity anyone is bound to ward off injury from his neighbour if he can. And because Moses could not do this by any blow unless the Egyptian died (for danger of death would hang over Moses if the Egyptian complained of his blow to the king), therefore Moses had to kill him. So there is no need to allege for this the Egyptian's adultery, of which no mention is made in Scripture. Thus far Rabbi Paul. His words do not seem learned enough, for (as was touched on) the doctors commonly say that it is lawful for no one to judge and kill another unless he is appointed his lawful judge. And although a member of the community is bound by charity to ward off injury from his neighbour as far as he can, yet not so as to hurt or punish the other, except (as was said) within the bounds of blameless defence. Nor is it lawful for a private person to kill one who is wronging another lest the wrongdoer complain of the private person to a superior and danger of death threaten the private person from this; for no one ought to sin to avoid the evil of punishment. Nor was danger of death necessarily hanging over Moses from the Egyptian's complaint. For he could have wounded the Egyptian and fled, and by flight escaped the king's hand, as he afterwards did.

paras.t: Et egressus die altero, scilicet immediate sequente, ut ex sequentibus constat, conspexit duos Hebræos rixantes contra se invicem. Atque ut refert Lyra, secundum Hebræos, isti duo fuerunt Dathan et Abiron. Quod verum non arbitror, quoniam Dathan et Abiron fuerunt filii Eliab filii Ruben, et de majoribus Israelitici populi. Unde non apparet, quod viri tam propinqui et potentes, ita contra se invicem contenderint, quod unus percusserit alterum. Dixitque Moyses ei qui faciebat injuriam : Quare percutis proximum tuum ? Secundum Stephanum in Actis : Viri, fratres estis, id est proximi : ut quid nocetis alterutrum ? quasi dicat : In hoc injuste et contra caritatem, insipienterque agitis, quum sitis tam proximi, et aliunde satis afflicti : propter quod unus vestrum non debet alteri augere afflictionem.
paras.en: [[2:13|And going out the next day|Et egressus die altero]], that is, the day immediately following, as is clear from what follows, [[2:13|he saw two Hebrews quarrelling|conspexit duos Hebræos rixantes]] with one another. And, as Lyra reports, according to the Hebrews these two were Dathan and Abiron. Which I do not think true, since Dathan and Abiron were the sons of Eliab the son of Ruben[[Num 16:1||]], and among the greater men of the Israelite people. Hence it does not seem likely that men so closely related and so powerful should have quarrelled with each other so far that one struck the other. [[2:13|and he said|Dixitque]] Moses [[2:13|to him that did the wrong|ei qui faciebat injuriam]]: [[2:13|Why strikest thou thy neighbour?|Quare percutis proximum tuum ?]] According to Stephen in the Acts: [[Acts 7:26|Men, ye are brethren|Viri, fratres estis]], that is, neighbours: [[Acts 7:26|Why hurt you one another?|ut quid nocetis alterutrum ?]] As if to say: In this you act unjustly, against charity and foolishly, since you are such close neighbours, and afflicted enough already besides; for which reason one of you ought not to add to the other's affliction.

paras.t: Qui respondit : Quis te constituit principem aut judicem super nos? quasi dicat : Ideo non debes te intromittere de nostra correctione, quum nullam præsidentiam aut jurisdictionem super nos habeas. Iste Hebræus graviter multipliciterque peccavit. Primo, per ingratitudinem. Nempe ut in Actibus S. Stephanus protestatur, Moyses reconciliavit, id est, reconciliare intendit illos in pace, et caritative corripuit ambos, sicut ex verbis beati Stephani patuit : quamvis hic legatur, quod illum corripuit qui injuriam intulit : quia videlicet illum specialiter increpavit et acrius. Ille autem pro verbis caritatis et pacificationis ac piæ correptionis, retribuit Moysi verba invectionis ; et de præsumptione et usurpatione, imo et homicidio redarguit illum. Secundo, quia non solum princeps et judex, sed et quilibet proximus, potest et debet delinquentes caritative corripere. Tertio, quoniam temere judicavit. Moyses namque ex ordinatione divina et inspiratione superna habuit jam quamdam auctoritatem corripiendi et judicandi Hebræos. Num occidere me tu vis, sicut heri occidisti Ægyptium? quasi dicat : Tu es violentus et homicida, idcirco emenda te ipsum.
paras.en: [[2:14|But he answered: Who hath appointed thee prince and judge over us?|Qui respondit : Quis te constituit principem aut judicem super nos?]] As if to say: So thou oughtest not to meddle with correcting us, since thou hast no headship or jurisdiction over us. This Hebrew sinned grievously and in many ways. First, by ingratitude. For, as St Stephen declares in the Acts, Moses reconciled them, that is, sought to reconcile them, in peace[[Acts 7:26||]], and charitably rebuked them both, as appeared from the words of blessed Stephen; although here we read that he rebuked the one who did the wrong: because, that is, he rebuked him in particular and more sharply. But he, in return for words of charity, peacemaking and loving correction, paid Moses back with words of invective, and charged him with presumption and usurpation, and indeed with murder. Second, because not only a prince and judge, but any neighbour can and should charitably correct wrongdoers. Third, because he judged rashly. For by divine ordinance and heavenly inspiration Moses already had a certain authority to correct and judge the Hebrews. [[2:14|wilt thou kill me, as thou didst yesterday kill the Egyptian?|Num occidere me tu vis, sicut heri occidisti Ægyptium?]] As if to say: Thou art violent and a murderer; therefore amend thyself.

paras.t: Timuit Moyses. Contrarium videtur ex verbo Apostoli : Fide reliquit Ægyptum, non veritus animositatem regis. Responderi potest, quod naturali timore timuit mortis discrimen, non timore carnali aut mundano. Et ait, vel intra se cogitando, vel alicui sibi familiari loquendo : Quomodo palam factum est verbum istud? id est, qualiter factum istud tam cito vulgatum est ? Ex hoc elicitur, quod Moyses commisit Hebræo, cujus injuriam vindicavit in Ægyptio, ne interfectionem Ægyptii propalaret, sed ille non tacuit. Denique in Scripturis verbum pro facto frequenter accipitur, sicut in Isaia : Hæc verba feci. Et quarto libro Regum : Non fuit verbum in domo mea, quod non ostenderim eis.
paras.en: [[2:14|Moses feared|Timuit Moyses]]. The contrary seems to follow from the word of the Apostle: [[Heb 11:27|By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the fierceness of the king|Fide reliquit Ægyptum, non veritus animositatem regis]]. It may be answered that he feared the danger of death with natural fear, not with carnal or worldly fear. [[2:14|and said|Et ait]], either thinking within himself, or speaking to someone close to him: [[2:14|How is this come to be known?|Quomodo palam factum est verbum istud?]] [Latin *verbum istud*, “this word”], that is, how has this deed been made public so quickly? From this it is gathered that Moses had charged the Hebrew whose wrong he avenged on the Egyptian not to make the killing of the Egyptian known, but he did not keep silent. Moreover, in the Scriptures *word* is often taken for the deed, as in Isaias: [[Is 42:16|these things have I done|Hæc verba feci]] [Latin *verba*, “words”]. And in the fourth book of Kings: There was not a *word* [that is, a thing] in my house which I have not shewn them[[4 Kings 20:15||]][[Is 39:2||]][[Is 39:4||]] [the margin gives IV Kings xx and Is. xxxix, 2, 4: Denis's words are those of Is 39:2 and 39:4; the same story in Kings is 4 Kings 20:15, which has “nothing” for “word”].

paras.t: Audivitque Pharao verbum hoc, quod scilicet Moyses occidisset Ægyptium. Et forsan impius ille Hebræus, per se aut per alium indicavit hoc regi. Et quærebat occidere Moysen : tum quia occiderat Ægyptium, regis præfectum super opera Hebræorum, quod rex reputavit in suam redundare injuriam : tum quia multi suggerebant regi, Moysen esse de quo ex deorum suorum oraculo audierunt, quod liberaturus esset Hebræos, et humiliaturus Ægyptios.
paras.en: [[2:15|And Pharao heard of this word|Audivitque Pharao verbum hoc]] [the margin gives the Vulgate's reading, *sermonem hunc*], namely that Moses had killed the Egyptian. And perhaps that wicked Hebrew made it known to the king, himself or through another. [[2:15|and sought to kill Moses|Et quærebat occidere Moysen]]: both because he had killed the Egyptian, the king's overseer over the works of the Hebrews, which the king considered to redound to his own injury; and because many suggested to the king that Moses was the one of whom they had heard from the oracle of their gods that he would deliver the Hebrews and humble the Egyptians.

paras.t: Qui fugiens de conspectu ejus. Hoc dupliciter explanatur. Primo, quod post prædicta venit ad regis præsentiam, et increpatus a rege, fugit de ejus conspectu. Dicunt enim Hebræi, quod Pharaone jubente, Moyses captus fuit et coram rege adductus, increpantique regi constanter respondit. Quumque spiculator ex regis præcepto voluisset Moysen decollare, percussus est cæcitate, quæ acrisia nuncupatur, qua aliquis non videt distincte quod cupit videre, quum tamen videat alia : qua angeli percusserant Sodomitas. Sicque Moyses miraculose evasit, Pharaone vidente : quem et Deus sic obstupefecit, quod nihil contra Moysen facere quivit. Huic recitationi favere videtur, quod ait Apostolus ad Hebræos : Fide reliquit Ægyptum, non veritus animositatem regis. Quocirca scribit Chrysostomus : Quod reliquit Ægyptum, fides fuit, non metus. Secundo exponitur sic : Qui fugiens de conspectu regis, id est, discedens ab Ægypto, ne amplius coram rege appareret. Moratus est in terra Madian. Madian quandoque est nomen regionis, interdum civitatis in terra illa, quæ sic vocatur ab uno filiorum Abrahæ ex Cetura, ut in historiis ait Magister. Fugitque Moyses per desertum, et ciborum inopiam virtute patientiæ vicit, ut Josephus dicit. Et sedit juxta puteum. Hoc fuit antequam fecit notabilem moram in Madian : seditque juxta puteum, quoniam illic solebant homines convenire atque divertere, quia et putei illis in locis sunt rari et cari.
paras.en: [[2:15|but he fled from his sight|Qui fugiens de conspectu ejus]]. This is explained in two ways. First, that after the things said above he came into the king's presence, and being rebuked by the king, fled from his sight. For the Hebrews say that at Pharao's order Moses was seized and brought before the king, and answered the king's rebukes steadfastly. And when the executioner, at the king's command, was about to behead Moses, he was struck with the blindness that is called *acrisia* [Denis's form of the word usually given as *aorasia*, Greek for “not seeing”], by which one does not see distinctly what he wishes to see, though he sees other things: the blindness with which the angels had struck the Sodomites. And so Moses escaped miraculously before Pharao's eyes, whom God so stupefied that he could do nothing against Moses. What the Apostle says to the Hebrews seems to favour this account: [[Heb 11:27|By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the fierceness of the king|Fide reliquit Ægyptum, non veritus animositatem regis]]. Hence Chrysostom writes: That he left Egypt was faith, not fear. Secondly, it is explained thus: [[2:15|but he fled from his sight|Qui fugiens de conspectu]] of the king, that is, departing from Egypt so as no longer to appear before the king. [[2:15|and abode in the land of Madian|Moratus est in terra Madian]]. Madian is sometimes the name of a region, sometimes of a city in that land, which is so called after one of the sons of Abraham by Cetura, as the Master says in the Histories. And Moses fled through the desert, and overcame the lack of food by the virtue of patience, as Josephus says. [[2:15|and he sat down by a well|Et sedit juxta puteum]]. This was before he made any notable stay in Madian; and he sat by the well because men used to gather and stop there, since wells in those places are rare and precious.

paras.t: Erant autem sacerdoti Madian septem filiæ. Aliqui dicunt, quod iste fuit idolorum sacerdos. In Scholastica vero historia dicitur, quod sacerdos sumitur hic pro primate, quoniam primas antiquitus dicebatur sacerdos. Cui concordat quod scribit Lyra: Secundum Hebræos, sacerdos hic accipitur pro majori aut magnate. An autem fuit sacerdos hoc modo civitatis unius Madian dictæ an regionis illius textus non exprimit; potiusque videtur, quod civitatis illius. Quæ venerunt ad hauriendum aquam pro suis pecoribus; et impletis canalibus, id est vasis seu lignis cavatis, in quæ fundebatur aqua hausta, adaquare cupiebant greges patris sui. Erat autem consuetudinis in terris illis, quod puellæ, etiam filiæ divitum et potentum, pecora custodiebant. Pecora namque erant præcipuæ illorum divitiæ.
paras.en: [[2:16|And the priest of Madian had seven daughters|Erant autem sacerdoti Madian septem filiæ]]. Some say that he was a priest of idols. But in the Scholastic History it is said that *priest* is taken here for a chief man, since in ancient times a chief was called a priest. With this agrees what Lyra writes: According to the Hebrews, *priest* here is taken for a great man or magnate. But whether he was priest in this sense of a single city called Madian, or of that region, the text does not say; it seems rather that he was of that city. [[2:16|who came to draw water|Quæ venerunt ad hauriendum aquam]] for their flocks; [[2:16|and when the troughs were filled|et impletis canalibus]], that is, vessels or hollowed-out logs into which the drawn water was poured, [[2:16|desired to water their father's flocks|adaquare cupiebant greges patris sui]]. Now it was the custom in those lands that girls, even the daughters of the rich and powerful, kept the flocks. For flocks were their chief wealth.

paras.t: Supervenere pastores, et ejecerunt eas, id est, ab actu adaquationis incepto, eas impediverunt et repulerunt. Nam sicut in Genesi habetur, consuetudinem in Mesopotamia exstitisse, ut cuncti greges ad puteum congregarentur, et pariter potarentur; sic et in Madian consuetum fuisse putatur: idcirco pastores indignabantur puellis, quod contra consuetudinem facere præsumpserunt. Surrexitque Moyses, et defensis puellis, adaquavit oves earum. Si Moyses solus venit in Madian, et sine adjutorio defendit illas puellas refrenando pastores, ostenditur vir valde robustus fuisse. Sed nonne peccavit, contra consuetudinem ibi agendo? Dici potest, quod ex quadam bona curialitate hoc egit, deferendo virginibus, quas vidit indecenter tractari.
paras.en: [[2:17|And the shepherds came and drove them away|Supervenere pastores, et ejecerunt eas]], that is, they hindered them from the watering they had begun, and drove them back. For as is found in Genesis, the custom in Mesopotamia was that all the flocks should be gathered at the well and watered together[[Gen 29:3||]]; and it is thought that this was the custom in Madian too: therefore the shepherds were angry with the girls, because they had presumed to act against the custom. [[2:17|and Moses arose, and defending the maids, watered their sheep|Surrexitque Moyses, et defensis puellis, adaquavit oves earum]]. If Moses came to Madian alone, and without help defended those girls by holding back the shepherds, he is shown to have been a very strong man. But did he not sin, by acting against the custom there? It can be said that he did this out of a certain good courtesy, showing deference to maidens whom he saw being treated unbecomingly.

paras.t: Quæ quum revertissent ad Jethro patrem suum: qui dicitur quatuor nomina habuisse, videlicet Jethro, Raguel, Cinæus, et Hobab: qui secundum Hebræos vocatus est Jethro, quod interpretatur adjiciens, quoniam unum capitulum addidit legi, hortando Moysen qualiter populum judicaret ac regeret per centuriones et decanos. Secundum Hebræos quoque aliquos, dictus est Hobab, id est diligens, quoniam dilexit legem, atque ad Judaismum fuit conversus. Dixit ad eas: Cur velocius venistis solito? Responderunt: Vir Ægyptius, non tamen de semine Ægyptiorum, sed natus et demoratus in Ægypto, liberavit nos de manu pastorum, qui cœperunt nos impedire. Insuper et hausit aquam nobiscum, potumque dedit ovibus. Quo constat, quod puellæ impleverunt canalia, Moyse adjuvante, qui in aula regia conversatus, scivit curialiter se ad puellas habere: nam et filiam regis ante jam habuit uxorem, juxta prælibata. At ille: Ubi est? inquit. Quare dimisistis hominem? Vocate eum, ut comedat panem. Puellæ forsan ex quadam verecundia dimiserunt Moysen, qui habuit valde honorabilem apparatum.
paras.en: [[2:18|And when they returned|Quæ quum revertissent]] to Jethro [the margin gives the Vulgate's reading, *Raguel*] [[2:18|their father|patrem suum]]: he is said to have had four names, namely Jethro, Raguel, Cinæus and Hobab. According to the Hebrews he was called Jethro, which is interpreted *adding*, because he added one chapter to the law, by advising Moses how to judge and govern the people through captains of hundreds and of tens[[Ex 18:21||]]. And according to some of the Hebrews he was called Hobab, that is, *loving*, because he loved the law and was converted to Judaism. [[2:18|he said to them: Why are ye come sooner than usual?|Dixit ad eas: Cur velocius venistis solito?]] [[2:19|They answered: A man of Egypt|Responderunt: Vir Ægyptius]], not however of Egyptian stock, but born and dwelling in Egypt, [[2:19|delivered us from the hands of the shepherds|liberavit nos de manu pastorum]], who had begun to hinder us. [[2:19|and he drew water also with us, and gave the sheep to drink|Insuper et hausit aquam nobiscum, potumque dedit ovibus]]. From which it is clear that the girls filled the troughs with the help of Moses, who, having lived at the royal court, knew how to behave courteously towards girls: for he had already had the king's daughter as his wife, as was said above. [[2:20|But he said: Where is he? why have you let the man go? call him that he may eat bread.|At ille: Ubi est? inquit. Quare dimisistis hominem? Vocate eum, ut comedat panem]] The girls perhaps let Moses go out of a certain bashfulness, since he had a very dignified bearing.

paras.t: Juravit ergo Moyses quod habitaret cum eo, id est, inter cetera cum Jethro colloquia habita, firmiter dixit aut juramento firmavit habitare cum ipso. Accepitque Sephoram filiam ejus uxorem. Mirum videri potest, quod Jethro vir tantus in terra sua, dedit filiam suam viro exsuli et in terra illa inopi, conjugem. Ad quod poterit responderi, quod consideravit elegantiam, amabilitatem, prudentiam, ceterasque Moysis sancti virtutes. Et forsan audivit ab eo vel aliis, qualis fuerat in Ægypto, et cur inde recesserit.
paras.en: [[2:21|And Moses swore that he would dwell with him|Juravit ergo Moyses quod habitaret cum eo]], that is, among the other conversations he had with Jethro, he said firmly, or confirmed by oath, that he would dwell with him. [[2:21|And he took Sephora his daughter to wife|Accepitque Sephoram filiam ejus uxorem]]. It may seem strange that Jethro, so great a man in his own land, gave his daughter in marriage to a man who was an exile and poor in that land. To this it may be answered that he considered the comeliness, the amiability, the prudence and the other virtues of holy Moses. And perhaps he heard from him or from others what he had been in Egypt, and why he had left it.

paras.t: Quæ peperit ei filium, quem vocavit Moyses Gersam, dicens: Advena fui in terra aliena, puta in Madian. Idcirco filium suum sic appellavit; nam Gersam interpretatur advena. Est autem consuetudo Hebræis, imponere pueris suis nomina ab aliqua proprietate, eventu, aut actu. Alterum vero peperit Sephora, quem vocavit Eliezer, dicens: Deus enim patris mei adjutor meus, et eripuit me de manu Pharaonis, per fugam meam, vel miraculose, ut tactum est. Eliezer autem interpretatur, adjutorium Dei mei. Sicque in appellatione filii sui, recognovit beneficia sibi desuper contributa.
paras.en: [[2:22|And she bore him a son|Quæ peperit ei filium]], [[2:22|whom he called|quem vocavit]] (Moses, that is) [[2:22|Gersam, saying: I have been a stranger in a foreign country|Gersam, dicens: Advena fui in terra aliena]], namely in Madian. Therefore he named his son so; for Gersam is interpreted *stranger*. Now it is the custom of the Hebrews to give their children names from some property, event or act. [[2:22|And she bore another|Alterum vero peperit]] (Sephora, that is), [[2:22|whom he called Eliezer, saying: For the God of my father, my helper, hath delivered me out of the hand of Pharao|quem vocavit Eliezer, dicens: Deus enim patris mei adjutor meus, et eripuit me de manu Pharaonis]], by my flight, or miraculously, as was touched on. And Eliezer is interpreted, *help of my God*. And so in naming his son he acknowledged the benefits bestowed on him from above.

paras.t: Post multum vero temporis mortuus est rex Ægypti, qui Moysen persequebatur, et præ ceteris regibus Ægypti dure nimis afflixit Hebræos. Et ingemiscentes filii Israel propter opera eis a rege injuncta, quæ et successor defuncti continuari voluit, vociferati sunt, Dei auxilium invocando, et suam calamitatem deflendo. Ascenditque clamor eorum ad Deum ab operibus. Servierunt etenim regi, nec tamen mercedem tribuit eis. In quo commisit unum de quatuor vitiis clamantibus ad Deum. Dicitur quoque clamor Israelitarum ascendisse ad Deum, quia exauditus fuit ab eo.
paras.en: [[2:23|Now after a long time the king of Egypt died|Post multum vero temporis mortuus est rex Ægypti]], who had persecuted Moses, and had afflicted the Hebrews far more harshly than the other kings of Egypt. [[2:23|and the children of Israel groaning|Et ingemiscentes filii Israel]], [[2:23|because of the works|propter opera]] laid on them by the king, which the dead king's successor also wished to be continued, [[2:23|cried out|vociferati sunt]], calling on God's help and bewailing their calamity. [[2:23|and their cry went up unto God from the works|Ascenditque clamor eorum ad Deum ab operibus]]. For they served the king, and yet he gave them no wages; in which he committed one of the four sins that cry to God [the sins crying to heaven for vengeance: wilful murder, the sin of Sodom, oppression of the poor, and defrauding labourers of their wages]. The cry of the Israelites is also said to have gone up to God because it was heard by him.

paras.t: Et audivit gemitum eorum, id est, per modum audientis se habuit succurrendo : ac recordatus est fœderis, hoc est, memorem se esse ostendens, aut ostendere volens, quum tamen invariabilis sit Deus, in quem nec recordatio, nec oblivio cadit. Sed Scriptura loquitur de Deo more humano, nostræ capacitati in hoc condescendens. Itaque recordatus est fœderis, quod pepigerat, id est inierat et firmaverat, cum Abraham, Isaac et Jacob, videlicet quod eorum posteros ex Ægypto educeret, et terram Chanaan eis conferret, sicut in Genesi per plura capitula demonstratur. Et respexit Dominus filios Israel oculo pietatis, et cognovit eos, id est, eos ad se pertinere, ac sibi aliquo modo placere, testatus est.
paras.en: [[2:24|And he heard their groaning|Et audivit gemitum eorum]], that is, he behaved in the manner of one who hears, by coming to their help: [[2:24|and remembered the covenant|ac recordatus est fœderis]], that is, showing himself mindful, or wishing to show it; though God is unchangeable, and neither remembering nor forgetting can befall him. But Scripture speaks of God in human fashion, condescending in this to our capacity. So he [[2:24|remembered the covenant|recordatus est fœderis]] [[2:24|which he made|quod pepigerat]], that is, had entered into and confirmed, [[2:24|with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob|cum Abraham, Isaac et Jacob]], namely that he would lead their descendants out of Egypt and give them the land of Chanaan, as is shown in Genesis over many chapters. [[2:25|And the Lord looked upon the children of Israel|Et respexit Dominus filios Israel]] with the eye of pity, [[2:25|and he knew them|et cognovit eos]], that is, he bore witness that they belonged to him and in some way pleased him.

2.title: Spiritualis intelligentia ejusdem capituli secundi
2.title_en: The spiritual sense of the same second chapter

paras.t: Egressus est post hæc vir. Per Moysen allegorice intelligitur Christus. Et sicut Moyses fuit infantulus elegans, sic Christus infans, fuit speciosus præ filiis hominum. Quemadmodum etiam parentes Moysis cum suo periculo absconderunt Moysen a tyrannide Pharaonis, sic beatissima ac Deifera Virgo et ejus minister S. Joseph, abscondérunt puerum Jesum a persecutione scelerati Herodis. Quemadmodum etiam Moyses, quum diutius abscondi non potuisset a suis parentibus, expositus est in fiscella gurgiti fluminis: sic Dominus Jesus, quum in Judæa diutius propter Herodis furorem servari non posset, in Ægyptum vitiorum fluctibus plenam, delatus est. Deinde quum gloriosa Virgo Filium suum secum in secreto degentem, non posset detinere diutius, recessit ab ea Filius, volens Dei Patris implere mandatum, prædicando publice in omni Judæa; descenditque primitus in Jordanem, ut baptizaretur a beato Joanne. Sicque per fiscellam in qua Moyses est locatus, intelligi potest caro Christi, in qua ejus anima atque divinitas latuit. Porro per sororem, Moysen procul sequentem, et rei eventum considerantem, designatur plebs Judaica, Christo secundum carnem propinqua, quæ eum familiarius sequebatur, observans quid ei acciderit.
paras.en: [[2:1|After this there went a man|Egressus est post hæc vir]]. By Moses is understood, allegorically, Christ. And as Moses was a goodly little babe, so Christ as an infant was [[Ps 44:3|beautiful above the sons of men|speciosus præ filiis hominum]]. As, too, the parents of Moses, at their own peril, hid Moses from the tyranny of Pharao, so the most blessed and God-bearing Virgin [Deifera, that is, she who bore God: the Mother of God] and her minister St. Joseph hid the child Jesus from the persecution of the wicked Herod[[Matt 2:14||]]. As, too, Moses, when he could be hidden no longer by his parents, was exposed in a basket to the stream of the river, so the Lord Jesus, when he could no longer be kept safe in Judea because of Herod's fury, was carried down into Egypt, full of the waves of vices. Then, when the glorious Virgin could no longer keep her Son living with her in seclusion, the Son went away from her, wishing to fulfil the command of God the Father by preaching publicly in all Judea; and first he went down into the Jordan, to be baptized by blessed John[[Matt 3:13||]]. And so by the basket in which Moses was placed can be understood the flesh of Christ, in which his soul and his Godhead lay hidden. Further, by the sister, following Moses afar off and watching how the matter would turn out, is signified the Jewish people, near to Christ according to the flesh, which followed him more familiarly, observing what would befall him.

paras.t: Ecce autem descendebat filia Pharaonis, ut lavaretur in flumine. Per filiam Pharaonis, significatur Ecclesia ex gentibus congregata, et ex principibus regibusque terrenis progenita; vel diaboli filia, quantum ad pristina vitia sua. Propter quod dicitur ei: Audi, filia, et vide, et obliviscere populum tuum et domum patris tui. Quemadmodum itaque filia Pharaonis, descendens ad flumen ut lavaretur, reperit Moysen; sic plebs gentilis se ipsam humilians, atque ad fontem Baptismi pro sua purgatione accedens, invenit Christum, et consecuta est gratiam ejus. Quemadmodum autem filia Pharaonis miserabatur Moysis vagientis, sic Ecclesia ex gentibus constans, intime condolet Christo in universis quæ pro nostra salute sustinuit. Denique sicut filia Pharaonis amplexata est Moysen a suis relictum, sic Ecclesia devotissime apprehendit Dominum Jesum a Synagoga contemptum.
paras.en: [[2:5|And behold the daughter of Pharao came down to wash herself in the river|Ecce autem descendebat filia Pharaonis, ut lavaretur in flumine]]. By the daughter of Pharao is signified the Church gathered from the Gentiles, and born of the princes and kings of the earth; or the daughter of the devil, as regards her former vices. For which reason it is said to her: [[Ps 44:11|Hearken, O daughter, and see|Audi, filia, et vide]], and [[Ps 44:11|forget thy people and thy father's house|obliviscere populum tuum et domum patris tui]]. As, then, the daughter of Pharao, coming down to the river to wash herself, found Moses, so the Gentile people, humbling itself and coming to the fountain of Baptism for its cleansing, found Christ and obtained his grace. And as the daughter of Pharao had pity on Moses crying, so the Church made up of the Gentiles grieves inwardly with Christ in all that he bore for our salvation. Lastly, as the daughter of Pharao embraced Moses, forsaken by his own, so the Church most devoutly lays hold of the Lord Jesus, despised by the Synagogue.

paras.t: Insuper sicut filia Pharaonis reddidit Moysen mulieri Hebrææ, matri videlicet ejus, nutriendum; ita Ecclesia ipsis quoque Judæis ex quibus natus est, rursus obtulit prædicavitque Christum. Quem et aliqui Judæi susceperunt per fidem sicque Christum spiritualiter refecerunt, secundum quod ipse in Apocalypsi testatur : Si quis aperuerit mihi, cœnabo cum illo, et ipse mecum. Refecerunt quoque eum in membris suis de quibus lætatur : Quod uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis. Amplius, sicut filia Pharaonis promisit mercedem mulieri Hebrææ Moysen educanti, sic Ecclesia multa contulit beneficia Synagogæ conversæ : imo ut Paulus scribit apostolus, necessaria vitæ misit eidem. Synagoga quoque conversa, videns tanta gratiarum charismata Ecclesiæ condonata, admirata est, et gratias egit Deo, atque in fide est roborata, prout in Actibus docetur Apostolorum. Insuper, sicut mater Moysis adultum Moysen tradidit filiæ Pharaonis, sic Synagoga conversa, Dominum Jesum Christum sua prædicatione detulit ad gentiles. Sed quomodo Ecclesia adoptavit Christum in filium, sicut Pharaonis filia Moysen, nisi secundum quod Dominus ipse in Evangelio loquitur. Qui fecerit voluntatem Patris mei, ipse meus frater et soror et mater est ? Ecclesia etenim pro magna et nobiliori sua parte, ab omni carnali concubitu abstinens, Filium Dei intra se spiritualiter concipit, parit, amplectitur : Christum quoque quasi in infantia constitutum, sincere contemplatur, ac materno affectu complectitur, quem tulit de aqua Baptismi.
paras.en: Moreover, as the daughter of Pharao gave Moses back to the Hebrew woman, namely his mother, to be nursed, so the Church in turn offered and preached Christ to the very Jews of whom he was born. And some Jews received him by faith, and so refreshed Christ spiritually, as he himself testifies in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:20|If any man|Si quis]] [[Apoc 3:20|open to me|aperuerit mihi]], [[Apoc 3:20|will sup with him: and he with me|cœnabo cum illo, et ipse mecum]]. They refreshed him also in his members, in whom he rejoices: [[Matt 25:40|as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me|Quod uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis]]. Further, as the daughter of Pharao promised wages to the Hebrew woman who brought Moses up, so the Church bestowed many benefits on the converted Synagogue: indeed, as Paul the Apostle writes, she sent it the necessaries of life[[1 Cor 16:1||]] [the margin's verse number is lost (it reads "I Cor. […]"); the collection sent to the saints at Jerusalem is 1 Cor 16:1–3]. The converted Synagogue, too, seeing such great gifts of graces bestowed on the Church, marvelled, and gave thanks to God, and was strengthened in the faith, as is taught in the Acts of the Apostles[[Acts 5:12||]][[Acts 4:32||]]. Moreover, as the mother of Moses delivered Moses, grown up, to the daughter of Pharao, so the converted Synagogue by its preaching brought the Lord Jesus Christ to the Gentiles. But how did the Church adopt Christ for a son, as the daughter of Pharao did Moses, unless according to what the Lord himself says in the Gospel: [[Matt 12:50|whosoever shall do the will of my Father|Qui fecerit voluntatem Patris mei]], [[Matt 12:50|he is my brother, and sister, and mother|ipse meus frater et soror et mater est]]? For the Church, in her great and nobler part, abstaining from all carnal intercourse, spiritually conceives within herself the Son of God, brings him forth and embraces him; and she sincerely contemplates Christ as though set in infancy, and clasps him with a mother's affection, whom she took out of the water of Baptism.

paras.t: In diebus illis postquam creverat Moyses, etc. Quemadmodum Moyses factus virilis ætatis, visitavit fratres suos Hebræos, Ægyptiumque injuriantem Hebræo, occidit ac sabulo texit : sic Christus per Moysen præfiguratus, quum jam esset ætatis virilis, in carne assumpta visitavit Judæos, prædicando et signa exhibendo eisdem ; diabolum quoque illos graviter opprimentem, prorsus devicit et conculcavit. Propter quod beatissimus princeps Apostolorum ait de Christo : Qui pertransiit benefaciendo, et sanando omnes oppressos a diabolo.
paras.en: [[2:11|In those days, after Moses was grown up|In diebus illis postquam creverat Moyses]], etc. As Moses, having come to man's age, visited his brethren the Hebrews, and killed the Egyptian who was wronging a Hebrew and covered him with sand, so Christ, prefigured by Moses, when he was now of man's age, visited the Jews in the flesh he had taken, preaching to them and showing them signs; and the devil, who was grievously oppressing them, he utterly overcame and trampled down. For which reason the most blessed prince of the Apostles says of Christ: [[Acts 10:38|who went about doing good and healing all that were oppressed by the devil|Qui pertransiit benefaciendo, et sanando omnes oppressos a diabolo]].

paras.t: Et egressus die altero, conspexit duos Hebræos rixantes, dixitque ei qui faciebat injuriam : Quare percutis proximum tuum ? Sic et Christus post suam resurrectionem egressus de limbo patrum et monumento, vidit duos Hebræos contra se contendentes, videlicet eos qui crediderunt ex Judaismo, et eos qui in Judaica perstiterunt perfidia, qui per allegationes Scripturarum invicem disputabant et contendebant de Jesu. Increduli autem injurias multas intulerunt credentibus, ut patet in Actibus. Ideo Christus redarguit perfidos illos, quibus per os protomartyris Stephani dixit : Dura cervice et incircumcisi cordibus et auribus, vos semper restitistis Spiritui Sancto. Illi vero Christi auctoritatem negantes, indignati dixerunt : Quis te constituit principem aut judicem super nos ? Dixerunt enim : Nolumus hunc regnare super nos. Num occidere me tu vis, etc. ? Imposuerunt enim Christo, quod per se et suos discipulos false docuerit eos, et quod ex ejus prædicatione immineret eis destructio. Collegerunt quippe pontifices et Pharisæi concilium, dicentes : Quid facimus, quia hic homo multa signa facit ? Si dimittimus eum sic, omnes credent in eum : et venient Romani, et tollent nostrum locum et gentem. Timuit Moyses, et ait : Quomodo palam factum est verbum istud ? Sic et Christus naturali timore timuit mortem, ostendens in se humanæ naturæ veritatem. Signa quoque sua interdum occultari præcepit.
paras.en: [[2:13|And going out the next day, he saw two Hebrews quarrelling: and he said to him that did the wrong: Why strikest thou thy neighbour?|Et egressus die altero, conspexit duos Hebræos rixantes, dixitque ei qui faciebat injuriam : Quare percutis proximum tuum]] So too Christ, after his resurrection, going out from the limbo of the fathers and from the tomb, saw two Hebrews contending against each other: namely those who believed from among the Jews, and those who persisted in Jewish unbelief, who disputed and contended with one another about Jesus by appeals to the Scriptures. And the unbelievers did many wrongs to the believers, as is plain in the Acts. Therefore Christ rebuked those unbelievers, saying to them by the mouth of the protomartyr Stephen: [[Acts 7:51|You stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Ghost|Dura cervice et incircumcisi cordibus et auribus, vos semper restitistis Spiritui Sancto]]. But they, denying Christ's authority, said indignantly: [[Acts 7:27|Who hath appointed thee prince and judge over us|Quis te constituit principem aut judicem super nos]]? [these are the words of Ex 2:14, as Stephen recalls them in Acts 7:27] For they said: [[Luke 19:14|We will not have this man to reign over us|Nolumus hunc regnare super nos]]. [[2:14|wilt thou kill me|Num occidere me tu vis]], etc.? For they charged Christ with having taught them falsely, by himself and his disciples, and said that destruction threatened them from his preaching. For the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered a council, saying: [[John 11:47|What do we, for this man doth many miracles?|Quid facimus, quia hic homo multa signa facit]] [[John 11:48|If we let him alone so, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come, and take away our place and nation|Si dimittimus eum sic, omnes credent in eum : et venient Romani, et tollent nostrum locum et gentem]]. [[2:14|Moses feared, and said: How is this come to be known?|Timuit Moyses, et ait : Quomodo palam factum est verbum istud]] So too Christ, with natural fear, feared death, showing in himself the truth of human nature. He also at times commanded that his signs be kept hidden.

paras.t: Audivitque Pharao verbum hoc, et quærebat occidere Moysen. Sic et principes Judæorum cogitaverunt interficere Christum, eo quod tantis præfulsit miraculis, propter quæ merito credidissent in eum. Qui fugiens de conspectu Pharaonis, etc. Sic Salvator interdum fugit rabiem Judæorum, juxta illud Joannis : Jesus ergo jam non in palam ambulabat apud Judæos, sed abiit trans Jordanem in civitatem quæ dicitur Ephrem, et ibi morabatur cum discipulis suis. Et sedit juxta puteum, id est, fontem Baptismi constanter edocuit, et profunditati sapientiæ saluberrimæ indesinenter adhæsit. Ad litteram quoque, fatigatus ex itinere, sedit juxta puteum.
paras.en: [[2:15|And Pharao heard of this word, and sought to kill Moses|Audivitque Pharao verbum hoc, et quærebat occidere Moysen]]. So too the princes of the Jews thought to kill Christ, because he shone forth with such great miracles, on account of which they would rightly have believed in him. [[2:15|but he fled|Qui fugiens]] from the sight of Pharao, etc. So the Saviour at times fled the rage of the Jews, according to that of John: [[John 11:54|Wherefore Jesus walked no more openly among the Jews: but he went|Jesus ergo jam non in palam ambulabat apud Judæos, sed abiit]] beyond the Jordan [[John 11:54|unto a city that is called Ephrem. And there he abode with his disciples|in civitatem quæ dicitur Ephrem, et ibi morabatur cum discipulis suis]] [the Vulgate has "into a country near the desert"; "beyond the Jordan" is from John 10:40]. [[2:15|and he sat down by a well|Et sedit juxta puteum]]: that is, he taught the fountain of Baptism steadfastly, and clung unceasingly to the depth of most wholesome wisdom. And literally, too, [[John 4:6|being wearied with his journey|fatigatus ex itinere]], he sat by the well.

paras.t: Erant autem sacerdoti Madian septem filiæ, quæ venerunt ad hauriendam aquam, etc. Per has septem filias viri gentilis, intelliguntur universæ ecclesiæ gentium, quæ ex auditione prædicationis evangelicæ legis, venerunt per mentis conversionem ad hauriendam aquam doctrinæ salubris, fluentaque gratiæ ex sacramentis Christi, et maxime ex immensitate pietatis divinæ, sicut Isaias prædixit: Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris. Et impletis canalibus, adaquare cupiebant greges patris sui: hoc est, quum corda eorum fuissent impleta septemplici gratia Spiritus Sancti, optabant et alios gentiles nondum conversos illuminare, et donis Dei reficere, communicando eis charismata sibi donata, juxta illud principis Apostolorum: Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes. Supervenere pastores, et ejecerunt eas. Isti pastores fuerunt pontifices Judæorum, ac paganorum imperatores et principes infideles, qui persequendo Ecclesiam, conati sunt aliorum impedire conversionem ad Christum. Surrexitque Moyses, et adaquavit oves earum. Sic Christus supernaturaliter et gratiosissime subvenit suis fidelibus, et eorum subditos illustravit ac pavit, in tantum, quod Ecclesia tandem omnibus hostibus suis prævaluit, et reges ac principes crediderunt.
paras.en: [[2:16|And the priest of Madian had seven daughters, who came to draw water|Erant autem sacerdoti Madian septem filiæ, quæ venerunt ad hauriendam aquam]], etc. By these seven daughters of a Gentile man are understood all the churches of the Gentiles, which, from hearing the preaching of the Gospel law, came by the turning of their minds to draw the water of wholesome doctrine and the streams of grace from the sacraments of Christ, and above all from the immensity of the divine goodness, as Isaias foretold: [[Is 12:3|Thou shall draw waters with joy out of the saviour's fountains|Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris]]. [[2:16|and when the troughs were filled, desired to water their father's flocks|Et impletis canalibus, adaquare cupiebant greges patris sui]]: that is, when their hearts had been filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Ghost, they longed also to enlighten other Gentiles not yet converted and to refresh them with the gifts of God, sharing with them the gifts bestowed on themselves, according to that of the prince of the Apostles: [[1 Pet 4:10|As every man hath received grace, ministering the same one to another|Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes]]. [[2:17|And the shepherds came and drove them away|Supervenere pastores, et ejecerunt eas]]. These shepherds were the high priests of the Jews, and the emperors of the pagans and unbelieving princes, who, by persecuting the Church, tried to hinder the conversion of others to Christ. [[2:17|and Moses arose|Surrexitque Moyses]], [[2:17|watered their sheep|et adaquavit oves earum]]. So Christ supernaturally and most graciously came to the help of his faithful, and enlightened and fed those under them, so much that the Church at length prevailed over all her enemies, and kings and princes believed.

paras.t: Quæ quum revertissent ad patrem suum, dixit ad eas: Cur velocius venistis solito? Responderunt: Vir Ægyptius liberavit nos, etc. Sic patriarchæ gentilium conversi, admirati sunt vehementer celerrimam gentium conversionem inquirentesque causam a subditis, audierunt quod vir Ægyptius. Christus videlicet, qui in infantia sua septem circiter annis moratus est in Ægypto, eos adjuvit, redemit, refecit. At ille: Ubi est? inquit, etc. Per hoc designatur, quod bonus prælatus increpat animas subditorum suorum relinquentium Christum, hortaturque eos, ut orando revocent Salvatorem; et cum talibus dignatur Dominus habitare per gratiam.
paras.en: [[2:18|And when they returned|Quæ quum revertissent]] to their father, [[2:18|he said to them: Why are ye come sooner than usual?|dixit ad eas: Cur velocius venistis solito?]] They answered: [[2:19|A man of Egypt delivered us|Vir Ægyptius liberavit nos]], etc. So the converted patriarchs of the Gentiles marvelled greatly at the very swift conversion of the Gentiles, and, asking the cause of those under them, heard that a man of Egypt (namely Christ, who in his infancy stayed about seven years in Egypt) had helped them, redeemed them, refreshed them. [[2:20|But he said: Where is he?|At ille: Ubi est?]] etc. By this is signified that a good prelate rebukes the souls of those under him who forsake Christ, and urges them to call the Saviour back by prayer; and with such the Lord deigns to dwell by grace.

paras.t: Porro, per nuptias Moysis cum filia Jethro, præfiguratur spirituale connubium Christi cum quacumque Ecclesia, seu persona particulari ex gentilitate exorta, ex qua generat filios duos, videlicet contemplativum et activum.
paras.en: Further, by the marriage of Moses with the daughter of Jethro is prefigured the spiritual wedlock of Christ with any church, or any particular person, sprung from the Gentiles, of whom he begets two sons, namely the contemplative and the active.

paras.t: Tropologice per Moysen aquæ expositum, significatur quicumque fidelis, abundantia tribulationum atque tentationum vallatus, et vitæ hujus deplorans exsilium, quem suscipit filia regis, id est misericordia et gratia Salvatoris, adoptans illum sibi in filium, traditque illum Ecclesiæ educandum: qui quum creverit in virum virtutum, visitat proximos suos, quando rite præficitur ac digne præsidet aliis, et discordantes pacificat, dum reos redarguit.
