Per Hebræum vero, qui Moysi dixit, Quis te constituit principem et judicem super nos? designantur perversi, ingratique subditi: qui dum caritative et juste corripiuntur et corriguntur, ægre ferunt, verba pungitiva, contumeliosa, criminatoriaque respondent, in tantum quod suam correctionem quasi interfectionem existiment.
paras.en: Tropologically, by Moses exposed to the water is signified any one of the faithful who is hemmed in by an abundance of tribulations and temptations and bewails the exile of this life; whom the king's daughter takes up, that is, the mercy and grace of the Saviour, adopting him as her son, and she gives him to the Church to be brought up: and when he has grown into a man of virtues, he visits his neighbours, when he is duly set over others and worthily presides over them, and he makes peace between those at variance while he rebukes the guilty. And by the Hebrew who said to Moses, [[2:14|Who hath appointed thee prince and judge over us?|Quis te constituit principem et judicem super nos?]], are signified perverse and ungrateful subjects, who, when they are charitably and justly reproved and corrected, take it ill and answer with stinging, insulting and accusing words, so much that they count their correction as a kind of killing.

3.title: Elucidatio litteralis capituli tertii: Moyses autem pascebat oves Jethro
3.title_en: Literal explanation of the third chapter: “Now Moses fed the sheep of Jethro”

paras.t: Consequenter describitur qualiter Deus apparuit, prædixit, et commisit Moysi, ut educeret populum Israel ex Ægypto. Moyses autem pascebat oves Jethro cognati, id est soceri sui, sacerdotis Madian, qui curam gregum suorum commiserat Moysi, ejus fidelitatem atque prudentiam fuit satis expertus. In isto quoque monstratur humilitas Moysis, qui quum antea fuerit tantus vir, non recusavit illud officium. Et puto, quod ideo illud libenter assumpsit atque exercuit, quatenus sequestratus ab idololatris Madianitis, aptius Deo vacaret in campis et locis eremi solus, et etiam quoniam Jacob patriarcha et filii ejus, ovium erant pastores.
paras.en: Next is described how God appeared to Moses, foretold things to him, and charged him to lead the people of Israel out of Egypt. [[3:1|Now Moses fed the sheep of Jethro|Moyses autem pascebat oves Jethro]], his kinsman [Latin *cognati*; the Vulgate here reads *soceri*, which Denis gives as his gloss], that is, his father-in-law, [[3:1|the priest of Madian|sacerdotis Madian]], who had entrusted the care of his flocks to Moses, having well proved his faithfulness and prudence. In this, too, the humility of Moses is shown: though he had formerly been so great a man, he did not refuse that office. And I think he took it up and carried it out willingly for this reason: that, set apart from the idolatrous Madianites, he might be the freer for God alone in the fields and places of the wilderness; and also because Jacob the patriarch and his sons were shepherds of sheep.

paras.t: Quumque minasset gregem ad interiora, id est remotiora loca deserti, quærendo uberes alimonias ovium, venit ad montem Dei Horeb, id est montem Sinai, cujus pes dicitur Horeb, et vertex Sinai: de quo aliqui dicunt, quod dicitur hic mons Dei, propter eventum futurum, quoniam Deus in eo erat legem daturus. Verumtamen, quando Moyses scripsit hæc, fuit lex data, dicebaturque mons Dei propter eventum præteritum. Porro in Scholastica historia ex Josepho fertur: Mons ille ad pasturas fuit egregius, herbis abundans, quia pastores illuc ascendere non præsumebant, tum quia excelsus fuit, tum quia fama erat Deum habitare in eo. Et juxta hoc dicebatur mons Dei, non tantum propter futurum eventum, sed propter legem in eo datam.
paras.en: [[3:1|and he drove the flock to the inner parts|Quumque minasset gregem ad interiora]], that is, the more remote places, [[3:1|of the desert|deserti]], seeking rich pasture for the sheep, [[3:1|and came to the mountain of God, Horeb|venit ad montem Dei Horeb]], that is, Mount Sinai, whose foot is called Horeb and its summit Sinai. Of this some say that it is called here the mountain of God because of what was to happen, since God was to give the law on it. Yet when Moses wrote these things the law had been given, and it was called the mountain of God because of what had happened. Further, in the Scholastic History it is related from Josephus: That mountain was excellent for pasture and abounded in grass, because the shepherds did not presume to go up there, both because it was high and because there was a report that God dwelt on it. And according to this it was called the mountain of God, not only because of the event to come, but because of the law given on it.

paras.t: Apparuitque ei Dominus in flamma ignis de medio rubi. Ista apparitio Dei, fuit per creaturam subjectam, quia in angelo et per angelum apparebat et loquebatur Dominus Deus. Sicque angelus in Dei persona loquens et apparens, Dominus appellatur et Deus, in quantum Dei personam repræsentavit. In hac quoque visione non apparuit angelus Moysi in forma sensibili et humana, aut visibiliter in propria persona. Unde nec Moyses scivit angelum esse juxta rubum vel in igne quem vidit, quando primo ipsum ignem conspexit. Sed sicut angelus interdum apparet in forma humana, ita apparuit nunc in specie ignis, quemadmodum et Apostolis apparuit Spiritus Sanctus in igneis linguis.
paras.en: [[3:2|And the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush|Apparuitque ei Dominus in flamma ignis de medio rubi]]. This appearing of God was through a subject creature [that is, a created thing used by God as his instrument], for the Lord God appeared and spoke in an angel and through an angel. And so the angel, speaking and appearing in the person of God, is called Lord and God, inasmuch as he represented the person of God. In this vision, moreover, the angel did not appear to Moses in a sensible and human form, or visibly in his own person. Hence Moses did not know that an angel was beside the bush or in the fire that he saw, when he first beheld the fire. But as an angel sometimes appears in human form, so now he appeared in the likeness of fire, just as the Holy Ghost appeared to the Apostles in fiery tongues[[Acts 2:3||]].

paras.t: Quod si quæratur, cur Dominus apparuit in specie ignis: respondent quidam, quod ideo, quoniam populus Israel fuit ad idololatriam pronus: idcirco apparebat in flamma, quæ non potest imagine figurari. Sed ultimum verbum hoc, falsum et contra experientiam esse videtur. Flamma quippe ascendendo, paulatim ad formam angularem pertingit, et sic potest depingi ac figurari: magisque terminatur proprio termino in se ipso, quam aër aut aqua. Aptius ergo dicendum, quod ideo, quoniam juxta divinum Dionysium, proprietates actionesque Dei, per proprietates et actiones ignis præcipue designantur. Unde et Deus ignis vocatur, dicente Apostolo: Etenim Deus noster ignis consumens est. Quod ex Deuteronomio sumptum est, quo habetur: Dominus Deus tuus ignis consumens est, Deus æmulator. Quemadmodum enim ignis consumit ac devorat et inflammat, sic Deus consumit peccata, accenditque corda. In igne quoque sunt splendor et calor, per quæ lux sapientiæ et fervor caritatis notantur. Rursus, quia per ignem quæcumque grandis afflictio designatur, apparuit Dominus in igne, ad insinuandum magnitudinem afflictionis Israelitarum. Sed cur apparebat in rubo? Ad hoc respondetur in Glossa: Dicunt Hebræi, ideo Deum apparuisse in rubo, ne possent sibi inde occasionem idololatriæ sumere. Ex ligno etenim rubi non potest idolum fieri. Apparuit autem Dominus in flamma ignis, de medio rubi, id est de rubo forinsecus, præsertim de medio rubi inter extrema ipsius.
paras.en: But if it is asked why the Lord appeared in the likeness of fire, some answer that it was because the people of Israel were prone to idolatry: therefore he appeared in a flame, which cannot be represented by an image. But this last statement seems false and contrary to experience. For a flame, as it rises, gradually comes to an angular shape, and so it can be painted and represented; and it is bounded within itself by a limit of its own more than air or water are. It is better, then, to say that it was because, according to the divine Dionysius, the properties and actions of God are signified chiefly by the properties and actions of fire. Hence God is also called fire, as the Apostle says: [[Heb 12:29|For our God is a consuming fire|Etenim Deus noster ignis consumens est]]. This is taken from Deuteronomy, where we read: [[Deut 4:24|the Lord thy God is a consuming fire, a jealous God|Dominus Deus tuus ignis consumens est, Deus æmulator]]. For as fire consumes and devours and sets aflame, so God consumes sins and kindles hearts. In fire, moreover, there are brightness and heat, by which the light of wisdom and the fervour of charity are signified. Again, since every great affliction is signified by fire, the Lord appeared in fire to suggest the greatness of the affliction of the Israelites. But why did he appear in a bush? To this the Gloss answers: The Hebrews say that God appeared in a bush so that they could not take from it an occasion of idolatry; for an idol cannot be made from the wood of a bush. Now [[3:2|the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush|Apparuit autem Dominus in flamma ignis, de medio rubi]], that is, from the bush on its outside, and especially from the midst of the bush, between its outer parts.

paras.t: Et videbat quod rubus arderet, id est, igne opertus esset absque sua læsione. Ideo subditur, et non comburetur: quia non viriditas rubi, nec ejus substantia lædebatur, nec flos. Per quod Deus omnipotentiam suam monstravit, ac mystice designavit, quod tribulatio Hebræorum in Ægypto, non fuit eos penitus consumptura, sed occasio magnificæ liberationis eorumdem. Circa hoc dicit Gregorius: Deus ignem rubumque sociavit, atque aliud superius, aliud inferius junxit: quod tunc solum agitur, quum aliquid magnum ex conjunctione significatur. Nam per succensum rubum Moysen alloquens, ostendit quod Moyses fieret doctor populi, qui et legis flammam perciperet, et peccati spinam non vitaret; vel quod ex Israelitico populo nasceretur, qui similitudinem carnis et peccati spinam assumeret, et substantiam humanitatis inconsumptam, in flamma deitatis servaret.
paras.en: [[3:2|and he saw that the bush was on fire|Et videbat quod rubus arderet]], that is, it was covered with fire without being harmed. Therefore it is added, [[3:2|and was not burnt|et non comburetur]]: for neither the greenness of the bush, nor its substance, nor its flower was harmed. By this God showed his almighty power, and signified mystically that the tribulation of the Hebrews in Egypt was not going to consume them utterly, but would be the occasion of their magnificent deliverance. On this Gregory says: God joined fire and the bush together, and united one thing higher with another lower: which is done only when something great is signified by the union. For in speaking to Moses through the burning bush, he showed that Moses would become the teacher of a people who would both receive the flame of the law and not avoid the thorn of sin; or that from the people of Israel One would be born who would take on the likeness of flesh and of the thorn of sin, and would keep the substance of his humanity unconsumed in the flame of the Godhead.

paras.t: Circa præhabita scribit Rabbi Paulus: Non videtur necessarium dicere, quod idem angelus quandoque in persona Domini loquebatur, et ideo Dominus nominatur. Nam secundum seriem litteræ, prout etiam verba plane sonant, potest dici, quod ille qui apparuit in flamma et forma ignis, erat angelus apparens ad excitandum mentem Moysis, ut cernens miraculum, attenderet ad audiendum vocem ac verba divina. Sed quum sequitur, Dixit ergo Moyses: Vadam, et videbo visionem hanc magnam, quare non comburatur rubus. Cernens autem Dominus quod pergeret ad videndum, etc.: et postea, Ego sum Deus patris tui, etc.: hæc verba et sequentia intelligi possunt a Deo dicta, ut sonant. Hæc Paulus. Cujus verba omnino imperita videntur. In littera namque et serie ejus non dicitur, Apparuit ei angelus in flamma ignis, sed, Apparuit ei Dominus, etc., et tamen non ipse Dominus in propria persona, sed angelus ibi apparuit. Nec verior ratio dari potest, cur angelus ille, Dominus appelletur, nisi quia in ejus persona loquebatur, sicut sanctus ait Gregorius, et communiter dicunt doctores. Deinde quod dicit, verba prætacta intelligi posse dicta a Domino, stare non potest, ita ut intelligantur immediate a Deo prolata. Nam tales vocales locutiones non proferuntur immediate a Deo, sed per creaturam subjectam, ut super Genesim loquitur Augustinus. Denique, quum in textu dictum est, Apparuit ei Dominus in flamma ignis; et paulo post sub eodem contextu subjungitur, Cernens autem Dominus quod pergeret ad videndum, vocavit eum de medio rubi, et ait, etc. Quo constat quod utrumque de eodem Domino asseratur, nec ex serie litteræ aliud insinuetur. Rursus, secundum expositores super illud Lucæ, Vox de cœlo facta est, dicens, Hic est Filius meus dilectus: vox illa ab angelo est formata in aere in Dei Patris persona: quemadmodum et dum in Joanne Christus legitur dixisse, Pater, clarifica filium tuum: venit vox, dicens, Et clarificavi, et iterum clarificabo: qua audita, asseruit turba tonitruum factum esse. Alii autem dicebant: Angelus ei locutus est. Et hoc verum fuit.
paras.en: On what has been said, Rabbi Paul writes: It does not seem necessary to say that the same angel sometimes spoke in the person of the Lord and is therefore named Lord. For according to the order of the letter, and as the words plainly sound, it can be said that he who appeared in the flame and form of fire was an angel appearing in order to rouse the mind of Moses, so that, seeing the miracle, he might give heed to hear the divine voice and words. But when there follows, [[3:3|And Moses said: I will go, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt|Dixit ergo Moyses: Vadam, et videbo visionem hanc magnam, quare non comburatur rubus]]. [[3:4|And when the Lord saw that he went forward to see|Cernens autem Dominus quod pergeret ad videndum]], etc.; and afterwards, [[3:6|I am the God of thy father|Ego sum Deus patris tui]], etc.: these words and those following can be understood as spoken by God, as they sound. Thus far Paul. His words seem altogether unlearned. For in the letter and its order it is not said, The angel appeared to him in a flame of fire, but, [[3:2|And the Lord appeared to him|Apparuit ei Dominus]], etc.; and yet it was not the Lord himself in his own person, but an angel, that appeared there. Nor can a truer reason be given why that angel is called Lord than that he spoke in his person, as St. Gregory says and the doctors commonly say. Next, what he says, that the words touched on above can be understood as spoken by the Lord, cannot stand, if they are to be understood as uttered by God immediately. For such spoken utterances are not uttered by God immediately, but through a subject creature, as Augustine says on Genesis. Finally, since in the text it is said, [[3:2|And the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire|Apparuit ei Dominus in flamma ignis]], and a little after, in the same context, it is added, [[3:4|And when the Lord saw that he went forward to see, he called to him out of the midst of the bush. and said|Cernens autem Dominus quod pergeret ad videndum, vocavit eum de medio rubi, et ait]], etc., it is plain from this that both are asserted of the same Lord, and that nothing else is suggested by the order of the letter. Again, according to the expositors on that passage of Luke, [[Luke 3:22|And a voice came from heaven|Vox de cœlo facta est]], saying, [[Matt 3:17|This is my beloved Son|Hic est Filius meus dilectus]] [the margin note here is unreadable; Luke 3:22 has Thou art my beloved Son, and Denis's words are those of Matt 3:17]: that voice was formed by an angel in the air in the person of God the Father; just as when Christ is read in John to have said, Father, [[John 17:1|Glorify thy Son|clarifica filium tuum]], there came a voice saying, [[John 12:28|I have both glorified it and will glorify it again|Et clarificavi, et iterum clarificabo]] [the margin note here is unreadable; the voice answers the prayer of John 12:28, Father, glorify thy name, which Denis gives in the words of John 17:1]: on hearing which the multitude [[John 12:29|said that it thundered|tonitruum factum esse]]. [[John 12:29|Others said: An angel spoke to him|Alii autem dicebant: Angelus ei locutus est]]. And this was true.

paras.t: Vocavit itaque Dominus eum, Moysen, de medio rubi, et ait: Moyses, Moyses. Repetitio nominis, signum fuit dilectionis, et excitatio advertentiæ diligentioris, indicium quoque seriositatis et magnitudinis dicendorum.
paras.en: So [[3:4|he called to him|Vocavit itaque Dominus eum]], that is, Moses, [[3:4|out of the midst of the bush. and said: Moses, Moses|de medio rubi, et ait: Moyses, Moyses]]. The repetition of the name was a sign of love and a rousing to more careful attention, and also an indication of the seriousness and greatness of what was to be said.

paras.t: Qui respondit: Adsum. At ille: Ne appropies, inquit, huc. Hoc propter spiritualem et mysticam rationem Dominus dixit, sicut et Christus post resurrectionem suam, ad beatissimam Mariam Magdalenam locutus est: Noli me tangere. Cur ergo Dominus dixit ad Moysen, Ne appropies huc, nisi ad innuendum, quod nemo accedere debet ad Deum, nec perscrutari divina, nisi cum reverentia magna? quum et Salomon protestetur, Qui perscrutator est majestatis, opprimetur a gloria.
paras.en: [[3:4|And he answered: Here I am|Qui respondit: Adsum]]. [[3:5|And he said: Come not nigh hither|At ille: Ne appropies, inquit, huc]]. The Lord said this for a spiritual and mystical reason, as Christ too after his resurrection said to the most blessed Mary Magdalen: [[John 20:17|Do not touch me|Noli me tangere]]. Why then did the Lord say to Moses, [[3:5|Come not nigh hither|Ne appropies huc]], except to intimate that no one ought to approach God, or search into divine things, except with great reverence? For Solomon too declares: [[Prov 25:27|he that is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory|Qui perscrutator est majestatis, opprimetur a gloria]].

paras.t: Solve calceamentum de pedibus tuis. Cujus præcepti causa subjungitur: Locus enim in quo stas, terra sancta est. Idcirco propter reverentiam loci sancti, imo ob Dei honorem, hoc jussum est Moysi. Sed unde et qualiter locus ille exstitit terra sancta? Dicendum, quod inde et ideo, quia fuit electus et deputatus a Deo, ut in eo contingerent sacra mysteria ac multa divina, utpote apparitio ista divina, et collocutio sancta, multaque alia, scilicet datio legis, et quæ fiebant in ea.
paras.en: [[3:5|put off the shoes from thy feet|Solve calceamentum de pedibus tuis]]. The reason for this command is added: [[3:5|for the place, whereon thou standest, is holy ground|Locus enim in quo stas, terra sancta est]]. This, then, was enjoined on Moses out of reverence for the holy place, or rather for the honour of God. But whence and how was that place holy ground? It must be said: from this and for this reason, that it was chosen and appointed by God for sacred mysteries and many divine things to take place in it, such as this divine apparition and holy colloquy, and many other things, namely the giving of the law and what was done at it.

paras.t: Et ait: Ego sum Deus patris tui, qui Amram vocatus est. Ex quo constat, quod pater Moysis fuit vir justus, in tantum, quod Deus universorum fuit specialiter Deus viri illius per dilectionem et cultum præcipuum. Ideo quoque Deus vocavit se Deum patris Moysis, ut in spe et amore Dei magis accenderetur, patrisque sui meritis se crederet adjuvari. Hinc ait Glossa interlinearis: Merita parentum bonorum sæpe filiis subvenerunt.
paras.en: [[3:6|And he said: I am the God of thy father|Et ait: Ego sum Deus patris tui]], who was called Amram. From this it is plain that the father of Moses was a just man, so much so that the God of all things was in a special way the God of that man, through a special love and worship. God also called himself the God of Moses' father so that Moses might be kindled the more in hope and in the love of God, and might believe that he was helped by his father's merits. Hence the Interlinear Gloss says: The merits of good parents have often come to the help of their children.

paras.t: Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, et Deus Jacob. Deus æternus, verus, atque omnipotens, universorum Deus est jure creationis et gubernationis ac incessabilis conservationis, omniumque hominum Deus est per providentiam et judiciariam potestatem, imo per prædestinationem æternam et dilectionem præcipuam, et item per specialem illorum devotionem ad Deum, atque assiduum Dei cultum, ferventissimumque amorem. Præterea, sicut sanctus Papa Sylvester disseruit, Deus voluit specialiter horum trium Patriarcharum Deus vocari, et sub eorum nominibus invocari, ad insinuandum superbeatissimæ Trinitatis mysterium in unitate divinæ essentiæ. Hac demum auctoritate utitur in Evangelio Christus contra perfidiam Sadducæorum, dicentium animas hominum esse mortales: quarum immortalitatem probat Salvator per hoc, quod Deus dixit se esse Deum Abrahæ, Isaac, et Jacob. Non autem est Deus mortuorum, sed vivorum.
paras.en: [[3:6|the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob|Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, et Deus Jacob]]. God, eternal, true and almighty, is the God of all things by right of creation, of government and of unceasing conservation; and he is the God of all men by his providence and judicial power, and more than that, of these by eternal predestination and special love, and also by their special devotion to God, their constant worship of God, and their most fervent love. Moreover, as the holy Pope Sylvester taught, God willed to be called in a special way the God of these three patriarchs, and to be invoked under their names, to suggest the mystery of the supremely blessed Trinity in the unity of the divine essence. Finally, Christ in the Gospel uses this authority against the faithlessness of the Sadducees, who said that men's souls are mortal; and the Saviour proves their immortality by this, that God said he was the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. [[Matt 22:32|He is not the God of the dead but of the living|Non autem est Deus mortuorum, sed vivorum]].

paras.t: Abscondit Moyses faciem suam, hoc est, vultum declinavit in terram: quod faciendo, creditur Deum adorasse. Sic et in Evangelio recitantur sanctæ mulieres, quæ ad Christi venerunt sepulcrum, angelis visis, vultum suum declinasse in terram. Vel abscondit faciem suam, eam quasi velando, seu manus suas faciei suæ ac oculis superponendo. Cujus subjungitur ratio: Non enim audebat adspicere contra Deum, id est, ignem in quo apparuit Dominus, non audebat intueri, nec visum dirigere ex opposito versus locum, in quo Dominus apparebat, non principaliter ex terribilitate dignitateve ignis aut loci, sed ex consideratione majestatis divinæ, ibidem in creatura subjecta, seu in angelo apparentis. Item ex consideratione propriæ indignitatis et fragilitatis, sicut et publicanus in Evangelio legitur nec oculos ausus fuisse in cœlum levare, ex consideratione suorum excessuum. Nempe quum opposita juxta se posita, clarius innotescant: quanto fragilis homo excellentiam Dei altius contemplatur ac experitur, tanto propriam defectuositatem clarius intuetur, profundiusque se ipsum humiliat: nec ad intuendum incircumscriptibilem illam superexcellentiam Dei se audet indecenter ingerere, sed suum moderatur intuitum. Hinc scriptum est in Job: Ecce excelsus Deus in fortitudine, et nullus ei similis in legislatoribus. Et subditur ibi sequenti capitulo: Ideo timebunt eum viri, et non audebunt contemplari omnes qui sibi videntur esse sapientes.
paras.en: [[3:6|Moses hid his face|Abscondit Moyses faciem suam]], that is, he bowed his countenance to the ground; and in doing so he is believed to have adored God. So also in the Gospel the holy women who came to Christ's sepulchre are related, on seeing the angels, to have [[Luke 24:5|bowed down their countenance towards the ground|vultum suum declinasse in terram]]. Or, he [[3:6|hid his face|abscondit faciem suam]] as though veiling it, or putting his hands over his face and eyes. The reason for this is added: [[3:6|for he durst not look at God|Non enim audebat adspicere contra Deum]] [Latin *contra Deum*, literally facing God, over against him], that is, he did not dare to gaze at the fire in which the Lord appeared, nor to direct his sight straight toward the place where the Lord was appearing: not chiefly because of the terribleness or dignity of the fire or of the place, but from considering the divine majesty that was appearing there in a subject creature, or in an angel. Again, from considering his own unworthiness and frailty, as the publican too in the Gospel is read not to have dared to lift up his eyes to heaven[[Luke 18:13||]], from considering his own transgressions. For since opposites set side by side are known more clearly, the more highly frail man contemplates and experiences the excellence of God, the more clearly he sees his own defectiveness and the more deeply he humbles himself; nor does he dare to thrust himself unbecomingly into gazing at that uncircumscribable super-excellence of God, but he moderates his gaze. Hence it is written in Job: [[Job 36:22|Behold, God is high in his strength, and none is like him among the lawgivers|Ecce excelsus Deus in fortitudine, et nullus ei similis in legislatoribus]]. And it is added there in the following chapter: [[Job 37:24|Therefore men shall fear him, and all that seem to themselves to be wise, shall not dare to behold him|Ideo timebunt eum viri, et non audebunt contemplari omnes qui sibi videntur esse sapientes]].

paras.t: Cui, videlicet Moysi, ait Dominus: Vidi oculo pietatis et quasi compassionis et miserationis, afflictionem populi mei, utpote Hebræorum, qui erant specialiter populus Dei præ ceteris per electionem, juxta illud Deuteronomii, Te elegit Dominus, ut sis ei populus peculiaris de cunctis populis qui sunt super terram: in Ægypto, et clamorem ejus audivi, id est, preces quibus me invocant, jam implere decrevi; vel clamorem, id est ululatum et gemitum quos emittunt; propter duritiam eorum qui præsunt operibus, id est propter angustias et labores quibus premuntur.
paras.en: [[3:7|And the Lord said to him|Cui]], that is, to Moses: [[3:7|I have seen|Vidi]], with the eye of pity, and as it were of compassion and mercy, [[3:7|the affliction of my people|afflictionem populi mei]], namely of the Hebrews, who were specially the people of God above the others by election, according to that passage of Deuteronomy: [[Deut 7:6|God hath chosen thee, to be his peculiar people of all peoples that are upon the earth|Te elegit Dominus, ut sis ei populus peculiaris de cunctis populis qui sunt super terram]]; [[3:7|in Egypt|in Ægypto]], [[3:7|and I have heard their cry|et clamorem ejus audivi]], that is, I have now decided to fulfil the prayers with which they call upon me; or *cry*, that is, the wailing and groaning which they utter; [[3:7|because of the rigour of them that are over the works|propter duritiam eorum qui præsunt operibus]], that is, because of the straits and labours by which they are oppressed.

paras.t: Et sciens dolorem ejus, descendi ut liberem eum de manibus Ægyptiorum. Deus incircumscriptibilis et immensus, in propria persona nequaquam descendit, aut locum mutat; sed dicitur descendere per effectum, in quantum de novo succurrit, punit, aut aliquid facit. Unde oravit Psalmista: Domine, inclina cœlos tuos, et descende. Et Isaias: Utinam, inquit, dirumperes cœlos, et descenderes.
paras.en: [[3:8|And knowing their sorrow, I am come down to deliver them out of the hands of the Egyptians|Et sciens dolorem ejus, descendi ut liberem eum de manibus Ægyptiorum]]. God, who is uncircumscribable and immense, in no way comes down in his own person or changes place; but he is said to come down by his effect, inasmuch as he newly gives help, punishes, or does something. Hence the Psalmist prayed: [[Ps 143:5|Lord, bow down thy heavens and descend|Domine, inclina cœlos tuos, et descende]]. And Isaias: [[Is 64:1|O that|Utinam]], he says, [[Is 64:1|thou wouldst rend the heavens, and wouldst come down|dirumperes cœlos, et descenderes]].

paras.t: Et educam eos de terra illa, scilicet ex Ægypto, in terram bonam et spatiosam, in terram quæ fluit lacte et melle, id est, omni genere victualium abundat, ad loca Chananæi, et Hethæi, et Amorrhæi, et Pherezæi, et Hevæi, et Jebusæi, hoc est ad terram Chanaan seu promissionis, in qua hinc inde in diversis locis et urbibus habitaverunt sex gentes, quæ exprimuntur in littera; septima vero tacetur hoc loco, et alibi sæpe, scilicet Gergesæi, qui tamen in Deuteronomio et Josue libro exprimuntur. Cur autem tam raro nominantur, causa est secundum Hebræos, quia non restiterunt filiis Israel ingredientibus terram promissionis, ut aliæ gentes: sed recesserunt de terra illa ex timore ante introitum Israelitarum in eam.
paras.en: [[3:8|and to bring them out of that land|Et educam eos de terra illa]], namely out of Egypt, [[3:8|into a good and spacious land, into a land that floweth with milk and honey|in terram bonam et spatiosam, in terram quæ fluit lacte et melle]], that is, which abounds in every kind of food, [[3:8|to the places of the Chanaanite, and Hethite, and Amorrhite, and Pherezite, and Hevite, and Jebusite|ad loca Chananæi, et Hethæi, et Amorrhæi, et Pherezæi, et Hevæi, et Jebusæi]], that is, to the land of Chanaan or of promise, in which six nations dwelt here and there in various places and cities, which are named in the letter; but the seventh is passed over here and often elsewhere, namely the Gergesite, who is, however, named in Deuteronomy[[Deut 7:1||]] and in the book of Josue[[Jos 3:10||]]. And the reason why they are so seldom named, according to the Hebrews, is that they did not resist the children of Israel as they entered the land of promise, as the other nations did, but withdrew from that land out of fear before the Israelites entered it.

paras.t: Clamor ergo filiorum Israel venit ad me; vidique afflictionem eorum qua ab Ægyptiis opprimuntur. Sed veni, id est, mente paratus esto ad executionem præcepti mei, mittam te ad Pharaonem, ut educas populum meum filios Israel de Ægypto. Dixitque Moyses ad Deum: Quis sum ego, ut vadam ad Pharaonem, et educam filios Israel de Ægypto? quasi dicat: Insufficiens sum ad tantum opus, quum nec potestas prævalendi Pharaoni, nec facundia coram eo loquendi, existant in me. Qui dixit ei: Ego cui nihil difficile est, et cui nullus resistere valet, ero tecum per gratiam adjutricem, et dando tibi omne, quo indigebis, auxilium.
paras.en: [[3:9|For the cry of the children of Israel is come unto me|Clamor ergo filiorum Israel venit ad me]]; [[3:9|and I have seen their affliction, wherewith they are oppressed by the Egyptians|vidique afflictionem eorum qua ab Ægyptiis opprimuntur]]. [[3:10|But come|Sed veni]], that is, be ready in mind to carry out my command, [[3:10|and I will send thee to Pharao, that thou mayst bring forth my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt|mittam te ad Pharaonem, ut educas populum meum filios Israel de Ægypto]]. [[3:11|And Moses said to God: Who am I that I should go to Pharao, and should bring forth the children of Israel out of Egypt?|Dixitque Moyses ad Deum: Quis sum ego, ut vadam ad Pharaonem, et educam filios Israel de Ægypto?]] As if to say: I am not sufficient for so great a work, since there is in me neither the power to prevail over Pharao nor the eloquence to speak before him. [[3:12|And he said to him: I|Qui dixit ei: Ego]], to whom nothing is difficult and whom no one can resist, [[3:12|will be with thee|ero tecum]] by helping grace, and by giving thee every help that thou shalt need.

paras.t: Et hoc habebis signum quod miserim te. Hoc Hebræi ad præcedentia referunt, ut sit sensus: Miraculum istud quod vidisti in rubo ardente nec læso, erit tibi signum quod vere te mitto: idcirco ex consideratione insufficientiæ tuæ noli diffidere, sed ex intuitu assistentiæ meæ confide. Catholici autem expositores referunt istud ad verba sequentia, eritque sensus: Quod subditur, habebis pro signo legationis meæ tibi injunctæ. Quum eduxeris populum meum de Ægypto, immolabis Deo super montem istum, id est, in monte hoc Horeb seu Sinai, offeres Deo corporales spiritualesque hostias, per quod agnosces te missum esse a me. Fuit quoque istud impletum, quando post egressum Hebræorum ex Ægypto, obtulit Moyses in hoc monte sacrificium laudis, gratiarum actionem, et orationem, et quædam etiam legalia sacrificia Deo, ut infra patebit: sicque immolatio illa fuit signum memorativum præteriti, in quantum fuit indicium, quod Deo jubente atque auxiliante, Moyses filios Israel perducturus erat usque ad terram promissionis. Horum autem utrumque prædixerat Moysi Deus. Verumtamen immolatio illa non fuit res in se miraculosa, sed signum fuit ex institutione et ordinatione divina, quemadmodum iris signum est fœderis inter Deum et terram, juxta illud in Genesi: Arcum meum ponam in nubibus, et erit signum fœderis mei: quum tamen arcus seu iris, sit naturalis effectus. Verumtamen prænuntiatio immolationis illius, tanquam futuri contingentis, fuit quid miraculosum seu super naturam, quemadmodum quod Christus prædixit duobus Apostolis: Ecce introeuntibus vobis in civitatem, occurret vobis homo lagenam aquæ bajulans: et quod Samuel prædixit Sauli quorumdam occursum, sibi in hoc et illo loco futurum.
paras.en: [[3:12|and this thou shalt have for a sign that I have sent thee|Et hoc habebis signum quod miserim te]]. The Hebrews refer this to what goes before, so that the sense is: This miracle that thou hast seen in the bush, burning and not harmed, will be a sign to thee that I truly send thee; therefore do not lose heart from considering thy insufficiency, but trust, looking to my assistance. The Catholic expositors, however, refer it to the words that follow, and the sense will be: What is added thou shalt have as a sign of the embassy I have laid upon thee: [[3:12|When thou shalt have brought my people out of Egypt, thou shalt offer sacrifice to God upon this mountain|Quum eduxeris populum meum de Ægypto, immolabis Deo super montem istum]], that is, on this mountain Horeb or Sinai thou shalt offer to God bodily and spiritual victims, by which thou shalt know that thou hast been sent by me. And this was fulfilled when, after the Hebrews had gone out of Egypt, Moses offered to God on this mountain the sacrifice of praise, thanksgiving and prayer, and also certain legal sacrifices[[Ex 24:4||]], as will appear below; and so that sacrifice was a sign recalling the past, inasmuch as it was a token that, at God's command and with his help, Moses was going to lead the children of Israel as far as the land of promise. Now God had foretold both of these to Moses. Yet that sacrifice was not a thing miraculous in itself, but was a sign by divine institution and ordinance, as the rainbow is a sign of the covenant between God and the earth, according to that passage in Genesis: [[Gen 9:13|I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be the sign of a covenant|Arcum meum ponam in nubibus, et erit signum fœderis mei]], though the bow or rainbow is a natural effect. Yet the foretelling of that sacrifice, as of a future contingent thing, was something miraculous or above nature; as when Christ foretold to two Apostles: [[Luke 22:10|Behold, as you go into the city, there shall meet you a man carrying a pitcher of water|Ecce introeuntibus vobis in civitatem, occurret vobis homo lagenam aquæ bajulans]] [the margin note here is unreadable; the words are those of Luke 22:10, but lagenam aquæ bajulans is as in Mark 14:13, where the Douay-Rheims is the same]; and as Samuel foretold to Saul that certain men would meet him in this place and in that.

paras.t: Præterea duas præinductas expositiones reprobat Rabbi Paulus: et primam primo per hoc, quod Moyses non petivit tale signum. Secundo, quoniam sequeretur quod Moyses fuisset modicæ fidei, si ei datum fuisset hujusmodi signum, et ita peccaset in hoc, quum tamen nil tale referatur de eo hoc loco. Verum hæ duæ objectiones nullius exstant valoris. Deus namque multa impendit dona et signa non petentibus, quemadmodum per Samuelem legitur prædixisse Sauli aliqua signa, ex quorum eventu Saul cognosceret vera esse, quæ ei prænuntiavit Samuel. Similiter in Luca angelus legitur dixisse pastoribus: Et hoc vobis signum: Invenietis infantem pannis involutum, etc. Et tamen pastores non petiverunt hoc signum super his quæ audierunt, nec dubitaverunt de veritate angelicæ denuntiationis. Per quod patet secundi solutio. Signa quippe hujusmodi, non semper dantur propter incredulitatem aut diffidentiam eorum quibus donantur, sed dantur interdum pro consolatione et majori confortatione illorum, imo et propter aliorum ædificationem, quemadmodum Dominus contulit Noe signum fœderis sui, arcum, ut tactum est. Sic quoque contulit Moysi signum istud. Denique, non oportet Moysen hoc loco excusare a culpa, et veniali incredulitatis motu: quem constat diu postea, quando majoris erat perfectio[…]riis, per incredulitatem percussit mortaliter ad aquam Contradictionis, ubi Dominus dixit ad eum ac Aaron: Quia non credidistis mihi, non introducetis hos populos, etc. Unde fertur in Psalmo: Absorpti sunt juncti petræ judices eorum, id est, Moyses et Aaron judices Judæorum spiritualiter sunt absorpti per culpam incredulitatis juncti petræ, id est juxta petram, de qua dixerunt: Num de petra hac poterimus vobis aquam ejicere? Per Isaiam quoque Dominus contestatur populo Judæorum: Interpretes tui prævaricati sunt in me. Ubi, secundum expositores, per interpretes intelliguntur Moyses et Aaron, qui verba Dei populo exposuerunt. Infra quoque patebit, quod Moyses in collocutione ista cum Deo, peccavit, ita quod Deus iratus fuit in eum, ut sequenti habetur capitulo.
paras.en: Moreover, Rabbi Paul rejects the two expositions given above: the first, first, on the ground that Moses did not ask for such a sign; secondly, because it would follow that Moses had been of little faith, if a sign of this kind had been given him, and so would have sinned in this, though nothing of the kind is related of him in this place. But these two objections are of no worth. For God bestows many gifts and signs on those who do not ask for them, as Samuel is read to have foretold to Saul certain signs[[1 Kings 10:1||]], from whose coming to pass Saul would know that what Samuel had foretold to him was true. Likewise in Luke the angel is read to have said to the shepherds: [[Luke 2:12|And this shall be a sign unto you|Et hoc vobis signum]]: [[Luke 2:12|You shall find the infant wrapped in swaddling clothes|Invenietis infantem pannis involutum]], etc. And yet the shepherds did not ask for this sign about what they had heard, nor did they doubt the truth of the angel's message. By this the answer to the second objection is plain. For signs of this kind are not always given because of the unbelief or distrust of those to whom they are granted, but are sometimes given for their consolation and greater strengthening, and also for the edification of others; as the Lord gave Noe the sign of his covenant, the bow, as has been touched on. So too he gave Moses this sign. Lastly, there is no need to excuse Moses in this place from fault and from a venial movement of unbelief, since it is known that long afterwards, when he was of greater perfection […], through unbelief he struck mortally at the water of Contradiction [the text is damaged here at a page break and reads percussit mortaliter, struck mortally; the sense seems to be that he sinned mortally through unbelief], where the Lord said to him and to Aaron: [[Num 20:12|Because you have not believed me|Quia non credidistis mihi]], [[Num 20:12|you shall not bring these people|non introducetis hos populos]], etc. Hence it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 140:6|Their judges falling upon the rock have been swallowed up|Absorpti sunt juncti petræ judices eorum]] [the Latin juncti petræ, joined to the rock, is rendered falling upon the rock in the Douay-Rheims; Denis's gloss turns on it]: that is, Moses and Aaron, the judges of the Jews, were spiritually swallowed up through the fault of unbelief, joined to the rock, that is, beside the rock of which they said: [[Num 20:10|Can we bring you forth water out of this rock?|Num de petra hac poterimus vobis aquam ejicere]] Through Isaias too the Lord protests to the people of the Jews: [[Is 43:27|thy teachers have transgressed against me|Interpretes tui prævaricati sunt in me]]. Where, according to the expositors, by the interpreters [Latin interpretes, the Douay-Rheims teachers] are understood Moses and Aaron, who expounded the words of God to the people. It will also appear below that Moses sinned in this colloquy with God, so that God was angry with him[[Ex 4:14||]], as is found in the following chapter.

paras.t: Deinde reprobat expositionem secundam: et primo probat, quod immolatio facta in monte illo, non potuit esse signum præteriti, quia tunc omnibus per experientiam patuit, quod Deus fuit cum Moyse in eductione filiorum Israel. Ad quod respondetur, quod pari ratione sequetur, nullum esse signum memorativum præteriti, quoniam re jam præterita et peracta, omnibus, quantum est ex natura rei, constat, rem illam esse præteritam et peractam. Nihilo minus dicitur signum præteriti, quia valet ad remedium, rememorationem et majorem certificationem præteriti. Amplius, quod immolatio illa non fuit signum futuri, videlicet introductionis Israeliticæ plebis in terram promissionis, probat ex hoc, quia (ut ait) Deus non fecit aliquam mentionem de introductione populi ad terram promissionis. Sed istud est evidenter falsum, et contra textum. Jam enim in isto capitulo Dominus dixit ad Moysen: Descendi, ut liberem eum de manibus Ægyptiorum, et educam de terra illa in terram bonam et spatiosam, in terram quæ fluit lacte et melle, etc. Itaque dicit verba illa, Hoc habebis signum, esse referenda ad inhabilitatem Moysis ad hoc, ut educeret filios Israel. Quod rursus stare non potest: Primo, quia in textu apertissime Dominus ait, Hoc habebis signum quod miserim te, etc. Non dicit, Hoc habebis signum quod inhabilis seu insufficiens sis ex te ipso ad tantum opus. Secundo, quoniam tam Moysi quam cunctis constabat insufficientia illa.
paras.en: Next he rejects the second exposition: and first he proves that the sacrifice made on that mountain could not be a sign of the past, because then it was plain to all by experience that God was with Moses in bringing out the children of Israel. To this it is answered that by the same reasoning it would follow that there is no sign recalling the past, since, when a thing is already past and done, it is plain to all, as far as the nature of the thing goes, that the thing is past and done. Nevertheless it is called a sign of the past, because it serves as a remedy, a reminder and a fuller assurance of the past. Further, he proves that that sacrifice was not a sign of the future, namely of the bringing of the Israelite people into the land of promise, from this, that (as he says) God made no mention of bringing the people into the land of promise. But this is evidently false and against the text. For already in this chapter the Lord said to Moses: [[3:8|I am come down to deliver them out of the hands of the Egyptians|Descendi, ut liberem eum de manibus Ægyptiorum]], [[3:8|and to bring them out of that land into a good and spacious land, into a land that floweth with milk and honey|et educam de terra illa in terram bonam et spatiosam, in terram quæ fluit lacte et melle]], etc. And so he says that the words, [[3:12|this thou shalt have for a sign|Hoc habebis signum]], are to be referred to Moses' unfitness to bring out the children of Israel. This again cannot stand: first, because in the text the Lord says most plainly, [[3:12|this thou shalt have for a sign that I have sent thee|Hoc habebis signum quod miserim te]], etc. He does not say, This thou shalt have for a sign that thou art unfit or insufficient of thyself for so great a work. Secondly, because that insufficiency was plain both to Moses and to all.

paras.t: Ait Moyses ad Deum: Ecce ego vadam ad filios Israel, et dicam eis: Deus patrum vestrorum misit me ad vos. Si dixerint mihi, Quod est nomen ejus, videlicet Dei? quid dicam eis? Dixit Dominus ad Moysen: Ego sum qui sum. Ait: Sic dices filiis Israel: Qui est, misit me ad vos. Ista responsio Dei, profunditate et subtilitate sententiæ plena est. Asserit etenim quod nomen suum sit, Esse, vel, Qui est, ad insinuandum quod ei soli competat esse, cum omnimoda plenitudine et infinita nobilitate atque absoluta perfectione essendi, ita quod comparatione increati divinique esse, omne esse creatum est magis non esse, quam esse: sicut et lux et sapientia creata, est quasi caligo et insipientia respectu lucis et sapientiæ increatæ et infinitæ. Iterum protestatus est Deus, quod Esse sit proprium nomen suum, quoniam Esse est actualissimum et formalissimum; et tanquam pelagus quoddam immensum, includit in se omnem perfectionem et nobilitatem. Propter quod maxime competit Deo, qui est purus incircumscriptusque actus, et forma omnia formans. Hinc sanctus Job loquitur Deo: Quis potest facere mundum de immundo? Nonne tu qui solus es? Et rursus: Deus solus est, et cogitationem ejus nemo avertere potest. Jeremias quoque fatetur: Qui creavit omnia, ipse est, et Israel sceptrum hereditatis ejus.
paras.en: [[3:13|Moses said to God: Lo, I shall go to the children of Israel, and say to them: The God of your fathers hath sent me to you. If they shall say to me: What is his name?|Ait Moyses ad Deum: Ecce ego vadam ad filios Israel, et dicam eis: Deus patrum vestrorum misit me ad vos. Si dixerint mihi, Quod est nomen ejus]], that is, of God? [[3:13|What shall I say to them?|quid dicam eis]] [[3:14|God said to Moses: I AM WHO AM. He said: Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you|Dixit Dominus ad Moysen: Ego sum qui sum. Ait: Sic dices filiis Israel: Qui est, misit me ad vos]]. This answer of God is full of depth and subtlety of meaning. For he asserts that his name is Being, or He Who Is, to suggest that being belongs to him alone, with every kind of fullness, infinite nobility and absolute perfection of being, so that, compared with the uncreated and divine being, all created being is rather not-being than being: just as created light and wisdom are as it were darkness and folly in respect of the uncreated and infinite light and wisdom. Again, God declared that Being is his proper name because Being is the most actual and the most formal of all [that is, what is most fully in act and gives the last perfection to everything, as form does to matter]; and like some boundless ocean it includes in itself every perfection and nobility. For this reason it belongs most of all to God, who is pure and uncircumscribed act, and the form that forms all things. Hence holy Job says to God: [[Job 14:4|Who can make him clean|Quis potest facere mundum]] from the unclean? [[Job 14:4|is it not thou who only art?|Nonne tu qui solus es]] And again: [[Job 23:13|he is alone, and no man can turn away his thought|Deus solus est, et cogitationem ejus nemo avertere potest]]. Jeremias too confesses: [[Jer 51:19|he that made all things he it is, and Israel is the sceptre of his inheritance|Qui creavit omnia, ipse est, et Israel sceptrum hereditatis ejus]].

paras.t: De hoc in libro de Divinis nominibus profundissime scribit D. Dionysius. Hilarius quoque: Esse, inquit, non est accidens Deo, sed subsistens veritas, manens causa, et naturalis generis proprietas. Porro octavo de Civitate Dei, videtur Augustinus sentire, quod Plato per interpretem didicit libros Moysis: præsertim quia quod Dominus ad Moysen ait, Ego sum qui sum; Hæc dices filiis Israel: Qui est, misit me ad vos; Plato vehementer tenuit, et diligentissime commendavit.
paras.en: Of this St. Dionysius writes most profoundly in the book On the Divine Names. Hilary too: Being, he says, is not an accident in God, but subsisting truth, an abiding cause, and the natural property of his kind. Further, in the eighth book of The City of God, Augustine seems to think that Plato learned the books of Moses through an interpreter, especially because Plato held firmly and commended most diligently what the Lord said to Moses: [[3:14|I AM WHO AM|Ego sum qui sum]]; [[3:14|Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you|Hæc dices filiis Israel: Qui est, misit me ad vos]].

paras.t: De hoc nomine Dei, loquitur Thomas in prima parte Summæ suæ, quæstione 13: Hoc nomen, Qui est, est maxime proprium Deo: Primo, propter suam significationem. Significat enim non aliquam formam, sed ipsum esse. Solus autem Deus est suum esse. Secundo, propter suam communitatem. Alia enim nomina, sunt vel minus communia, aut minus absoluta: sicque quodammodo determinant et informant ipsum esse: ideo minus proprie nominant Deum, quum Deus sit simplicissimum ac separatissimum esse. Tertio, propter suam consignificationem. Designat etenim esse, ut in præsenti. Deus autem æterna præsentia invariabiliter est in se ipso. Itaque, Qui est, est magis proprium nomen Dei, quam hoc nomen, Deus, quantum ad id a quo nomen imponitur, et item quantum ad significationem et consignificationem: sed quantum ad id cui nomen imponitur, hoc nomen, Deus, est magis proprium nomen ejus, quia impositum est ad significandum essentiam Dei, propter quod est nomen magis incommunicabile, quam hoc nomen, Qui est. Sicque adhuc magis proprium Dei nomen est τετράγραμματον, quod impositum est ad significandum divinam essentiam ut incommunicabilem, atque ut sic liceat fari, ut singularem. Bonum vero, est maxime proprium nomen Dei, secundum quod est causa rerum. Esse quippe, intelligitur ante rationem causæ. Hinc tertio capitulo de Divinis nominibus S. Dionysius ait, quod nominatio Boni, sit omnium divinarum processionum manifestativa. Hæc Thomas.
paras.en: Of this name of God Thomas speaks in the first part of his Summa, question 13: This name, He Who Is, is most properly the name of God. First, because of what it signifies: for it signifies not some form, but being itself; and God alone is his own being. Secondly, because of its universality: for other names are either less universal or less absolute, and so in some way determine and inform being itself; therefore they name God less properly, since God is being most simple and most separate. Thirdly, because of its consignification [that is, what a word signifies along with its meaning, as the tense of a verb]: for it designates being as in the present, and God is unchangeably in himself in an eternal present. And so He Who Is is more properly the name of God than this name, God, as regards that from which the name is taken, and likewise as regards its signification and consignification; but as regards that to which the name is given, this name, God, is more properly his name, because it was given to signify the essence of God, and so it is a more incommunicable name than this name, He Who Is. And so a still more proper name of God is the *tetragrammaton* [the name of four letters, the Hebrew name of God], which was given to signify the divine essence as incommunicable, and, if one may so speak, as singular. But Good is most properly the name of God inasmuch as he is the cause of things; for being is understood before the notion of cause. Hence St. Dionysius says in the third chapter of On the Divine Names that the naming of the Good shows forth all the divine processions. Thus far Thomas.

paras.t: Verumtamen Nicolaus de Lyra, et Rabbi Paulus concorditer dicunt, quod Hebraica veritas non habet, Ego sum qui sum, et, Qui est, misit me; sed, Ero qui ero, et, Qui erit, misit me. Porro in hoc isti duo discordant, quia secundum Lyram, per utramque litteram idem significatur, videlicet necessitas, æternitas, et invariabilitas esse ipsius Dei; sed secundum Rabbi Paulum, istud dici non potest, quoniam verbum hoc, Ero, designat successionem vel progressionem a non esse, vel a præsenti aut præterito esse in futurum. Insuper dicit Paulus iste, quod translatio Hieronymi in hoc passu manifeste deviat ab Hebraica veritate, quod male sonat. Tertio dicit, quod per verba ista, Ero qui ero, Deus non ostendit Moysi aliquod novum nomen divinum, sed quod non erat ei necessarium quærere novum nomen, quia sufficiebat ei nomen istud, Deus patrum vestrorum, etc. Quarto dicit, quod iste sit sensus horum verborum, Ero qui ero, id est, Ego qui ero tecum, ero cum filiis Israel.
paras.en: Nevertheless Nicholas of Lyra and Rabbi Paul [that is, Paul of Burgos, a convert from Judaism who wrote additions to Lyra's commentary] say with one accord that the Hebrew text does not have [[3:14|I AM WHO AM|Ego sum qui sum]], and [[3:14|HE WHO IS, hath sent me|Qui est, misit me]], but, I WILL BE WHO WILL BE, and, HE WHO WILL BE hath sent me. But in this the two disagree: for according to Lyra the same thing is signified by either reading, namely the necessity, eternity and unchangeableness of the being of God himself; but according to Rabbi Paul this cannot be said, since this word, I will be, designates a succession or progression from not-being, or from present or past being into the future. Further, this Paul says that Jerome's translation plainly departs from the Hebrew text in this passage, which has an ill sound. Thirdly he says that by these words, I will be who will be, God did not show Moses any new divine name, but showed that there was no need for him to seek a new name, because this name was enough for him: [[3:13|The God of your fathers|Deus patrum vestrorum]], etc. Fourthly he says that the sense of these words, I will be who will be, is this: I who will be with thee will be with the children of Israel.

paras.t: Circa hæc dico, S. Hieronymum in hoc loco vere atque fideliter transtulisse, etsi non secundum formam verborum, tamen secundum intentionem et verum intellectum Scripturæ. Quemadmodum quod apud Michæam habetur, Et tu Bethlehem Ephrata, parvulus es in millibus Juda: Matthæus evangelista in evangelio suo sic allegat, Tu Bethlehem terra Juda, nequaquam minima es in principibus Juda. Ubi videtur contrarietas in forma verborum, et tamen in sensu et intentione concordia est, sicut super Matthæum expositum est. Itaque, sicut asserit Lyra, per utramque litteram idem significatur. Quamvis enim verba præsentis temporis, magis proprie conveniant Deo, quam verba temporis præteriti ac futuri, quantum ad hoc quod aliquid principaliter et quasi stabiliter, non succedenter designant: non tamen, quantum ad hoc quod designant illud temporaliter aut subita certa differentia temporis, quum nullum tempus conveniat proprie Deo, tanquam mensura ipsius: sed in Scripturis frequenter enuntiantur de Deo verba cujuslibet differentiæ temporis, ad innuendum quod Deus omni tempori coexsistit, et omne tempus sua æternitate complectitur et transcendit, prout super primum Sententiarum scribunt doctores. Hinc æternitas Dei aliquando designatur per verba trium differentiarum temporis simul expressa et sumpta, juxta illud Apocalypsis: Gratia vobis et pax ab eo, qui est, et qui erat, et qui venturus est. Quemadmodum ergo hoc verbum, Sum, et Est, adscribitur Deo, in quantum designat æternam et incommutabilem præsentiam esse divini, absque commutatione præsentis temporalitatis; ita hoc verbum, Ero, et Erit, adscribitur Deo, in quantum designat esse æternum, quod numquam poterit terminari, deficere, aut finiri modo quocumque; ut sit sensus: Ero qui ero, id est, æternaliter idem manebo. Et ita nulla successio designatur in esse divino, sicut nec quum loquitur per Prophetam: Ero illorum Dominus in perpetuum.
paras.en: On these points I say that St. Jerome translated this place truly and faithfully, if not according to the form of the words, yet according to the intention and true understanding of Scripture. In the same way, what is found in Micheas, [[Mich 5:2|And thou Bethlehem Ephrata, art a little one among the thousands of Juda|Et tu Bethlehem Ephrata, parvulus es in millibus Juda]], Matthew the evangelist cites thus in his gospel: [[Matt 2:6|thou Bethlehem the land of Juda art not the least among the princes of Juda|Tu Bethlehem terra Juda, nequaquam minima es in principibus Juda]]. Here there seems to be a contradiction in the form of the words, and yet in sense and intention there is agreement, as has been explained on Matthew. So, as Lyra asserts, the same thing is signified by either reading. For although verbs of the present tense suit God more properly than verbs of the past and future tense, inasmuch as they designate something chiefly and as it were stably, not successively, yet not inasmuch as they designate it in time, or under a definite difference of time, since no time properly suits God as his measure; but in the Scriptures verbs of every difference of time are often spoken of God, to intimate that God coexists with every time, and embraces and transcends all time by his eternity, as the doctors write on the first book of the Sentences. Hence the eternity of God is sometimes designated by verbs of the three differences of time, expressed and taken together, according to that of the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 1:4|Grace be unto you and peace, from him that is and that was and that is to come|Gratia vobis et pax ab eo, qui est, et qui erat, et qui venturus est]]. As therefore this verb, I am, and Is, is ascribed to God inasmuch as it designates the eternal and unchangeable presence of the divine being, without the change of present time, so this verb, I will be, and Will be, is ascribed to God inasmuch as it designates eternal being, which can never be ended, fail, or be finished in any way; so that the sense is: I will be who will be, that is, I will remain the same eternally. And so no succession is designated in the divine being, as neither when he speaks by the Prophet: I will be their Lord for ever[[Wis 3:8||]] [the margin note is partly unreadable (Cf. Wis. iii, …); the nearest words are Wis 3:8, where the Douay-Rheims has: their Lord shall reign for ever].

paras.t: Illa quoque expositio, Ero qui ero, id est, Ero cum eis qui ero tecum, est impropria et extorta; imo secundum eam, Deus magis apte dixisset, Adero qui adero, id est, adero eis qui adero tibi. Denique dicere, quod per verba illa, Ero qui ero, Deus non ostendit Moysi novum nomen divinum, est evidenter contra tenorem ac seriem textus. Non enim solum dixit Deus, Ero qui ero: sed addidit, Hæc dices filiis Israel: Qui est, misit me ad vos. Per quod apertissime datur intelligi, quod Deus protulit verba illa, ostendendo Moysi nomen novum divinum. Josephus quoque ait: Deus dixit Moysi appellationem suam, quam homines prius non audierunt, nec mihi fas est dicere. Multa alia scribit Paulus iste circa hæc, quæ implicare videntur; sed brevitati studens, pertranseo.
paras.en: That exposition too, I will be who will be, that is, I will be with them, I who will be with thee, is improper and forced; indeed, according to it God would more fittingly have said, I will be at hand who will be at hand, that is, I will be at hand to them who will be at hand to thee. Lastly, to say that by those words, I will be who will be, God did not show Moses a new divine name, is plainly against the tenor and order of the text. For God did not only say, I will be who will be, but added: [[3:14|Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you|Hæc dices filiis Israel: Qui est, misit me ad vos]]. By this it is most plainly given to understand that God uttered those words in showing Moses a new divine name. Josephus too says: God told Moses his name, which men had not heard before, and which it is not lawful for me to speak. This Paul writes many other things on these matters which seem to involve contradictions; but, keen to be brief, I pass them over.

paras.t: Dixitque iterum Deus ad Moysen: Hæc dices filiis Israel: Dominus Deus patrum vestrorum, videlicet Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, et Deus Jacob, misit me ad vos. Moyses audito nomine illo antea inaudito, videlicet, Ego sum qui sum, et, Hæc dices filiis Israel: Qui est, misit me ad vos: præ admiratione et contemplationis vigore, quasi stupidus siluit: ideo Dominus protulit ei nomen facilius, quod etiam a filiis Israel capi celerius potuit, majorem quoque spem et devotionem eis imprimere quivit, dicens: Hæc dices filiis Israel: Dominus Deus patrum vestrorum, etc. Hoc nomen mihi est in æternum, id est, per hoc complexum, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, et Deus Jacob, volo necessabiliter et usque in finem mundi exprimi, nominari, laudari, et invocari, propter causam prælibatam; et hoc memoriale meum in generationem et generationem, id est, idem complexum universos fideles inducet ad recordationem et memoriam mei usque in finem mundi, secundum quod nomen est memoriale et recordativum rei designatæ per ipsum. Sic quoque in verbis his insinuatur nobis inæstimabilis caritas, pietas atque dignatio Dei ad suos electos, eo quod ipse Dominus majestatis immensæ, creator et rex universorum, dignatur tam peculiariter ac familiariter Deus hominum nuncupari.
paras.en: [[3:15|And God said again to Moses: Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: The Lord God of your fathers|Dixitque iterum Deus ad Moysen: Hæc dices filiis Israel: Dominus Deus patrum vestrorum]], namely [[3:15|the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob hath sent me to you|Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, et Deus Jacob, misit me ad vos]]. Moses, having heard that name unheard before, namely [[3:14|I AM WHO AM|Ego sum qui sum]], and [[3:14|Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you|Hæc dices filiis Israel: Qui est, misit me ad vos]], was silent as if stunned, from wonder and the force of contemplation; therefore the Lord gave him an easier name, which could also be grasped more quickly by the children of Israel, and could impress on them greater hope and devotion, saying: [[3:15|Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: The Lord God of your fathers|Hæc dices filiis Israel: Dominus Deus patrum vestrorum]], etc. [[3:15|this is my name for ever|Hoc nomen mihi est in æternum]], that is, by this phrase, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, I will to be expressed, named, praised and called upon unceasingly [the print has *necessabiliter*, apparently for *incessabiliter*, unceasingly], even to the end of the world, for the reason already given; [[3:15|and this is my memorial unto all generations|et hoc memoriale meum in generationem et generationem]], that is, the same phrase will bring all the faithful to remember me and be mindful of me even to the end of the world, inasmuch as a name is a memorial and a reminder of the thing designated by it. So too in these words is suggested to us the inestimable charity, kindness and condescension of God towards his elect, in that the Lord himself, of boundless majesty, creator and king of all things, deigns so particularly and familiarly to be called the God of men.

paras.t: Vade in Ægyptum, congrega ibi seniores Israel, id est aliquos seniores et majores Israelitici populi: et dices ad eos: Dominus Deus patrum vestrorum apparuit mihi, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, et Deus Jacob, dicens: Visitans visitavi vos, id est, visitare vos pie jam tam certe decrevi atque prænuntio, quasi jam fecissem hoc ipsum. Solet autem Deus sic loqui de futuro per modum præteriti, propter certitudinem veritatis verborum suorum. Vel, Visitavi, id est, visitare vos cœpi apparendo loquendoque Moysi, et dirigendo eum ad vos. Et sumitur visitatio nunc in bono, videlicet pro gratiosa subventione, sicut in Psalmo: Visita nos in salutari tuo. Et in Luca: Visitavit nos Oriens ex alto. Frequenter autem sumitur visitatio in malo, puta pro punitione, secundum quod per Sophoniam Dominus contestatur: Visitabo super omnem qui arroganter ingreditur.
paras.en: [[3:16|Go and gather together the ancients of Israel|Vade in Ægyptum, congrega ibi seniores Israel]] [Denis reads: Go into Egypt, gather together there the ancients of Israel], that is, some of the elders and chief men of the Israelite people; [[3:16|and thou shalt say to them: The Lord God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, hath appeared to me, saying: Visiting I have visited you|et dices ad eos: Dominus Deus patrum vestrorum apparuit mihi, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, et Deus Jacob, dicens: Visitans visitavi vos]], that is, I have now so surely decreed to visit you in mercy, and foretell it, as if I had already done this very thing. For God is wont so to speak of the future in the manner of the past, because of the certain truth of his words. Or, I have visited, that is, I have begun to visit you, by appearing and speaking to Moses, and directing him to you. And visitation is here taken in a good sense, namely for gracious help, as in the Psalm: [[Ps 105:4|visit us with thy salvation|Visita nos in salutari tuo]]. And in Luke: [[Luke 1:78|the Orient from on high hath visited us|Visitavit nos Oriens ex alto]]. But visitation is often taken in a bad sense, for instance for punishment, as the Lord declares through Sophonias: [[Soph 1:9|I will visit in that day upon every one that entereth arrogantly|Visitabo super omnem qui arroganter ingreditur]].

paras.t: Et vidi omnia quæ acciderunt vobis in Ægypto; et dixi ut educam vos de afflictione Ægypti in terram Chananæi, et Hethæi, et Amorrhæi, et Pherezæi, et Hevæi, et Jebusæi, et in terram fluentem lacte et melle. Et audient vocem tuam, id est, credent et acquiescent tibi, quoniam seniores illi noverunt promissiones Dei sanctis Patriarchis, Abrahæ, Isaac et Jacob, factas de liberatione posteritatis eorum ex Ægypto, et introductione in terram promissionis. Tempus quoque a Deo præfixum, jam esse impletum viderunt ex numero generationum et annorum decursu. Dixerat namque Deus ad Abraham: Generatione quarta revertentur huc.
paras.en: [[3:16|and I have seen all that hath befallen you in Egypt|Et vidi omnia quæ acciderunt vobis in Ægypto]]; [[3:17|And I have said the word to bring you forth out of the affliction of Egypt, into the land of the Chanaanite, and Hethite, and Amorrhite, and Pherezite, and Hevite, and Jebusite, to a land that floweth with milk and honey|et dixi ut educam vos de afflictione Ægypti in terram Chananæi, et Hethæi, et Amorrhæi, et Pherezæi, et Hevæi, et Jebusæi, et in terram fluentem lacte et melle]]. [[3:18|And they shall hear thy voice|Et audient vocem tuam]], that is, they will believe thee and assent to thee, since those elders knew the promises of God made to the holy Patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, of the deliverance of their posterity out of Egypt and their bringing into the land of promise. They saw too, from the number of the generations and the passing of the years, that the time fixed beforehand by God was now fulfilled. For God had said to Abraham: [[Gen 15:16|in the fourth generation they shall return hither|Generatione quarta revertentur huc]].

paras.t: Ingredierisque tu et seniores Israel ad regem Ægypti, et dicetis ad eum: Dominus Deus Hebræorum vocavit nos, id est, Deus noster præcepit nobis ire ad locum certum; ibimus viam trium dierum in solitudinem juxta præceptum Dei, id est, petimus ut hoc placeat tibi: ut immolemus Domino Deo nostro. Istud fuit verum: non tamen voluit Deus, ut Moyses prima facie exprimeret Pharaoni suum propositum: quo patet, quod aliquando liceat veritatem caute celare. Hinc voluit Deus, ut Moyses et seniores proponerent Pharaoni petitionem istam rationabilem et non gravem, ex qua videbatur quod essent celeriter redituri. Sed cur Dominus jussit ut peterent licentiam eundi viam trium dierum, et non pauciorum, nec plurium? Ad hoc sunt multæ mysticæ rationes, ut patebit sequenti articulo. Porro, ad litteram dici potest, quod ideo, quia infra tres dies poterant se tantum ab Ægyptiis elongare, quod eis non instabat periculum a plebe Ægypti. Nec petierunt dies plures, ne nimis multum petendo, videretur Pharao aliqualiter excusabilis de repulsa petitionis eorum, et de inobedientia sua ad Deum.
paras.en: [[3:18|and thou shalt go in, thou and the ancients of Israel, to the king of Egypt|Ingredierisque tu et seniores Israel ad regem Ægypti]], [[3:18|and thou shalt say to him: The Lord God of the Hebrews hath called us|et dicetis ad eum: Dominus Deus Hebræorum vocavit nos]], that is, our God has commanded us to go to a certain place; [[3:18|we will go three days' journey into the wilderness|ibimus viam trium dierum in solitudinem]] according to God's command, that is, we ask that this may please thee: [[3:18|to sacrifice unto the Lord our God|ut immolemus Domino Deo nostro]]. This was true; yet God did not will that Moses should lay open his purpose to Pharao at the outset: by which it is clear that it is sometimes lawful to conceal the truth with prudence. Hence God willed that Moses and the elders should put to Pharao this request, reasonable and not burdensome, from which it would seem that they would soon return. But why did the Lord command them to ask leave to go three days' journey, and not fewer, nor more? For this there are many mystical reasons, as will appear in the following article. But according to the letter it can be said that it was because within three days they could get so far from the Egyptians that no danger threatened them from the people of Egypt. Nor did they ask for more days, lest by asking too much Pharao might seem in some way excusable for refusing their request, and for his disobedience to God.

paras.t: Sed ego scio quod non dimittet vos rex Ægypti ut eatis de sua tellure, nisi per manum validam, id est, nisi quasi compulsus per plagas horribiles. Extendamque manum meam, id est, potentiam meam evidenter ostendam, atque in actus justitiæ eam procedere faciam: et percutiam Ægyptum, videlicet terram, terræ nascentia, homines et jumenta Ægypti; in cunctis mirabilibus meis, non absolute in cunctis mirabilibus et supernaturalibus plagis, sed in cunctis mirabilibus de quibus subjungitur, quæ facturus sum in medio eorum.
paras.en: [[3:19|But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go|Sed ego scio quod non dimittet vos rex Ægypti ut eatis]] out of his land, [[3:19|but by a mighty hand|nisi per manum validam]], that is, unless as it were compelled by dreadful plagues. [[3:20|For I will stretch forth my hand|Extendamque manum meam]], that is, I will show my power plainly, and make it go forth into acts of justice; [[3:20|and will strike Egypt|et percutiam Ægyptum]], namely the land, what the land brings forth, the men and the beasts of Egypt; [[3:20|with all my wonders|in cunctis mirabilibus meis]]: not absolutely with all wonders and supernatural plagues, but with all the wonders of which it is added, [[3:20|which I will do in the midst of them|quæ facturus sum in medio eorum]].

paras.t: Post hæc dimittet vos. Nam post ultimam plagam, quæ fuit percussio primogenitorum, fuerunt rex et Ægyptii ita perterriti, quod rogaverunt et quasi compellebant Hebræos exire, dicentes: Omnes moriemur.
paras.en: [[3:20|after these he will let you go|Post hæc dimittet vos]]. For after the last plague, which was the striking of the firstborn, the king and the Egyptians were so terrified that they begged the Hebrews, and as it were compelled them, to go out, saying: [[Ex 12:33|We shall all die|Omnes moriemur]].

paras.t: Daboque gratiam populo huic coram Ægyptiis, id est, Hebræos faciam acceptos, amabiles ac venerabiles ipsis Ægyptiis, movendo corda Ægyptiorum, ut bene sic afficiantur Hebræis tanquam summi Dei cultoribus, propter quos tanta peregit Deus. Deo etenim omnipotenti immenso est proprium, voluntates et mentes hominum ad libitum immutare, afficere, et quocumque ei placuerit, vertere. Et quum egrediemini Ægyptum, non exibitis vacui. Sub persona Moysis, loquitur Deus ad totum populum Moysi committendum.
paras.en: [[3:21|And I will give favour to this people, in the sight of the Egyptians|Daboque gratiam populo huic coram Ægyptiis]], that is, I will make the Hebrews acceptable, lovable and venerable to the Egyptians themselves, moving the hearts of the Egyptians to be well disposed towards the Hebrews as worshippers of the most high God, for whose sake God has done such great things. For it is proper to the almighty and boundless God to change the wills and minds of men at his pleasure, to move them, and to turn them whithersoever he pleases. [[3:21|and when you go forth, you shall not depart empty|Et quum egrediemini Ægyptum, non exibitis vacui]] [Denis reads: when you go forth out of Egypt]. Under the person of Moses God speaks to the whole people that was to be entrusted to Moses.

paras.t: Sed postulabit mulier a vicina sua et ab hospita sua. Ponitur hic singulare pro plurali, ut sit sensus: Mulieres Hebrææ petent a feminis Ægyptiis sibi vicinis ac hospitantibus se, vasa argentea et aurea, ac vestes: imo et alia quædam jocalia atque clenodia pretiosa, quæ postea obtulerunt filii Israel in ædificationem tabernaculi et sacerdotalium ornamentorum, ut infra patebit. Ponetisque ea super filios vestros et filias, ut portent ea super humeros suos; et spoliabitis Ægyptum, id est, has Ægyptiorum divitias auferetis ab eis per modum prædantium. Non tamen fuit spoliatio proprie dicta, sed justa sublatio, quoniam omnium rerum Dominus et Creator præcepit sic fieri. Ipse enim potest justissime bona terrena quibusdam, præsertim indignis, auferre, aliisque conferre. Hebræi quoque diu ac laboriose servierunt Ægyptiis, et maximam passi erant injuriam ab eisdem, præsertim in submersione infantium: ideo Deus justissimus judex, rectissime fecit eis hanc recompensationem. Dicunt Hebræi, quod mulieres illæ Hebrææ petierunt sibi talia ab Ægyptiis dari: sed verius creditur, quod postulaverunt sibi hæc mutuari; nec ab egredientibus Hebræis ea repetierunt, vel quia putabant eos mox redituros, vel præ nimia occupatione in sepelitione mortuorum suorum.
paras.en: [[3:22|But every woman shall ask of her neighbour, and of her that is in her house|Sed postulabit mulier a vicina sua et ab hospita sua]]. The singular is put here for the plural, so that the sense is: the Hebrew women will ask of the Egyptian women who are their neighbours and who give them lodging [[3:22|vessels of silver and of gold, and raiment|vasa argentea et aurea, ac vestes]]: and indeed certain other precious jewels and trinkets too, which the children of Israel afterwards offered for the making of the tabernacle and of the priestly vestments, as will appear below. [[3:22|and you shall put them on your sons and daughters|Ponetisque ea super filios vestros et filias]], that they may carry them on their shoulders; [[3:22|and shall spoil Egypt|et spoliabitis Ægyptum]], that is, you shall carry off these riches of the Egyptians from them in the manner of plunderers. Yet it was not a spoiling properly so called, but a just taking away, since the Lord and Creator of all things commanded it to be so done. For he can most justly take earthly goods from some, especially the unworthy, and confer them on others. The Hebrews too had long and laboriously served the Egyptians, and had suffered very great injury from them, especially in the drowning of their infants: therefore God, the most just judge, most rightly made them this recompense. The Hebrews say that those Hebrew women asked that such things be given them by the Egyptians; but it is more truly believed that they asked to borrow them; and the Egyptians did not ask them back from the Hebrews as they went out, either because they thought they would soon return, or because they were too much taken up with the burial of their dead.

3.title: De spirituali sensu ejusdem capituli tertii
3.title_en: On the spiritual sense of the same third chapter

paras.t: Moyses pascebat oves Jethro cognati sui. Per Moysen intelligitur pastor et prælatus fidelis, qui filiam Jethro soceri sui duxit uxorem, id est, Ecclesiæ sibi commissæ, filiæ Christi, est sponsus, et eam caritatis ulnis amplectitur et fecundat. Sicque oves Christi pascit scientia et doctrina, oratione atque exemplo, fama et ecclesiasticis sacramentis. Christus quoque dici potest sacerdos Madian, id est gentilitatis conversæ. Quumque minasset gregem ad interiora deserti, hoc est, fideles sibi commissos perduxerit ad secretiora cœlestis mysterii, exponendo eis arcana et spiritualia documenta de lege Christi, quantum ipsi capere queunt, et eis expedit dici, venit ad montem Dei Horeb, hoc est ad cacumen et apicem ecclesiasticæ theoriæ, quoniam subditos suos tam efficaciter instruendo, meretur valde illuminari a Domino, cui nil gratius potest offerri, quam ut oves suæ salubriter gubernentur.
paras.en: [[3:1|Moses fed the sheep of Jethro|Moyses pascebat oves Jethro]] his kinsman [Denis reads *cognati*, “kinsman”, where the Vulgate has *soceri*, “father-in-law”]. By Moses is understood the faithful shepherd and prelate, who took to wife the daughter of Jethro his father-in-law: that is, he is the bridegroom of the Church committed to him, the daughter of Christ, and he embraces her in the arms of charity and makes her fruitful. And so he feeds the sheep of Christ with knowledge and teaching, with prayer and example, with good repute and with the sacraments of the Church. Christ too can be called the priest of Madian, that is, of the converted Gentiles. And [[3:1|he drove the flock to the inner parts of the desert|Quumque minasset gregem ad interiora deserti]], that is, when he has led the faithful committed to him into the more secret places of the heavenly mystery, setting forth to them the hidden and spiritual teachings of the law of Christ, as far as they are able to take them in and as it is good for them to be told, [[3:1|came to the mountain of God, Horeb|venit ad montem Dei Horeb]], that is, to the summit and peak of the Church's contemplation [*theoria*]; for by instructing his subjects so effectively he deserves to be greatly enlightened by the Lord, to whom nothing more pleasing can be offered than that his sheep be governed to their salvation.

paras.t: Apparuitque ei Dominus in flamma ignis rubi. Per rubum apte signatur humanitas Salvatoris, cujus caritas ferventissima, qua tradidit se pro nobis, est flamma ignis in qua Deus apparet. Quia qui Christi caritatem rite perpendit, ad contemplationis altitudinem elevatur, et superbenedictæ Trinitatis pietatem et gratiam circa genus humanum, imo et altitudinem consilii ejus super nostra redemptione, fideliter speculatur. Et ita potissime illuminari meretur, quia tumultibus et inquietudinibus societatis humanæ et sæcularium rerum se abstrahit, et solitarium petit locum, in quo solus soli vacet Altissimo.
paras.en: [[3:2|And the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire|Apparuitque ei Dominus in flamma ignis]] [[3:2|of a bush|rubi]]. By the bush is fitly signified the humanity of the Saviour, whose most fervent charity, with which he delivered himself up for us, is the flame of fire in which God appears. For he who duly weighs the charity of Christ is raised to the height of contemplation, and faithfully beholds the loving-kindness and grace of the supremely blessed Trinity towards the human race, and indeed the depth of his counsel concerning our redemption.
