And he deserves to be enlightened in this way above all because he withdraws himself from the tumults and disquiet of human society and of worldly affairs, and seeks a solitary place in which, alone, he may give himself to the Most High alone.

paras.t: Videbat quod rubus arderet, et non combureretur. Humanitas etenim Filii Dei, inflammatissima erat igne Spiritus Sancti, qui innocue ac superdulcissime arsit in ea. Quod fidelis admirans, pergit, id est disponit se, ad videndum tam sublime mysterium, qualiter scilicet humana natura ab increato Verbo assumpta, manet in tali unione ab ardore Solis justitiæ inconsumpta, atque in naturalibus viribus suis ac proprietatibus salva et integra. Quod revera grande et impenetrabile exstat mysterium.
paras.en: [[3:2|he saw that the bush was on fire, and was not burnt|Videbat quod rubus arderet, et non combureretur]]. For the humanity of the Son of God was most fully aflame with the fire of the Holy Ghost, which burned in it harmlessly and with surpassing sweetness. Marvelling at this, the faithful man goes forward, that is, disposes himself, to see so sublime a mystery: namely how the human nature assumed by the uncreated Word remains in such a union unconsumed by the burning of the Sun of justice, and safe and whole in its natural powers and properties. And this is truly a great and impenetrable mystery.

paras.t: Cernens autem Dominus quod pergeret ad videndum, vocavit eum de medio rubi, et ait: Ne appropies huc. Solve calceamentum de pedibus tuis. Locus enim in quo stas, terra sancta est. Sic deitas summa in Christo habitans, videns fidelem contemplatorem ad considerandum mirabilia legis divinæ ac fidei christianæ accedere, vocat eum, interius inspirando eidem, ne supra virium suarum mensuram præsumat divina scrutari secreta, juxta quod scriptum est: Altiora te ne quæsieris, et fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris; sed quæ præcepit tibi Deus, illa cogita semper. Jubet quoque Dominus homini tali auferre calceamenta de pedibus suis, hoc est, actiones carnales et opera prava, excusationesque frivolas auferre a cordis sui affectibus, qui sunt animæ pedes. Non enim aptus est contemplari divina, nisi qui abjicit a suis desideriis hujuscemodi calceamenta, quæ multi pessime induunt et assumunt, qui ex aliorum perversitatibus se excusant. Locus vero in quo stat contemplator et fidelis prælatus, est sancta Ecclesia.
paras.en: [[3:4|And when the Lord saw that he went forward to see, he called to him out of the midst of the bush. and said|Cernens autem Dominus quod pergeret ad videndum, vocavit eum de medio rubi, et ait]]: [[3:5|Come not nigh hither, put off the shoes from thy feet; for the place, whereon thou standest, is holy ground|Ne appropies huc. Solve calceamentum de pedibus tuis. Locus enim in quo stas, terra sancta est]]. So the supreme Godhead dwelling in Christ, seeing the faithful contemplative drawing near to consider the wonders of the divine law and of the Christian faith, calls him, inspiring him inwardly, not to presume to search into divine secrets beyond the measure of his powers, according to what is written: [[Ecclus 3:22|Seek not the things that are too high for thee, and search not into things above thy ability: but the things that God hath commanded thee, think on them always|Altiora te ne quæsieris, et fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris; sed quæ præcepit tibi Deus, illa cogita semper]]. The Lord also bids such a man put off the shoes from his feet, that is, put away carnal actions and wicked works and frivolous excuses from the affections of his heart, which are the feet of the soul. For no one is fit to contemplate divine things unless he casts from his desires shoes of this kind, which many most wrongly put on and take up, excusing themselves by the perversities of others. And the place on which the contemplative and faithful prelate stands is holy Church.

paras.t: Abscondit Moyses faciem suam. Sic dum homo sublimiter illustratur a Deo, in tantum miratur et obstupescit ex inspecta altitudine Creatoris, quod se ipsum in totius humilitatis abyssum demergit.
paras.en: [[3:6|Moses hid his face|Abscondit Moyses faciem suam]]. So when a man is sublimely enlightened by God, he so marvels and is so astonished at the height of the Creator he has beheld that he plunges himself into the abyss of all humility.

paras.t: Vidi afflictionem populi mei in Ægypto. Considerat etenim pius Dominus, qualiter veraciter Christiani a visibilibus ac invisibilibus hostibus, ab acie vitiorum, ab impedimentis virtutum multipliciter acriterque affliguntur: et quasi compatiens eis, consolationem impendit, promittens quod cito perducentur ad regnum cælorum.
paras.en: [[3:7|I have seen the affliction of my people in Egypt|Vidi afflictionem populi mei in Ægypto]]. For the loving Lord considers how true Christians are afflicted in many ways and sharply by visible and invisible enemies, by the battle-line of the vices, by hindrances to the virtues; and as though suffering with them, he grants them consolation, promising that they will soon be brought into the kingdom of heaven.

paras.t: Tunc Moyses mittitur ad Pharaonem, ut populum Dei educat de tenebris vitiorum, quando ex divina commissione is qui præsidet aliis, opponit se fortiter pro defensione gregis sui, diabolicam crudelitatem atque versutiam orationibus ac virtuosis exercitiis reprimendo, et vasa ejus ei auferendo, per hoc quod iniquos trahit ad viam salutis.
paras.en: Then Moses is sent to Pharao, to bring God's people out of the darkness of the vices, when he who is set over others, by divine commission, sets himself stoutly in defence of his flock, checking the devil's cruelty and cunning by prayers and virtuous exercises, and taking his vessels from him by drawing the wicked to the way of salvation.

paras.t: Verumtamen ad hæc peragenda, humiliter recognoscit se præsidens, nequaquam viribus suis sufficere: ideo Dominus consolatur et roborat eum, dicendo: Ego ero tecum. Et hoc habebis signum quod miserim te: Quum eduxeris populum meum de Ægypto, hoc est, ex vitiosa et tenebrosa conversatione converteris eos ad lucem gratiæ et splendorem virtutum, immolabis Deo super montem istum, id est, super altare et in Ecclesia offeres Deo sacrificium gratiarum actionis et laudis, et Eucharistiæ sacramentum, omnem fructum tuæ prædicationis et sancti laboris Deo totis præcordiis adscribendo.
paras.en: Yet he who presides humbly acknowledges that he is by no means equal to accomplishing these things by his own strength; therefore the Lord comforts and strengthens him, saying: [[3:12|I will be with thee; and this thou shalt have for a sign that I have sent thee: When thou shalt have brought my people out of Egypt|Ego ero tecum. Et hoc habebis signum quod miserim te: Quum eduxeris populum meum de Ægypto]], that is, when thou shalt have turned them from a vicious and darksome way of life to the light of grace and the splendour of the virtues, [[3:12|thou shalt offer sacrifice to God upon this mountain|immolabis Deo super montem istum]], that is, upon the altar and in the Church thou shalt offer to God the sacrifice of thanksgiving and praise, and the sacrament of the Eucharist, ascribing to God with all thy heart all the fruit of thy preaching and holy labour.

paras.t: Ait Moyses ad Deum: Ecce ego vadam ad filios Israel, et dicam eis: Deus patrum vestrorum misit me ad vos, hoc est, Christianos meo regimini informationive creditos accedam, dicamque eis, quod Deus Apostolorum injunxit mihi, ut prædicem eis verbum salutis. Si dixerint mihi, Quod est nomen ejus? quid dicam eis? hoc est, si petierint aliqualiter edoceri ac scire quid sit Deus (quia nil potest amari ac timeri et venerari, nisi aliquatenus cognitum), quid dicturus sum ipsis?
paras.en: [[3:13|Moses said to God: Lo, I shall go to the children of Israel, and say to them: The God of your fathers hath sent me to you|Ait Moyses ad Deum: Ecce ego vadam ad filios Israel, et dicam eis: Deus patrum vestrorum misit me ad vos]]: that is, I will go to the Christians entrusted to my rule or instruction, and I will tell them that the God of the Apostles has charged me to preach to them the word of salvation. [[3:13|If they shall say to me: What is his name? What shall I say to them?|Si dixerint mihi, Quod est nomen ejus? quid dicam eis?]] That is, if they ask to be taught in some measure and to know what God is (for nothing can be loved and feared and revered unless it is known in some degree), what am I to tell them?

paras.t: Dixit Dominus: Ego sum qui sum. Sic dices: Qui est, misit me ad vos. Sic plane, sic debet prælatus et prædicator instruere populum, exponendo ei, qualiter ipse Dominus Deus noster, sit ipsum esse purum, incircumscriptum, et separatum, in se ipso incommutabiliter æternaliterque […], in quo vere, et sine omni mensura ac termino est infinita perfectio, immensa dulcedo, sapientia, beatitudo, et quidquid excogitari potest pertinere ad nobilitatem eminentiamque essendi, hoc est, superpurissima bonitas, omnipotens virtus, interminata voluptas, pulchritudo illimitata, sempiterna libertas. Propter quod Deus est pro universis et singulis creaturis incomparabiliter amabilis, desiderandus, metuendus, colendus, et contemplandus; et quidquid ab ipso est aversivum, est cum infinito horrore ac nausea respuendum. Sic ergo instruendus ac inflammandus est populus ad Dei contemplationem, amorem, cultum, ac filialem timorem.
paras.en: The Lord said: [[3:14|I AM WHO AM|Ego sum qui sum]]. [[3:14|Thus shalt thou say|Sic dices]]: [[3:14|HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you|Qui est, misit me ad vos]]. Plainly so, so ought the prelate and preacher to instruct the people, setting forth to them how the Lord our God himself is pure being itself, uncircumscribed and separate [that is, distinct from every creature and mixed with none], unchangeably and eternally […] in himself; in whom truly, and without any measure or limit, there is infinite perfection, boundless sweetness, wisdom, beatitude, and whatever can be thought to belong to the nobility and eminence of being: that is, a goodness pure beyond all purity, almighty power, unending delight, unlimited beauty, everlasting freedom. For this reason God is, for each and every creature, beyond compare lovable, to be desired, feared, worshipped and contemplated; and whatever turns away from him is to be spurned with infinite horror and loathing. Thus, then, the people is to be instructed and kindled to the contemplation, love and worship of God, and to filial fear.

paras.t: Quod si homines rudes et idiotæ capere ista nequiverint, sufficiat ut eis dicatur: Deus patrum vestrorum, Deus Apostolorum, martyrum, confessorum, virginum, et omnium electorum, misit me ad vos.
paras.en: But if rude and unlettered men cannot take this in, let it be enough to tell them: The [[3:15|God of your fathers|Deus patrum vestrorum]], the God of the Apostles, martyrs, confessors, virgins and of all the elect, [[3:15|hath sent me to you|misit me ad vos]].

paras.t: Vade, congrega seniores Israel, et dices ad eos: Deus patrum vestrorum apparuit mihi, dicens: Visitans visitavi vos. Istud committit Deus superioribus prælatis, qui præsunt aliis multis pastoribus. Illis ergo superioribus Deus jubet, ut seniores Israel, id est inferiores prælatos ac sacerdotes, prædicatoresque congregent, id est, ad celebrationem synodi et salubris concilii convocent, insinuando eisdem qualiter Deus omnipotens paratus sit eis succurrere ad hoc, quod se ipsos ac subditos suos digne reforment, gubernent, salvificent: quoniam Deus vidit omnia quæ eis in Ægypto, id est in hoc sæculo nequam, contigerunt, et qualiter ibi a diabolo, mundo et carne decepti et victi sint sæpe, in tantum quod crudelissimo suæ salutis adversario servierunt.
paras.en: [[3:16|Go and gather together the ancients of Israel, and thou shalt say to them|Vade, congrega seniores Israel, et dices ad eos]]: The [[3:16|God of your fathers|Deus patrum vestrorum]] [[3:16|hath appeared to me, saying|apparuit mihi, dicens]]: [[3:16|Visiting I have visited you|Visitans visitavi vos]]. This God commits to the higher prelates, who are set over many other shepherds. To those superiors, then, God commands that they gather the ancients of Israel, that is, the lower prelates and priests and preachers; that is, that they call them together to hold a synod and a wholesome council, making known to them how almighty God is ready to help them to reform, govern and save themselves and their subjects worthily: since God has seen all that has befallen them in Egypt, that is, in this wicked world, and how there they have often been deceived and overcome by the devil, the world and the flesh, so far that they have served the most cruel adversary of their salvation.

paras.t: Ingredierisque tu et seniores Israel ad regem Ægypti, id est ad principem hujus mundi, dicens: Dominus Deus Hebræorum vocavit nos, hoc est, diabolo te oppones, insultabis et dices: Deus nobis præcepit, ut te relicto, accedamus ad thronum gratiæ ejus, et per mentis conversionem applacemus nos adhæreamusque ei. […] trium dierum in solitudinem, id est, per tres partes Pœnitentiæ, quæ sunt contritio, confessio, satisfactio, tendamus ad mentis tranquillitatem a strepitu mundi et inquietudine vitiorum: ut immolemus Domino Deo nostro nos ipsos in holocaustum, mancipando nos totos cultui ejus.
paras.en: [[3:18|thou shalt go in, thou and the ancients of Israel, to the king of Egypt|Ingredierisque tu et seniores Israel ad regem Ægypti]], that is, to the prince of this world, saying: [[3:18|The Lord God of the Hebrews hath called us|Dominus Deus Hebræorum vocavit nos]]; that is, thou shalt set thyself against the devil, defy him and say: God has commanded us to leave thee and draw near to the throne of his grace, and by conversion of mind to reconcile ourselves to him and cleave to him. […] [[3:18|three days' journey into the wilderness|trium dierum in solitudinem]] [some words are lost here in the print, presumably *ibimus viam*, “we will go”], that is, through the three parts of Penance, which are contrition, confession and satisfaction, let us make our way to tranquillity of mind, away from the din of the world and the disquiet of the vices, [[3:18|to sacrifice unto the Lord our God|ut immolemus Domino Deo nostro]] ourselves as a holocaust, giving ourselves over wholly to his worship.

paras.t: Insuper, via trium dierum, est exercitatio mentis in fide, spe et caritate, per quam ad salutis pertingitur finem. Rursus, via trium dierum, est servitus Dei exhibita in adolescentia, in juventute et senectute. Iterum, via trium dierum, est observantia legis naturalis, legis evangelicæ, et legis positivæ seu statutorum Ecclesiæ: quas omnes observare tenemur, unusquisque juxta exigentiam suæ vocationis. Adhuc autem, via trium dierum, est lumen naturæ, lumen gratiæ, lumenque gloriæ. Item status incipientium, proficientium, et perfectorum.
paras.en: Further, the three days' journey is the exercise of the mind in faith, hope and charity, by which the goal of salvation is reached. Again, the three days' journey is the service of God shown in youth, in manhood and in old age. Again, the three days' journey is the observance of the natural law, the law of the Gospel, and positive law, that is, the statutes of the Church, all of which we are bound to observe, each according to what his calling requires. And again, the three days' journey is the light of nature, the light of grace and the light of glory. Likewise, the state of beginners, of the proficient and of the perfect.

paras.t: Sed ego scio quod non dimittet vos rex Ægypti ut eatis, nisi per manum validam. Princeps etenim tenebrarum et ejus satellites, non cessant eos qui volunt se emendare, acriter impugnare: imo tanto validius, quanto hi qui ei servierant, fortius se convertunt ad viam salutis. Ideo necessaria est valde gratiosa subventio Dei, qui manum suam extendat, percutiatque Ægyptum in cunctis mirabilibus suis, et variis modis faciat suos prævalere electos, et machinamenta dæmonum prorsus evacuet, eosque contribulet per virtuosa exercitia conversorum, quorum humilitate, caritate, patientia, perseverantia et profectu ac prævalentia, dæmones exuruntur. Hæc etenim dona virtutum, et varii effectus gratiæ, ac triumphi fidelium contra aereas potestates, sunt vere mirabilia Dei, quæ Deus operatur in suis, videntibus impiis illis: sicque dimittit diabolus eos, qui sibi sic renituntur ac prævalent.
paras.en: [[3:19|But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go, but by a mighty hand|Sed ego scio quod non dimittet vos rex Ægypti ut eatis, nisi per manum validam]]. For the prince of darkness and his minions never cease to attack fiercely those who wish to amend themselves; indeed, all the more strongly, the more vigorously those who had served him turn to the way of salvation. Therefore the gracious help of God is very necessary: that he stretch forth his hand and strike Egypt with all his wonders, and in various ways make his elect prevail, and bring the devices of the demons utterly to nothing, and crush them through the virtuous exercises of the converted, by whose humility, charity, patience, perseverance, progress and prevailing the demons are burned up. For these gifts of the virtues, and the various effects of grace, and the triumphs of the faithful over the powers of the air, are truly the wonders of God, which God works in his own while those wicked ones look on; and so the devil lets go those who thus resist him and prevail.

paras.t: Daboque gratiam populo huic coram Ægyptiis. Hoc impletur quotidie, quando Altissimo disponente, servi Dei et vere religiosi, qui mundum et ea quæ mundi sunt deserunt, inveniunt gratiam coram mundanis hominibus, eleemosynas quoque et beneficia quædam sortiuntur ab illis.
paras.en: [[3:21|And I will give favour to this people, in the sight of the Egyptians|Daboque gratiam populo huic coram Ægyptiis]]. This is fulfilled daily when, by the disposing of the Most High, the servants of God and true religious, who forsake the world and the things of the world, find favour in the sight of worldly men, and receive from them alms and certain benefits.

paras.t: Postulabit mulier a vicina sua et ab hospita sua vasa argentea et aurea ac vestes. Hoc spiritualiter adimpletur, dum animæ christianæ ex dictis philosophorum et poetarum ac rhetorum accipiunt aliqua utilia documenta, et eloquentiæ flores, naturalemque sapientiam, per quæ omnia adjuvantur ad intelligendum et exponendum Scripturas, ad fidei defensionem, ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ. Nam et Paulus in suis epistolis allegat nonnulla hujusmodi dicta. Hæc quoque ponunt fideles super filios suos ac filias, id est, cordibus discipulorum et subditorum ac posterorum suorum imprimunt ea; spoliantque Ægyptum, dum illorum dogmatibus in evangelica lege utuntur.
paras.en: [[3:22|every woman shall ask of her neighbour, and of her that is in her house, vessels of silver and of gold, and raiment|Postulabit mulier a vicina sua et ab hospita sua vasa argentea et aurea ac vestes]]. This is fulfilled spiritually when Christian souls take from the sayings of the philosophers, poets and rhetoricians some useful teachings, and flowers of eloquence, and natural wisdom, by all of which they are helped to understand and expound the Scriptures, to defend the faith, and to build up the Church. For Paul too cites a number of such sayings in his epistles [for instance a line of Menander at 1 Cor 15:33 and one of Epimenides at Tit 1:12]. These too the faithful put on their sons and daughters, that is, they impress them on the hearts of their disciples and subjects and those who come after them; and they spoil Egypt when they use those men's teachings in the law of the Gospel.

4.title: Elucidatio capituli quarti: Respondens Moyses, ait: Non credent mihi
4.title_en: Explanation of the fourth chapter: “Moses answered, and said: They will not believe me”

paras.t: Moyses prudenter considerans magnitudinem legationis, quam sibi proposuit et injunxit Dominus, diu se excusavit, insufficientiam suam allegans, etiam quodammodo importune. Idcirco nunc recitatur qualiter Deus roboravit eum per miracula et promissa.
paras.en: Moses, prudently considering the greatness of the embassy which the Lord had set before him and laid upon him, excused himself for a long time, alleging his own insufficiency, and even somewhat importunately. Therefore it is now related how God strengthened him by miracles and promises.

paras.t: Si autem objiciatur, quia præhabitum est quod Moyses ex revelatione cognovit se electum a Deo, ad hoc quod liberaret filios Israel, etiam antequam fugit a facie Pharaonis, ergo se excusare non debuit, aut de veritate divinæ revelationis dubitare: dicendum, quod viri virtutum nunc actioni unius virtutis, nunc actioni virtutis alterius sunt intenti; diversas quoque habent considerationes, et secundum hoc diversimode judicant etiam de eodem, quemadmodum Paulus uno in loco: Non sum, inquit, dignus vocari apostolus; et tamen alibi sæpe se vocat apostolum. Sic et David scivit se unctum et electum in regem, et tamen quandoque desperavit se posse evadere manus Saulis, atque ad Jonatham lacrimans dixit: Ego et mors uno tantum gradu dividimur. Sic viri virtuosi quandoque insistunt actibus et considerationibus humilitatis, sicque reputant se ineptos et indignos ad ardua: quandoque vero insistunt considerationibus et actibus magnanimitatis, et ita ex confidentia divini subsidii offerunt se paratos ad magna. Una etenim virtus alteri cedit, et circa eamdem materiam humilitas magnanimitasque versantur. Sic ergo nunc Moyses se excusat, propriam insufficientiam humiliter pensans, non tamen de veritate revelationis divinæ ambigens per considerationem supernaturalium auxiliorum Omnipotentis.
paras.en: But if it be objected that, as was said before, Moses knew by revelation that he had been chosen by God to set the children of Israel free, even before he fled from the face of Pharao, and that he therefore ought not to have excused himself or to have doubted the truth of the divine revelation: it must be said that men of virtue are intent now on the act of one virtue, now on the act of another; they also have different considerations, and accordingly judge differently even of the same thing. So Paul in one place: [[1 Cor 15:9|who am not|Non sum]], he says, [[1 Cor 15:9|worthy to be called an apostle|dignus vocari apostolus]]; and yet elsewhere he often calls himself an apostle[[Rom 11:13||]][[1 Cor 1:1||]]. So too David knew that he had been anointed and chosen king, and yet at times despaired of being able to escape the hands of Saul, and said to Jonathan with tears: [[1 Kings 20:3|there is but one step (as I may say) between me and death|Ego et mors uno tantum gradu dividimur]]. So virtuous men at times dwell on the acts and considerations of humility, and so reckon themselves unfit and unworthy for hard things; but at times they dwell on the considerations and acts of magnanimity [that is, greatness of soul, the virtue that reaches out to great things], and so, from confidence in God's help, offer themselves ready for great things. For one virtue gives way to another, and humility and magnanimity are concerned with the same matter. In this way, then, Moses now excuses himself, humbly weighing his own insufficiency, yet not doubting the truth of the divine revelation, since he considers the supernatural helps of the Almighty.

paras.t: Nunc itaque dicitur: Respondens Moyses, ait: Non credent mihi, neque audient vocem meam auribus cordis, acquiescendo verbis meis, sed dicent: Non apparuit tibi Dominus. Præcedenti capitulo Dominus ait ad Moysen, Audient vocem tuam: quomodo ergo Moyses nunc affirmat, Neque audient vocem meam? Sed hoc faciliter concordatur, quoniam Dominus dixit illud de senioribus, qui promissiones patribus suis factas noverunt; Moyses vero nunc loquitur de plebe communi, in qua multi erant ad credendum difficiles. Vel Moyses protulit verba hæc non simpliciter affirmando, sed probabiliter conjiciendo. Est enim frequens talis modus loquendi.
paras.en: Now therefore it is said: [[4:1|Moses answered, and said: They will not believe me, nor hear my voice|Respondens Moyses, ait: Non credent mihi, neque audient vocem meam]] with the ears of the heart, by acquiescing in my words, [[4:1|but they will say: The Lord hath not appeared to thee|sed dicent: Non apparuit tibi Dominus]]. In the preceding chapter the Lord said to Moses: [[Ex 3:18|they shall hear thy voice|Audient vocem tuam]]. How then does Moses now affirm: [[4:1|nor hear my voice|Neque audient vocem meam]]? But this is easily reconciled, since the Lord said that of the elders, who knew the promises made to their fathers, while Moses is now speaking of the common people, among whom many were hard to bring to belief. Or Moses uttered these words not as a plain assertion but as a likely conjecture; for such a manner of speaking is frequent.

paras.t: Dixit ergo ad eum: Quid est hoc quod tenes in manu tua? Interrogatio non semper ex ignorantia venit, sicut nec ista. Sed ideo Dominus quod scivit quæsivit, ut ex responsione Moysis proportionate præciperet ei. Respondit: Virga est. Fuit namque virga seu baculus pastoralis.
paras.en: [[4:2|Then he said to him: What is that thou holdest in thy hand?|Dixit ergo ad eum: Quid est hoc quod tenes in manu tua?]] A question does not always come from ignorance, and neither does this one. But the Lord asked what he knew so that he might give Moses a command fitted to his answer. [[4:2|He answered: A rod|Respondit: Virga est]]. For it was a rod, that is, a shepherd's staff.

paras.t: Dixitque Dominus: Projice eam in terram. Projecit, et versa est in colubrum, ita ut fugeret Moyses; quia coluber ille fuit serpens magnus atque terribilis, et (ut Josephus scribit) erat draco repens, convolutus spiris ingentibus, et tanquam contra persequentes suum caput sævissimum movens: et ita ex naturali timore, concepto ex naturali consideratione et imaginatione serpentis, Moyses fugere cœpit, quasi lædi posset a colubro, non attendens actualiter satis præsentiam Dei, ex qua debuit esse securus. Et venit hoc ex subreptione et fragilitate humana, ideo excusabile fuit. Dixitque Dominus: Extende manum tuam, et apprehende caudam ejus. Extendit, et tenuit; et versus est in virgam. Et in hoc commendatur obedientia Moysis, quod bestiam illam tam abominabilem, Deo jubente, mox apprehendit. Istud miraculum excessit naturalem cursum, causalitatem et ordinem rerum: quia tam subito virgam in serpentem mutari, atque serpentem in virgam, per naturalium applicationem causarum fieri nequit, prout de hoc infra circa opera magorum Pharaonis, magis dicetur.
paras.en: [[4:3|And the Lord said: Cast it down upon the ground. He cast it down, and it was turned into a serpent, so that Moses fled from it|Dixitque Dominus: Projice eam in terram. Projecit, et versa est in colubrum, ita ut fugeret Moyses]]; for that serpent was a great and terrible snake, and (as Josephus writes) it was a crawling dragon, coiled in huge folds, and moving its most savage head as if against pursuers. And so, from natural fear, conceived from the natural thought and image of a serpent, Moses began to flee, as though the serpent could hurt him, not actually attending enough to the presence of God, which ought to have made him feel safe. This came from a sudden movement [subreptio: a stirring that steals upon one before reason can weigh it] and from human frailty; therefore it was excusable. [[4:4|And the Lord said: Put out thy hand, and take it by the tail. He put forth his hand, and took hold of it, and it was turned into a rod|Dixitque Dominus: Extende manum tuam, et apprehende caudam ejus. Extendit, et tenuit; et versus est in virgam]]. And in this Moses's obedience is commended, that at God's command he at once took hold of so loathsome a beast. This miracle surpassed the natural course, causality and order of things: for a rod cannot be changed so suddenly into a serpent, and the serpent into a rod, by bringing natural causes to bear, as will be said more fully below concerning the works of Pharao's magicians.

paras.t: Ut credant, inquit, tibi, quod apparuerit tibi Dominus Deus patrum tuorum, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, et Deus Jacob: id est, ad hoc ipse Deus fecit et demonstravit signum hoc Moysi, quatenus Moyse illud coram filiis Israel faciente, ipsi crederent Deum vere ipsi Moysi apparuisse, eumque misisse ad eos.
paras.en: [[4:5|That they may believe, saith he|Ut credant, inquit]], thee, [[4:5|that the Lord God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, hath appeared to thee|quod apparuerit tibi Dominus Deus patrum tuorum, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, et Deus Jacob]]: that is, God himself did and showed this sign to Moses for this purpose, that when Moses performed it before the children of Israel they might believe that God had truly appeared to Moses and had sent him to them.

paras.t: Dixitque Dominus rursum ad Moysen: Mitte manum tuam in sinum tuum. Quam quum misisset in sinum, protulit leprosam instar nivis, id est, retraxit eam tam leprosam, quod præ magnitudine lepræ fuit candens et alba ut nix. Albor quippe lucens in superficie cutis, argumentum est lepræ, ut in Levitico scriptum est.
paras.en: [[4:6|And the Lord said again|Dixitque Dominus rursum]] to Moses: [[4:6|Put thy hand into thy bosom. And when he had put it into his bosom, he brought it forth leprous as snow|Mitte manum tuam in sinum tuum. Quam quum misisset in sinum, protulit leprosam instar nivis]]: that is, he drew it out so leprous that, through the greatness of the leprosy, it was shining and white as snow. For a whiteness shining on the surface of the skin is a sign of leprosy, as is written in Leviticus[[Lev 13:3||]].

paras.t: Retrahe, ait, manum tuam in sinum tuum: id est, Dominus dixit ad Moysen, ut manum suam rursus in suo poneret sinu. Retraxit, id est, iterum traxit eam in gremium, et protulit iterum, inde retrahendam eamdem: et erat similis carni reliquæ: utpote sanata a lepra, quum tamen lepra, præsertim tam ingens, sit naturaliter incurabilis morbus.
paras.en: [[4:7|And he said: Put back thy hand into thy bosom|Retrahe, ait, manum tuam in sinum tuum]]: that is, the Lord told Moses to put his hand back into his bosom. [[4:7|He put it back|Retraxit]], that is, he drew it again into his lap, [[4:7|and brought it out again|et protulit iterum]], drawing the same hand out from there: [[4:7|and it was like the other flesh|et erat similis carni reliquæ]], being healed of the leprosy, although leprosy, especially so great a leprosy, is by nature an incurable disease.

paras.t: Si non crediderint filii Israel tibi, inquit Dominus, neque audierint sermonem signi prioris: id est, non acquieverint verbis quibus probabas te missum a me, per exhibitionem præfati miraculi, utpote mutationis virgæ in colubrum. In quo tamen signo totali duo continebantur prodigia: unum erat tam repentina conversio virgæ in aspidem; alterum æque repentina conversio serpentis in virgam. Credent verbo signi sequentis, id est assertioni tuæ, qua probabis te missum a me, faciendo hoc signum secundum. In quo itidem duo continebantur miracula: unum, tam supernaturalis inductio lepræ; aliud, tam supernaturalis curatio ejus.
paras.en: [[4:8|If they will not believe|Si non crediderint]] (the children of Israel) [[4:8|thee, saith he|tibi, inquit]] (the Lord), [[4:8|nor hear the voice of the former sign|neque audierint sermonem signi prioris]]: that is, if they do not acquiesce in the words by which thou provedst that thou wast sent by me, by showing the aforesaid miracle, namely the changing of the rod into a serpent. In this one sign, however, two prodigies were contained: one was the sudden turning of the rod into an asp; the other the equally sudden turning of the serpent into the rod. [[4:8|they will believe the word of the latter sign|Credent verbo signi sequentis]], that is, thy assertion, by which thou wilt prove that thou art sent by me, by doing this second sign. In it likewise two miracles were contained: one, the supernatural bringing on of the leprosy; the other, its equally supernatural cure.

paras.t: Quod si nec duobus quidem his signis crediderint. Si Dominus noverat, et vere jam dixerat, eos credituros duobus signis prædictis, cur nunc conditionaliter addit, Quod si nec duobus? Dici potest, quod multi Israelitarum credituri erant illis duobus signis; sed propter quosdam ad credendum duriores, Dominus addidit hæc de tertio signo, vel ex superabundanti hoc fecit, et item propter mysticas rationes infra tangendas, atque ut Moysen plenius consoletur ac roboraret. Neque audierint vocem tuam; sume aquam fluminis, id est, aliquid aquæ hauri ex Nilo, et effunde eam super aridam; et quidquid hauseris de flumine, vertetur in sanguinem. Josephus vero dicit, quod Deo jubente, Moyses sumpsit aquam de proximo sibi loco, et fudit in terram, quæ mox in sanguinem vertebatur, quod fuit grande prodigium. An tamen per magicam artem et diabolicam opem fieri hoc quiverit, infra discutietur in septimi expositione capituli.
paras.en: [[4:9|But if they will not even believe these two signs|Quod si nec duobus quidem his signis crediderint]]. If the Lord knew, and had already truly said, that they would believe the two signs aforesaid, why does he now add conditionally: [[4:9|But if they will not even believe these two|Quod si nec duobus]]? It can be said that many of the Israelites were going to believe those two signs; but because of some who were harder to bring to belief the Lord added these words about a third sign. Or he did it out of superabundance, and also for mystical reasons to be touched on below, and to console and strengthen Moses more fully. [[4:9|nor hear thy voice|Neque audierint vocem tuam]]: [[4:9|take of the river water|sume aquam fluminis]], that is, draw some water from the Nile, [[4:9|and pour it out upon the dry land, and whatsoever thou drawest out of the river, shall be turned into blood|et effunde eam super aridam; et quidquid hauseris de flumine, vertetur in sanguinem]]. Josephus, however, says that at God's command Moses took water from the place nearest him and poured it on the ground, and it was at once turned into blood, which was a great prodigy. Whether this could nonetheless be done by magic art and the devil's help will be discussed below, in the exposition of the seventh chapter.

paras.t: Præterea si quæratur, cur Dominus fecit ac demonstravit, imo et facere jussit Moysi tria hæc signa: ad hoc aliqui dicunt, quod signum factum in virga, correspondet statui Hebræorum, quantum ad eorum introitum in Ægyptum, et quoad mansionem eorum ibidem sub domino Joseph, quod significatur per virgam. Hoc dominium fuit quasi conculcatum in terra, quando post mortem Joseph, tam ejus posteritas quam reliqui filii Israel, compulsi sunt servire Ægyptiis in duris vilibusque operibus: sicque dominium illud fuit quasi versum in colubrum, utpote in serpentinam adversitatem mutatum. Tandem vero educti sunt Hebræi a servitute Ægypti, quod significavit apprehensio serpentis cum cauda; atque ad regiam dignitatem in terra promissionis promoti, quod præfiguravit conversio serpentis in virgam. Porro signum factum in manu Moysis, designavit statum Hebræorum, quo esse cœperunt sub cura ducatuque Moysis: quo tempore eorum calamitas fuit aucta, quia tunc ab Ægyptiis gravius premebantur, quod infectio manus Moysis per lepram signavit. Sed paulo post per manum Moysis sunt educti, quod curatio manus illius monstravit. Tertium autem signum factum in flumine, designavit statum Judæorum in Ægypto, quando eorum infantuli mergebantur in Nilo, quod conversio aquæ in sanguinem prætendebat; quæ etiam innuebat, quod Deus vindicaret sanguinem infantulorum illorum in Ægyptiis per plagas, et submersionem eorum in mari Rubro.
paras.en: Further, if it is asked why the Lord made and showed these three signs to Moses, and indeed commanded him to perform them: to this some say that the sign done with the rod corresponds to the state of the Hebrews as regards their entry into Egypt and their dwelling there under the lordship of Joseph, which is signified by the rod [virga, which also means a sceptre, the sign of rule]. This lordship was as it were trodden into the ground when, after the death of Joseph, both his posterity and the rest of the children of Israel were forced to serve the Egyptians in hard and base works; and so that lordship was as it were turned into a serpent, that is, changed into a serpent-like adversity. But at length the Hebrews were led out of the servitude of Egypt, which the seizing of the serpent by the tail signified; and they were raised to royal dignity in the land of promise, which the turning of the serpent back into the rod prefigured. Next, the sign done in Moses's hand designated the state of the Hebrews when they began to be under the care and leadership of Moses: at that time their calamity was increased, because they were then more heavily oppressed by the Egyptians, which the infection of Moses's hand with leprosy signified. But a little later they were led out by the hand of Moses, which the healing of that hand showed. And the third sign, done in the river, designated the state of the Jews in Egypt when their little ones were drowned in the Nile, which the turning of the water into blood foreshadowed; it also intimated that God would avenge the blood of those little ones on the Egyptians by the plagues and by their drowning in the Red Sea.

paras.t: Ait Moyses: Obsecro, Domine, non sum eloquens ab heri et nudiustertius, id est a tempore evoluto, vel ut quidam exponunt, a pueritia mea, vel nativitatis meæ exordio; et ex quo locutus es ad servum tuum, impeditioris et tardioris linguæ sum. Quasi dicat: Ab hac hora qua mecum loqui cœpisti, aucta est infacundia mea: tum quoniam comparatione eloquentiæ tuæ, mea loquela amplius sordet et deficit: tum quia ex hac apparitione et allocutione divina, ex signis quoque jam visis, multum in me ipso debilitata est mea natura et complexio alterata, et virtus obriguit, ita ut vocem formare vix queam: quemadmodum ex talibus supernaturalibus et insolitis visionibus, allocutionibus et portentis, solet humana debilitari et alterari ac vereri fragilitas: propter quod Prophetæ in talibus corruerunt in terram. Isaias quoque dixit: Corrui, quum viderem. Emarcuit cor meum; tenebræ obstupefecerunt me. Joannes quoque in Apocalypsi: Quum vidissem, inquit, eum, cecidi ad pedes ejus quasi mortuus. Sic et Daniel dixit ad angelum: Quomodo poterit servus tuus loqui cum domino meo? Nihil enim in me remansit virium. Sed et halitus meus intercluditur, et in visione tua dissolutæ sunt compages meæ. Itaque Moyses adhuc a tanto se excusavit officio propter ineloquentiam suam. Qui enim regibus loqui debent, præsertim extranei, et pro arduis causis, indigent voce tubali, quum et remote soleant stare a rege.
paras.en: [[4:10|Moses said: I beseech thee, Lord, I am not eloquent from yesterday and the day before|Ait Moyses: Obsecro, Domine, non sum eloquens ab heri et nudiustertius]], that is, from time past, or, as some explain it, from my boyhood, or from the beginning of my life; [[4:10|and since thou hast spoken to thy servant, I have more impediment and slowness of tongue|et ex quo locutus es ad servum tuum, impeditioris et tardioris linguæ sum]]. As if to say: From this hour in which thou didst begin to speak with me my want of eloquence has grown: both because, compared with thy eloquence, my speech is all the more worthless and falls short; and because, from this divine apparition and address, and from the signs already seen, my nature has been much weakened in me, my bodily constitution altered and my strength numbed, so that I can scarcely form a word. For human frailty is wont to be weakened, shaken and made afraid by such supernatural and unwonted visions, addresses and portents: which is why in such cases the Prophets fell to the ground. Isaias too said: [[Is 21:3|I fell down|Corrui]] [[Is 21:3|at the seeing of it|quum viderem]]. [[Is 21:4|My heart failed, darkness amazed me|Emarcuit cor meum; tenebræ obstupefecerunt me]] [the margin gives Is. xxi, 3; Denis joins words from the beginning and the end of that verse, and the rest is from v. 4]. John too, in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 1:17|when I had seen|Quum vidissem]], he says, [[Apoc 1:17|him, I fell at his feet as dead|eum, cecidi ad pedes ejus quasi mortuus]]. So also Daniel said to the angel: [[Dan 10:17|how can the servant of my lord speak with my lord? for no strength remaineth in me; moreover, my breath is stopped|Quomodo poterit servus tuus loqui cum domino meo? Nihil enim in me remansit virium. Sed et halitus meus intercluditur]], and [[Dan 10:16|at the sight of thee my joints are loosed|in visione tua dissolutæ sunt compages meæ]]. And so Moses still excused himself from so great an office because of his lack of eloquence. For those who have to speak to kings, especially foreigners and in weighty causes, need a voice like a trumpet, since they are also wont to stand at a distance from the king.

paras.t: Circa hæc quæritur, an Moyses habuit impeditam aut balbutientem loquelam. Ad hoc Origenes respondet: Quamdiu Moyses fuit in Ægypto, et erudiebatur omni sapientia Ægyptiorum, non erat gracili voce, nec tardus in lingua, nec profitebatur se esse ineloquentem. Ubi autem cœpit audire vocem Dei, et eloquia divina suscipere, tunc sensit exilem et gracilem esse vocem suam, tardamque et impeditam esse suam intellexit linguam. Tunc pronuntiavit se mutum, quum cœpit agnoscere verum illud Verbum quod erat in principio apud Deum. Quemadmodum homo imperitus et infacundus, comparatione brutorum eloquens esse videtur; si autem eloquentibus atque doctissimis hominibus comparetur, ineloquens et mutus esse videtur. At si quis contempletur Verbum divinum, sapientiamque divinam perspiciat, quantumcumque sit eruditus, multo plus apud Deum se profitebitur animal mutum, quam apud nos sunt pecudes. Huic Origenis opinioni favere videtur, quod S. Stephanus testatur: Eruditus est, inquiens, Moyses omni sapientia Ægyptiorum, et erat potens in verbis et operibus suis. Alii dicunt, quod postquam misit prunam ardentem in os suum, ut recitatum est supra, læsa est extremitas suæ linguæ, et defectum incurrit loquelæ. Cæteri asserunt, quod ex naturali dispositione habuit parvam, tardam, ac gracilem vocem: Aaron vero tubalem ac promptam. Quamvis autem in verbis Origenis quædam vera et subtilia continentur, verumtamen non creditur, quod Moyses absolute loquendo, fuerit eloquens aut incomparabilis eloquentiæ. Sic enim fuisset eloquentior Aaron fratre suo, nec indiguisset ejus ad loquendum auxilio, nec dedisset ei Deus ipsum Aaron ad loquendum pro ipso Moyse ad regem Ægypti ac filios Israel: cujus oppositum infra habetur. Porro verba beatissimi Stephani intelliguntur, quod erat potens et prudens, efficaxque in verbis.
paras.en: Concerning this it is asked whether Moses had an impeded or stammering speech. To this Origen answers: As long as Moses was in Egypt and was being instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, he was not thin of voice nor slow of tongue, nor did he profess himself to be no speaker. But when he began to hear the voice of God and to receive the divine utterances, then he felt his voice to be weak and thin, and understood his tongue to be slow and impeded. He declared himself dumb when he began to know that true Word which [[John 1:2|was in the beginning with God|erat in principio apud Deum]]. Just as an unlearned man without eloquence seems eloquent in comparison with the brute beasts, but if he is compared with eloquent and very learned men seems ineloquent and dumb; so if anyone contemplates the divine Word and looks into the divine wisdom, however learned he may be, he will profess himself a dumb animal before God much more truly than cattle are such beside us. This opinion of Origen seems to be supported by what St. Stephen testifies: [[Acts 7:22|Moses was instructed|Eruditus est]], he says, [[Acts 7:22|in all the wisdom of the Egyptians: and he was mighty in his words and in his deeds|Moyses omni sapientia Ægyptiorum, et erat potens in verbis et operibus suis]]. Others say that after he put a burning coal into his mouth, as was related above, the tip of his tongue was hurt and he incurred a defect of speech. Others again assert that by natural disposition he had a small, slow and thin voice, but Aaron a ready voice like a trumpet. Now although some true and subtle things are contained in Origen's words, yet it is not believed that Moses, absolutely speaking, was eloquent, or of incomparable eloquence. For then he would have been more eloquent than his brother Aaron, and would not have needed his help in speaking, nor would God have given him Aaron to speak for Moses to the king of Egypt and to the children of Israel: the opposite of which is found below. And the words of the most blessed Stephen are to be understood to mean that he was mighty, prudent and effective in words.

paras.t: Dixit Dominus ad eum: Quis fecit os hominis? aut quis fabricatus est surdum et mutum, videntem et cæcum? Nonne ego? Quasi dicat: Ego universorum creator ac dominus, qui omnem rerum naturam, ordinemque institui, et loquelam hominibus præstiti, possum facillime tuum implere defectum, et infacundo eloquentiam dare. Nam et ego instar fabricantis, ex semine humano compegi, formavi, et edidi tam eos qui in naturalibus sunt perfecti, quam eos qui monstruosi seu in naturalibus defectuosi exsistunt, ut surdi, cæci, et muti. Opus quippe causarum naturalium et secundarum, est opus primæ causæ, quæ plus influit quam quæcumque causa secunda. Unde et sanctus Job loquitur Deo: Nonne sicut lac mulsisti me, et sicut caseum me coagulasti? Pelle et carnibus vestisti me: ossibus et nervis compegisti me. Verumtamen monstruositas non habet proprie causam efficientem, sed magis deficientem, loquendo quantum ad causas naturales: nec est intenta, sed contingit per accidens ex indispositione materiæ. Natura vero facit melius id quod potest, ut docet Philosophus. Verum per respectum ad Omnipotentis providentiam, cuncta et singula perfectissime complectentem, nihil est casuale, aut improvisum, aut absque certa et legitima ratione proveniens. Propter quod de cæco a nativitate disserit Christus, quod ideo natus est cæcus, ut manifestarentur in eo opera Dei. Hinc loquitur Augustinus: Quidam Deum veteris Testamenti, et ejus Scripturas seu vetus Testamentum calumniantur, quoniam dixit Deus, quod fecit mutum. Quid ergo dicent de Christo, qui apertissime protestatur, Ego veni ut qui non vident, videant; et qui vident, cæci fiant? Quis autem nisi ignarus, crediderit aliquid secundum corporalia vitia talia posse accidere homini, quod nolit Deus? Sed eum totum juste velle, ambigit nemo. Hæc Augustinus. Itaque surdos, mutos, et cæcos ac similes monstruosos fecit Deus, quantum ad id quod substantialiter et perfectionaliter sunt: quia et corpora eorum, quantum ad materiam primam, creavit, et ea per causas secundas formavit, animasque creando infudit. Monstruositas vero, quæ non est nisi privatio, non aliquid positivum, non sine dispositione divina accidit eis ex rationabilibus causis Deo notis.
paras.en: [[4:11|The Lord said to him: Who made man's mouth? or who made the dumb and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? did not I?|Dixit Dominus ad eum: Quis fecit os hominis? aut quis fabricatus est surdum et mutum, videntem et cæcum? Nonne ego?]] As if to say: I, the creator and lord of all things, who established the whole nature and order of things and gave men speech, can most easily make good thy defect and give eloquence to one who lacks it. For I too, like a craftsman, have put together, formed and brought forth from human seed both those who are whole in their natural powers and those who are misshapen or lacking in their natural powers, as the deaf, the blind and the dumb. For the work of natural and secondary causes is the work of the first cause, which has more influence than any secondary cause whatever. Hence holy Job too says to God: [[Job 10:10|Hast thou not milked me as milk, and curdled me like cheese?|Nonne sicut lac mulsisti me, et sicut caseum me coagulasti?]] [[Job 10:11|Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh: thou hast put me together with bones and sinews|Pelle et carnibus vestisti me: ossibus et nervis compegisti me]]. Yet a deformity has properly no efficient cause, but rather a deficient one [that is, it comes not from a cause that acts but from one that falls short], speaking of natural causes: nor is it intended, but happens accidentally from the unfitness of the matter. For nature does the best it can, as the Philosopher teaches. But with respect to the providence of the Almighty, which embraces each and every thing most perfectly, nothing is by chance or unforeseen, or comes about without a sure and lawful reason. That is why Christ says of the man blind from birth[[John 9:1||]] that he was born blind for this reason, [[John 9:3|that the works of God should be made manifest in him|ut manifestarentur in eo opera Dei]]. Hence Augustine says: Some slander the God of the Old Testament and his Scriptures, that is, the Old Testament, because God said that he made the dumb. What then will they say of Christ, who most openly declares: [[John 9:39|I am come|Ego veni]] [[John 9:39|that they who see not may see; and they who see may become blind|ut qui non vident, videant; et qui vident, cæci fiant?]]? Who but an ignorant man would believe that such bodily defects can befall a man which God does not will? But that he wills it all justly, no one doubts. Thus Augustine. So God made the deaf, the dumb, the blind and others misshapen like them, as regards what they are in their substance and their perfection: for he both created their bodies as regards prime matter and formed them through secondary causes, and infused their souls by creating them. But the deformity, which is nothing but a privation, not something positive, befalls them not without God's disposing, for reasonable causes known to God.

paras.t: Hebræi (ut fertur) aliter hæc exponunt, quia (ut tactum est in expositione capituli secundi) asserunt Moysen captum et Pharaoni adductum, quia occidit Ægyptium, tunc quoque imperterrite respondisse Moysen regi. Itaque sensus esset: Quis fecit os hominis? id est, quis fecit te coram Pharaone respondere constanter in tali articulo? Aut quis fabricatus est surdum et mutum? id est, quis fecit Pharaonem tunc instar surdi mutique stupidum? Videntem et cæcum? id est, quis fecit spiculatorem, cui rex jussit te decollare, sic cæcum per acrisiam, quod te videre nequivit, quum tamen alia cerneret? Sicque evasisti regis manum, ita quod te insequi et revocare nequivit. Quasi dicat: Ego qui mirabilia illa feci in te, possum tibi nunc dare facundiam, et quidquid adjutorii voluero.
paras.en: The Hebrews (it is said) explain these words otherwise. For (as was touched on in the exposition of the second chapter) they assert that Moses was seized and brought before Pharao because he had killed the Egyptian[[Ex 2:11||]][[Ex 2:12||]], and that Moses then answered the king fearlessly. So the sense would be: [[4:11|Who made man's mouth?|Quis fecit os hominis?]] that is, who made thee answer steadfastly before Pharao at such a moment? [[4:11|or who made the dumb and the deaf|Aut quis fabricatus est surdum et mutum?]] that is, who made Pharao stunned at that time like one deaf and dumb? [[4:11|the seeing and the blind?|Videntem et cæcum?]] that is, who made the executioner whom the king ordered to behead thee so blind, by acrisia [a Greek word: a failing of the power to discern], that he could not see thee, though he saw other things? And so thou didst escape the king's hand, so that he could not pursue thee and call thee back. As if to say: I who did those wonders in thee can now give thee eloquence, and whatever help I will.

paras.t: Circa hæc Rabbi Paulus scribit: Non videtur rationabile ut Moyses dubitasset, quod Deus posset supplere defectum suum. Fateor verum hoc esse, nec legi aliquem dicentem hoc. Tamen Rabbi Paulus videtur hoc introducere in reprehensionem Nicolai de Lyra. Præfatis etenim verbis Paulus præmittit: In quarto capitulo ubi dicitur in postilla, Dixit Dominus ad eum. Attamen Lyra non dicit verba illa in sua postilla, sed rationabiliter scribit, quod Dominus protulit verba illa præhabita, Quis fecit os hominis, etc., ad ostendendum, quod posset supplere defectum Moysis allegatum. Ex hoc non sequitur, quod Moyses dubitaverit inde; sed potuit dubitare, an et qualiter vellet Dominus defectum suæ loquelæ supplere. Itaque verba doctorum et expositorum non sunt captiose sumenda, nec reprobanda, quando rationabiliter queunt salvari.
paras.en: On this Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, a converted rabbi, who wrote Additions to Lyra's Postil] writes: It does not seem reasonable that Moses should have doubted that God could make good his defect. I grant that this is true, nor have I read anyone who says the contrary. Yet Rabbi Paul seems to bring this in as a criticism of Nicholas of Lyra; for before the words just quoted Paul sets: In the fourth chapter, where it is said in the Postil, [[4:11|The Lord said to him|Dixit Dominus ad eum]]. Yet Lyra does not say those words in his Postil, but writes reasonably that the Lord spoke the words quoted above, [[4:11|Who made man's mouth|Quis fecit os hominis]], etc., to show that he could make good the defect Moses had alleged. It does not follow from this that Moses doubted it; but he could have doubted whether, and how, the Lord would make good the defect of his speech. So the words of the doctors and expositors are not to be taken captiously, nor rejected, when they can reasonably be saved.

paras.t: Perge igitur, et ego ero in ore tuo, id est, defectum naturæ tuæ supplebo per gratiam; doceboque te quid loquaris. Magna et gratiosa promissio. Sic et Salvator suis promisit discipulis: Ego dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri.
paras.en: [[4:12|Go therefore, and I will be in thy mouth|Perge igitur, et ego ero in ore tuo]], that is, I will make good the defect of thy nature by grace; [[4:12|and I will teach thee what thou shalt speak|doceboque te quid loquaris]]. A great and gracious promise. So too the Saviour promised his disciples: [[Luke 21:15|I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to resist and gainsay|Ego dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri]].

paras.t: At ille, videlicet Moyses: Obsecro, inquit, Domine, mitte quem missurus es. Hoc in Glossa exponitur sic: Humiliter se excusat Moyses, petens aliquem digniorem se mitti. Quidam exponunt de Aaron, ita quod Moyses per verba hæc intendebat orare, ut Deus associaret sibi in adjutorem fratrem suum Aaron, qui senior atque facundior Moyse fuit. Huicque expositioni videntur verba illa consonare sequentia: Iratus Dominus in Moysen, ait: Aaron frater tuus Levites, scio quod eloquens sit. Hanc explanationem sequitur Lyra. Quocirca scribit Rabbi Paulus: Quidam Hebræorum, et specialiter Rabbi Moyses, aliter exponunt hunc passum, dicentes quod Moyses non fuit introducturus populum in terram promissionis, prout in prima revelatione ei facta dictum fuit. Credidit quoque, quod alius fuit a Deo mittendus in redemptionem finalem. Idcirco petebat ut alter illorum mittendorum mitteretur, quorum utrumque digniorem se æstimabat.
paras.en: [[4:13|But he said|At ille]], namely Moses: [[4:13|I beseech thee, Lord, send whom thou wilt send|Obsecro, inquit, Domine, mitte quem missurus es]]. In the Gloss this is explained thus: Moses humbly excuses himself, asking that someone worthier than himself be sent. Some explain it of Aaron, as though by these words Moses meant to pray that God would join to him as a helper his brother Aaron, who was older than Moses and more eloquent. And the words that follow seem to agree with this explanation: [[4:14|The Lord being angry at Moses, said: Aaron the Levite is thy brother, I know that he is eloquent|Iratus Dominus in Moysen, ait: Aaron frater tuus Levites, scio quod eloquens sit]]. Lyra follows this explanation. On this Rabbi Paul writes: Some of the Hebrews, and especially Rabbi Moses, explain this passage otherwise, saying that Moses was not to bring the people into the land of promise, as had been told him in the first revelation made to him. He also believed that another was to be sent by God for the final redemption. Therefore he asked that one of those who were to be sent should be sent, each of whom he reckoned worthier than himself.

paras.t: Circa istud dicendum videtur, quod in prima revelatione Moysi facta, quæ supra descripta est, non continetur in textu, quod Moyses non fuit populum Israel introducturus in terram promissionis, ut patet textum legentibus: imo frequenter locutus est Dominus Moysi, quasi introducturo populum illam in terram, sicut et populo ex Ægypto educto, frequenter denuntiavit per Moysen, quod introduceret eos in terram promissionis. Quod tamen impletum non fuit, quia demeruerunt induci; et promissiones hujusmodi sub conditione intelligendæ fuerunt, videlicet nisi peccando redderent se indignos divinarum adimpletione promissionum. Porro, quod Deus interdum locutus sit Moysi, quod introduceret filios Israel in terram eis promissam, constat ex hoc quod infra Dominus ait ad ipsum: Tu autem vade, et duc populum istum de quo locutus sum tibi. Infra quoque habetur alio loco, quod locutus est Dominus ad Moysen, dicens: Vade, ascende de loco isto tu et populus tuus in terram quam juravi Abraham, Isaac et Jacob. Itemque, Mittam præcursorem tuum angelum, et ejiciam Chananæum et Amorrhæum et Hethæum, et intrabis in terram fluentem lacte et melle. Præterea, quod Moyses non esset introducturus filios Israel in terram promissam, videtur ei tunc primo dictum, quum ad aquas Contradictionis incredulus exstitit Domino, qui tunc dixit ad eum et Aaron: Quia non credidistis mihi, etc., non introducetis hos populos, etc.
paras.en: On this it seems we must say that in the first revelation made to Moses, which was described above[[Ex 3:1||]] [the margin gives Exod. iii and following], it is not contained in the text that Moses was not to bring the people of Israel into the land of promise, as is plain to those who read the text. On the contrary, the Lord often spoke to Moses as to one who would bring the people into that land; just as He often declared through Moses to the people, once they had been led out of Egypt, that He would bring them into the land of promise. Yet this was not fulfilled, because they forfeited by their deserts being brought in; and promises of this kind were to be understood under a condition, namely, unless by sinning they made themselves unworthy of the fulfilment of the divine promises. Further, that God sometimes told Moses that he would bring the children of Israel into the land promised them is clear from what the Lord says to him below: [[Ex 32:34|But go thou, and lead this people whither I have told thee|Tu autem vade, et duc populum istum de quo locutus sum tibi]]. In another place below, too, we read that the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: [[Ex 33:1|Go, get thee up from this place, thou and thy people|Vade, ascende de loco isto tu et populus tuus]] [[Ex 33:1|into the land concerning which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob|in terram quam juravi Abraham, Isaac et Jacob]]. And again: [[Ex 33:2|I will send an angel before thee, that I may cast out the Chanaanite, and the Amorrhite, and the Hethite|Mittam præcursorem tuum angelum, et ejiciam Chananæum et Amorrhæum et Hethæum]], and [[Ex 33:3|thou mayst enter into the land that floweth with milk and honey|intrabis in terram fluentem lacte et melle]]. Moreover, that Moses was not to bring the children of Israel into the promised land seems to have been told him then for the first time, when at the waters of Contradiction he showed himself unbelieving towards the Lord, who then said to him and to Aaron: [[Num 20:12|Because you have not believed me|Quia non credidistis mihi]], etc., [[Num 20:12|you shall not bring these people|non introducetis hos populos]], etc.

paras.t: Attamen verba hæc Moysis, Obsecro, Domine, mitte quem missurus es, secundum quod sonant, videntur satis apte posse exponi de eo, qui fuit ad plenam redemptionem Hebræorum mittendus, ita quod Moyses audiens Deum fari de eductione Israel ex Ægypto, oculum mentis direxit ad liberationem finalem, sive ad Christi missionem. Quemadmodum in Evangelio per istud complexum, Propheta qui venturus est in mundum, intelligitur Christus; ita in veteri Testamento per verba hæc, Veniat qui mittendus est, et, Mitte quem missurus es, Christus solet insinuari. Sed huic expositioni non videtur consonare quod subditur, Iratus Dominus in Moysen. Siquidem propter illam petitionem non fuisset, ut apparet, et iratus: nisi forte dicatur, quod quantum ad hoc, Moyses inordinate oravit, quod voluit fieri pro tunc, quod diu postea fuit agendum: vel quia nimis importune se excusavit, atque pusillanimis aliqualiter fuit in acceptando legationem sibi injunctam, fuitque ejus peccatum veniale.
paras.en: And yet these words of Moses, [[4:13|I beseech thee, Lord, send whom thou wilt send|Obsecro, Domine, mitte quem missurus es]], taken as they sound, seem fittingly enough to be explained of Him who was to be sent for the full redemption of the Hebrews: so that Moses, hearing God speak of leading Israel out of Egypt, directed the eye of his mind to the final deliverance, that is, to the sending of Christ. For as in the Gospel Christ is understood by the phrase [[John 6:14|the prophet that is to come into the world|Propheta qui venturus est in mundum]], so in the Old Testament Christ is usually intimated by these words: [[Gen 49:10|he come that is to be sent|Veniat qui mittendus est]], and [[4:13|send whom thou wilt send|Mitte quem missurus es]]. But what follows does not seem to agree with this explanation: [[4:14|The Lord being angry at Moses|Iratus Dominus in Moysen]]. For on account of such a request He would not, it seems, have been angry; unless perhaps it be said that in this Moses prayed inordinately, in that he wished to be done then what was to be done long afterwards; or that he excused himself too importunately and was somewhat faint-hearted in accepting the embassy laid upon him, and his sin was venial.

paras.t: Ecce ipse Aaron egredietur in occursum tuum: quia (ut infra describitur) ex revelatione divina Aaron exivit ex Ægypto in occursum Moysis fratris sui; vidensque te, lætabitur corde, id est valde intense, tum ex spirituali affectu, et quia pro magnis et prosperis causis sciet te advenisse. Loquere ad eum, et pone verba mea in ore ejus, id est, dic ei quid debeat loqui ex mea commissione. Et ego ero in ore tuo, et in ore illius, id est, linguas vestras dirigam ad loquendum. Nempe ut in Proverbiis legitur: Cor hominis disponit viam suam, sed Domini est gubernare linguam. Propter quod oravit Apostolus: Ut detur mihi sermo in apertione oris mei. Et sancta Esther Dominum exoravit: Da in ore meo sermonem bene sonantem. Et ostendam vobis quid agere debeatis. Ipse loquetur pro te ad populum, et erit os tuum, id est, ex parte tui et juxta tuam informationem loquetur filiis Israel, quæcumque præcepero aut commisero eis. Tu autem eris ei in his quæ ad Deum pertinent, id est, a me per te ipsum accipies divina præcepta ac documenta, quæ docebis et ipsum Aaron.
paras.en: [[4:14|behold he cometh forth to meet thee|Ecce ipse Aaron egredietur in occursum tuum]]: for (as is told below) by divine revelation Aaron went out of Egypt to meet Moses his brother; [[4:14|and seeing thee, shall be glad at heart|vidensque te, lætabitur corde]], that is, very intensely, both from spiritual affection and because he will know that thou hast come for great and happy causes. [[4:15|Speak to him, and put my words in his mouth|Loquere ad eum, et pone verba mea in ore ejus]], that is, tell him what he is to say by my commission. [[4:15|and I will be in thy mouth, and in his month|Et ego ero in ore tuo, et in ore illius]], that is, I will direct your tongues in speaking. For, as we read in the Proverbs: [[Prov 16:9|The heart of man disposeth his way|Cor hominis disponit viam suam]]: but it is [[Prov 16:1|of the Lord to govern the tongue|Domini est gubernare linguam]] [the margin gives Prov. xvi, 9; these last words are from Prov 16:1]. For this reason the Apostle prayed [[Eph 6:19|that speech may be given me|Ut detur mihi sermo]], [[Eph 6:19|that I may open my mouth|in apertione oris mei]]. And holy Esther besought the Lord: [[Esth 14:13|Give me a well ordered speech in my mouth|Da in ore meo sermonem bene sonantem]] [Denis has "a well-sounding speech", where the Vulgate has *sermonem compositum*]. [[4:15|and will shew you what you must do|Et ostendam vobis quid agere debeatis]]. [[4:16|He shall speak in thy stead to the people, and shall be thy mouth|Ipse loquetur pro te ad populum, et erit os tuum]], that is, on thy behalf and according to thy instruction he shall speak to the children of Israel whatever I shall command or commit to them. [[4:16|but thou shalt be to him in those things that pertain to God|Tu autem eris ei in his quæ ad Deum pertinent]], that is, thou shalt receive from me by thyself the divine commands and teachings, which thou shalt teach to Aaron himself too.

paras.t: Virgam quoque hanc pastoralem, quam consuevisti ferre in manibus tuis pro ovium directione, sume in manu tua, id est, tecum porta: et forsitan Moyses habuit eam in manu, quando Dominus protulit verba ista; in qua facturus es signa. Etenim virga illa fuit causa materialis seu materia, in qua factum est istud primum miraculum, puta conversio ejus in serpentem, et rursus serpentis in virgam. Per virgam quoque quasi per instrumentum, facta est conversio aquæ in sanguinem, atque divisio maris Rubri: quia ut infra narratur Deo jubente Moyses percussit fluvium, similiter mare Rubrum cum virga.
paras.en: [[4:17|And take this rod|Virgam quoque hanc]], the shepherd's rod which thou art wont to carry in thy hands to guide the sheep, [[4:17|in thy hand|sume in manu tua]], that is, carry it with thee; and perhaps Moses had it in his hand when the Lord spoke these words; [[4:17|wherewith thou shalt do the signs|in qua facturus es signa]]. For that rod was the material cause, or matter, in which this first miracle was done, namely its turning into a serpent, and again of the serpent into a rod. By the rod too, as by an instrument, the water was turned into blood and the Red Sea divided: for, as is told below, at God's command Moses struck the river[[Ex 7:20||]], and likewise the Red Sea, with the rod[[Ex 14:16||]] [the margin note here cannot be read; the passages are 7:20 and 14:16].

paras.t: Abiit Moyses, id est, completa allocutione et apparitione prælata, disparenteque angelo, recessit Moyses a monte Sinai, et reversus est ad Jethro socerum suum. Forsitan reduxit et oves secum, aut sub aliorum manu pastorum eas reliquit. Forte enim habuit aliquos sibi subjectos pastores in intermediis locis; nam montem Sinai solus accessisse censetur. Dixitque ei: Vadam et revertar ad fratres, id est cognatos et proximos meos in Ægyptum, ut videam si adhuc vivant. Non dubitavit Moyses, quin Aaron et ceteri sibi propinqui adhuc viverent in Ægypto; sed (ut putatur) noluit ex humilitate socero suo revelare, qualiter Dominus ei apparuit, arduamque legationem injunxit: sicut nec Saul, adhuc bonus et humilis, indicavit patri suo Cis, quemadmodum Samuel unxit eum in regem. Ideo Moyses excogitavit aliam causam sui reditus in Ægyptum, quæ tamen exstitit vera, quia ad hoc quoque illuc revertebatur, ut videret an viverent, id est sani et bene dispositi essent.
paras.en: [[4:18|Moses went his way|Abiit Moyses]], that is, when the address and the apparition described above were ended and the angel had vanished, Moses withdrew from Mount Sinai, [[4:18|and returned to Jethro his father in law|et reversus est ad Jethro socerum suum]]. Perhaps he also brought the sheep back with him, or left them in the hands of other shepherds. For perhaps he had some shepherds under him in the places between; since he is thought to have gone up to Mount Sinai alone. [[4:18|and said to him|Dixitque ei]]: [[4:18|I will go and return to my brethren|Vadam et revertar ad fratres]], that is, my kinsmen and neighbours, [[4:18|into Egypt, that I may see if they be yet alive|in Ægyptum, ut videam si adhuc vivant]]. Moses did not doubt that Aaron and his other kin were still living in Egypt; but (as it is thought) out of humility he would not reveal to his father-in-law how the Lord had appeared to him and laid on him a hard embassy: just as Saul, while still good and humble, did not tell his father Cis how Samuel had anointed him king[[1 Kings 10:16||]] [in 1 Kings 10:16 it is Saul's uncle whom he does not tell]. So Moses thought out another reason for his return into Egypt, which was nevertheless a true one, since he was going back there for this too, to see whether they were alive, that is, well and in good case.

paras.t: Cui ait Jethro: Vade in pace pectoris et temporis, ut mente tranquillus sis, nec ab extra turberis. Per quæ verba dedit Jethro licentiam Moysi, ut pergeret in Ægyptum. Nam sine ejus consensu saltem optato, atque licentia saltem petita, noluit Moyses in Ægyptum reverti, præsertim quum esset gener illius, voluitque uxorem et liberos secum deducere. Quod si objiciatur, quia obedire oportet Deo magis quam hominibus, ergo suscepta jussione divina, non debuit ab homine licentiam postulare, præsertim quia et Jacob patriarcha rediit a Mesopotamia ex jussione divina, non petita a Laban licentia: respondetur, quod jussio illa divina non exclusit humilem postulationem licentiæ ab homine superiore. Tamen si Jethro renuisset Moysen licentiare, non ob hoc omisisset divini exsecutionem mandati. Porro Jacob non petiit a Laban licentiam, quia jam vidit illum esse aversum a se, et timuit injurias pati ab ipso: Jethro autem fuit vir magnæ prudentiæ, unde et consensit cito Moysi ut rediret: non quod libenter separabatur ab eo, aut quod modice eum dilexit, sed quia postulatio Moysis rationabilis fuit, nec voluit Jethro propria commoda præferre utilitatibus honestisque causis Moysis generi sui. Denique, quamvis Moyses istam historiam descripsit tam breviter, est tamen probabile, quod ipse et Jethro latius contulerunt de ista materia, tandemque Jethro locutus sit, Vade in pace.
paras.en: [[4:18|And Jethro said to him: Go in peace|Cui ait Jethro: Vade in pace]], peace of heart and of circumstance, that thou mayest be tranquil in mind and not troubled from without. By these words Jethro gave Moses leave to go into Egypt. For Moses would not go back into Egypt without his consent, at least wished for, and his leave, at least asked, above all since he was his son-in-law and wanted to take his wife and children with him. If it be objected that [[Acts 5:29|we ought to obey God rather than men|obedire oportet Deo magis quam hominibus]], and that therefore, having received the divine command, he ought not to have asked leave of a man, all the more because the patriarch Jacob too returned from Mesopotamia by divine command[[Gen 31:3||]] without asking leave of Laban: the answer is that that divine command did not exclude a humble request for leave from a man who was his superior. Yet had Jethro refused Moses leave, he would not on that account have left the divine command unperformed. Jacob, moreover, did not ask leave of Laban[[Gen 31:20||]] because he already saw that he had turned against him, and he feared to suffer wrongs from him; but Jethro was a man of great prudence, and so he quickly consented that Moses should return: not that he parted from him gladly, or loved him little, but because Moses's request was reasonable, and Jethro would not put his own advantage before the interests and honest reasons of Moses his son-in-law. Lastly, though Moses wrote this story down so briefly, it is nevertheless likely that he and Jethro spoke of this matter at greater length, and that at last Jethro said, [[4:18|Go in peace|Vade in pace]].

paras.t: Dixit ergo Dominus ad Moysen in Madian. Quum enim Moyses faceret adhuc aliquantulam moram in terra Madian, locutus est ei Dominus verba sequentia: Vade de terra hac, et revertere in Ægyptum. Mortui sunt enim omnes qui quærebant animam tuam, id est qui te nitebantur occidere, scilicet Pharao, et consensores seu complices ejus. Tulit ergo Moyses uxorem, et filios suos. Quare hoc fecit, quum sciret se non diu moraturum in Ægypto? Dici potest, quod putavit se cum filiis Israel infra breve tempus terram Chanaan ingressurum ad habitandum ibidem. Ideo duxit eos secum, et forte uxor sua desideravit pergere secum, ut moris est feminarum; itemque quoniam mariti et conjugis, ac sobolis eorumdem, debet contubernium esse unum.
paras.en: [[4:19|And the Lord said to Moses, in Madian|Dixit ergo Dominus ad Moysen in Madian]]. For while Moses was still staying a little while in the land of Madian, the Lord spoke to him the following words: [[4:19|Go|Vade]] from this land, [[4:19|and return into Egypt|et revertere in Ægyptum]]; [[4:19|for they are all dead that sought thy life|Mortui sunt enim omnes qui quærebant animam tuam]], that is, who were trying to kill thee, namely Pharao and those who consented with him or were his accomplices. [[4:20|Moses therefore took his wife, and his sons|Tulit ergo Moyses uxorem, et filios suos]]. Why did he do this, when he knew that he would not stay long in Egypt? It may be said that he thought that within a short time he would enter the land of Chanaan with the children of Israel, to dwell there. So he took them with him; and perhaps his wife wished to go with him, as is the way of women; and again, because husband and wife and their offspring ought to share one dwelling.

paras.t: Et imposuit eos super asinum. Circa hoc refert Lyra: Dicunt Hebræi, quod iste est asinus qui portavit ligna quando Abraham perrexit ad Isaac immolandum, quodque super eumdem asinum equitabit Messias in suo adventu, juxta illud Zachariæ, Ecce rex tuus venit tibi, sedens super asinam, etc.; sicque asinus ille tam fortis, super se vehere potuit tantum onus, videlicet matrem cum filiis duobus. Sed assertio ista tam fatua est, ut sit reprobatione indigna. Neque enim naturaliter poterat asinus ille vivere ita diu. Messias quoque jam venit, nec usus est ad equitandum asino illo; nec asinus Abrahæ portando ligna pro combustione corporis Isaac, […] meruerunt, hoc agendo, talem ac tantam vitæ prolongationem. Idcirco, si asinus Moysis ferre non potuit super se onus uxoris duorumque filiorum: dicendum, quod ponitur hic singulare pro plurali, intelligendo nomine asini, asinum […]. Reversusque est in Ægyptum, portans virgam Dei in manu sua.
paras.en: [[4:20|and set them upon an ass|Et imposuit eos super asinum]]. On this Lyra reports: The Hebrews say that this is the ass that carried the wood when Abraham went to sacrifice Isaac, and that the Messias will ride upon the same ass at His coming, according to that saying of Zacharias: [[Zach 9:9|BEHOLD THY KING will come to thee|Ecce rex tuus venit tibi]], [[Zach 9:9|riding upon an ass|sedens super asinam]], etc. [the margin gives Zach. ix, without a verse]; and that so that ass was strong enough to carry so great a load upon itself, namely the mother with two sons. But this assertion is so foolish that it does not deserve refuting. For that ass could not naturally have lived so long. Moreover, the Messias has already come, and did not use that ass to ride on; nor did the ass of Abraham, by carrying the wood for the burning of Isaac's body, […] merit by doing so such and so great a lengthening of life. Therefore, if Moses's ass could not bear upon itself the load of the wife and two sons, it must be said that the singular is put here for the plural, understanding by the word *ass* ass […]. [[4:20|and returned into Egypt, carrying the rod of God in his hand|Reversusque est in Ægyptum, portans virgam Dei in manu sua]].

paras.t: Dixitque ei Dominus, videlicet Moysi, revertenti in Ægyptum: Vide ut omnia ostenta, id est opera miraculosa ostentu dignissima, quæ posui in manu tua, id est, quæ per tuum ministerium perpetrare decrevi, facias coram Pharaone, id est coram ejus præsentia, vel evidenter ita, ut ea percipiat, imo et sentiat. Ego indurabo, id est indurari permittam, cor ejus. Dicitur enim Deus facere quod fieri sinit, præsertim quando oppositum fieri non valet, nec res illa vitari potest, nisi Deo agente. Itaque Deus est causa indurationis et obstinationis, non directe influendo malitiam, aut culpam causando, sed indirecte et quasi per accidens, in quantum justo judicio gratiam subtrahit aut non confert: quemadmodum sol recedendo ab hemisphærio nostro, est causa frigoris et corruptionis: et nauta per suam absentiam, est causa periclitationis navigantium. Etenim Dei solius est, mentem vitiosam ad pœnitentiam emollire, convertere, et salvare. Juxta hunc modum loquendi Psalmista loquitur Deo: Declinasti semitas nostras a via tua. Isaias quoque dicit de Deo: Quare nos errare fecisti a viis tuis, indurasti corda nostra, ne timeremus te? Sed et in Ezechiele Dominus protestatur: Propheta quum erraverit, ego Dominus decepi Prophetam illum. Per quem loquendi modum innuitur, quod sine ope et gratia Dei, nil boni habemus aut possumus. Et non dimittet populum per multas vices. Tandem vero plagis, terroribusque devictus, fecit populum egredi festinanter.
paras.en: [[4:21|And the Lord said to him|Dixitque ei Dominus]], namely to Moses, [[4:21|as he was returning into Egypt|revertenti in Ægyptum]]: [[4:21|See that thou do all the wonders|Vide ut omnia ostenta]], that is, miraculous works most worthy to be displayed [Latin *ostenta*, literally "things for showing"], [[4:21|which I have put in thy hand|quæ posui in manu tua]], that is, which I have decreed to accomplish through thy ministry, [[4:21|before Pharao|facias coram Pharaone]], that is, in his presence, or so plainly that he perceives them, nay, even feels them. [[4:21|I shall harden|Ego indurabo]], that is, I shall permit to be hardened, [[4:21|his heart|cor ejus]]. For God is said to do what He allows to be done, above all when the opposite cannot come about and the thing cannot be avoided except by God's acting. So God is the cause of hardening and obstinacy, not directly, by pouring in malice or causing guilt, but indirectly and as it were accidentally, inasmuch as by a just judgement He withdraws grace or does not bestow it: as the sun, by withdrawing from our hemisphere, is the cause of cold and decay, and a pilot by his absence is the cause of the peril of those at sea. For it belongs to God alone to soften a vicious mind to penance, to convert it and to save it. In this manner of speaking the Psalmist says to God: [[Ps 43:19|hast thou turned aside our steps from thy way|Declinasti semitas nostras a via tua]] [the Douay-Rheims reads this verse as a denial, "neither hast thou turned aside…"; Denis takes it, as the Latin allows, as "thou hast turned aside our steps"]. Isaias too says of God: [[Is 63:17|Why hast thou made us to err|Quare nos errare fecisti]] [[Is 63:17|from thy ways|a viis tuis]], [[Is 63:17|why hast thou hardened our heart, that we should not fear thee?|indurasti corda nostra, ne timeremus te?]] And in Ezechiel the Lord declares: [[Ezech 14:9|when the prophet shall err|Propheta quum erraverit]], [[Ezech 14:9|I the Lord have deceived that prophet|ego Dominus decepi Prophetam illum]].
