By this manner of speaking it is intimated that without God's help and grace we have and can do nothing good. [[4:21|and he will not let the people go|Et non dimittet populum]], many times over. But at last, overcome by plagues and terrors, he made the people go out in haste[[Ex 12:31||]].

paras.t: Dicesque ad eum, scilicet Pharaonem: Hæc dicit Dominus: Filius meus primogenitus, Israel. Hic loquitur Deus de toto populo Hebræorum, quasi de homine uno, ut sit sensus: Israeliticus populus carior mihi est ceteris gentibus, et majora beneficia ei impendo: quemadmodum parentes filios multos habentes, primogenitum communiter plus amant et ditant. Sic in Jeremia Dominus ait: Ephraim primogenitus meus. Porro in Glossa habetur: Filius meus primogenitus Israel, quia in Patriarchis primus electus est ad cultum unius Dei: hoc est, idcirco populus Hebræorum primogenitus meus est, quoniam ceteris ad idololatriam declinantibus, patres eorum primi vocati sunt ad cultum unius Dei. Ideo quoque populus ille primogenitus Dei vocatur, quia ex eo incarnatus ac natus est Unigenitus Patris, primogenitus omnis creaturæ, ut ad Romanos docetur.
paras.en: [[4:22|And thou shalt say to him|Dicesque ad eum]], namely to Pharao: [[4:22|Thus saith the Lord: Israel is my son, my firstborn|Hæc dicit Dominus: Filius meus primogenitus, Israel]]. Here God speaks of the whole Hebrew people as of one man, so that the sense is: The people of Israel is dearer to me than the other nations, and I bestow greater benefits on it; as parents who have many sons commonly love their firstborn more and enrich him more. So in Jeremias the Lord says: [[Jer 31:9|Ephraim is my firstborn|Ephraim primogenitus meus]] [the margin note here cannot be read; the passage is Jer 31:9]. Further, in the Gloss we have: [[4:22|Israel is my son, my firstborn|Filius meus primogenitus Israel]], because in the Patriarchs he was the first chosen for the worship of the one God: that is, the Hebrew people is my firstborn for this reason, that while the rest turned aside to idolatry, their fathers were the first called to the worship of the one God. That people is also called God's firstborn for this reason, that from it was made flesh and born the Only-begotten of the Father, [[Col 1:15|the firstborn of every creature|primogenitus omnis creaturæ]], as is taught in Romans[[Rom 8:29||]] [the margin gives Rom. viii, 29, and Col. i, 15; the words are those of Colossians].

paras.t: Dixi tibi, id est, tibi, o Pharao, per Moysen jussi: Dimitte filium meum, id est, populum Hebræorum mihi instar filii carum permitte egredi de Ægypto, ut serviat mihi servitute latriæ, et sacrificet in deserto: et noluisti dimittere eum. Ecce ego interficiam filium tuum primogenitum. Qualiter hoc sit impletum, infra describitur. In ultima etenim plaga, primogenita Ægyptiorum sunt occisa, a primogenito Pharaonis, etc. Porro ultima illa plaga fuit principalis et gravior ceteris, ideo tanquam præcipuam prænuntiari eam Pharaoni Dominus Deus jussit. Et quamvis infra non legatur in textu, quando aut ubi Moyses dixerit hæc verba Pharaoni, tamen quia hic scribitur Dominum istud Moysi commisisse, credendum est quod ita explevit.
paras.en: [[4:23|I have said to thee|Dixi tibi]], that is, to thee, O Pharao, I have commanded through Moses: [[4:23|Let my son go|Dimitte filium meum]], that is, let the Hebrew people, dear to me as a son, go out of Egypt, [[4:23|that he may serve me|ut serviat mihi]] with the service of latria [that is, the worship due to God alone], and sacrifice in the desert: [[4:23|and thou wouldst not let him go|et noluisti dimittere eum]]. [[4:23|behold I will kill thy son, thy firstborn|Ecce ego interficiam filium tuum primogenitum]]. How this was fulfilled is told below. For in the last plague the firstborn of the Egyptians were slain, from the firstborn of Pharao, etc. Now that last plague was the chief one and heavier than the others; therefore the Lord God commanded that it be foretold to Pharao as the principal one. And though we do not read in the text below when or where Moses said these words to Pharao, yet since it is written here that the Lord entrusted this to Moses, we must believe that he carried it out.

paras.t: Quumque esset in itinere in diversorio, id est in hospitio ad quod divertit, ad Ægyptum pergendo: unde Septuaginta transtulerunt, Et factum est in via ad refectionem; occurrit ei Dominus, et volebat occidere eum. Secundum Augustinum, istud potest exponi tam de Moyse, eo quod unum filiorum suorum dimisit incircumcisum contra præceptum Domini in Genesi scriptum, ubi dicitur, Infans octo dierum circumcidetur; quam de filio illo incircumciso, ut per hoc insinuaretur, quam districte servanda sint Dei præcepta. Verumtamen ex circumstantia litteræ videtur istud de Moyse intelligendum, non de ejus filio, qui secundum Augustinum tunc fuit infantulus: propter quod non apparet, quod puero illi nondum adulto Deus imputasset ad culpam personalem pœna sensibili puniendam, quod circumcisus non fuit.
paras.en: [[4:24|And when he was in his journey, in the inn|Quumque esset in itinere in diversorio]], that is, in the lodging to which he turned aside on his way to Egypt; whence the Septuagint translated: And it came to pass on the way, at the resting place; [[4:24|the Lord met him, and would have killed him|occurrit ei Dominus, et volebat occidere eum]]. According to Augustine this can be explained both of Moses, because he had left one of his sons uncircumcised against the Lord's precept written in Genesis, where it is said, [[Gen 17:12|An infant of eight days old shall be circumcised|Infans octo dierum circumcidetur]], and of that uncircumcised son, so that it might be intimated by this how strictly God's precepts are to be kept. Yet from the circumstances of the letter it seems this is to be understood of Moses, not of his son, who according to Augustine was then a little infant: for which reason it does not seem that God would have imputed to that child, not yet grown, as a personal fault to be punished with a sensible penalty, that he had not been circumcised.

paras.t: Tulit illico Sephora acutissimam petram, et circumcidit præputium filii sui. Per hæc verba innuitur, quod Sephora cognovit, cur angelus Moysi in forma visibili humana occurrens, voluerit eum occidere: quod vel ex revelatione angeli, vel ex Moysis informatione cognovit. Idcirco, ne suus occideretur maritus, circumcidit mox filium suum. Vel, quum esset gentilis, more gentilium putavit, angelum effusione sanguinis posse placari. Ex quibus putatur, quod femina illa gentilis voluit unum filiorum suorum tenere in ritu gentilitatis suæ. Alterum vero juxta legem divinam Moyses circumcidit. Fuit quoque culpabilis, quod quum esset caput mulieris, permisit eam tenere in suo ritu unum ex pueris illis.
paras.en: [[4:25|Immediately Sephora took a very sharp stone|Tulit illico Sephora acutissimam petram]], [[4:25|and circumcised the foreskin of her son|et circumcidit præputium filii sui]]. By these words it is intimated that Sephora knew why the angel, meeting Moses in a visible human form, wished to kill him: which she knew either by the angel's revelation or from Moses's telling her. Therefore, lest her husband be killed, she at once circumcised her son. Or, since she was a gentile, she thought after the manner of the gentiles that the angel could be appeased by the shedding of blood. From this it is thought that that gentile woman wished to keep one of her sons in the rite of her own heathenism; the other Moses had circumcised according to the divine law. And he too was blameworthy, in that, being the head of the woman, he allowed her to keep one of those boys in her own rite.

paras.t: Tetigitque pedes ejus, id est, sanguis de parte corporis circumcisi emanans, cecidit super pedes pueri circumcisi vel matris ejus, aut etiam Moysis, cui mater puerum circumcisum forsitan præsentavit ad intuendam læsionem infantuli. Vel, ut aliqui putant, quia ad pedes Moysis projecit abscisum filii sui præputium, cui sensui videtur consonare quod subditur: Et ait Sephora: Sponsus sanguinum tu mihi es. Quasi dicat: An ideo te sumpsi in sponsum, aut idcirco videor te in sponsum sumpsisse, ut propter te et ritum tuum, aut propter liberationem tuam de manu angeli comminantis, effunderem sanguinem filii mei? Et ita Sephora protulit hæc quasi indignans suo marito, quia multum condoluit puero circumciso; atque (ut in Scholastica historia tangitur) reputavit scelus esse, sic proprii filii sanguinem fundere. Sed mirum si indignabatur, aut illud esse peccatum arbitrabatur, quum angelum Dei visibiliter coram se cerneret. Hinc in Glossa insinuatur: Sanguis tetigit pedes angeli, cui Sephora fortassis ostendit puerum circumcisum, ut placaretur. Deinde angelo quasi blandiens, dixit: Sponsus sanguinum tu mihi es, id est, sicut Moysi carnaliter nupsi, ita nunc quodammodo tibi effusione sanguinis filii mei.
paras.en: [[4:25|and touched his feet|Tetigitque pedes ejus]], that is, the blood flowing from the circumcised part of the body fell upon the feet of the circumcised boy, or of his mother, or even of Moses, to whom the mother perhaps presented the circumcised boy for him to look at the little one's wound. Or, as some think, because she threw her son's severed foreskin at Moses's feet; and what follows seems to agree with this sense: [[4:25|and said|Et ait]] Sephora: [[4:25|A bloody spouse art thou to me|Sponsus sanguinum tu mihi es]]. As if to say: Did I take thee as my spouse for this, or do I seem to have taken thee as spouse for this, that for thy sake and thy rite, or for thy deliverance from the hand of the threatening angel, I should shed the blood of my son? And so Sephora said these words as though indignant with her husband, because she grieved much for the circumcised boy; and (as the Scholastic History touches on) she counted it a crime thus to shed the blood of her own son. But it would be strange if she was indignant, or thought it a sin, when she saw the angel of God visibly before her. Hence the Gloss intimates: The blood touched the feet of the angel, to whom Sephora perhaps showed the circumcised boy, that he might be appeased. Then, as though coaxing the angel, she said: [[4:25|A bloody spouse art thou to me|Sponsus sanguinum tu mihi es]]; that is, as I was wedded to Moses in the flesh, so now in a manner to thee by the shedding of my son's blood.

paras.t: Et dimisit eum, postquam dixerat ei, Sponsus sanguinum tu mihi es, ob circumcisionem. Totus hic passus sua brevitate valde obscurus est, ut etiam asserit Augustinus. Unde et clausula ista, juxta præhabita multipliciter explanatur. Magister namque in historia sic exponit: Angelus dimisit Moysen. Unde Hebræus habet: Relaxavit eum angelus, quem (scilicet Moysen) prius usque ad mortem arctavit. In Glossa exponitur sic: Sephora irata et indignans ex causa prætacta, dimisit Moysen, rediens ad Jethro suum parentem cum puero circumciso. Quidam tamen dicunt, quod dimisit puerum circumcisum: quod non videtur, quoniam infra fertur, quod Jethro venit ad Moysen in desertum, adducens secum uxorem et filios ejus. Ideo magis apparet, quod Sephora cum ambobus filiis suis et asino ad proprium rediit patrem: quod etiam creditur Moysi placuisse. Imo, ut tetigit Augustinus, aliqui putaverunt angelum propter hoc Moysen terruisse, ne ad impedimentum ministerii sibi impositi, duceret secum uxorem atque puerulos. Verumtamen Rabbi Paulus objicit præinductis, videlicet quod uxor Moysis non dimisit Moysen, præsertim quasi indignans: nam infra habetur præallegato loco, quod Jethro tulit uxorem Moysis quam remiserat. Ex quo apparet, quod uxor non dimisit Moysen, sed econtra. Ad quod ex dictis patet solutio. Siquidem potuit esse, quod quamvis mulier ex causa præhabita fuit indignans, tamen Moyses vir mitissimus eam placavit, reditumque persuasit, propter quod eam scribitur remisisse.
paras.en: [[4:26|And he let him go after she had said: A bloody spouse art thou to me, because of the circumcision.|Et dimisit eum, postquam dixerat ei, Sponsus sanguinum tu mihi es, ob circumcisionem]] This whole passage is very obscure from its brevity, as Augustine too declares. Hence this clause also is explained in many ways, according to what has gone before. For the Master in the History explains it thus: The angel let Moses go. Whence the Hebrew has: The angel released him, whom (namely Moses) he had before pressed hard even to death. In the Gloss it is explained thus: Sephora, angry and indignant for the reason touched on above, left Moses, going back to Jethro her father with the circumcised boy. Some, however, say that she let go the circumcised boy: which does not seem right, since it is related below that Jethro came to Moses into the desert, bringing with him his wife and sons[[Ex 18:5||]]. So it rather appears that Sephora went back to her own father with both her sons and the ass; and this too is believed to have pleased Moses. Indeed, as Augustine touches on, some have thought that the angel frightened Moses for this reason, that he should not take his wife and little boys with him to the hindrance of the ministry laid upon him. Rabbi Paul, however, objects to what has been brought forward, namely that Moses's wife did not leave Moses, least of all as if indignant: for in the place cited below we find that Jethro took the wife of Moses [[Ex 18:2|whom he had sent back|quam remiserat]]. From which it appears that the wife did not leave Moses, but the contrary. The answer to this is plain from what has been said. For it may be that, although the woman was indignant for the reason given, yet Moses, a most mild man, calmed her and persuaded her to go back; for which reason he is written to have sent her back.

paras.t: Circa hæc in Scholastica recitatur historia: Hinc aliqui dicunt morem circumcidendi petrinis cultellis habuisse principium, vel a Josue in Galgalis. Tamen ubi nos habemus, petram, Hebræus habet aciem; et acutissimam aciem vocat novaculam. Unde et Judæi novaculis circumcidunt. Fabulantur tamen quidam Hebræi, usque ad David circumcisionem factam cum petra; sed quia in dejiciendo Goliath, ferrum loricæ et galeæ cessit lapidi jacto, quasi dans ei locum, deinceps lapis cessit ferro in circumcisione. Hæc ibi. Lyra quoque testatur, pro Acutissima petra, apud Hebræos dici aciem sive novaculam.
paras.en: On these things the Scholastic History relates: Hence some say that the custom of circumcising with knives of stone had its beginning, or else from Josue in Galgal[[Jos 5:2||]]. Yet where we have *stone*, the Hebrew has *edge*, and by "a very sharp edge" it means a razor. And so the Jews circumcise with razors. Some Hebrews, however, tell the fable that circumcision was done with a stone until David; but because in the felling of Goliath the iron of the coat of mail and of the helmet gave way to the stone that was thrown, as it were yielding place to it, thenceforth the stone yielded to iron in circumcision[[1 Kings 17:49||]] [the margin gives 1 Kings xvii and following]. So far the History. Lyra too testifies that for [[4:25|a very sharp stone|Acutissima petra]] the Hebrews say *edge*, or *razor*.

paras.t: Dixit autem Dominus ad Aaron. Probabile est, quod per angelum sensibiliter apparentem locutus sit ista Deus ad Aaron in Ægypto, et forte idem angelus qui apparuit Moysi, ejus quoque fratri apparuit, vel per inspirationem et visionem in somno locutus est Dominus ista ad Aaron. Hinc primo Regum ait Dominus Heli de Aaron descendenti: Numquid non aperte revelatus sum domui patris tui, quum essent in Ægypto? Vade in occursum Moysi in desertum. Qui perrexit obviam ei in montem Dei: perrexit enim tamdiu, donec reperit Moysen, invenitque eum in monte Sinai; […] et osculatus est eum, etc.
paras.en: [[4:27|And the Lord said to Aaron|Dixit autem Dominus ad Aaron]]. It is likely that God said this to Aaron in Egypt through an angel appearing to the senses, and perhaps the same angel who appeared to Moses appeared to his brother too; or else the Lord said this to Aaron by inspiration and a vision in sleep. Hence in the first book of Kings the Lord says to Heli, a descendant of Aaron: [[1 Kings 2:27|Did I not plainly appear to thy father's house, when they were in Egypt|Numquid non aperte revelatus sum domui patris tui, quum essent in Ægypto?]]? [[4:27|Go into the desert to meet Moses|Vade in occursum Moysi in desertum]]. [[4:27|And he went forth to meet him in the mountain of God|Qui perrexit obviam ei in montem Dei]]: for he went on until he found Moses, and he found him on Mount Sinai; […] [[4:27|and kissed him|et osculatus est eum]], etc.

paras.t: Veneruntque simul, et congregaverunt cunctos seniores filiorum Israel: quos primo collegerunt tanquam prudentiores, quatenus eis rationabiliter informatis atque credentibus, ceteri Israelitæ facilius crederent ac parerent.
paras.en: [[4:29|And they came together, and they assembled all the ancients of the children of Israel|Veneruntque simul, et congregaverunt cunctos seniores filiorum Israel]]: these they gathered first as being the more prudent, so that once they had been reasonably instructed and believed, the other Israelites might the more readily believe and obey.

paras.t: Locutusque est Aaron omnia verba quæ dixerat Dominus ad Moysen; et fecit signa coram populo. Ex his videtur, quod Moyses per se ipsum exposuit senioribus suam legationem: quibus credentibus, convocaverunt Moyses et Aaron et seniores plebem communem totam, vel potius pro magna parte: quibus collectis, exposuit ipse Aaron, tanquam magis tubalis in voce et eloquens, universa quæ Deus præcepit Moysi dicere illis. Porro, quod dictum est, Et fecit signa coram populo, melius intelligitur de Moyse quam de Aaron. Moyses etenim non per Aaron, sed per se, Deo agente, exhibuit signa hæc; Aaron vero ea non fecit, nisi aliquo modo dispositive, et excitans Moysen ad signa agenda. Signa autem quæ fecit, fuerunt conversio virgæ in colubrum, atque conversio colubri in virgam; infectioque manus Moysis per lepram, et ejusdem curatio. Seniores demum crediderunt Moysi, ante ostensionem signorum istorum, ut in expositione tertii capituli patuit, et aliqui tenent. Josephus tamen sentit, quod non crediderunt Moysi, nisi signis ab eo coram ipsis peractis. Vulgus vero credidit visis signis. Ideo subditur: Et credidit populus. Audieruntque, tam illi qui ibi fuerunt, quam ceteri Hebræi hinc inde dispersi, quod visitasset Dominus filios Israel, utpote eos. Nam loquitur hæc scriptura de eisdem, quasi de aliis. Visitavit autem Dominus eos, mittendo Moysen ad liberationem eorum, et faciendo signa præfata in testimonium veritatis. Et quod respexisset afflictionem illorum: et proni adoraverunt, hoc est, prostrati gratias Deo egerunt, exorantes eumdem, ut sua promissa impleret in eis.
paras.en: [[4:30|And Aaron spoke all the words which the Lord had said to Moses|Locutusque est Aaron omnia verba quæ dixerat Dominus ad Moysen]]: [[4:30|and he wrought the signs before the people|et fecit signa coram populo]]. From this it seems that Moses himself set out his embassy to the elders; and when they believed, Moses and Aaron and the elders called together the whole common people, or rather the greater part of them; and when these were gathered, Aaron himself, as having the more trumpet-like voice and being eloquent, set out to them all that God had commanded Moses to tell them. Further, what is said, [[4:30|and he wrought the signs before the people|Et fecit signa coram populo]], is better understood of Moses than of Aaron. For Moses showed these signs not through Aaron but by himself, God working; while Aaron did them only in some preparatory way, and by stirring Moses to do the signs. And the signs that he did were the turning of the rod into a serpent and of the serpent into the rod, and the striking of Moses's hand with leprosy and its healing. The elders, for their part, believed Moses before these signs were shown, as was made plain in the exposition of the third chapter[[Ex 3:16||]][[Ex 3:18||]] [the margin gives Exod. iii, 16–18], and as some hold. Josephus, however, thinks that they did not believe Moses until he had done the signs before them. But the common people believed when they had seen the signs. Therefore it is added: [[4:31|And the people believed|Et credidit populus]]. [[4:31|And they heard|Audieruntque]], both those who were there and the other Hebrews scattered here and there, [[4:31|that the Lord had visited the children of Israel|quod visitasset Dominus filios Israel]], that is, them; for this Scripture speaks of them as though of others. And the Lord visited them by sending Moses to deliver them, and by doing the signs mentioned in witness of the truth. [[4:31|and that he had looked upon their affliction|Et quod respexisset afflictionem illorum]]: [[4:31|and falling down they adored|et proni adoraverunt]], that is, prostrate, they gave thanks to God, beseeching Him to fulfil His promises in them.

4.title: Spiritualis explanatio ejusdem capituli quarti
4.title_en: Spiritual explanation of the same fourth chapter

paras.t: Per hoc quod dixit Moyses ad Dominum, Non credent mihi, sed dicent, Non apparuit tibi Dominus: præfiguratum est, quod gentilitas non credidit evangelicæ prædicationi, nisi per signa, miracula, portentaque maxima.
paras.en: By Moses' saying to the Lord, [[4:1|They will not believe me|Non credent mihi]], [[4:1|but they will say: The Lord hath not appeared to thee|sed dicent, Non apparuit tibi Dominus]], it was prefigured that the Gentiles would not believe the preaching of the Gospel except through signs, miracles and the greatest portents.

paras.t: Porro, per hoc quod Moyses virgam suam, Deo jubente, projecit in terram, et in colubrum est conversa, signatur, quod Christus suam judiciariam potestatem humiliavit usque ad infima, in tantum, quod ipse omnium judex ac dominus, dignatus est ab hominibus impiis, tanquam a colubris, judicari ac condemnari. Sed virga hæc ad pristinam redit suæ celsitudinis speciem, quando post passionem suam glorificatus est Christus, ita quod dixit, Data est mihi omnis potestas in cælo et in terra: quod per apprehensionem caudæ serpentis est præmonstratum. Hinc in Actibus princeps ait Apostolorum: Præcepit nobis Deus testificari, quia Christus constitutus est judex vivorum et mortuorum. Per fugam demum Moysis a facie colubri, intelligi potest fuga Apostolorum, quando captus et apprehensus est Jesus ut judicaretur.
paras.en: Further, by Moses' casting his rod upon the ground at God's command, and its being turned into a serpent, it is signified that Christ humbled his judiciary power down to the lowest things, so far that he, the judge and lord of all, deigned to be judged and condemned by wicked men, as by serpents. But this rod returns to the former appearance of its loftiness when Christ, after his passion, was glorified, so that he said: [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|Data est mihi omnis potestas in cælo et in terra]]: and this was shown beforehand by the taking hold of the serpent's tail. Hence the prince of the Apostles says in the Acts: God [[Acts 10:42|commanded us|Præcepit nobis]] [[Acts 10:42|to testify|testificari]] that Christ [[Acts 10:42|was appointed by God to be judge of the living and of the dead|constitutus est judex vivorum et mortuorum]] [the margin gives Acts v, 32; the words are those of Acts 10:42]. Lastly, by Moses' flight from the face of the serpent can be understood the flight of the Apostles[[Mark 14:50||]] [the margin's numbers are lost (Marc. …); Mark 14:50, where the disciples all fled, fits], when Jesus was taken and seized to be judged.

paras.t: Insuper, per manum Moysis factam leprosam, quum missa fuisset in sinum ipsius, significatum est, quod Christi humanitas tempore passionis instar leprosi apparuit, juxta quod ab Isaia fuit prædictum: Reputavimus eum quasi leprosum, et percussum a Deo, et humiliatum. Moyses quippe figura est Christi. Sicque manus Moysis humanam Christi designat naturam, quæ fuit quasi manus et instrumentum suæ divinitatis. Per missionem vero manus Moysis in sinum ipsius, exprimitur mysterium humanitatis, quo factum est, ut per passionis acerbitatem et ignominiam videretur quasi lepra perfusa. Per hoc autem quod Moyses manum suam retraxit, et retractam reperit sanam: notatur, quod Christo resurgente a mortuis, quando corpus suum a sepulcro, animamque a limbo retraxit, humanitas ejus ad pristinam, imo ad multo majorem rediit venustatem, secundum quod ipse passione instante oravit: Et nunc clarifica me tu, Pater, apud temetipsum. Et: Pater, clarifica ea filium tuum.
paras.en: Moreover, by the hand of Moses being made leprous when it had been put into his bosom, it was signified that the humanity of Christ in the time of his passion appeared like a leper, according to what was foretold by Isaias: [[Is 53:4|we have thought him as it were a leper, and as one struck by God and afflicted|Reputavimus eum quasi leprosum, et percussum a Deo, et humiliatum]]. For Moses is a figure of Christ. And so the hand of Moses designates the human nature of Christ, which was as it were the hand and instrument of his Godhead. By the putting of Moses' hand into his bosom is expressed the mystery of the humanity, whereby it came about that through the bitterness and ignominy of the passion it seemed as if overspread with leprosy. But by Moses' drawing back his hand and finding it whole when drawn back, it is noted that when Christ rose from the dead, when he drew back his body from the tomb and his soul from limbo, his humanity returned to its former beauty, nay, to a far greater one, according to what he himself prayed as his passion drew near: [[John 17:5|And now glorify thou me, O Father, with thyself|Et nunc clarifica me tu, Pater, apud temetipsum]]. And: Father, [[John 17:1|Glorify thy Son|clarifica ea filium tuum]].

paras.t: Amplius, per aquam, populi designantur; per conversionem aquæ in sanguinem, conversio infidelium ad fidem incarnationis passionisque Christi: ita quod quidquid Moyses hausit de fluvio, in sanguinem vertebatur, hoc est, quidquid Salvator de populo tumultuantium sæcularium hominum elegit, et sibi assumpsit, ad fidem crucis et sanguinis ejus exstat conversum.
paras.en: Further, by the water peoples are designated; by the turning of the water into blood, the conversion of unbelievers to faith in the incarnation and passion of Christ: so that whatever Moses drew from the river was turned into blood; that is, whatever the Saviour chose out of the people of tumultuous worldly men, and took to himself, stands converted to faith in his cross and blood.

paras.t: Per ineloquentiam Moysis, accipi potest simplicitas stili evangelicæ legis. Eos autem qui infacundi sunt, et spiritualiter muti, surdi ac cæci, Christus per gratiam Spiritus Sancti facit facundos ad eloquendum verba Dei, atque paratos ad audiendum quidquid pertinet ad salutem. Sed et visum eorum internum clarificat ad contemplandum.
paras.en: By Moses' lack of eloquence can be understood the simplicity of style of the law of the Gospel. But those who are without eloquence, and spiritually dumb, deaf and blind, Christ by the grace of the Holy Ghost makes eloquent to speak forth the words of God, and ready to hear whatever pertains to salvation. He also clears their inward sight for contemplation.

paras.t: Per Aaron vero facundum, signatur chorus Apostolorum, quem Spiritus Sanctus eloquentissimum fecit, et eumdem Christo in adjutorium prædicationis concessit. Qui chorus Apostolorum occurrit Christo in monte, hoc est in sublimitate virtutum, et in exordio primitivæ Ecclesiæ. Posuitque Christus verba Dei in ore ipsorum, qui ex parte Christi prædicaverunt primo Judæis, deinde gentilibus, atque per signa eis collata, converterunt ex utrisque millia multa.
paras.en: By the eloquent Aaron is signified the company of the Apostles, which the Holy Ghost made most eloquent, and granted to Christ as a help in preaching. This company of the Apostles met Christ in the mountain, that is, in the height of the virtues, and at the beginning of the primitive Church. And Christ put the words of God in their mouth; and on Christ's behalf they preached first to the Jews, then to the Gentiles, and through the signs bestowed on them they converted many thousands from both.

paras.t: Quemadmodum etiam Moyses rediit ad Jethro suum cognatum, antequam descendit in Ægyptum: sic Christus antequam per Apostolos prædicavit evangelium suum gentilibus, prædicavit illud per se ipsum Judæis, suis secundum carnem cognatis. Quumque gentiles cognovissent se visitari a Deo per ejus Apostolos, gavisi sunt valde, et proni adoraverunt, sicut in Actibus Apostolorum copiose docetur.
paras.en: And just as Moses returned to Jethro his kinsman [Denis says cognatum, "kinsman", where the text has socerum, "father-in-law", to fit the comparison with Christ's kinsmen] before he went down into Egypt, so Christ, before he preached his gospel to the Gentiles through the Apostles, preached it himself to the Jews, his kinsmen according to the flesh. And when the Gentiles knew that they were visited by God through his Apostles, they rejoiced greatly, and [[4:31|falling down they adored|proni adoraverunt]], as is copiously taught in the Acts of the Apostles.

paras.t: Postremo, quid per Sephoram Moysis conjugem, ejusque filios designetur, præhabitum est.
paras.en: Lastly, what is designated by Sephora, the wife of Moses, and by her sons has been set out already.

5.title: Elucidatio litteralis capituli quinti: Post hæc ingressi sunt Moyses et Aaron
5.title_en: Literal explanation of the fifth chapter: “After these things, Moses and Aaron went in”

paras.t: NUNC describitur, qualiter Moyses executus sit legationem sibi commissam quantum ad regem Ægypti. Post hæc ingressi sunt Moyses et Aaron palatium regis, et dixerunt Pharaoni. Aaron autem fuit dux verbi, et Moyses introivit ut principalis. Porro supra Dominus dixit ad Moysen : Ingredieris tu et seniores Israel ad regem Ægypti : idcirco credendum videtur, quod hac vice seniores Israel intraverunt cum Moyse et Aaron ad Pharaonem, nec ex humano timore hoc dimiserunt, ut dicunt Judæi. Moyses tamen et Aaron, tanquam principales præ illis, nunc exprimuntur. Et dixerunt Pharaoni : Hæc dicit Dominus Deus Israel : Dimitte populum meum, ut sacrificet mihi in deserto. At ille respondit : Quis est Dominus, ut audiam vocem ejus, et dimittam Israel ? id est, qualis aut quantæ auctoritatis est Dominus Deus vester, de quo mihi loquimini, ut ei obediam ? quasi dicat : Non est tantæ auctoritatis. Ideo subjungitur : Nescio Dominum, et Israel, id est Israeliticum populum, non dimittam.
paras.en: Now it is described how Moses carried out the embassy committed to him, as regards the king of Egypt. [[5:1|After these things, Moses and Aaron went in|Post hæc ingressi sunt Moyses et Aaron]] to the king's palace, [[5:1|and said to Pharao|et dixerunt Pharaoni]]. Aaron was the leader in speech [*dux verbi*: the one who did the speaking], and Moses went in as the principal. Further, the Lord said to Moses above: [[Ex 3:18|thou shalt go in, thou and the ancients of Israel, to the king of Egypt|Ingredieris tu et seniores Israel ad regem Ægypti]]: hence it seems we should believe that on this occasion the elders of Israel went in with Moses and Aaron to Pharao, and did not hold back from it out of human fear, as the Jews say. Moses and Aaron, however, are named here as the principal ones before them. And they said to Pharao: [[5:1|Thus saith the Lord God of Israel: Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me in the desert|Hæc dicit Dominus Deus Israel : Dimitte populum meum, ut sacrificet mihi in deserto]]. [[5:2|But he answered: Who is the Lord, that I should hear his voice, and let Israel go?|At ille respondit : Quis est Dominus, ut audiam vocem ejus, et dimittam Israel ?]] That is, of what kind, or of how great authority, is the Lord your God of whom you speak to me, that I should obey him? As if to say: He is of no such authority. Hence there follows: [[5:2|I know not the Lord|Nescio Dominum]], [[5:2|neither will I let Israel|et Israel]], that is, the Israelite people, [[5:2|go|non dimittam]].

paras.t: Circa hoc quæritur, qualiter Pharao dicere potuit, Nescio Dominum, quum Deum esse, naturaliter sit insertum menti humanæ, secundum Damascenum primo libro : imo secundum Anselmum in Monologio, Deum esse, est per se notum. Ad hoc quidam respondent, quod quamvis Deum esse sit per se notum, in quantum mens humana Deum esse cogitat id, quod æstimat in entibus maximum, vel sub ratione summi boni, tamen sub hac determinatione, quod fuerit Deus populi Israel per fidem et cultum, non est per se notum. Unde et alii dicunt, quod quamvis per se notum, vel saltem demonstrabile sit, Deum esse, non tamen quod sit omnium rector, provisor ac judex, secundum quod fides docet. Sed contra solutionem hanc objici potest, quod utique Pharao et populus ejus sciverunt Hebræos colere Deum specialem, quem ipsi non coluerunt, atque habere circumcisionem et specialem ritum colendi, sicque aliquo modo cognoverunt Dominum Hebræorum. Ad istud arbitror respondendum, quod Pharao dixit hæc verba ex mera et cruda superbia, et tanquam summi Dei providentiam negans, ut sit sensus : Nescio Dominum, id est, non curo de eo, nec ejus dominium recognosco. Sic quippe et Ezechiel loquitur Pharaoni temporis sui : Audi, Pharao, draco magne, qui dicis : Meus est fluvius, et ego feci me ipsum. Denique in quibusdam ratio tam densissime excæcatur, quod naturalis notitia exsistendi Deum, aufertur a corde ipsorum, juxta quod scriptum est : Dixit insipiens in corde suo, Non est Deus. Et in Judith libro Holofernes ait ad Achior : Ostendam tibi quod non sit Deus, nisi Nabuchodonosor. Augustinus quoque libro de Civitate Dei, refert de quodam philosopho, qui contendebat non esse Deum.
paras.en: On this it is asked how Pharao could say, [[5:2|I know not the Lord|Nescio Dominum]], since it is naturally implanted in the human mind that God exists, according to Damascene in his first book; nay, according to Anselm in the Monologion, that God exists is self-evident [*per se notum*: known of itself, as soon as its terms are understood; the argument is in fact in Anselm's Proslogion]. To this some answer that, although it is self-evident that God exists, inasmuch as the human mind thinks of God as that which it reckons greatest among beings, or under the aspect of the highest good, yet under this determination, that he was the God of the people of Israel by faith and worship, it is not self-evident. Hence others also say that, although it is self-evident, or at least demonstrable, that God exists, it is not self-evident that he is the ruler, provider and judge of all, as faith teaches. But against this solution it can be objected that Pharao and his people certainly knew that the Hebrews worshipped a special God whom they themselves did not worship, and had circumcision and a special rite of worship; and so in some way they knew the Lord of the Hebrews. To this I think it must be answered that Pharao said these words out of sheer, crude pride, and as one denying the providence of the most high God, so that the sense is: [[5:2|I know not the Lord|Nescio Dominum]], that is, I care nothing for him, nor do I acknowledge his lordship. So indeed Ezechiel too speaks to the Pharao of his own time: Hear, Pharao, [[Ezech 29:3|thou great dragon|draco magne]], who sayest: [[Ezech 29:3|The river is mine, and I made myself|Meus est fluvius, et ego feci me ipsum]]. Lastly, in some men reason is so very thickly blinded that the natural knowledge that God exists is taken away from their heart, according to what is written: [[Ps 13:1|The fool hath said in his heart: There is no God|Dixit insipiens in corde suo, Non est Deus]][[Ps 52:1||]]. And in the book of Judith Holofernes says to Achior: I will [[Jdt 6:2|shew thee that there is no God, but Nabuchodonosor|Ostendam tibi quod non sit Deus, nisi Nabuchodonosor]]. Augustine too, in the book of the City of God, tells of a certain philosopher who maintained that there is no God.

paras.t: Dixeruntque Moyses et Aaron : Deus Hebræorum, qui ratione et jure creationis, et universalis gubernationis atque provisionis, est Deus universorum : tunc vero exstitit speciali modo Deus Hebræorum, utpote Judæorum ex Heber oriundorum : vocavit nos per inspirationem internam, et per Moysis hujus denuntiationem, per angelum quoque qui locutus est Moysi, ut eamus viam trium dierum in solitudinem, et sacrificemus Domino Deo nostro, ne forte accidat nobis pestis aut gladius, id est interfectio pestilentialis, aut persecutio hostium, si inobedientes Deo fuerimus in isto præcepto.
paras.en: [[5:3|And they said|Dixeruntque]], Moses and Aaron: [[5:3|The God of the Hebrews|Deus Hebræorum]], who by reason and right of creation, and of universal government and providence, is the God of all things, but was then in a special manner the God of the Hebrews, that is, of the Jews descended from Heber, [[5:3|hath called us|vocavit nos]] by inward inspiration, and by the announcement of this Moses, and also by the angel who spoke to Moses, [[5:3|to go three days' journey into the wilderness, and to sacrifice to the Lord our God|ut eamus viam trium dierum in solitudinem, et sacrificemus Domino Deo nostro]], [[5:3|lest a pestilence or the sword fall upon us|ne forte accidat nobis pestis aut gladius]], that is, death by pestilence, or persecution by enemies, if we are disobedient to God in this command.

paras.t: Sed videtur istud fuisse contectum mendacium. Deus enim in veritate præcepit, ut egrederentur Ægyptum ad habitandum in terra Chanaan, quatenus ibi servirent sibi, non ut immolarent ei in eremo expleto trium dierum itinere, ut pestem gladiumve evaderent. Neque post iter trium dierum sacrificaverunt Domino in deserto. Ad istud in Scholastica historia breviter respondetur: In his verbis nec duplicitas, nec contrarietas fuit. Eo enim forsitan ordine, et ea via qua dictum est, populus ille fuisset eductus, si a Pharaone fuisset statim dimissus. Fundatur quoque responsio ista in verbis Augustini, dicentis: Quæritur, quomodo populo dicatur, quod mandavit Dominus ejecturum se eos de Ægypto in terram Chanaan: Pharaoni autem dicatur, quod trium dierum itinere exire vellent in desertum immolare Deo ex ejus mandato. Sed intelligendum est, quamvis Deus sciret quid esset facturus, quoniam præsciebat non consensurum Pharaonem ad populum dimittendum, illud primo dictum esse a Deo quod fieret primo, si ille dimitteret populum: ut enim sic fierent omnia, sicut sequens scriptura testatur, Pharaonis et servorum ejus contumacia meruit.
paras.en: But this seems to have been a veiled lie. For in truth God commanded them to go out of Egypt to dwell in the land of Chanaan, so that they might serve him there; not to sacrifice to him in the wilderness when a three days' journey was completed, so as to escape pestilence or the sword. Nor did they sacrifice to the Lord in the desert after a three days' journey. To this the Scholastic History answers briefly: In these words there was neither duplicity nor contradiction. For perhaps in that order, and by that way which was said, that people would have been led out, had it been let go by Pharao at once. This answer is grounded also in the words of Augustine, who says: It is asked how it is said to the people that the Lord commanded that he would bring them out of Egypt into the land of Chanaan, while to Pharao it is said that they wished to go out a three days' journey into the desert to sacrifice to God at his command. But it must be understood that, although God knew what he was going to do, since he foreknew that Pharao would not consent to let the people go, God first spoke of that which would have come about first, if Pharao had let the people go: for that all things should come about as the following Scripture testifies was what the stubbornness of Pharao and his servants deserved.

paras.t: Ad aliud quoque, quod tactum est, Strabus respondet: Tertia mansione postquam Hebræi transierunt mare Rubrum, venerunt Etham, qui locus etiam dictus est Mara, propter aquas amaras quæ fuerunt ibidem: quibus dulcoratis, sacrificium laudis solverunt. Vel iter trium dierum, id est trium mensium. Tertio etenim mense venerunt in montem Sinai, ubi legem acceperunt, tabernaculum erexerunt, et sacrificaverunt. Quemadmodum etenim dies interdum pro anno accipitur, juxta illud in Ezechiele, Diem pro anno dedi tibi; ita sumitur nunc pro mense. Verumtamen istud superius aliter solutum est. Quamvis enim Deus ab exordio legationis Moysis intenderit populum illum de Ægypto in terram promissionis deducere, prima tamen fronte non insinuavit hoc Pharaoni, ne Pharao videretur aliquam justam habere persuasionem ad non consentiendum præcepto Dei, petitionique Moysis, sed primo proposuit aliquid parvi, quod tamen exstitit verum, nec exclusit majora.
paras.en: To the other point too that was touched on, Strabo answers: At the third station after the Hebrews crossed the Red Sea, they came to Etham, which place was also called Mara because of the bitter waters that were there; and when these had been sweetened, they paid a sacrifice of praise. Or, a journey of three days, that is, of three months. For in the third month they came to Mount Sinai, where they received the law, set up the tabernacle, and offered sacrifice. For just as a day is sometimes taken for a year, according to that in Ezechiel, [[Ezech 4:6|a day for a year I have appointed to thee|Diem pro anno dedi tibi]], so here it is taken for a month. The former difficulty, however, was resolved differently above. For although God from the beginning of Moses's embassy intended to lead that people out of Egypt into the land of promise, yet at the outset he did not intimate this to Pharao, lest Pharao should seem to have some just ground for not consenting to the command of God and to the petition of Moses; but first he put forward something small, which was nevertheless true, and did not exclude greater things.

paras.t: Aitque ad eos rex Ægypti: Quare, o Moyses et Aaron, sollicitatis populum ab operibus suis? id est, cur vestra persuasione inducitis populum Hebræorum ad cessandum ab operibus, eis a me injunctis? Refert Josephus, quod Moyses commemoravit tunc Pharaoni, quanta fecit Ægyptiis oppressis ab Æthiopibus, et pericula ac labores quos pro Ægyptiis toleravit, et quæ vidit in monte Sinai ei narravit. Quem rex deridens, servum suum fugitivum vocavit eum, et pro seditione excitanda dixit eum redisse. Ite ad onera vestra, hoc est, ad exercendum labores quos Hebræis indixi. Circa hoc aliqui dicunt, quod Pharao injunxit Moysi et Aaron ac senioribus ceteris, laborare cum ceteris reliquis Hebræis. Sed inferiores tanto plus laboraverunt, ut seniores superiores essent supportati.
paras.en: [[5:4|The king of Egypt said to them: Why do you Moses and Aaron draw off the people from their works?|Aitque ad eos rex Ægypti: Quare, o Moyses et Aaron, sollicitatis populum ab operibus suis?]] That is, why do you by your persuasion induce the people of the Hebrews to cease from the works I have laid upon them? Josephus relates that Moses then reminded Pharao how much he had done for the Egyptians when they were oppressed by the Ethiopians, and the dangers and labours he had borne for the Egyptians, and told him what he had seen on Mount Sinai. The king mocked him, called him his runaway slave, and said he had come back to stir up sedition. [[5:4|Get you gone to your burdens|Ite ad onera vestra]], that is, to carry out the labours that I have laid on the Hebrews. On this some say that Pharao enjoined Moses and Aaron and the other elders to labour together with all the rest of the Hebrews. But the lower ones laboured so much the more, that the elders, being their superiors, might be spared.

paras.t: Dixitque Pharao satellitibus et consiliariis suis: Multus est populus terræ, id est, Hebræi in terra Gessen morantes, multiplicati sunt valde: videtis quod turba succreverit, id est, multitudo eorum aucta sit nimis, non solum in feminis, sed item in viris. Ex quo elicitur, quod præceptum regis de Hebræorum infantulis submergendis, non diu duravit; sed ob suam excessivam et inhumanam crudelitatem, revocatum fuit a rege de suorum consilio, imo potius Deo sic ordinante: alias viri inter Hebræos pene jam defecissent. Quanto magis augebuntur, si dederitis, vos exactores operum, eis requiem ab operibus? quia tunc magis vacarent carnalitati atque amplexibus. Tamen (ut dictum est supra) afflictio operum non impedivit multiplicationem eorum.
paras.en: [[5:5|And Pharao said|Dixitque Pharao]] to his attendants and counsellors: [[5:5|The people of the land are numerous|Multus est populus terræ]], that is, the Hebrews dwelling in the land of Gessen have multiplied greatly; [[5:5|you see that the multitude is increased|videtis quod turba succreverit]], that is, their number has grown exceedingly, not only in women but also in men. From this it is gathered that the king's command about drowning the little ones of the Hebrews did not last long, but because of its excessive and inhuman cruelty was revoked by the king on the advice of his own people, or rather by God so ordaining: otherwise the men among the Hebrews would by now have almost died out. [[5:5|how much more|Quanto magis]] will they increase, [[5:5|if you give|si dederitis]], you taskmasters of the works, [[5:5|them rest from their works?|eis requiem ab operibus?]] For then they would give themselves the more to the flesh and to embraces. And yet (as was said above) the affliction of the works did not hinder their multiplying.

paras.t: Præcepit ergo Pharao in die illo præfectis operum, qui præfecti erant Hebræi, ut habitum est, et exactoribus populi, qui erant Ægyptii, et præfectis præfatis exigebant impletionem injuncti laboris commissi Hebræis, Dicens: Nequaquam ultra dabitis paleas populo, quæ paleæ miscebantur cum luto, ad conficiendos lateres, sicut prius: ut ex eis fierent lateres fortiores, quibus ad ædificandum utibantur pro saxis Ægyptii, quia (secundum Glossam) ibi lapides non abundant. In Scholastica vero historia dicitur, Pro penuria lignorum in Ægypto lateres coquebantur. Ipsi Hebræi vadant hinc inde per campos, et colligant stipulas. Quas paulo ante vocavit paleas, vocat nunc stipulas: idcirco per paleas intelligitur omne quod remanet, bladis excussis.
paras.en: [[5:6|Therefore he commanded|Præcepit ergo]], Pharao, [[5:6|the same day the overseers of the works|in die illo præfectis operum]], who were Hebrew overseers, as was said, [[5:6|and the task-masters of the people|et exactoribus populi]], who were Egyptians, and who exacted from the said overseers the fulfilment of the labour enjoined and committed to the Hebrews, [[5:6|saying|Dicens]]: [[5:7|You shall give straw no more to the people|Nequaquam ultra dabitis paleas populo]] (the straw was mixed with the clay) [[5:7|to make brick, as before|ad conficiendos lateres, sicut prius]], so that stronger bricks might be made with it: the Egyptians used these for building instead of stones, because (according to the Gloss) stones are not plentiful there. But in the Scholastic History it is said: Because of the scarcity of wood in Egypt, the bricks were baked. Let the Hebrews themselves [[5:7|go|vadant]] hither and thither through the fields, [[5:7|and gather straw|et colligant stipulas]]. What he called *paleæ* a little before, he now calls *stipulæ*: therefore by *paleæ* is understood everything that remains when the grain has been threshed out [*paleæ* is properly chaff, *stipulæ* stubble; the Douay-Rheims has "straw" for both].

paras.t: Et mensuram laterum quam prius faciebant, antequam scilicet Moyses venit ad me, imponetis super eos, id est, præcipietis ut jam de cetero faciant omni die tot lateres, quot fecerunt, quando paleæ eis dabantur; nec minuetis quidquam. Vacant enim, id est, non satis dure gravantur operibus, et idcirco vociferantur, dicentes: Eamus et sacrificemus Deo nostro. Opprimantur operibus et expleant ea, ut non acquiescant verbis mendacibus, etc., id est verbis quæ Moyses finxit, dicens se missum a Deo. Hoc Pharao suspicabatur.
paras.en: And [[5:8|the task of bricks, which they did before|mensuram laterum quam prius faciebant]], that is, before Moses came to me, [[5:8|you shall lay upon them|imponetis super eos]]: that is, you shall command that from now on they make every day as many bricks as they made when straw was given them; [[5:8|neither shall you diminish any thing thereof|nec minuetis quidquam]]. [[5:8|for they are idle|Vacant enim]], that is, they are not burdened hard enough with works, [[5:8|and therefore they cry. saying: Let us go and sacrifice to our God|et idcirco vociferantur, dicentes: Eamus et sacrificemus Deo nostro]]. [[5:9|Let them be oppressed with works, and let them fulfil them; that they may not regard lying words|Opprimantur operibus et expleant ea, ut non acquiescant verbis mendacibus]], etc., that is, words which Moses invented, saying that he was sent by God. This is what Pharao suspected.

paras.t: Dispersusque est populus Hebræorum per universam terram Ægypti ad colligendum paleas. Magister in historiis dicit: Opprimebantur Hebræi nocte paleas colligendo, et de die lateres faciendo. Et per noctem intelligit forte, quod valde tarde de sero, et valde mane paleas collegerunt.
paras.en: [[5:12|And the people was scattered|Dispersusque est populus]] of the Hebrews [[5:12|through all the land of Egypt to gather straw|per universam terram Ægypti ad colligendum paleas]]. The Master says in the Histories: The Hebrews were oppressed with gathering straw by night and making bricks by day. And by *night* perhaps he means that they gathered the straw very late in the evening and very early in the morning.

paras.t: Præfecti quoque, id est magistri operum instabant, id est, instanter et importune admonuerunt Hebræos, dicentes: Complete opus vestrum quotidie, ut facere solebatis prius quando dabantur vobis paleæ. Flagellatique sunt qui præerant operibus filiorum Israel, puta præfati præfecti Hebræi, ab exactoribus Pharaonis, dicentibus: Quare non impletis mensuram laterum, sicut prius, nec heri, nec hodie? id est, cur non facitis, ab Hebræis quibus præestis, quotidie fieri tot lateres, quot fecerunt, quando paleæ eis dabantur?
paras.en: [[5:13|And the overseers|Præfecti quoque]], that is, the masters, [[5:13|of the works|operum]] [[5:13|pressed them|instabant]], that is, urgently and importunately admonished the Hebrews, [[5:13|saying: Fulfil your work every day, as before ye were wont to do, when straw was given you|dicentes: Complete opus vestrum quotidie, ut facere solebatis prius quando dabantur vobis paleæ]]. [[5:14|And they that were over the works of the children of Israel, were scourged|Flagellatique sunt qui præerant operibus filiorum Israel]], namely the aforesaid Hebrew overseers, [[5:14|by Pharao's taskmasters, saying|ab exactoribus Pharaonis, dicentibus]]: [[5:14|Why have you not made up the task of bricks, both yesterday and to day, as before?|Quare non impletis mensuram laterum, sicut prius, nec heri, nec hodie?]] That is, why do you not have the Hebrews over whom you are set make as many bricks every day as they made when straw was given them?

paras.t: Veneruntque præpositi filiorum Israel, id est præfecti jam dicti, et conquesti sunt ad Pharaonem, dicentes: Cur ita agis contra servos tuos? id est, cur tam dure nos opprimis, et impossibilia præcipis? Ecce famuli tui flagellis cædimur ab exactoribus tuis, et injuste agitur contra populum tuum, id est Hebræos tibi subjectos.
paras.en: [[5:15|And the officers of the children of Israel came|Veneruntque præpositi filiorum Israel]], that is, the overseers just mentioned, [[5:15|and cried out to Pharao, saying: Why dealest thou so with thy servants?|et conquesti sunt ad Pharaonem, dicentes: Cur ita agis contra servos tuos?]] [Denis reads *conquesti sunt*, "complained", where the Vulgate has *vociferati sunt*, "cried out"] That is, why dost thou oppress us so hard, and command what is impossible? [[5:16|behold we, thy servants, are beaten with whips|Ecce famuli tui flagellis cædimur]] by thy taskmasters, [[5:16|and thy people is unjustly dealt withal|et injuste agitur contra populum tuum]], that is, the Hebrews subject to thee.

paras.t: Videbantque præpositi filiorum Israel, se in malo, id est, in angustia magna viderunt se positos, et cum gravi mœrore se invicem adspexerunt, eo quod diceretur eis a Pharaone. Non minuetur quidquam de lateribus per singulos dies, id est, non relaxabo præceptum meum de gravitate operum vobis injunctorum.
paras.en: [[5:19|And the officers of the children of Israel saw|Videbantque præpositi filiorum Israel]] [[5:19|that they were in evil case|se in malo]], that is, they saw themselves placed in great straits, and looked at one another in heavy grief, [[5:19|because it was said to them|eo quod diceretur eis]] by Pharao: [[5:19|There shall not a whit be diminished of the bricks for every day|Non minuetur quidquam de lateribus per singulos dies]], that is, I will not relax my command about the heaviness of the works laid upon you.

paras.t: Occurreruntque Moysi et Aaron, qui stabant ex adverso, egredientes a Pharaone, id est, præfecti operum egredientes a rege, occurrerunt Moysi et Aaron stantibus ex adverso, seu in aliquo intermedio loco præstolantes ibidem reditum præfectorum, ut scirent Pharaonis responsum. Et dixerunt præfecti ad eos: Videat Dominus et judicet, id est, per debitam ultionem ostendat se videre quam male fecistis nobis: quoniam fœtere fecistis odorem nostrum coram Pharaone, id est, aspernabiles et odiosos fecistis nos regi, ita quod nostram ferre non valet præsentiam, sicut ægre fertur præsentia ejus, qui fœtentem habet odorem: et præbuistis ei gladium ut occideret nos, id est, per verba vestra inflammastis eum adversus nos, ita quod usque ad mortem nos opprimit. Ita dixerunt præfecti ex impatientia et infidelitate. Nam et verbis Moysis quibus paulo ante crediderunt, jam discredebant, eo quod non viderunt se celeriter liberatos, sed dire præ solito pressos.
paras.en: [[5:20|And they met Moses and Aaron, who stood over against them as they came out from Pharao|Occurreruntque Moysi et Aaron, qui stabant ex adverso, egredientes a Pharaone]] [Denis reads *egredientes*, so that it is the overseers who come out from Pharao]: that is, the overseers of the works, coming out from the king, met Moses and Aaron, who were standing over against them, or, waiting in some place on the way for the overseers to come back, so as to learn Pharao's answer. [[5:21|And they said|Et dixerunt]], the overseers, [[5:21|to them|ad eos]]: [[5:21|The Lord see and judge|Videat Dominus et judicet]], that is, by due vengeance may he show that he sees how ill you have done by us: [[5:21|because you have, made our savour to stink before Pharao|quoniam fœtere fecistis odorem nostrum coram Pharaone]], that is, you have made us contemptible and hateful to the king, so that he cannot bear our presence, just as the presence of one who has a foul smell is hard to bear; [[5:21|and you have given him a sword, to kill us|et præbuistis ei gladium ut occideret nos]], that is, by your words you have inflamed him against us, so that he oppresses us even to death. So the overseers spoke out of impatience and unbelief. For they now disbelieved the words of Moses, which they had believed a little before, because they did not see themselves speedily set free, but cruelly pressed more than usual.

paras.t: Reversusque Moyses ad Dominum. Quo rediit ad incircumscriptibilem Deum ubique præsentem, nisi forsitan intra se, ad habitantem in corde suo, vel ad secretum aliquem locum orationis? Itaque reversus, id est, mente se convertens ad Dominum, ait: Domine, cur afflixisti, id est, ab Ægyptiis sic affligi et contristari permisisti, populum istum Hebræum? Quare misisti me ? etc. Quasi dicat : Admiror de isto, et quibusdam videtur quod inaniter, imo et nocive advenerim. Secundum Augustinum, ista non sunt verba contumaciæ aut indignationis, sed inquisitionis et occultæ orationis.
paras.en: [[5:22|And Moses returned to the Lord|Reversusque Moyses ad Dominum]]. Whither did he return, to God who cannot be circumscribed and is present everywhere, unless perhaps within himself, to him who dwells in his heart, or to some secret place of prayer? So, having returned, that is, turning himself in mind to the Lord, [[5:22|and said: Lord, why hast thou afflicted|ait: Domine, cur afflixisti]], that is, permitted to be so afflicted and saddened by the Egyptians, [[5:22|this people|populum istum]], the Hebrew people? [[5:22|wherefore hast thou sent me?|Quare misisti me ?]] etc. As if to say: I wonder at this, and it seems to some that I have come in vain, and even to their harm. According to Augustine, these are not words of defiance or indignation, but of inquiry and of hidden prayer.

5.title: De mystico ejusdem capituli quinti intellectu
5.title_en: On the mystical sense of the same fifth chapter

paras.t: Moyses et Aaron senioresque Israel, designant universos Christi vicarios, doctores et prælatos Ecclesiæ, qui verbo et opere instruunt plebem. Hi Christo jubente dicunt Pharaoni, hoc est diabolo, cuilibetque tyranno, aut hæresiarchæ, vel seductori, ut populum Christi dimittat, id est, pervertere et a sua salute impedire desistat. Hoc, inquam, dicunt Pharaoni, contra vitia prædicando, impios increpando, seductoribus resistendo, atque quam vile ac miserum sit diabolo ministrare et jugo vitiorum subjici declarando, quatenus populus christianus sacrificet Deo in deserto, id est, Altissimo offerat semetipsum, sacrificium quoque laudis, eleemosynas, decimas, oblationes, Hostiamque altaris in vera devotione, per recessum mentis ab omni sæculari tumultu, et carnali affectu, quatenus in solitudine, id est mentis abstractione et vacatione, qua soli intenditur Creatori, sacrificet obsequaturque Deo.
paras.en: [[5:1|Moses and Aaron|Moyses et Aaron]], and the elders of Israel, signify all the vicars of Christ, the doctors and prelates of the Church, who instruct the people by word and deed. At Christ's bidding these say to Pharao, that is, to the devil, and to every tyrant, heresiarch or seducer, that he let Christ's people go: that is, that he cease to pervert them and to hinder them from their salvation. This, I say, they say to Pharao by preaching against vices, rebuking the wicked, resisting seducers, and declaring how vile and wretched a thing it is to serve the devil and to be subjected to the yoke of vices; so that the Christian people may [[5:1|sacrifice|sacrificet]] to God [[5:1|in the desert|in deserto]]: that is, may offer themselves to the Most High, and also the sacrifice of praise, alms, tithes, oblations, and the Victim of the altar, in true devotion, by the mind's withdrawal from all worldly tumult and carnal affection; so that in solitude, that is, in the mind's abstraction and freedom from cares, in which it attends to the Creator alone, they may sacrifice to God and do him service.

paras.t: Præterea ad præfatam vicariorum Christi admonitionem, respondent designati per Pharaonem: Quis est Dominus, ut audiam vocem ejus, etc.? Nescio Dominum, et Israel non dimittam. Tales equidem etsi verbis dicant se recognoscere Deum, attamen factis negant: et quamvis eum agnoscant informi notitia, non tamen cognitione formata et affectiva, approbativaque boni, idcirco nec Deo obediunt, nec aliorum cessant impedire salutem, et ea quæ fidei sanctæ contrariantur, docere ac operari præsumunt. Omnes quoque superbi ac impii, propriam voluntatem præferendo, imo et superponendo voluntati divinæ, ipso facto effantur, Nescio Dominum: quia Deum creatorem suum non recognoscunt per veram subjectionem, sed illud Job dicunt effectu: Quis est Omnipotens, ut serviamus ei? De quibus ait Scriptura: Ipsi fuerunt rebelles lumini. Verumtamen hæc ipsa eorum cruda elatio, improba quoque rebellio, non cedent eis in bonum, sed velint nolint, tandem saltem per tormenta coacti, Dominum recognoscent, quemadmodum per Jeremiam et Ezechielem Deus de talibus sæpissime dixit: Et scietis quia ego Dominus. Et Psalmista: Imple, inquit, facies eorum ignominia; et cognoscant quia nomen tibi Dominus. Sic et Pharao qui nunc ait, Nescio Dominum, postea flagellis attritus, locutus est: Orate Dominum pro me.
paras.en: Further, to this admonition of the vicars of Christ those signified by Pharao answer: [[5:2|Who is the Lord, that I should hear his voice|Quis est Dominus, ut audiam vocem ejus]], etc.? [[5:2|I know not the Lord, neither will I let Israel go|Nescio Dominum, et Israel non dimittam]]. Such men, even if they say in words that they acknowledge God, yet deny him in deeds: and although they know him with an unformed knowledge [that is, a knowledge of faith not quickened by charity], yet not with a knowledge that is formed and affective and approves the good; and therefore they neither obey God nor cease to hinder the salvation of others, and they presume to teach and to do what is contrary to the holy faith. All the proud and wicked, too, by preferring, nay, by setting their own will above the divine will, by that very fact declare: [[5:2|I know not the Lord|Nescio Dominum]]; for they do not acknowledge God their creator by true subjection, but in effect they say that saying of Job: [[Job 21:15|Who is the Almighty, that we should serve him|Quis est Omnipotens, ut serviamus ei]]? Of whom the Scripture says: [[Job 24:13|They have been rebellious to the light|Ipsi fuerunt rebelles lumini]]. Yet this very raw pride of theirs, and their wicked rebellion, will not turn out to their good; but willing or unwilling, forced at last at least by torments, they will acknowledge the Lord, as God very often said of such men through Jeremias and Ezechiel: [[Ezech 6:7|and you shall know that I am the Lord|Et scietis quia ego Dominus]] [no margin reference; the refrain runs through Ezechiel, e.g. Ezech 6:7, where the Vulgate reads *ego sum Dominus*]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 82:17|Fill|Imple]], he says, [[Ps 82:17|their faces with shame|facies eorum ignominia]]; [[Ps 82:19|And let them know that the Lord is thy name|et cognoscant quia nomen tibi Dominus]]. So Pharao too, who now says, [[5:2|I know not the Lord|Nescio Dominum]], afterwards, worn down by the scourges, said: [[Ex 8:8|Pray ye to the Lord|Orate Dominum]] for me [Pharao's words at Ex 8:8 and 9:28; *pray for me* at Ex 8:28].

paras.t: Præterea, etsi designati per Pharaonem, renuant plebem christianam dimittere ad vivendum et sacrificandum catholice, nihilo minus egredi debet plebs Christi ab illorum jugo atque obsequio. Nec enim valent quempiam detinere invitum; sed unusquisque libere se potest ad suum convertere Salvatorem. Sic ergo, ut tactum est, sacrificemus Deo, ei soli vacando, ne accidat nobis pestis aut gladius, hoc est, ne aliquem scandalizemus, aut scandalizemur ab aliquo, et ne spiritualiter jugulemur ab hoste antiquo. Quid autem designetur per iter trium dierum, expressum est.
paras.en: Moreover, even if those signified by Pharao refuse to let the Christian people go to live and to sacrifice in the Catholic manner, none the less the people of Christ must go out from their yoke and service. For they cannot hold anyone back against his will; but each one can freely turn to his Saviour. So then, as was touched on, let us [[5:3|sacrifice|sacrificemus]] to God, giving ourselves to him alone, [[5:3|lest a pestilence or the sword fall upon us|ne accidat nobis pestis aut gladius]]: that is, lest we scandalize anyone, or be scandalized by anyone, and lest we be slain spiritually by the old enemy. What is signified by the [[5:3|three days' journey|iter trium dierum]] has already been set out [in Art. VI, on 3:18].

paras.t: Ait ad eos rex Ægypti: Quare sollicitatis populum ab operibus suis? Sic unusquisque animarum seductor tam invisibilis, quam visibilis hostis, respondet Christi vicariis, quoniam ægerrime fert, quod aliquis nititur ei subjectos a pristinis revocare operibus et a servitute peccati, et subdere obsequio Christi. Ideo præcipit sibi subjectis: Ite ad opera vestra, hoc est, pristina, quæ vobis suggessi, vitia exercete. In quibus est frequenter labor gravis et miser. Propter quod impii in libro Sapientiæ fatentur: Lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis, et ambulavimus vias difficiles.
paras.en: [[5:4|The king of Egypt said to them|Ait ad eos rex Ægypti]]: [[5:4|Why do you|Quare]] [[5:4|draw off the people from their works|sollicitatis populum ab operibus suis]]? So every seducer of souls, the invisible enemy as well as the visible, answers the vicars of Christ, since he takes it very ill that anyone strives to call those subject to him back from their former works and from the servitude of sin, and to bring them under the service of Christ. Therefore he commands those subject to him: [[5:4|Get you gone to your burdens|Ite ad opera vestra]] [Denis reads *ite ad opera vestra*, go to your works, where the Vulgate has *onera*, burdens], that is, practise the former vices that I suggested to you. In these there is often heavy and wretched labour. For this reason the wicked confess in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 5:7|We wearied ourselves in the way of iniquity and destruction, and have walked through hard ways|Lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis, et ambulavimus vias difficiles]].

paras.t: Denique, sicut Pharao tunc gravius afflixit filios Israel, quando volebant egredi terram ejus, ac Deo sacrificare in eremo: sic diabolus et adjutores ipsius, tunc acrius tentant fideles, quando suam volunt corrigere vitam, et Deo offerre se ipsos: imo toto conatu satagit eos tunc gravare adversis, ut tædio fracti, a salubri resipiscant proposito, quemadmodum de quibusdam instabilibus ac pusillis loquitur Christus, quia ad tempus credunt, et in tempore tentationis recedunt.
paras.en: Lastly, just as Pharao afflicted the children of Israel more heavily at the time when they wished to go out of his land and sacrifice to God in the wilderness, so the devil and his helpers tempt the faithful more fiercely at the time when they wish to amend their life and offer themselves to God: nay, he strives with all his might to weigh them down with adversities then, so that, broken by weariness, they may draw back from their wholesome purpose; as Christ says of certain unstable and faint-hearted ones, that [[Luke 8:13|they believe for a while and in time of temptation they fall away|ad tempus credunt, et in tempore tentationis recedunt]].

paras.t: Insuper, quemadmodum exactores Pharaonis flagellaverunt præfectos Hebræorum, quia Hebræi non impleverunt opus a Pharaone injunctum; sic dæmones principis tenebrarum satellites, gravius sæpe impugnant atque affligunt devotos Christi vicarios, qui subditos suos a diaboli retrahunt servitute, in tantum quod tales vicarii quandoque tentationi succumbunt, et in vitia corruunt carnis, incipiuntque Pharaoni servire, et ab impugnationum suarum cupiunt relevari molestia. Tunc quoque quodammodo indignantur his, a quibus ad viam virtutum erant inducti, in quantum fuerunt eis ruinæ gravioris occasio; feruntque ægre quod execrabiles facti sunt amatoribus et magnatibus sæculi hujus, ita quod eorum odor illis fœtere videtur. Tunc majores et perfectiores viri a quibus erant conversi, clamant ad Dominum, et ejus implorant auxilium, ut suæ subveniat plebi, et seductis ac victis auxiliari dignetur.
paras.en: Besides, just as Pharao's taskmasters scourged the overseers of the Hebrews because the Hebrews had not fulfilled the work Pharao had laid on them, so the demons, the henchmen of the prince of darkness, often assail and afflict more heavily the devout vicars of Christ who draw those under them back from the servitude of the devil; so much so that such vicars sometimes give way to temptation and fall into the vices of the flesh, and begin to serve Pharao, and long to be relieved of the trouble of their assaults. Then too they are in a manner indignant with those by whom they had been led into the way of the virtues, inasmuch as these were to them the occasion of a heavier fall; and they take it ill that they have become hateful to the lovers and great ones of this world, so that their savour seems to stink to them. Then the greater and more perfect men by whom they had been converted cry to the Lord and implore his help, that he may come to the aid of his people and deign to help those who have been led astray and overcome.

paras.t: Postremo, per hoc quod Moyses Aaronque tam patienter tulerunt injustam invectionem, reprehensionemque Hebræorum, ipsis dicentium, Videat Dominus et judicet, imo et pro suis reprehensoribus ingratisque subditis oraverunt: sic prælati interdum parcere, et disciplinam suspendere debent a subditis suis reis, dum eos conspiciunt aliunde dire afflictos, tentatos, ac passionatos, ne calamum quassatum aut fumigans linum penitus conterant et exstinguant, nisi forte ex tali pietate et dilatione periclitetur bonum commune, aut fidei veritas patiatur jacturam. Tunc quippe per disciplinæ rigorem compescere debent perversos.
paras.en: Lastly, as Moses and Aaron bore so patiently the unjust invective and reproach of the Hebrews, who said to them: [[5:21|The Lord see and judge|Videat Dominus et judicet]], and even prayed for their reproachers and ungrateful subjects, so prelates ought at times to spare their guilty subjects and hold back discipline from them, when they see them grievously afflicted, tempted and troubled by passions from other quarters, lest they utterly break the bruised reed or quench the smoking flax [an echo of Is 42:3, cited of Christ at Matt 12:20; no margin reference]; unless perhaps the common good is endangered by such kindness and delay, or the truth of the faith suffers loss. For then they must restrain the perverse by the rigour of discipline.

paras.t: Itaque egrediamur Ægyptum, id est vitiorum caliginem et inquietudinem sæcularium negotiorum, relinquamus mundum animo et affectu, sicut hortatur S. Joannes apostolus: Nolite diligere mundum, neque ea quæ in mundo sunt. Nec impatienter feramus, si odit nos mundus, si mundanis ac passionatis displicemus hominibus, quoniam Deus dissipavit ossa eorum qui hominibus placent; confusi sunt, quoniam Deus sprevit eos. Quid horribilius dici potest? Idcirco ait et Paulus: An quæro hominibus placere? Si adhuc hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem. Hinc ait Salvator discipulis: Si mundus vos odit, scitote quoniam me priorem vobis odio habuit. Verumtamen quantum in nobis est, studeamus universis in Deo placere, exempla virtutum præbere, nemini ullam dare offensionem.
paras.en: Let us therefore go out of Egypt, that is, out of the darkness of vices and the restlessness of worldly business; let us leave the world in mind and affection, as St. John the Apostle exhorts: [[1 John 2:15|Love not the world, nor the things which are in the world|Nolite diligere mundum, neque ea quæ in mundo sunt]]. Nor let us bear it impatiently if the world hates us, if we displease worldly men and men ruled by passion; for [[Ps 52:6|God hath scattered the bones of them that please men: they have been confounded, because God hath despised them|Deus dissipavit ossa eorum qui hominibus placent; confusi sunt, quoniam Deus sprevit eos]]. What more dreadful thing can be said? Therefore Paul too says: [[Gal 1:10|Or do I seek to please men? If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ|An quæro hominibus placere? Si adhuc hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem]]. Hence the Saviour says to the disciples: [[John 15:18|If the world hate you, know ye that it hath hated me before you|Si mundus vos odit, scitote quoniam me priorem vobis odio habuit]]. Yet, as far as in us lies, let us strive to please all men in God, to give examples of the virtues, and to give no offence to anyone.

6.title: Expositio litteralis capituli sexti: Dixit Dominus ad Moysen
6.title_en: Literal exposition of the sixth chapter: “And the Lord said to Moses”

paras.t: Modo describitur qualiter Deus Moysen vehementer afflictum confortavit et consolatus est, dicens : Nunc videbis quæ facturus sum Pharaoni, hoc est, quibus plagis eum et terram ac populum ejus percutiam. Per manum enim fortem dimittet eos, hoc est, mediantibus magnis prodigiis permittet exire Hebræos, et in manu robusta, id est per plagas ei potenter infligendas, ejiciet illos, id est velociter exire compellet, de terra sua. Percussis namque primogenitis Ægyptiorum ita fuerunt perterriti, quod dixerunt : Omnes moriemur. Ideo non permiserunt Hebræos aliquam facere moram in terra Ægypti, ut infra describitur.
paras.en: Now it is described how God strengthened and consoled Moses in his great affliction, saying: [[6:1|Now thou shalt see what I will do to Pharao|Nunc videbis quæ facturus sum Pharaoni]], that is, with what plagues I will strike him and his land and people. [[6:1|For by a mighty hand shall he let them go|Per manum enim fortem dimittet eos]], that is, by means of great wonders he will allow the Hebrews to go out; [[6:1|and with a strong hand|et in manu robusta]], that is, through the plagues to be mightily inflicted on him, [[6:1|shall he cast them out|ejiciet illos]], that is, he will force them to go out with speed, [[6:1|of his land|de terra sua]]. For when the firstborn of the Egyptians had been struck down, they were so terrified that they said: We shall all die. And so they did not let the Hebrews make any delay in the land of Egypt, as is described below.

paras.t: Locutusque est Dominus ad Moysen, dicens : Ego Dominus qui apparui Abraham, Isaac et Jacob in Deo omnipotente, hoc est, qui eis apparendo, ostendi eisdem me esse Deum omnipotentem. Unde in Genesi legitur : Dixit Dominus ad Abraham : Ego sum Dominus Deus omnipotens, ambula coram me, et esto perfectus. Alibi quoque Isaac ait ad Jacob : Deus meus omnipotens benedicat tibi. Similiter alio loco Dominus ad Jacob locutus est : Ego sum fortissimus Deus patris tui. Sed quum Dominus etiam apparuerit Noe atque Melchisedech, imo et Adæ ac aliis quibusdam Patriarchis in lege naturæ, ut creditur, cur de his tribus solum nunc facit mentionem ad Moysen ? Ad hoc breviter Glossa respondet, quod Deus mentionem facit antiquæ promissionis, tanquam eam in proximo completurus. Itaque respondendum, quod ideo mentionem facit horum trium Patriarcharum, quoniam ipsi specialiter patres Hebræorum vocantur, eisque specialiter ac frequenter Deus promisit, quod posteritati eorum terram Chanaan condonaret.
paras.en: [[6:2|And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: I am the Lord|Locutusque est Dominus ad Moysen, dicens : Ego Dominus]] [[6:3|that appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, by the name of God Almighty|qui apparui Abraham, Isaac et Jacob in Deo omnipotente]], that is, who, in appearing to them, shewed them that I am God almighty. Hence we read in Genesis: The Lord said to Abraham: [[Gen 17:1|I am the Almighty God: walk before me, and be perfect|Ego sum Dominus Deus omnipotens, ambula coram me, et esto perfectus]]. Elsewhere too Isaac says to Jacob: [[Gen 28:3|God almighty bless thee|Deus meus omnipotens benedicat tibi]] [Denis reads *Deus meus*, “my God”]. Likewise in another place the Lord spoke to Jacob: [[Gen 46:3|I am the most mighty God of thy father|Ego sum fortissimus Deus patris tui]]. But since the Lord also appeared to Noe and to Melchisedech, and indeed to Adam and to certain other Patriarchs under the law of nature, as is believed, why does he now mention only these three to Moses? To this the Gloss answers briefly that God makes mention of the ancient promise, as one about to fulfil it shortly. And so we must answer that he mentions these three Patriarchs because they in particular are called the fathers of the Hebrews, and it was to them in particular and often that God promised to give the land of Chanaan to their posterity.

paras.t: Et nomen meum Adonai, quod secundum Glossam, interpretatur generaliter Dominus, non indicavi eis, supple, tam clare, ut tibi. Circa quod fertur in Glossa : Non indicavi eis sicut tibi. Per successiones enim ætatum crevit divinæ cognitionis augmentum. Apparuit Deus Abrahæ, locutus est facie ad faciem cum Moyse. David ait : Super senes intellexi. Apostoli Dei Filium præsentem viderunt, et quidquid volebant, interrogabant. Quibus et dictum est : Multi reges et Prophetæ voluerunt videre, quæ vos videtis, et non viderunt. Hæc Glossa. Porro in Scholastica fertur historia : Nomen meum Adonai non indicavi eis, id est fortitudinem et potentiam meam, ad quas pertinet nomen istud, sed pietatem et sapientiam meam, ad quas pertinet Eli, et Eloi. Sed huic dicto objici potest, quod dictum est, Deum dixisse ad Abraham, Ego sum Dominus Deus omnipotens, atque ad Jacob, Ego sum fortissimus Deus. Quod Isaac sciens : Deus, inquit, omnipotens benedicat tibi. Apostolus quoque in epistola ad Romanos de Abraham protestatur, quod non hæsitavit diffidentia, sed confortatus est fide, dans gloriam Deo, plenissime sciens, quia quæcumque promisit Deus, potens est et facere. Itemque : Arbitrans, scilicet ipse Abraham, quia a mortuis suscitare potens est Deus. Rursus fortitudinem et omnipotentiam suam Deus monstravit Abrahæ et Isaac facto, dando eis supernaturalem fecunditatem. Sed et cognoverunt hi Patriarchæ Deum cuncta creasse, sicque omnipotentiam ejus noverunt, sed et pietatem sapientiamque ipsius.
paras.en: [[6:3|And my name ADONAI|Et nomen meum Adonai]], which according to the Gloss is interpreted “Lord” in a general sense, [[6:3|I did not shew them|non indicavi eis]]: understand, so clearly as to thee. On this the Gloss says: [[6:3|I did not shew them|Non indicavi eis]] as I did thee. For with the succession of the ages the knowledge of God grew and increased. God appeared to Abraham; he spoke with Moses face to face. David says: [[Ps 118:100|I have had understanding above ancients|Super senes intellexi]]. The Apostles saw the Son of God present, and asked him whatever they wished; and to them it was said: [[Luke 10:24|many prophets and kings have desired to see the things that you see and have not seen them|Multi reges et Prophetæ voluerunt videre, quæ vos videtis, et non viderunt]] [the margin gives Matth. xiii, 17; the wording, with *kings*, is that of Luke 10:24]. Thus the Gloss. And in the Scholastic History it is said: [[6:3|my name ADONAI I did not shew them|Nomen meum Adonai non indicavi eis]], that is, my strength and power, to which this name belongs, but rather my goodness and wisdom, to which Eli and Eloi belong. But against this saying it may be objected that God is said to have said to Abraham, [[Gen 17:1|I am the Almighty God|Ego sum Dominus Deus omnipotens]], and to Jacob, [[Gen 46:3|I am the most mighty God|Ego sum fortissimus Deus]]. Knowing this, Isaac says: [[Gen 28:3|God almighty bless thee|Deus, inquit, omnipotens benedicat tibi]]. The Apostle too, in the Epistle to the Romans, testifies of Abraham that [[Rom 4:20|he staggered not by distrust: but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God|non hæsitavit diffidentia, sed confortatus est fide, dans gloriam Deo]], [[Rom 4:21|Most fully knowing that whatsoever he has promised, he is able also to perform|plenissime sciens, quia quæcumque promisit Deus, potens est et facere]]. And again: [[Heb 11:19|Accounting|Arbitrans]], that is, Abraham himself, [[Heb 11:19|that God is able to raise up even from the dead|quia a mortuis suscitare potens est Deus]]. Again, God shewed his strength and almighty power to Abraham and Isaac in deed, by giving them a fruitfulness beyond nature. And these Patriarchs knew that God created all things, and so they knew his almighty power, and also his goodness and wisdom.

paras.t: Insuper circa locum hunc scribit Lyra : Aliqui dicunt, quod hoc nomen Adonai significat generale dominium.
