Et quamvis patribus præcedentibus Moysen, Deus ostendit se Dominum totius creaturæ, non tamen ita perfecte, ut Moysi. Contra quod objicit Lyra, quoniam per inundationem diluvii, et conversionem uxoris Lot in statuam salis, in combustione quoque Pentapolis, imo et in mundi creatione, Deus ostendit generale dominium suum. Et talia fecit, qualia et per Moysen egit. Et omnia illa fuerunt Abrahæ notificata. Hæc autem objectio non est fortis. Nam sicut omnia illa ante Moysen facta, fuerunt Abrahæ patefacta, ita et Moysi. Et ultra illa fecit Deus per Moysen multa et præclara prodigia, multo copiosius, quam unquam ante per aliquem hominem unum. Sicque sublimius atque splendidius manifestavit Deus Moysi generale dominium suum ac robur immensum, quam præcedentibus Patriarchis, non solum per miraculosos effectus, sed per illuminationes supernas et apparitiones, ac allocutiones angelicas, quas per annos quadraginta ad libitum habuit.
paras.en: Further, on this place Lyra writes: Some say that this name *Adonai* signifies universal lordship; and although God shewed himself Lord of all creation to the fathers who went before Moses, yet not so perfectly as to Moses. Against this Lyra objects that in the flooding of the deluge, in the turning of Lot's wife into a pillar of salt, in the burning of the Pentapolis [that is, the five cities of the plain, Sodom and its neighbours], and indeed in the creation of the world, God shewed his universal lordship; and he did such things as he also did through Moses; and all these were made known to Abraham. But this objection is not strong. For just as all those things done before Moses were made known to Abraham, so were they to Moses as well; and beyond them God worked through Moses many and glorious wonders, far more abundantly than ever before through any one man. And so God manifested his universal lordship and his boundless might to Moses more sublimely and splendidly than to the Patriarchs before him, not only through miraculous works but through heavenly enlightenments, and appearances and conversations of angels, which he had at will for forty years.

paras.t: Insuper scribit Lyra : Adonai non ponitur hic in Hebræo, sed nomen Dei tetragrammaton, vel Jehovah. Quod quum reputetur ab Hebræis tantæ sanctitatis, ut nominari non debeat, nisi a summo sacerdote, et solum in benedictionibus fiendis in templo, ideo loco ejus pronuntiatur hoc nomen Adonai : velut si apud nos hoc nomen Deus, non esset nominabile ob suam sanctitatem : et ubicumque scriptum est, loco ejus pronuntiaretur Dominus. Porro hoc nomen tetragrammaton, secundum Rabbi Moysen, significat divinam essentiam, prout in se ipsa consistit, circumscripto omni respectu ad alia : idcirco est nomen incommunicabile, solique Deo appropriatum, designans veritatem divinæ essentiæ in se. Hoc præsupposito, aliqui dicunt quod Deus apparens patribus præcedentibus Moysen, non nominavit se eis sub hoc nomine Jehovah. Sed hoc falsum videtur, quoniam in Genesi ubi Dominus ait ad Abraham, Ego sum Dominus qui eduxi te de Ur Chaldæorum, in Hebræo loco hujus nominis Dominus, habetur nomen Domini tetragrammaton : idcirco dicendum, quod hoc nomen tetragrammaton, Deus indicavit hic Moysi, non solum quantum ad vocem, sed etiam quantum ad significatum : quod est proprie indicare. Et hoc primo indicavit Moysi, quando dixit : Ego sum qui sum : quia per hoc nomen significatur necessitas, stabilitas, et plenitudo esse divini, ut dictum est in expositione capituli tertii. Secundo ostendit Moysi nomen istud, quando in raptu vidit clare divinam essentiam, secundum quod in Numeris legitur : Clare et non per ænigmata videt Deum. Neutro autem horum modorum legitur Deus patribus ante Moysen nomen suum tetragrammaton indicasse, sed usus est nomine, vel potius significato nominis, importante respectum ad creaturam. Unde et in Genesi, quando loquendo ad Abraham, usus est nomine suo tetragrammaton, non expressit proprium significatum, sed magis per nomen importans respectum ad creaturam determinavit, dicendo : Ego Dominus qui eduxi te de Ur Chaldæorum. Nulli quoque illorum ostendit essentiam suam clare, ut Moysi.
paras.en: Lyra writes further: *Adonai* is not put here in the Hebrew, but the four-lettered name of God [the *tetragrammaton*, the name written with the four Hebrew letters YHWH], or *Jehovah*. Since this is held by the Hebrews to be of such holiness that it may not be uttered except by the high priest, and only in giving the blessings in the temple, the name *Adonai* is pronounced in its place: as if among us the name *Deus* could not be uttered for its holiness, and wherever it was written, *Dominus* were pronounced in its place. Now this four-lettered name, according to Rabbi Moses [Maimonides], signifies the divine essence as it stands in itself, leaving aside every relation to other things; and therefore it is an incommunicable name, proper to God alone, designating the truth of the divine essence in itself. This being supposed, some say that God, in appearing to the fathers who went before Moses, did not name himself to them by this name *Jehovah*. But this seems false, since in Genesis, where the Lord says to Abraham, [[Gen 15:7|I am the Lord who brought thee out from Ur of the Chaldees|Ego sum Dominus qui eduxi te de Ur Chaldæorum]], the Hebrew has the four-lettered name of the Lord in place of this name *Lord*. Therefore it must be said that God shewed this four-lettered name to Moses here not only as to its sound but also as to its meaning, which is properly to shew it. And he first shewed it to Moses when he said: [[Ex 3:14|I AM WHO AM|Ego sum qui sum]] [the margin’s chapter and verse are lost; the words are Ex 3:14]: for by this name is signified the necessity, stability and fullness of the divine being, as was said in the exposition of the third chapter. Secondly, he shewed Moses this name when in rapture he saw the divine essence clearly, according to what we read in Numbers: [[Num 12:8|plainly, and not by riddles and figures doth he see the Lord|Clare et non per ænigmata videt Deum]] [the margin note here is unreadable; the words are Num 12:8]. But in neither of these ways do we read that God shewed his four-lettered name to the fathers before Moses; rather he used a name, or rather the meaning of a name, that implies a relation to creatures. Hence in Genesis too, when he used his four-lettered name in speaking to Abraham, he did not express its proper meaning, but rather defined it by a name implying a relation to creatures, saying: [[Gen 15:7|I am the Lord who brought thee out from Ur of the Chaldees|Ego Dominus qui eduxi te de Ur Chaldæorum]] [the margin’s numbers are lost here; the words are Gen 15:7 again]. Nor did he shew his essence clearly to any of them, as he did to Moses.

paras.t: Sed contra hæc scribit Rabbi Paulus, et primo reprobat prætactas rationes quas Lyra pro sua expositione inducit, et contra primam earum sic arguit : Indicare nomen secundum vocem tantum, et non secundum significatum, modicæ aut nullius est utilitatis, quum nomina ad significandum ordinentur. Sicque patres ante Moysen inutiliter cognovissent hoc nomen Jehovah. Contra secundam rationem argumentatur, quia dum Deus locutus est Moysi, Apparui Abrahæ, Isaac, et Jacob in Deo omnipotente, Moyses nondum vidit divinam essentiam. Hinc Rabbi Paulus circa hæc aliter sentit, in primis allegans Thomam, dicentem : Ad hoc Deus concedit homini miracula facere, ut per ea probet supernaturalem veritatem, quam docet. Deinde addit, quod quamvis ante Moysis tempora fecit supernaturalia aliqua, ut est tactum, nunquam tamen fuit concessum alicui antiquorum facere miracula, ut verbis ipsius crederetur, ut concessum est Moysi, cui datum est istud, ut ejus legationi ac legislationi crederetur. Lex enim per Moysen data, fuit miraculis confirmanda. Deo autem secundum significationem hujus nominis Jehovah, principaliter convenit miracula facere, in quantum omnipotentia fundatur in puritate et plenitudine infinita esse divini. Hinc Moysi, non patribus ante eum, concessum est miracula facere. Sicque intelligendum est quod dicitur, Nomen meum Adonai non indicavi eis, videlicet dando eis miracula facere, sicut tibi.
paras.en: But against this Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, in his *Additiones* to Lyra] writes, and first rejects the reasons mentioned above which Lyra brings for his exposition. Against the first of them he argues thus: To shew a name only as to its sound, and not as to its meaning, is of little or no use, since names are ordained to signify; and so the fathers before Moses would have known this name *Jehovah* to no purpose. Against the second reason he argues that when God said to Moses that he [[6:3|appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, by the name of God Almighty|Apparui Abrahæ, Isaac, et Jacob in Deo omnipotente]], Moses had not yet seen the divine essence. Hence Rabbi Paul thinks otherwise on this matter, first citing Thomas, who says: God grants man to work miracles for this purpose, that through them he may prove the supernatural truth which he teaches. Then he adds that although before the time of Moses God did some supernatural things, as has been mentioned, yet it was never granted to any of the ancients to work miracles so that his words should be believed, as it was granted to Moses, to whom this was given so that his mission and his lawgiving should be believed; for the Law given through Moses was to be confirmed by miracles. Now to work miracles belongs principally to God according to the meaning of this name *Jehovah*, inasmuch as almighty power is founded in the infinite purity and fullness of the divine being. Hence to Moses, and not to the fathers before him, it was granted to work miracles. And so what is said, [[6:3|my name ADONAI I did not shew them|Nomen meum Adonai non indicavi eis]], is to be understood thus: namely, by granting them to work miracles, as I did thee.

paras.t: Insuper Rabbi Paulus affirmat convenienter dici posse, quod nomen Jehovah non fuit patribus ante Moysen revelatum; atque ad id quod contra hoc objicit Lyra, utpote in Genesi scriptum esse nomen tetragrammaton, ubi habemus, Ego Dominus qui eduxi te, etc., respondet, argumentum istud esse invalidum. Nam illa sunt verba Moysis, describentis ea quæ transierunt inter Deum et Abraham: qui Moyses Deum cognovit sub hoc nomine tetragrammaton, ideo eum sic nominavit. Hæc Rabbi Paulus; qui circa hunc passum multa scribit contra Lyram, quæ quicumque intelligens satis faciliter perpendere valet, non esse idonee introducta; sed prolixitatem vitans, pertranseo. Verumtamen circa id quod asserit Lyra, Deum manifestasse Moysi hoc nomen Jehovah, dum dixit ad eum, Ego sum qui sum, et quod Patriarchis præcedentibus Moysen, non indicavit hoc nomen secundum significatum, sed secundum vocem, non videtur posse salvari. Non enim videtur Abraham, et ei consimiles viri contemplativi sublimiter illuminati, ignorasse, quod Deus sit ipsum purum, incommutabile, infinitum, ac necessarium esse, in se pure consistens, et quod esse sic sumptum, sit proprium nomen Dei, præsertim quum et naturalis ratio dictet hoc, et quidam puri philosophi hoc noverunt. Sanctus quoque Job id novisse videtur, dicendo ad Dominum : Quis potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine? nonne, tu qui solus es? Et rursus: Deus solus est.
paras.en: Further, Rabbi Paul affirms that it may fitly be said that the name *Jehovah* was not revealed to the fathers before Moses; and to what Lyra objects against this, namely that the four-lettered name is written in Genesis, where we have, [[Gen 15:7|I am the Lord who brought thee out|Ego Dominus qui eduxi te]], etc., he answers that this argument is invalid. For those are the words of Moses describing what passed between God and Abraham; and Moses, who knew God under this four-lettered name, therefore named him so. Thus Rabbi Paul, who writes much against Lyra on this passage; anyone of understanding can easily enough judge that it is not fitly brought in, but to avoid prolixity I pass it over. Nevertheless, what Lyra asserts, that God made this name *Jehovah* known to Moses when he said to him, [[Ex 3:14|I AM WHO AM|Ego sum qui sum]], and that he did not shew this name to the Patriarchs before Moses as to its meaning but only as to its sound, does not seem tenable. For it does not seem that Abraham, and contemplative men like him, sublimely enlightened, were ignorant that God is pure, unchangeable, infinite and necessary being itself, subsisting purely in itself, and that being so taken is the proper name of God; especially since natural reason too dictates this, and some mere philosophers knew it. Holy Job also seems to have known it, saying to the Lord: [[Job 14:4|Who can make him clean that is conceived of unclean seed? is it not thou who only art?|Quis potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine? nonne, tu qui solus es?]] And again: God [[Job 23:13|is alone|solus est]].

paras.t: Omnibus ergo pensatis, videtur littera ista sic exponenda: Nomen meum Adonai, hoc est universale dominium meum et omnipotentiam meam, seu nomen meum Jehovah, quod nude et pure designat divinam essentiam, non indicavi Abrahæ et Isaac et Jacob tam copiose et evidenter, ut tibi. Vel, non indicavi eorum alicui nomen istud Jehovah: si tamen verum est quod Rabbi Paulus insinuat, dicens, quod Moysi primo sit revelatum hoc nomen. Dicit etiam Rabbi Paulus, Nomen istud Jehovah, nunquam pronuntiatur ab Hebræis, prout in littera jacet ac scribitur, sed ubique loco ejus pronuntiant hoc nomen Adonai. Nec nomen illud tetragrammaton transferibile est: ideo translatores tam Chaldæi quam Latini, et etiam Arabici, loco illius transtulerunt Dominum, quod est translatio nominis hujus Adonai, non autem proprie nominis hujus tetragrammaton. Ideo dicit Rabbi Paulus, quod nomen istud Jehovah tantum significat, atque impositum est ex institutione divina, non humana: alias nomen hoc, seu ejus significatio, innotuisset saltem scientibus linguam Hebræam: cujus oppositum constat ex hoc, quod nec Moyses, nec filii Israel cognoverunt hoc nomen ante ipsius revelationem.
paras.en: All things considered, then, this text seems to be expounded thus: [[6:3|my name ADONAI|Nomen meum Adonai]], that is, my universal lordship and my almighty power, or my name *Jehovah*, which designates the divine essence nakedly and purely, [[6:3|I did not shew|non indicavi]] to Abraham and Isaac and Jacob so abundantly and evidently as to thee. Or: I did not shew this name *Jehovah* to any of them, if indeed what Rabbi Paul suggests is true, when he says that this name was first revealed to Moses. Rabbi Paul also says that this name *Jehovah* is never pronounced by the Hebrews as it stands and is written in the text, but everywhere they pronounce the name *Adonai* in its place. Nor can that four-lettered name be translated; and so the translators, Chaldean as well as Latin and Arabic too, have put *Lord* in its place, which is the translation of this name *Adonai*, not properly of the four-lettered name. And so Rabbi Paul says that this name *Jehovah* only signifies [that is, has its meaning only], and was imposed by divine, not human, institution: otherwise this name, or its meaning, would have been known at least to those who knew the Hebrew tongue; the opposite of which is clear from this, that neither Moses nor the children of Israel knew this name before its revelation.

paras.t: Pepigique fœdus cum eis, id est, ipsis promisi, pactumque inii, ut darem illis, hoc est posteritati eorum, terram Chanaan, terram peregrinationis eorum in qua fuerunt advenæ. Ego audivi gemitum filiorum Israel, id est, ad succurrendum nunc consideravi, et preces eorum cum gemitu fusas, jam exaudire decrevi; quo Ægyptii oppresserunt eos; et recordatus sum pacti mei, etc., id est, per modum reminiscentis me habeo, per effectum nunc demonstrando, quod intendo et implere jam volo promissionem præfatam.
paras.en: [[6:4|And I made a covenant with them|Pepigique fœdus cum eis]], that is, I promised them and entered into a pact with them, [[6:4|to give them|ut darem illis]], that is, to their posterity, [[6:4|the land of Chanaan, the land of their pilgrimage wherein they were strangers|terram Chanaan, terram peregrinationis eorum in qua fuerunt advenæ]]. [[6:5|I have heard the groaning of the children of Israel|Ego audivi gemitum filiorum Israel]], that is, I have now considered them, to help them, and have resolved now to hear their prayers poured out with groaning; [[6:5|wherewith the Egyptians have oppressed them|quo Ægyptii oppresserunt eos]]; [[6:5|and I have remembered my covenant|et recordatus sum pacti mei]], etc., that is, I behave like one who remembers, shewing now in deed that I intend, and now will, to fulfil the promise spoken of.

paras.t: Ego Dominus qui educam vos de ergastulo Ægyptiorum, hoc est de terra Ægypti, in qua demorati ac tribulati estis quasi in carcere. Porro ergastulum proprie dicitur locus, in quo rei ad opera facienda relegabantur. Et eruam vos de servitute, ac redimam vos in brachio extento, id est per evidentem et efficacem potentiam. Loquitur autem Deus de se ipso metaphorice, quasi de homine qui brachium suum extendit ad subveniendum. Et judiciis magnis, id est per miracula, hoc est miraculosos effectus punitivos, ex divina justitia magnifice infligendos Ægyptiis. Et assumam vos mihi in populum, id est, ad gloriam meam faciam vos devotos majestatis meæ cultores; et ero vester Deus per specialem provisionem et gratiam. Hoc impletum est, quando in monte Sinai acceperunt legem a Deo, ubi et Deus desponsavit sibi Synagogam, prout in Ezechiele fatetur, quando et filii Israel locuti sunt: Omnia quæ præcepit nobis Dominus Deus noster, faciemus, et erimus obedientes. Et scietis per experientiam beneficiorum meorum, et per mirabilia pro vestra liberatione patranda, quia ego sum Dominus Deus vester, qui mea potestate ac providentia vobis misericorditer dominor, et opem exhibeo: nam omnium Deus, dicitur specialiter Deus eorum, quibus specialia gratiæ dona confert; qui eduxerim vos de ergastulo Ægyptiorum, et induxerim vos in terram super quam levavi manum meam, id est, in qua potentiam declarare decrevi, dando vobis potenter eamdem, ut darem eam Abraham, Isaac et Jacob; daboque illam vobis possidendam, etc., si tamen vos ipsi non posueritis obicem. Non enim ingressi sunt eam propter murmurationes, perversitates, et diffidentias suas.
paras.en: [[6:6|I am the Lord who will bring you out from the work-prison of the Egyptians|Ego Dominus qui educam vos de ergastulo Ægyptiorum]], that is, from the land of Egypt, in which you have stayed and been afflicted as in a prison. Now an *ergastulum* [the word the Douay-Rheims renders “work-prison”] properly means a place to which the guilty were sent to do forced labour. [[6:6|And will deliver you from bondage|Et eruam vos de servitute]], [[6:6|and redeem you with a high arm|ac redimam vos in brachio extento]] [Denis reads *extento*, “stretched out”, where the Clementine text has *excelso*, “high”], that is, by evident and effective power. God speaks of himself here in a figure, as of a man who stretches out his arm to help. [[6:6|And great judgments|Et judiciis magnis]], that is, by miracles, that is, by miraculous punishments to be inflicted magnificently on the Egyptians by the divine justice. [[6:7|And I will take you to myself for my people|Et assumam vos mihi in populum]], that is, for my glory I will make you devout worshippers of my majesty; [[6:7|I will be your God|et ero vester Deus]] by special providence and grace. This was fulfilled when on Mount Sinai they received the Law from God[[Ex 20:3||]], where God also espoused the Synagogue to himself, as is declared in Ezechiel[[Ezech 36:24||]] [the margin gives Ezech. xxxvi, 24 and following; the espousal itself is told at Ezech 16:8], and when the children of Israel said: [[Ex 24:7|All things that the Lord hath spoken, we will do, we will be obedient|Omnia quæ præcepit nobis Dominus Deus noster, faciemus, et erimus obedientes]] [the margin gives Exod. xxiv, 3; Denis’s words, with *we will be obedient*, are closest to Ex 24:7]. [[6:7|And you shall know|Et scietis]] by the experience of my benefits, and through the wonders to be worked for your deliverance, [[6:7|that I am the Lord your God|quia ego sum Dominus Deus vester]], who by my power and providence rule over you in mercy and give you help: for the God of all is called in a special way the God of those on whom he bestows special gifts of grace; [[6:7|who brought you out from the work-prison of the Egyptians|qui eduxerim vos de ergastulo Ægyptiorum]], [[6:8|And brought you into the land, concerning which I lifted up my hand|et induxerim vos in terram super quam levavi manum meam]], that is, in which I have resolved to declare my power, by giving it to you mightily, [[6:8|to give it to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob|ut darem eam Abraham, Isaac et Jacob]]; [[6:8|and I will give it you to possess|daboque illam vobis possidendam]], etc., provided, however, that you yourselves do not put an obstacle in the way. For they did not enter it, because of their murmurings, their perversities and their distrust.

paras.t: Narravit ergo Moyses omnia, id est, præfata Dei promissa consolatoria exposuit, filiis Israel. Qui non acquieverunt ei, id est, verbis ejus non crediderunt sinceriter, nec consolationem acceperunt ex eis, propter angustiam spiritus et opus durissimum, id est ob nimiam suam afflictionem in corde et corpore. Erant enim pleni mœrore et anxietate in anima. Exterioribus quoque laboribus inhumaniter premebantur. Hujusmodi autem excessivæ passiones et afflictiones actum rationis impediunt, præsertim in imperfectis, quales fuerunt hi vulgares in populo Israel. Aliqui tamen seniores et meliores in eis, Moysi crediderunt.
paras.en: [[6:9|And Moses told all this|Narravit ergo Moyses omnia]], that is, set forth the comforting promises of God spoken of, [[6:9|to the children of Israel|filiis Israel]]: [[6:9|but they did not hearken to him|Qui non acquieverunt ei]], that is, they did not sincerely believe his words, nor take comfort from them, [[6:9|for anguish of spirit, and most painful work|propter angustiam spiritus et opus durissimum]], that is, because of their excessive affliction in heart and body. For they were full of grief and anxiety in soul, and outwardly too they were inhumanly oppressed with labours. Now such excessive passions and afflictions hinder the act of reason, especially in the imperfect, such as were these common folk among the people of Israel. Some of the elders and better men among them, however, believed Moses.

paras.t: Locutusque est Dominus ad Moysen, dicens: Ingredere, et loquere ad Pharaonem regem Ægypti, ut dimittat filios Israel de terra sua. Respondit Moyses: Ecce filii Israel non me audiunt auribus cordis, id est, non obtemperant mihi: et quomodo audiet me Pharao? quasi dicat, Multo minus acquiescet sermonibus meis. Hoc Moyses dixit, non contra Dominum proterviendo aut inobediendo, sed se humiliter excusando, et difficultatem negotii allegando. In talibus quippe, ubi alicui quid jubetur, quod ad ejus excellentiam pertinet, non est contra perfectionem obedientiæ, difficultatem et excusationem inducere. Præsertim quum incircumcisus sim labiis, id est ineptus ad loquendum coram rege, sicut expositum est.
paras.en: [[6:10|And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying|Locutusque est Dominus ad Moysen, dicens]]: [[6:11|Go in, and speak to Pharao king of Egypt, that he let the children of Israel go out of his land|Ingredere, et loquere ad Pharaonem regem Ægypti, ut dimittat filios Israel de terra sua]]. [[6:12|Moses answered|Respondit Moyses]]: [[6:12|Behold the children of Israel do not hearken to me|Ecce filii Israel non me audiunt]] with the ears of the heart, that is, they do not obey me: [[6:12|and how will Pharao hear me|et quomodo audiet me Pharao?]] As if to say: much less will he consent to my words. Moses said this not in insolence or disobedience against the Lord, but humbly excusing himself and pleading the difficulty of the task. For in such things, where someone is bidden to do what belongs to his own exaltation, it is not against the perfection of obedience to put forward the difficulty and to excuse oneself. [[6:12|Especially as I am of uncircumcised lips|Præsertim quum incircumcisus sim labiis]], that is, unfit to speak before a king, as has been explained.

paras.t: Circa quod Lyra scribit: Incircumcisus labiis proprie dicitur, qui verbis superfluis utitur: quod non est credendum de Moyse; sed large accipiendo, trahitur ad quemcumque defectum eloquentiæ designandum: sicque dicitur de Moyse, ex vocis suæ gracilitate. Contra hoc scribit Rabbi Paulus: Incircumcisus labiis magis proprie videtur dicendus, qui habet in labiis aliquod corporale impedimentum, quo prolatio litterarum quæ labiis proferuntur, impeditur. Unde supra conquerebatur Moyses de impedimento loquelæ ex parte oris et linguæ, nunc autem addit, ex parte labiorum: ut ita ostenderet, quod organa corporea, quibus verba exprimuntur, erant in eo inepta ad loquendum. De vocis autem gracilitate non fit mentio ulla in littera, nec oportet hoc fingere, præsertim quum Moyses in ultima sua senectute legatur omnibus filiis Israel simul locutus, ut in Deuteronomio patet: quod cum vocis tenuitate esse non potuit.
paras.en: On this Lyra writes: He is properly called of uncircumcised lips who uses superfluous words, which is not to be believed of Moses; but taken broadly, it is stretched to signify any defect of eloquence, and so it is said of Moses on account of the slenderness of his voice[[Ex 4:10||]]. Against this Rabbi Paul writes: He seems more properly to be called of uncircumcised lips who has some bodily impediment in the lips, by which the utterance of the letters that are pronounced with the lips is hindered. Hence above Moses complained of an impediment of speech on the part of the mouth and tongue, but now he adds, on the part of the lips: so as to shew that the bodily organs by which words are uttered were unfit in him for speaking. Of slenderness of voice, however, no mention at all is made in the text, nor need it be invented, especially since Moses in his extreme old age is read to have spoken to all the children of Israel together, as is plain in Deuteronomy[[Deut 33:1||]]; which could not have been with a thin voice.

paras.t: Ad ista respondeo, quod in Scripturis incircumcisio magis adscribitur corporalibus membris et organis, propter spiritualem, quam ob corporalem defectum. Et hoc in libris Prophetarum frequenter innuitur, in quibus incircumcisæ dicuntur aures Israelitarum. In Actis quoque S. Stephanus loquitur ad Judæos : Dura cervice et incircumcisi corde et auribus, vos semper resistitis Spiritui Sancto. Porro quod Moyses gracilem linguam habuerit, supra ex doctoribus catholicis et Hebræis probatum est, ideo non est hoc repudiandum fictitium. Denique, quod Rabbi Paulus asserit in Scriptura mentionem non fieri de hoc quod Moyses fuerit gracilis ac tenuis vocis, falsum censetur, saltem secundum antiquam translationem. Nam Septuaginta interpretes transtulerunt : Ecce ego gracili voce sum. Qua translatione utens Augustinus, disseruit : Non videtur se excusare de vocis gracilitate tantum propter multitudinem populi, sed etiam propter unum hominem, scilicet Pharaonem. Sed mirum si tam gracilis exstitit vocis, quod nec ab uno potuit audiri. An forte regius fastus non permitteret eum de proximo loqui ? Siquidem qui coram regibus habent loqui, a remote stare et loqui solent. Hæc Augustinus. Postremo, quod objicitur, Moysen per se esse locutum filiis Israel in senio suo, faciliter solvitur. Nam et qui gracilem habent vocem, interdum sibi vim faciunt ad loquendum quid altius. Poteratque gratia supplere defectum naturæ ad loquendum in Moyse, quod et Aaron jam defuncto, rationabiliter creditur factum.
paras.en: To this I answer that in the Scriptures uncircumcision is ascribed to the members and organs of the body more on account of a spiritual than a bodily defect. And this is often suggested in the books of the Prophets, in which the ears of the Israelites are called uncircumcised[[Jer 6:10||]] [the margin note here is unreadable; Jer 6:10 is such a place]. In the Acts too St. Stephen says to the Jews: [[Acts 7:51|You stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Ghost|Dura cervice et incircumcisi corde et auribus, vos semper resistitis Spiritui Sancto]] [the margin note here too is unreadable; the words are Acts 7:51]. Moreover, that Moses had a slender tongue was proved above from Catholic and Hebrew doctors; and so it is not to be rejected as an invention. Lastly, what Rabbi Paul asserts, that no mention is made in Scripture of Moses having been of a slender and thin voice, is judged false, at least according to the ancient translation. For the Seventy translators rendered: Behold, I am of a slender voice [the Old Latin rendering of the Septuagint at v. 30 of this chapter, where the Vulgate has “I am of uncircumcised lips”]. Using this translation, Augustine discussed it thus: He seems to excuse himself on account of the slenderness of his voice not only because of the multitude of the people, but also because of one man, namely Pharao. But it is strange if he was of so slender a voice that he could not be heard even by one man. Or perhaps the pride of royalty did not allow him to speak from close by? For those who have to speak before kings are wont to stand at a distance and speak. Thus Augustine. Finally, the objection that Moses himself spoke to the children of Israel in his old age is easily answered. For even those who have a slender voice sometimes force themselves to say something more loudly; and grace could make up for the defect of nature in Moses’ speaking, which it is reasonably believed was done once Aaron was dead.

paras.t: Locutusque est Dominus ad Moysen et Aaron, et dedit mandatum ad filios Israel, et ad Pharaonem regem Ægypti, id est, præcepit eis aliquid, quod pertinebat ad Hebræos ac regem Ægypti, videlicet ut educerent filios Israel de terra Ægypti. Per quod docemur, quod Dei voluntas sit, ut qui præsident aliis, non cito neque faciliter ab illorum, quamvis duri exsistant, exhortatione et informatione desistant ; sed eamdem sæpius repetendo, tandem verba salutis cordi illorum inculcent, sicut ad Timotheum scribit Apostolus : Prædica verbum, insta opportune, importune, argue, obsecra, increpa in omni patientia.
paras.en: [[6:13|And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, and he gave them a charge unto the children of Israel, and unto Pharao the king of Egypt|Locutusque est Dominus ad Moysen et Aaron, et dedit mandatum ad filios Israel, et ad Pharaonem regem Ægypti]], that is, he commanded them something which concerned the Hebrews and the king of Egypt, namely [[6:13|that they should bring forth the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt|ut educerent filios Israel de terra Ægypti]]. By this we are taught that it is God’s will that those who are set over others should not quickly or easily give up exhorting and instructing them, however hard they may be, but by repeating it often should at last press the words of salvation into their hearts; as the Apostle writes to Timothy: [[2 Tim 4:2|Preach the word: be instant in season, out of season: reprove, entreat, rebuke in all patience|Prædica verbum, insta opportune, importune, argue, obsecra, increpa in omni patientia]].

paras.t: Deinceps Moyses sui ipsius ac fratris sui prosapiam diligenter describit, ne in persona legislatoris Hebræorum quis erret. Isti sunt principes domorum per familias suas, id est, hi qui statim nominabuntur, sunt patres et capita tribuum ex se progenitarum in cognationibus suis. Filii Ruben primogeniti Israelis, id est Jacob patriarchæ, qui alio nomine dictus est Israel, fuerunt Henoch et Phallu, Esron et Charmi. Quamvis enim Ruben fuit primus et generalis pater omnium a se descendentium, tamen quatuor filii ejus fuerunt principales, unusquisque eorum inter natos ex semine suo. Deinde in littera exprimuntur filii Simeonis, quorum unusquisque exstitit princeps et caput prosapiæ ex se ortæ.
paras.en: Next Moses carefully describes his own and his brother’s lineage, so that no one may go astray about the person of the Hebrews’ lawgiver. [[6:14|These are the heads of their houses by their families|Isti sunt principes domorum per familias suas]], that is, those who will be named straightaway are the fathers and heads of the tribes descended from them, in their kindreds. [[6:14|The sons of Ruben the firstborn of Israel|Filii Ruben primogeniti Israelis]], that is, of Jacob the patriarch, who by another name was called Israel[[Gen 32:28||]], were [[6:14|Henoch and Phallu, Hesron and Charmi|Henoch et Phallu, Esron et Charmi]]. For although Ruben was the first and general father of all descended from him, yet his four sons were chief, each of them among those born of his own seed. Then the text names the sons of Simeon, each of whom was prince and head of the line sprung from him.

paras.t: Et hæc nomina filiorum Levi patriarchæ per cognationes suas, Gerson et Caath et Merari. Ex quibus natæ sunt tres familiæ Levitarum, videlicet Gersonitæ, Caathitæ et Meraritæ, ut infra, præsertim in libro Numerorum, copiose describitur. Anni autem vitæ Levi fuerunt centum triginta et septem. Et ita vixit decem annis minus quam Jacob.
paras.en: [[6:16|And these are the names of the sons of Levi|Et hæc nomina filiorum Levi]] the patriarch [[6:16|by their kindreds: Gerson, and Caath, and Merari|per cognationes suas, Gerson et Caath et Merari]]. From these were born the three families of the Levites, namely the Gersonites, the Caathites and the Merarites, as is described at length below, especially in the book of Numbers[[Num 26:57||]]. [[6:16|And the years of the life of Levi were a hundred and thirty-seven|Anni autem vitæ Levi fuerunt centum triginta et septem]]. And so he lived ten years less than Jacob.

paras.t: Accepit autem Amram uxorem Jochabed patruelem suam, id est neptem ex patruo, ut plenius secundo capitulo exstat expositum. Quæ peperit ei Aaron, et Moysen, et Mariam. Quæ quamvis ultimo loco nunc ponatur propter sexum inferiorem, tamen ante Aaron et Moysen fuit nata.
paras.en: [[6:20|And Amram took to wife Jochabed his aunt by the father's side|Accepit autem Amram uxorem Jochabed patruelem suam]], that is, a kinswoman [*neptis*] through his father’s brother [Denis takes *patruelis* as kin through a paternal uncle; the Douay-Rheims renders it “his aunt by the father’s side”], as was explained more fully in the second chapter. [[6:20|and she bore him Aaron and Moses|Quæ peperit ei Aaron, et Moysen]], and Mary [Denis’s text adds Mary here, as the Septuagint does; the Clementine Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims name only Aaron and Moses]. And although she is now put in the last place because of the weaker sex, yet she was born before Aaron and Moses.

paras.t: Accepit autem Aaron uxorem Elisabeth, filiam Aminadab, sororem Naasson, quæ peperit ei Nadab, et Abiu et Eleazar et Ithamar. Circa hoc scribit Lyra : Elisabeth filia Aminadab, fuit de tribu regia, quoniam propter dignitatem sacerdotalem tribus regia et sacerdotalis fuerunt commixtæ. Circa quod dico, quod tempore illius connubii, nec regia dignitas data fuit, aut inerat tribui Judæ, de qua fuit Aminadab, nec sacerdotalis dignitas fuit collata tribui Levi, de qua exstitit Aaron. Et quamvis Jacob prophetaverat regiam dignitatem tribui Judæ præstandam, tamen sacerdotii eminentiam tribui Levi esse donandam, prophetatum non fuit, neque innotuit ideo dictum illud non videtur alienum, nisi forsan quis dicat, Deo disponente sic factum esse, quoniam Deus præcognovit duabus tribubus illis præfatas dignitates fore contribuendas, quæ ambæ in Christo sunt counitæ.
paras.en: [[6:23|And Aaron took to wife Elizabeth the daughter of Aminadab, sister of Nahason, who bore him Nadab, and Abiu, and Eleazar, and Ithamar.|Accepit autem Aaron uxorem Elisabeth, filiam Aminadab, sororem Naasson, quæ peperit ei Nadab, et Abiu et Eleazar et Ithamar]]. On this Lyra writes: Elizabeth the daughter of Aminadab was of the royal tribe, for on account of the priestly dignity the royal and priestly tribes were mingled. On this I say that at the time of that marriage the royal dignity had neither been given to nor belonged to the tribe of Juda, of which Aminadab was, nor had the priestly dignity been conferred on the tribe of Levi, of which Aaron was. And although Jacob had prophesied that the royal dignity was to be given to the tribe of Juda[[Gen 49:8||]] [the margin gives Gen. xlix, 8–10], yet that the eminence of the priesthood was to be bestowed on the tribe of Levi was not prophesied, nor was it known; and so that saying does not seem to hold, unless perhaps one says that it was so done by God’s disposing, since God foreknew that those dignities were to be bestowed on those two tribes, both of which are united in Christ.

paras.t: At vero Eleazar filius Aaron, accepit uxorem de filiabus Phutiel : quem Hebræi dicunt fuisse Jethro, ut refert Lyra : quod verum non reor; sed Eleazar accepit uxorem ante egressum ex Ægypto : nam usque ad tempus illud non videtur habuisse notitiam Jethro illius.
paras.en: [[6:25|But Eleazar the son of Aaron took a wife of the daughters of Phutiel|At vero Eleazar filius Aaron, accepit uxorem de filiabus Phutiel]]: who, the Hebrews say, was Jethro, as Lyra reports; which I do not think true; but Eleazar took a wife before the going out from Egypt, for up to that time he does not seem to have had any knowledge of that Jethro.

paras.t: Hi, scilicet præfati tres filii Levi, sunt principes tribuum Leviticarum per familias suas. Iste est Aaron et Moyses, quibus præcepit Dominus, ut educerent filios Israel de terra Ægypti per turmas suas, etc. Interdum in textu Aaron exprimitur ante Moysen dum combinantur, interdum contra. Dicique potest, quod Moyses aliquando exprimit Aaron ante se, quoniam senior eo fuit, et in summum pontificem præelectus, atque in eloquentia præcellebat ; quandoque vero prænominat se, quoniam absolute principalior fuit et legislator, quem et Aaron ipse suum dominum appellavit. Iste est Moyses et Aaron, etc. Sicut Magister in historiis tangit, et Glossa ex Strabo allegat, Esdras ex suo addidit verbum istud, qui omnem bibliothecam Judæorum post Babylonicam captivitatem recuperavit, cunctis libris a Nabuchodonosor succensis; vel Moyses de se ipso, tanquam de alio loquitur : quod verius puto.
paras.en: [[6:25|These|Hi]], namely the three sons of Levi spoken of, [[6:25|are the heads of the Levitical families by their kindreds|sunt principes tribuum Leviticarum per familias suas]] [Denis reads *tribuum*, “tribes”, and *per familias suas*]. [[6:26|These are Aaron and Moses, whom the Lord commanded to bring forth the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt by their companies|Iste est Aaron et Moyses, quibus præcepit Dominus, ut educerent filios Israel de terra Ægypti per turmas suas]], etc. Sometimes in the text Aaron is named before Moses when they are joined, sometimes the other way round. And it may be said that Moses sometimes names Aaron before himself because he was older than he, and chosen beforehand as high priest, and excelled in eloquence; but sometimes he names himself first, because he was simply the more principal and the lawgiver, whom Aaron himself called his lord. [[6:27|These are that Moses and Aaron|Iste est Moyses et Aaron]], etc. As the Master [Peter Comestor] touches on in the Histories, and the Gloss cites from Strabo, Esdras, who restored the whole library of the Jews after the Babylonian captivity when all the books had been burnt by Nabuchodonosor, added this phrase of his own; or else Moses speaks of himself as of another, which I think the truer.

paras.t: Præterea mystica intelligentia hujus capituli ex præhabitis satis videtur patere.
paras.en: Furthermore, the mystical sense of this chapter seems clear enough from what has been said before.

paras.t: Moraliter vero ex isto capitulo instruimur, qualiter Deus omnipotens, pius, justus ac sapiens, suos permittit electos in vita hac ab impiis graviter ac multipliciter tribulari, finaliter tamen eos non deserit; imo et in ipsis eorum tribulationibus multipliciter consolatur eosdem per prædicatores atque prælatos, per angelicam inspirationem et consolationem divinam, denuntiant eis, quod in terram cælestis Jerusalem, in regionem civium superiorum ab Ægypto (id est hoc sæculo nequam) perducturus sit eos : quod quidam in afflictionibus positi non advertunt. Ideo in omni hujusmodi adversitate sint in Domino immobiliter confidentes, atque in persecutionibus gloriantes, certi quod Deus suos non deserit, et per adversa misericordissime providet ipsis, veniam gratiamque largitur, et felicitatem accelerat.
paras.en: In the moral sense, we are taught by this chapter how God, almighty, good, just and wise, permits his elect to be grievously and in many ways afflicted by the wicked in this life, yet in the end does not forsake them; nay, in their very afflictions he consoles them in many ways through preachers and prelates, and by the inspiration of angels and divine consolation they announce to them that he will lead them out of Egypt (that is, this wicked world) into the land of the heavenly Jerusalem, into the country of the citizens on high; which some, set in afflictions, do not heed. Therefore in every such adversity let them trust unshakably in the Lord, and glory in persecutions, sure that God does not forsake his own, but through adversities provides for them most mercifully, grants them pardon and grace, and hastens their happiness.

paras.t: Rursus docemur ex dictis, exemplo sancti Moysis, humilitatem amplecti, et omnem detestari ambitionem; nostram quoque insufficientiam et defectuositatem in donis naturæ ac gratiæ, ex sincero corde humiliter, imo et sæpius allegare, ut ex promotione, etiam dum non quæsita offertur, sic evadamus. Quod, proh dolor! multi non advertentes, præcipitant semetipsos, proni ad regimen aliorum, qui nec se ipsos regere queunt nec regunt.
paras.en: Again we are taught by what has been said, after the example of holy Moses, to embrace humility and to abhor all ambition; and also humbly, from a sincere heart, and often, to plead our insufficiency and defectiveness in the gifts of nature and of grace, so that thus we may escape promotion, even when it is offered unsought. Not heeding this, alas, many cast themselves headlong, eager to rule others, who neither can nor do rule themselves.

paras.t: Præterea circa textum inquiritur, cur Moyses præfatas tres tribus, videlicet Ruben, Simeon et Levi, easque dumtaxat, hoc loco describit. Et respondendum, quod ideo, ut designet ducatum Israeliticæ plebis non esse commissum alicui viro ex primogenito Jacob nato, neque alicui nato ex secundogenito ejus, scilicet Simeone, sed ex tertiogenito ejus, puta ex Levi : ideo ultra tribum Levi non descendit ad alias tribus. In Glossa quoque habetur : Non primam aut secundam, sed tertiam tribum elegit Deus in sacerdotium et ducatum : quia in nomine sanctæ ac summæ Trinitatis consecrati sunt sacerdotes, ut fidem Trinitatis in se conservare, et alios studeant edocere, et quoniam numero impare gaudet Deus.
paras.en: Furthermore, it is asked about the text why Moses describes here these three tribes, namely Ruben, Simeon and Levi, and those alone. And we must answer that he does so to shew that the leadership of the people of Israel was not entrusted to any man born of Jacob’s firstborn, nor to any born of his second son, namely Simeon, but to one from his third son, namely Levi: and so he does not go on beyond the tribe of Levi to the other tribes. The Gloss also says: God chose not the first or the second but the third tribe for the priesthood and the leadership, because the priests are consecrated in the name of the holy and supreme Trinity, so that they may be zealous to keep the faith of the Trinity in themselves and to teach it to others; and because God delights in an odd number.

paras.t: Rursus, secundum Strabum, Amram interpretatur pater excelsus, per quem significatur Christus. Jochabed vero interpretatur gratia Dei, per quam significatur Ecclesia. Ex Christo igitur et Ecclesia nascitur Moyses, id est lex spiritualis, et Aaron, id est sacerdotium verum. Amplius circa illud, Accepit Aaron uxorem Elisabeth, ait Glossa : De tribu Juda fuit uxor Aaron. Nondum enim præceptum erat, ut unusquisque de tribu sua conjugem duceret. Ideo autem hæ tribus, puta Levitica et regalis, tunc matrimonio jungebantur, ut intelligeretur Christus ex eis futurus, qui est rex et summus sacerdos.
paras.en: Again, according to Strabo, *Amram* is interpreted “lofty father”, by whom Christ is signified; and *Jochabed* is interpreted “grace of God”, by which the Church is signified. From Christ, then, and the Church is born Moses, that is, the spiritual law, and Aaron, that is, the true priesthood. Further, on the words [[6:23|Aaron took to wife Elizabeth|Accepit Aaron uxorem Elisabeth]], the Gloss says: Aaron’s wife was of the tribe of Juda; for it had not yet been commanded that each should take a wife of his own tribe. And these tribes, the Levitical and the royal, were joined in marriage at that time so that it might be understood that Christ was to come from them, who is king and high priest[[Heb 7:1||]] [the margin gives Hebr. vii].

7.title: Expositio capituli septimi: Et locutus est Dominus ad Moysen, dicens: Ego Dominus
7.title_en: Exposition of the seventh chapter: And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: I am the Lord

paras.t: Excellentia et efficacia, quas Deus contulit Moysi in verbis et signis ac aliis supernaturalibus donis, in præsenti describuntur capitulo. Et locutus est Dominus ad Moysen, dicens: Ego Dominus. Quasi dicat: Quam verum est, quod ego solus sum omnium Dominator omnipotens, qui solo jussu omnia possum, tam securus et constans esse debes in his, quæ tibi dico ac jubeo, et certus de veritate verborum meorum. Ideo subditur: Loquere ad Pharaonem regem Ægypti omnia quæ loquor tibi, ita ut prorsus non timeas eum.
paras.en: The excellence and power which God conferred on Moses in words and signs and other supernatural gifts are described in the present chapter. [[Ex 6:29|And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: I am the Lord|Et locutus est Dominus ad Moysen, dicens: Ego Dominus]]. As if he said: As truly as I alone am the almighty Ruler of all things, who can do all things by my command alone, so secure and steadfast oughtest thou to be in the things that I say and command to thee, and certain of the truth of my words. Therefore it is added: [[Ex 6:29|speak thou to Pharao, king of Egypt, all that I say to thee|Loquere ad Pharaonem regem Ægypti omnia quæ loquor tibi]], so that thou fear him not at all.

paras.t: Et ait Moyses: En incircumcisus labiis sum. Quomodo audiet me Pharao? id est, qualiter acquiescet verbis meis? Non ex diffidentia, sed ex humilitate ait hoc Moyses, non obstante quod jam ante dixerit ei Deus, quod loqueretur Aaron pro eo. Et forsan nunc rursus allegavit insufficientiam suæ loquelæ, quoniam Dominus dixit ad eum, Loquere ad Pharaonem; et non addidit, Per Aaron loquere ei. Hinc Dominus pandit ac subdit modum, qualiter audiret Pharao Moysen.
paras.en: [[Ex 6:30|And Moses said|Et ait Moyses]]: [[Ex 6:30|Lo I am of uncircumcised lips, how will Pharao hear me?|En incircumcisus labiis sum. Quomodo audiet me Pharao?]] that is, how will he give heed to my words? Moses says this not from distrust but from humility, notwithstanding that God had already told him before that Aaron would speak for him[[Ex 4:16||]]. And perhaps he now again pleaded the insufficiency of his speech because the Lord had said to him, [[Ex 6:29|speak thou to Pharao|Loquere ad Pharaonem]], and had not added, Speak to him through Aaron. Hence the Lord sets out and adds the manner in which Pharao would hear Moses.

paras.t: Dixitque Dominus ad Moysen: Ecce constitui te deum Pharaonis, id est, quasdam divinas excellentias tibi do super eum, ita ut instar Dei possis ei præcipere, comminari, nocere et subvenire. Sicque per participationem quamdam dici poteris deus ipsius. Nam quamvis sit unus solus verus Deus substantialiter, tamen participative sunt plures dii, in quantum aliquid divinarum proprietatum et excellentiarum ac potestatum participant in judiciaria potestate, sapientia, sanctitate, præsidentia, signis, virtutibus atque miraculis. Propter quod scriptum est: Non est similis tui in diis, Domine. Et: Quoniam dii fortes terræ vehementer elevati sunt. Itemque: Ego dixi, dii estis. Circa quod ait in Evangelio Christus: Illos dixit deos, ad quos sermo Dei factus est. Et Aaron frater tuus erit propheta tuus, id est, quæ ventura sunt, ex mea revelatione ei denuntiabis, et ipse ex parte tui illa loquetur, sicque per modum prophetæ habebit se ad te. Nam ille vocatur propheta, cui Deus contingentia futura revelat, et ille ex parte Dei illa prædicit. Unde Dominus hoc loco non ait, Aaron erit propheta; sed, Erit propheta tuus: sicut nec Moysi dixerat absolute, Constitui te deum, sed addidit, Pharaonis. Sicque in verbis istis servavit Deus metaphoram, quoniam juxta analogiam seu proportionem qua constituit Moysen deum Pharaonis, constituit et ipsum Aaron prophetam Moysis. Nam soli vero Deo proprie competit habere Prophetam, quoniam futurorum pure contingentium certa præcognitio ponitur propria Deo, nec competit aliis, nisi in quantum revelatur ipsis a Domino. Propter quod loquitur Isaias: Quæ ventura sunt, annuntiate nobis, et sciemus quia dii estis vos.
paras.en: [[7:1|And the Lord said to Moses|Dixitque Dominus ad Moysen]]: [[7:1|Behold, I have appointed thee the god of Pharao|Ecce constitui te deum Pharaonis]], that is, I give thee certain divine excellences over him, so that like God thou canst command him, threaten, harm and help him. And so by a certain participation thou canst be called his god. For although there is substantially only one true God, yet by participation there are many gods, in so far as they share in something of the divine properties, excellences and powers: in judicial power, wisdom, holiness, rule, signs, mighty works and miracles. For which reason it is written: [[Ps 85:8|There is none among the gods like unto thee, O Lord|Non est similis tui in diis, Domine]]. And: [[Ps 46:10|for the strong gods of the earth are exceedingly exalted|Quoniam dii fortes terræ vehementer elevati sunt]]. And again: [[Ps 81:6|I have said: You are gods|Ego dixi, dii estis]]. On which Christ says in the Gospel: [[John 10:35|he called them gods to whom the word of God was spoken|Illos dixit deos, ad quos sermo Dei factus est]]. [[7:1|and Aaron, thy brother, shall be thy prophet|Et Aaron frater tuus erit propheta tuus]], that is, thou shalt make known to him by my revelation the things that are to come, and he shall speak them on thy behalf, and so he will stand towards thee after the manner of a prophet. For he is called a prophet to whom God reveals future contingent things, and who foretells them on God's behalf. Hence the Lord does not say in this place, Aaron shall be a prophet, but, [[7:1|shall be thy prophet|Erit propheta tuus]]; just as he had not said to Moses absolutely, [[7:1|I have appointed thee the god|Constitui te deum]], but added, [[7:1|of Pharao|Pharaonis]]. And so in these words God kept up the metaphor: by the analogy or proportion by which he appointed Moses the god of Pharao, he also appointed Aaron the prophet of Moses. For to have a Prophet belongs properly to the true God alone, since sure foreknowledge of purely contingent future things is held to be proper to God, and belongs to others only in so far as it is revealed to them by the Lord. For which reason Isaias says: [[Is 41:23|Shew the things that are to come hereafter, and we shall know that ye are gods|Quæ ventura sunt, annuntiate nobis, et sciemus quia dii estis vos]] [Denis's wording, "tell us the things that are to come", runs a little differently from the Vulgate].

paras.t: Circa hæc scribit Lyra: In Hebræo habetur Elohim, quod est pluralis numeri, et significat deos. Ideo translatio nostra magis propria esset, si ita haberet, Constitui te deos Pharaonis: quod non apparet. Non enim proprie diceretur singulari personæ pluraliter, Constitui te deos. In expositione quoque primi capituli Genesis, ex Scholastica historia allegavi super illud, In principio creavit Deus cælum et terram, Hebræus habet Elohim, quod tam singulare quam plurale est: idcirco tenendum, quod Hieronymus proprie transtulit in hoc loco singulariter, Constitui te deum Pharaonis. Satis tamen credendum, quod Elohim in Hebræo communius atque frequentius sumitur pluraliter quam singulariter. Amplius Magister in historiis ait, Constitui te deum Pharaonis, id est potentem in Pharaone et in terra ejus facere signa ad modum Dei. Et Aaron frater tuus erit propheta, id est prælocutor tuus. Non tamen fuit Moyses nec Aaron propheta. Circa quod dico, quod quamvis ex hoc loco non sequatur, Aaron fuisse prophetam, aliunde tamen probatur, quod propheticas revelationes a Deo sortitus sit, quum et Maria soror ejus prophetissa infra vocetur. Et supra legitur, qualiter Deus apparuit atque locutus sit Aaron in Ægypto. Infra tamen hoc clarius innotescet. Id quoque pensandum, quod etiam in novo Testamento propheta interdum dicatur, qui verba divina interpretatur, eloquitur, seu exponit, ut dum ad Corinthios scribit Apostolus: Prophetæ duo aut tres dicant. Potestis enim per singulos prophetare.
paras.en: On this Lyra writes: In the Hebrew there stands *Elohim*, which is of the plural number and means "gods". So our translation would be more exact if it read, *I have appointed thee gods of Pharao*. But that does not seem right: for it would not properly be said in the plural to a single person, *I have appointed thee gods*. Also, in the exposition of the first chapter of Genesis I cited from the Scholastic History, on the words [[Gen 1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cælum et terram]], that the Hebrew has *Elohim*, which is both singular and plural. It must therefore be held that Jerome rightly translated it in the singular in this place, [[7:1|I have appointed thee the god of Pharao|Constitui te deum Pharaonis]]. Yet it is surely to be believed that *Elohim* in Hebrew is more commonly and more often taken in the plural than in the singular. Further, the Master in the Histories [that is, Peter Comestor in the *Historia scholastica*] says: [[7:1|I have appointed thee the god of Pharao|Constitui te deum Pharaonis]], that is, mighty to work signs in the manner of God upon Pharao and in his land. [[7:1|and Aaron, thy brother, shall be thy prophet|Et Aaron frater tuus erit propheta]], that is, thy spokesman [*prælocutor*, one who speaks on another's behalf]. Yet neither Moses nor Aaron was a prophet. On this I say that although it does not follow from this place that Aaron was a prophet, it is proved from elsewhere that he received prophetic revelations from God, since his sister Mary also is called a prophetess below[[Ex 15:20||]]. And we read above how God appeared to Aaron and spoke to him in Egypt[[Ex 4:27||]]. But this will be made clearer below. This too is to be weighed: that in the New Testament also he is sometimes called a prophet who interprets, utters or expounds the divine words, as when the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 14:29|let the prophets speak, two or three|Prophetæ duo aut tres dicant]]. [[1 Cor 14:31|For you may all prophesy, one by one|Potestis enim per singulos prophetare]] [no margin note; the words are 1 Cor 14:31, where Denis leaves out "all"].

paras.t: Tu loqueris ei omnia quæ mando tibi, et ille loquetur ad Pharaonem, ut dimittat filios Israel de terra sua. Sed ego indurabo cor ejus, videlicet Pharaonis, gratiam emollientem cordis duritiam non infundendo ei, exigente justitia mea. Et multiplicabo signa et ostenta mea in terra Ægypti, id est miracula, meam potentiam et verborum meorum veritatem monstrantia, quæ signa ostensione et admiratione sunt digna. Vel per signa, intelliguntur minora prodigia; per ostenta autem, majora. Circa quod loquitur Augustinus, quod Deus bene utitur cordibus malis, quia ad hoc permisit Pharaonem sceleratum sic indurari, ut ea occasione fierent in Ægypto plura et præclariora miracula, per quæ Deus suam omnipotentiam declaravit, et suos electos ædificavit, convertit, omnesque homines in admirationem divinæ majestatis induxit. Et non audiet vos. Immittamque manum meam super Ægyptum, id est, per effectus potentiæ meæ castigabo Ægyptios, et educam exercitum et populum meum filios Israel de terra Ægypti per judicia maxima, id est per gloriosissima signa, justo judicio Ægyptiis infligenda ac nocitura.
paras.en: [[7:2|Thou shalt speak to him all that I command thee; and he shall speak to Pharao, that he let the children of Israel go out of his land.|Tu loqueris ei omnia quæ mando tibi, et ille loquetur ad Pharaonem, ut dimittat filios Israel de terra sua]] [[7:3|But I shall harden his heart|Sed ego indurabo cor ejus]], that is, Pharao's, by not pouring into him the grace that softens the hardness of the heart, as my justice requires. [[7:3|and shall multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt|Et multiplicabo signa et ostenta mea in terra Ægypti]], that is, miracles that show my power and the truth of my words, signs worthy to be shown and wondered at. Or by *signs* are meant the lesser prodigies, by *wonders* the greater. On this Augustine says that God makes good use of evil hearts: for he permitted the wicked Pharao to be so hardened to this end, that on that occasion more and more glorious miracles might be wrought in Egypt, by which God declared his almighty power, edified and converted his elect, and moved all men to wonder at the divine majesty. [[7:4|And he will not hear you|Et non audiet vos]]: [[7:4|and I will lay my hand upon Egypt|Immittamque manum meam super Ægyptum]], that is, I will chastise the Egyptians by the effects of my power, [[7:4|and will bring forth my army and my people, the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt, by very great judgments|et educam exercitum et populum meum filios Israel de terra Ægypti per judicia maxima]], that is, by most glorious signs, to be inflicted on the Egyptians by a just judgment, to their hurt.

paras.t: Erat autem Moyses octoginta annorum, et Aaron octoginta trium, quando locuti sunt ad Pharaonem. Et ita ex parte ætatis patet idoneitas eorumdem ad tantum officium.
paras.en: [[7:7|And Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three, when they spoke to Pharao.|Erat autem Moyses octoginta annorum, et Aaron octoginta trium, quando locuti sunt ad Pharaonem]] And so, as regards their age, their fitness for so great an office is plain.

paras.t: Dixitque Dominus ad Moysen et Aaron: Quum dixerit vobis Pharao, ostendite signa, id est opera mira, et tanta ac talia, ut dignum sit quod credamus vos esse missos a Deo, quem dicitis esse summum Deum, dices tu, o Moyses, ad Aaron: Tolle virgam tuam, id est, in manu accipe, vel acceptam ex manu ejice, et projice coram Pharaone, et vertetur in colubrum.
paras.en: [[7:8|And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron:|Dixitque Dominus ad Moysen et Aaron:]] [[7:9|When Pharao shall say to you, Shew signs|Quum dixerit vobis Pharao, ostendite signa]], that is, wondrous works, so great and of such a kind that it is fitting we should believe you to be sent by God, who you say is the supreme God, [[7:9|thou shalt say|dices]] (thou, O Moses) [[7:9|to Aaron: Take thy rod|ad Aaron: Tolle virgam tuam]], that is, take it in thy hand, or, having taken it, throw it from thy hand, [[7:9|and cast it down before Pharao, and it shall be turned into a serpent|et projice coram Pharaone, et vertetur in colubrum]].

paras.t: Cur Moyses virgam non projecit? Respondent quidam, quod ideo, ne Ægyptii dicerent eum magicis artibus facere signum hoc. Nempe quum diu absens fuerit ab Ægypto, poterant suspicari Ægyptii, quod in terra aliena magicas didicerit artes: quod de Aaron suspicari nequibant, quia a juventute fuerat commoratus inter Ægyptios, sine quorum voluntate ac scitu non valuit artes illas addiscere. Hæc ratio non videtur magni vigoris. Primo, quoniam infra Moyses legitur per se ipsum quædam signa cum virga fecisse. Secundo, quoniam Aaron potuisset occulte artes didicisse præfatas. Tertio, quia Ægyptii poterant suspicari, quod Moyses instruxisset seorsum ipsum Aaron magicas artes. Aptius igitur arbitror responderi, quod Aaron virgam projecit, quoniam Deus hoc jussit, sicut in textu evidenter exprimitur. Et cur Deus hoc jussit, quis novit? Tamen ex circumstantia litteræ conjici potest, quod ideo, ut ordo mediationis ipsius Aaron inter Moysen et Pharaonem, superioritas quoque Moysis in hoc commendatur. Jam enim dixerat Deus ad Moysen: Constitui te deum Pharaonis, et Aaron frater tuus erit propheta tuus. Ideo Moyses quasi superior, et quasi quidam deus Pharaonis, per intermedium fratrem suum jussit virgam projici, et eadem ratione Deus Moysi præcepit sic facere.
paras.en: Why did Moses not cast down the rod? Some answer that it was so that the Egyptians might not say he worked this sign by magic arts. For since he had been long absent from Egypt, the Egyptians could suspect that he had learned magic arts in a foreign land; but they could not suspect this of Aaron, since he had lived among the Egyptians from his youth, and could not have learned those arts without their will and knowledge. This reason does not seem of much force. First, because we read below that Moses himself worked certain signs with the rod. Second, because Aaron could have learned those arts in secret. Third, because the Egyptians could suspect that Moses had taught Aaron the magic arts in private. I think, then, that it is more fittingly answered that Aaron cast down the rod because God commanded it, as is plainly expressed in the text. And why God commanded it, who knows? Yet from the circumstances of the letter it can be conjectured that it was so that the order of Aaron's mediation between Moses and Pharao, and also the superiority of Moses, might be set forth in this. For God had already said to Moses: [[7:1|I have appointed thee the god of Pharao|Constitui te deum Pharaonis]], [[7:1|and Aaron, thy brother, shall be thy prophet|et Aaron frater tuus erit propheta tuus]]. So Moses, as the superior and as a kind of god of Pharao, ordered the rod to be cast down through his brother as intermediary; and for the same reason God commanded Moses to do so.

paras.t: Præterea advertendum, quod virga hæc interdum dicitur virga Dei, quia in ea Deus potentiam suam monstravit, miraculoseque egit. Aliquando appellatur virga Moysis, quia eam habebat quum Dominus in monte Sinai ei apparuit, et secum detulit eam. Nunc vero vocatur virga Aaron, quia ipse gestavit, projecitque eam.
paras.en: It is further to be noted that this rod is sometimes called the rod of God, because in it God showed his power and worked miracles. Sometimes it is called the rod of Moses, because he had it when the Lord appeared to him on Mount Sinai, and he brought it with him. But now it is called Aaron's rod, because he carried it and cast it down.

paras.t: Ingressi itaque Moyses et Aaron, et forte quidam ex senioribus Israel cum eis, ad Pharaonem, fecerunt sicut præceperat Dominus. Quod qualiter factum sit, subditur: Tulitque Aaron, id est, in terram projecit, virgam coram Pharaone, quum dixisset, Ostendite signa, aut aliquid simile protulisset, et coram servis ejus; quæ versa est in colubrum: et hoc miraculose, puta repente, sine naturalium applicatione agentium, per omnipotentiam Dei.
paras.en: [[7:10|So Moses and Aaron went in|Ingressi itaque Moyses et Aaron]], and perhaps some of the ancients of Israel with them, [[7:10|unto Pharao, and did as the Lord had commanded|ad Pharaonem, fecerunt sicut præceperat Dominus]]. How this was done is added: [[7:10|And Aaron took|Tulitque Aaron]], that is, cast down on the ground, [[7:10|the rod before Pharao|virgam coram Pharaone]], when he had said, Shew signs, or had said something like it, [[7:10|and his servants|et coram servis ejus]]; [[7:10|and it was turned into a serpent|quæ versa est in colubrum]]: and this miraculously, that is, suddenly, without the applying of natural agents, by the almighty power of God.

paras.t: Vocavit autem Pharao sapientes, id est eos qui in scientia Ægyptiorum erant instructi, vel philosophos, qui ante Pythagoram vocabant se sapientes: quod Pythagoras reputans esse præsumptuosum, interrogatus a quodam an sapiens esset, respondit se esse philosophum, id est sapientiæ amatorem. Quæ responsio tantum placuit studentibus sapientiæ naturali, quod omnes de cetero vocabant se philosophos, non sapientes, prout in libro de Civitate Dei recitat Augustinus. Et maleficos, id est necromanticos, et dæmoniacis artibus auxiliisque intentos; et fecerunt etiam ipsi per incantationes Ægyptiacas, id est invocationes seu adjurationes diabolicas, quibus intenti erant Ægyptii, et arcana quædam, id est per quasdam occultas maneries aut virtutes, quæ communem plebem latebant, ut infra magis tangetur, similiter, projiciendo virgas suas seu baculos, qui in Alcorano impii Mahometi vocantur hastilia. Hinc subditur: Projeceruntque singuli virgas suas, quæ versæ sunt in dracones. Qualiter factum sit hoc, jam inquiretur.
paras.en: [[7:11|And Pharao called the wise men|Vocavit autem Pharao sapientes]], that is, those who were learned in the knowledge of the Egyptians; or the philosophers, who before Pythagoras called themselves wise men. Pythagoras, thinking this presumptuous, when someone asked him whether he was a wise man, answered that he was a philosopher, that is, a lover of wisdom. This answer so pleased those who studied natural wisdom that from then on they all called themselves philosophers, not wise men, as Augustine relates in the book of the City of God. [[7:11|and the magicians|Et maleficos]] [*malefici*, literally "evil-doers", the common Latin word for sorcerers], that is, necromancers, men given to devilish arts and aids; [[7:11|and they also by Egyptian enchantments|et fecerunt etiam ipsi per incantationes Ægyptiacas]], that is, devilish invocations or conjurations, to which the Egyptians were given, [[7:11|and certain secrets|et arcana quædam]], that is, by certain hidden ways or powers unknown to the common people, as will be touched on more fully below, [[7:11|did in like manner|similiter]], casting down their rods or staves, which in the Koran of the impious Mahomet are called *hastilia* [that is, shafts or spear-staves]. Hence it is added: [[7:12|And they every one cast down their rods, and they were turned into serpents|Projeceruntque singuli virgas suas, quæ versæ sunt in dracones]]. How this was done will be inquired into presently.

paras.t: Sed devoravit virga Aaron virgas eorum. Hoc dupliciter exponitur. Primo, quod coluber in quem virga Aaron fuit conversa, devoravit dracones seu serpentes, in quos versæ fuerunt vere aut apparenter virgæ magorum. Et si fuerunt versæ realiter in dracones, tunc coluber ille realiter devoravit dracones illos. Si autem apparenter duntaxat, tunc coluber ille devoravit apparenter dracones, et realiter virgas. Juxta hanc expositionem, devoratio illa facta est, antequam coluber Aaron in virgæ naturam mutatus atque reversus est. Et ita intelligit Josephus, dicens quod draco Aaron insiliit in illos, donec devoravit universos. Sed cur Scriptura ait, Devoravit virga, et non potius, Devoravit coluber Aaron virgas seu dracones illorum, præsertim quum devorare non proprie competat virgæ, sed magis serpenti? Ad hoc B. Augustinus respondet: Si dictum esset, Absorbuit draco, id est coluber Aaron, virgas illorum, intelligeretur verus draco Aaron absorbuisse, non phantastica figmenta magorum, sed virgas. Hoc enim potuit absorbere quod erant, non quod videbantur et non erant. Sed quia dixit Scriptura, Absorbuit virga Aaron virgas illorum, draco Aaron potuit absorbere virgas magorum, non virga Aaron. Sed eo nomine vocata est res, ex qua versa est, non nomine rei in quam versa est, quia in eam rem, scilicet virgam, etiam reversa est: ideo hoc vocari debuit, quod principaliter erat. Itaque draco seu coluber Aaron vocatur virga, quamvis tempore devorationis illius non erat virga, quia primo exstitit virga, et rursus in speciem virgæ mutatus est. Hanc expositionem sequuntur Catholici.
paras.en: [[7:12|but Aaron's rod devoured their rods|Sed devoravit virga Aaron virgas eorum]]. This is expounded in two ways. First, that the serpent into which Aaron's rod had been turned devoured the dragons or serpents into which the magicians' rods had been turned, truly or in appearance. And if they had been really turned into dragons, then that serpent really devoured those dragons; but if only in appearance, then that serpent devoured the dragons in appearance, and the rods in reality. According to this exposition, the devouring took place before Aaron's serpent was changed back into the nature of a rod. And so Josephus understands it, saying that Aaron's dragon sprang upon them until it had devoured them all. But why does Scripture say, The [[7:12|rod devoured|Devoravit virga]], and not rather, The serpent of Aaron devoured their rods or dragons, especially since devouring does not properly belong to a rod, but rather to a serpent? To this blessed Augustine answers: If it had been said, The dragon (that is, Aaron's serpent) swallowed up their rods, it would have been understood that Aaron's true dragon swallowed up not the phantasms of the magicians but the rods; for it could swallow up what they were, not what they seemed to be and were not. But since Scripture said, [[7:12|Aaron's rod devoured their rods|Absorbuit virga Aaron virgas illorum]], it was Aaron's dragon that could swallow up the magicians' rods, not Aaron's rod. But the thing was called by the name of that from which it was turned, not by the name of the thing into which it was turned, because it was also turned back into that thing, namely the rod: therefore it had to be called what it principally was. So Aaron's dragon or serpent is called a rod, although at the time of that devouring it was not a rod, because it was a rod first and was changed again into the form of a rod. This exposition the Catholics follow.

paras.t: Secundo exponitur ab Hebræis, quod post reditionem colubri Aaron in virgam, ipsa virga Aaron devoravit dracones magorum miraculose divina virtute, loquendo metaphorice de devoratione, eo modo quo loquitur Isaias: Sicut devorat stipulam lingua ignis et calor flammæ exurit, sic radix eorum quasi favilla erit. Sicque divina potestate in virgam illam fuissent conversi dracones, quoniam Deus potest unum corpus in aliud convertere: vel virga illa per omnipotentiam Dei consumpsisset, et quasi in nihilum redegisset dracones magorum, quemadmodum calor solis dissolvit naturaliter glaciem, et consumit humorem. Prima autem expositio, aptior reputatur. Si enim Hebræi litteræ volunt inniti, dicendo quod non coluber, sed virga devoravit, quia in textu habetur, Devoravit virga Aaron, consequens est ut dicant, dracones magorum redisse et rursus esse mutatos in virgas, quia in textu asseritur: Devoravit virga Aaron virgas eorum. Insuper videtur verbum istud sic posse intelligi: Devoravit virga Aaron virgas eorum, id est, mirabilia facta per virgam Aaron, prævaluerunt signis factis vere seu apparenter per virgas magorum. Et si iste non est sensus litteralis, hoc tamen ad minus significatum est per devorationem præfatam. Denique devoratio virgarum seu draconum a virga seu colubro Aaron, fuit speciale prodigium.
paras.en: Second, it is expounded by the Hebrews that after Aaron's serpent had returned into a rod, Aaron's rod itself devoured the magicians' dragons miraculously by divine power; the devouring being spoken of metaphorically, in the way in which Isaias says: [[Is 5:24|as the tongue of the fire devoureth the stubble, and the heat of the flame consumeth it: so shall their root be as ashes|Sicut devorat stipulam lingua ignis et calor flammæ exurit, sic radix eorum quasi favilla erit]]. And so the dragons would have been turned into that rod by divine power, since God can turn one body into another; or that rod, by the almighty power of God, would have consumed the magicians' dragons and brought them as it were to nothing, as the heat of the sun naturally melts ice and consumes moisture. But the first exposition is held to be the more fitting. For if the Hebrews wish to rely on the letter, saying that not the serpent but the rod devoured, because the text has, [[7:12|Aaron's rod devoured|Devoravit virga Aaron]], it follows that they must say the magicians' dragons had returned and been changed again into rods, since the text asserts: [[7:12|Aaron's rod devoured their rods|Devoravit virga Aaron virgas eorum]]. Besides, it seems that these words can be understood thus: [[7:12|Aaron's rod devoured their rods|Devoravit virga Aaron virgas eorum]], that is, the wonders done by Aaron's rod prevailed over the signs done, truly or in appearance, by the magicians' rods. And if this is not the literal sense, this at least is signified by that devouring. Lastly, the devouring of the rods or dragons by Aaron's rod or serpent was a special prodigy.

paras.t: Circa præhabita quæritur, quid sit catholice sentiendum de facto magorum Pharaonis, an scilicet virgæ eorum conversæ fuerint in dracones. Et videtur quod non, quia tam repentina virgarum in dracones conversio, non videtur per naturam, neque per magicam artem possibilis. Miracula quoque Dei debent differre a miris magorum effectibus. Quod si conversio illa fuit per naturam aut magicam artem vere possibilis et peracta, ergo conversio virgæ Aaron in serpentem, non fuit sufficiens signum quo Moysi et Aaron crederetur; nec Pharao videretur peccasse non credendo, nec obtemperando propter signum illud. Oppositum probatur ex textu, in quo simpliciter affirmatur, quod virgæ magorum versæ sunt in dracones.
paras.en: On what has been said, it is asked what is to be held, in the Catholic way, about the deed of Pharao's magicians: namely, whether their rods were turned into dragons. And it seems that they were not: for so sudden a turning of rods into dragons does not seem possible either by nature or by magic art. Also the miracles of God ought to differ from the wondrous effects of the magicians. And if that turning was truly possible by nature or magic art, and was done, then the turning of Aaron's rod into a serpent was not a sufficient sign for Moses and Aaron to be believed; nor would Pharao seem to have sinned in not believing and not obeying because of that sign. The opposite is proved from the text, in which it is plainly affirmed that the magicians' rods [[7:12|were turned into serpents|versæ sunt in dracones]].

paras.t: Ad hæc dissolvenda est triplex responsio. Nam aliqui dicunt, quod virgæ magorum non fuerunt veraciter in dracones conversæ, sed apparenter et ludificatorie tantum, ita quod ibi non erant dracones realiter, sed præstigialiter solum. Hinc Strabus et Magister in historiis dicunt: Magi diabolicis figmentis spectantium oculos deludebant, ut res in sua natura manentes, aliud viderentur. Huic autem responsioni videtur favere, quod jam ex Augustino est allegatum: Si dictum esset, Absorbuit draco Aaron virgas eorum, intelligeretur verus draco Aaron absorbuisse, non phantastica figmenta, sed virgas. Hoc enim poterat absorbere quod erant, non quod videbantur et non erant.
paras.en: To resolve this there is a threefold answer. For some say that the magicians' rods were not truly turned into dragons, but only in appearance and by way of illusion, so that there were no dragons there in reality, but only by sleight [*præstigialiter*, by a conjuror's trick that deceives the eye]. Hence Strabo and the Master in the Histories say: The magicians deceived the eyes of the onlookers by devilish figments, so that things remaining in their own nature seemed something else. This answer seems to be favoured by what has already been cited from Augustine: If it had been said, Aaron's dragon swallowed up their rods, it would have been understood that Aaron's true dragon swallowed up not the phantasms but the rods; for it could swallow up what they were, not what they seemed to be and were not.

paras.t: Secunda responsio est, quod virgæ magorum vere convertebantur in dracones, per applicationes virium ac seminum naturalium rerum, quæ maligni spiritus celerrime colligere, adducere, applicareque poterant, et ita repente transmutare virgarum materiam, ut in dracones converterentur. Hanc quoque responsionem Strabus et auctor Scholasticæ historiæ tangunt, dicendo: Dum per incantationem dæmonum malefici aliquid operari conantur, dæmones ipsi per mundum discurrunt, et subito semina rerum, de quibus hoc agitur, afferunt; sicque ex illis, Deo permittente, nova quædam producunt. Ista item responsio in verbis Augustini fundatur, dicentis: Insunt corporeis rebus per omnia mundi elementa quædam occultæ seminariæ rationes, quibus quum data fuerit opportunitas temporalis, prorumpunt in species debitas suis modis ac finibus. Et qui faciunt hæc, non dicuntur animalium creatores, sicut nec agricolæ, segetum. Quod autem hi faciunt visibiliter, hoc angeli boni vel mali invisibiliter. Solus autem Deus creator est, qui causas ipsas et rationes seminarias rebus inseruit. Hæc vero responsio quibusdam non placet. Nam dicunt, quod licet ex virgis possunt generari serpentes per naturalium applicationem virtutum ac seminum, hoc tamen non fieret tam repente, sed per intermedias transmutationes et per moram notabilem. Ideo dicunt quod dæmones celerrime et imperceptibiliter subtraxerunt virgas a magis projectas, et loco earum supposuerunt dracones aliunde invisibiliter allatos, vel ibi de novo generatos, per hoc quod supposuerunt materiam de propinquo dispositam ad inductionem formarum serpentium. Textum autem solvunt, dicendo quod consuetudo Scripturæ est, aliquid recitare sicut ab omnibus reputatum est, et sicut apparuit quando fiebat, secundum quod super Matthæum scribit S. Hieronymus.
paras.en: The second answer is that the magicians' rods were truly turned into dragons, by the applying of the powers and seeds of natural things, which the evil spirits could gather, bring and apply with the greatest speed, and so suddenly transform the matter of the rods that they were turned into dragons. Strabo and the author of the Scholastic History touch on this answer too, saying: When sorcerers try to work something through the incantation of demons, the demons themselves run about the world and suddenly bring the seeds of the things in question; and so from them, God permitting, they produce certain new things. This answer is likewise founded on the words of Augustine, who says: There are in bodily things, throughout all the elements of the world, certain hidden seminal reasons [*rationes seminariæ*, Augustine's term for the hidden powers placed in things at the creation, from which new things later spring], which, when a fitting time is given them, break forth into their due kinds by their own ways and ends. And those who bring this about are not called the creators of the animals, any more than farmers are called the creators of the crops. What these do visibly, good or evil angels do invisibly. But God alone is the creator, who put those causes and seminal reasons into things. Some, however, do not like this answer. For they say that although serpents can be generated from rods by the applying of natural powers and seeds, this would not happen so suddenly, but through intermediate changes and over a notable length of time.
