So they say that the demons, with the greatest speed and imperceptibly, took away the rods cast down by the magicians, and in their place put dragons brought invisibly from elsewhere, or newly generated there, by putting in matter disposed at hand for the bringing in of the forms of serpents. And they explain the text by saying that it is the custom of Scripture to relate a thing as it was thought by all, and as it appeared when it was done, as St. Jerome writes on Matthew.

paras.t: Præterea ut sciatur, quæ harum responsionum verior probabiliorque putetur, advertendum in primis quod in prima parte Summæ suæ, quæstione 110, scribit S. Thomas, dicendo : Secundum divinum Dionysium capitulo 7 de Divinis nominibus, Deus conjungit infimum superioris ordinis cum supremo ordinis inferioris. Hinc angeli tam boni quam mali ratione suæ spiritualis naturæ, dignitatis ac potestatis, agere possunt in corporalem naturam, quantum ad motum localem. Porro ad rationem miraculi non sufficit, quod aliquid fiat præter ordinem naturæ particularis : alioqui qui projicit lapidem sursum, perpetraret miraculum : sed oportet ut fiat præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ : sicque Deo proprium est miracula facere, juxta illud, Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, qui facit mirabilia solus. Verumtamen homines sancti et angeli gloriosi dicuntur patrare miracula, in quantum propter eorum preces et vota Deus efficit ea, aut quia ministerium exhibent in operatione miraculi. His verbis addit Thomas : Dæmones aliqua agere possunt ex naturali industria per occulta rerum semina, quorum nos ignoramus virtutem, sicut fecerunt per magos Pharaonis. Unde talia, quamvis sint miracula, quantum ad nos, non tamen simpliciter, quia in naturali potestate est creaturæ quidquid efficiunt. Ex his constat, quid de conversione virgarum magorum Pharaonis senserit Thomas, utpote quod in dracones vere conversæ sunt per modum prætactum.
paras.en: Further, so that it may be known which of these answers is to be thought the truer and more probable, we must note first what St Thomas writes in the first part of his Summa, question 110, saying: According to the divine Dionysius, in chapter 7 of the Divine Names, God joins the lowest of a higher order to the highest of a lower order. Hence angels, good as well as bad, by reason of their spiritual nature, dignity and power, can act upon bodily nature as regards local motion. Moreover, for something to be a miracle it is not enough that it happen outside the order of some particular nature: otherwise whoever throws a stone upwards would be working a miracle; it must happen outside the order of the whole of created nature. And so it belongs to God alone to work miracles, according to that saying: [[Ps 71:18|Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone doth wonderful things|Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, qui facit mirabilia solus]]. Yet holy men and glorious angels are said to work miracles inasmuch as God brings them about on account of their prayers and petitions, or because they render a ministry in the working of the miracle. To these words Thomas adds: Demons can do some things by natural skill, through the hidden seeds of things whose power we do not know, as they did through Pharao's magicians. Hence such things, although they are miracles as far as we are concerned, are not miracles simply speaking, since whatever they bring about lies within the natural power of a creature. From this it is clear what Thomas thought about the turning of the rods of Pharao's magicians: namely, that they were truly turned into serpents, in the manner touched on above.

paras.t: Insuper in eadem parte Summæ suæ, quæstione 114, ait : Dicuntur dæmones miracula facere posse, quoniam per occulta rerum semina, aut simili modo aliqua efficere possunt, quæ facultatem et considerationem humanam transcendunt. Quæ autem naturali virtute fieri nequeunt, non faciunt vere, sed apparenter dumtaxat, videlicet decipiendo sensus humanos, aliquas formas seu similitudines imprimendo exterioribus sensibus, aut phantasiam et sensum communem interius immutando, ex qua immutatione refluunt species rerum ad sensus exteriores : et ita videtur homini quod sentiat, quod non sentit. Denique sicut diabolus potest ex aere corpus formare atque assumere, sic potest aliis rebus corporeis quamcumque formam et figuram circumponere, ita ut corpus humanum videatur in figuram bestialem conversum : quam conversionem non potest diabolus vere efficere. Unde octavodecimo de Civitate Dei loquitur Augustinus : Nec ulla ratione crediderim, dæmonum potestate et arte in bestialia posse lineamenta et membra converti corpus humanum. De hac autem materia, et quid sit proprie miraculum, de diversitate quoque ac gradibus miraculorum, et qualiter dæmonum ope, magorum opera fiant, qualiter etiam dæmones valeant imaginativam vim, exterioresque sensus hominum immutare ac fallere, valde magistraliter atque subtiliter scribit sanctus Doctor in prima parte Summæ suæ, et super secundum Sententiarum, distinctione 7 ; itemque in Summa contra gentiles libro tertio.
paras.en: Moreover, in the same part of his Summa, question 114, he says: Demons are said to be able to work miracles because, through the hidden seeds of things or in some like way, they can bring about certain things that surpass human ability and understanding. But what cannot be done by natural power they do not do truly but only in appearance, namely by deceiving the human senses: by impressing certain forms or likenesses on the outward senses, or by changing the imagination and the common sense [*sensus communis*: the inner sense that gathers and compares what the outward senses perceive] within, from which change the images of things flow back to the outward senses; and so a man seems to perceive what he does not perceive. Lastly, just as the devil can form a body out of air and assume it, so he can put any form and shape around other bodily things, so that a human body seems turned into the shape of a beast: a change which the devil cannot truly bring about. Hence Augustine says in the eighteenth book of the City of God: Nor would I on any account believe that the human body can be changed into the features and limbs of a beast by the power and art of demons. On this matter, and on what a miracle properly is, on the diversity and degrees of miracles too, and how the works of magicians are done by the help of demons, and also how demons are able to change and deceive the imaginative power and the outward senses of men, the holy Doctor writes very masterfully and subtly in the first part of his Summa, and on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 7, and also in the Summa contra Gentiles, book three.

paras.t: Itaque verius reor, quod virgæ magorum Pharaonis fuerunt vere in dracones conversæ, et quod magi, ut infra habetur, vere converterunt aquam in sanguinem, ranasque produxerunt. Primo, quoniam hoc magis consonat textui veritatis, videlicet sacræ huic historiæ, quæ absolute ac apertissime protestatur et asserit, quod virgæ illæ in dracones sint versæ, etc. Secundo, quoniam doctores egregii, super secundum Sententiarum, distinctione 7, communiter dicunt hoc, et ipse Magister in textu ibidem idem affirmat. Tertio, quoniam effectus illi non transcendunt virtutes naturalium seminum et causarum, ac angelorum sive bonorum sive malorum. Quarto, quia beatissimus Augustinus tertio libro de Trinitate per diversa capitula, hoc ipsum contestatur atque declarat : Video, inquit, quid infirmæ cogitationi possit occurrere, cur scilicet mirabilia ista etiam magicis artibus fiant. Nam et magi Pharaonis, serpentes et alia quædam fecerunt aerearum potestatum auxilio. Nam et dæmones nihil possunt, nisi data eis desuper potestate, quæ datur eis ad fallendum fallaces, sicut data est eis in ipsos Ægyptios et in magos, ut in eorum spirituum seductione viderentur admirandi a quibus fiebant, a Dei veritate damnandi : vel ad monendum fideles, ne tale aliquid facere pro magno reputent : vel ad exercendam, manifestandamque justorum patientiam. Nec ideo putandum est, transgressoribus angelis ad nutum servire hanc visibilium rerum materiam, sed Deo potius, a quo hæc datur potestas. Nec mali angeli illi dicendi sunt creatores, quia magi famulo Dei Moysi resistentes, ranas et serpentes fecerunt per illos. Omnium quippe rerum quæ corporaliter visibiliterque nascuntur, occulta quædam semina in corporeis hujus mundi elementis latent : alias non nascerentur plerumque ex terra, quæ in ea seminata non sunt.
paras.en: And so I think it truer that the rods of Pharao's magicians were truly turned into serpents, and that the magicians, as is related below, truly turned water into blood and brought forth frogs. First, because this agrees better with the text of truth, that is, with this sacred history, which states and asserts absolutely and most openly that those rods were turned into serpents, etc. Secondly, because the eminent doctors on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 7, commonly say this, and the Master himself affirms the same in the text there. Thirdly, because those effects do not surpass the powers of natural seeds and causes, and of angels, whether good or bad. Fourthly, because the most blessed Augustine, in the third book On the Trinity, in several chapters, bears witness to this very thing and declares it. I see, he says, what may occur to a weak mind: why, that is, these wonders are done by magic arts as well. For the magicians of Pharao too made serpents and certain other things by the help of the powers of the air. For the demons too can do nothing unless power be given them from above; and it is given them to deceive the deceitful, as it was given them against the Egyptians themselves and against the magicians, so that, in being led astray by those spirits by whom these things were done, they might seem worthy of wonder, while they were to be condemned by the truth of God; or to warn the faithful not to count it a great thing to do anything of the kind; or to exercise and make manifest the patience of the just. Nor is it therefore to be thought that this matter of visible things serves the angels who transgressed at their nod, but rather God, by whom this power is given. Nor are those wicked angels to be called creators because the magicians, resisting Moses the servant of God, made frogs and serpents through them. For of all things that are born bodily and visibly, certain hidden seeds lie in the bodily elements of this world: otherwise things that were not sown in the earth would not so often spring from it.

paras.t: Sed nunc restat objectio illa solvenda quæ tacta est, quia apparet quod per magicam artem et dæmonum operationem non potuerint virgæ magorum tam repente in dracones converti. Quam objectionem Nicolaus de Lyra sic ponderat, quod ob eam negat virgas fuisse in dracones conversas. Verum ex verbis Augustini tertio de Trinitate, habetur solutio. Ait equidem ibi : Angeli ex sua subtilitate et agilitate semina rerum nobis occultiora noverunt, et ea per congruas temperationes latenter spargunt, atque ita gignendarum rerum et accelerandorum incrementorum præbent occasiones. Multi etiam homines noverunt, ex quibus herbis aut carnibus, vel quarumlibet rerum succis et humoribus, sic vel sic positis, obrutis, contritis aut commixtis, quæ animalia soleant nasci. Quid igitur mirum, si quemadmodum potest cognoscere quilibet nequissimus homo, unde illi vel illi vermes aut muscæ nascantur, sic angeli mali in occultioribus elementorum seminibus norunt, unde ranæ serpentesque nascantur, et hæc per certas ac eis notas temperationum opportunitates seu convenientias, occultis motibus adhibeant et procurent ? Quod si quis celeritates incrementorum forte miratur, quod animalia illa tam cito sunt facta, attendat quemadmodum ista pro modulo facultatis humanæ ab hominibus procurentur. Sed hæc ab hominibus tanto difficilius adhibentur, quanto desunt sensuum subtilitates, et corporum mobilitates in membris terrenis. Hinc quanto facilius est angelis, et malis, intimas causas ab elementis contrahere, tanto mirabiliores exsistunt celeritates in talibus eorum operibus.
paras.en: But now that objection which was touched on remains to be answered: that it appears the magicians' rods could not have been turned into serpents so suddenly by magic art and the working of demons. Nicholas of Lyra weighs this objection so heavily that on account of it he denies that the rods were turned into serpents. But the answer is found in the words of Augustine in the third book On the Trinity. For he says there: The angels, by their subtlety and swiftness, know the seeds of things that are more hidden from us, and scatter them secretly by fitting combinations, and so furnish occasions for things to be begotten and for their growth to be hastened. Many men too know from what herbs or flesh, or from the juices and moistures of any things whatever, placed, buried, crushed or mixed in this way or that, certain animals are wont to be born. What wonder then if, just as any wicked man can know whence these or those worms or flies are born, so the evil angels know, in the more hidden seeds of the elements, whence frogs and serpents are born, and apply and procure these by hidden movements, through certain favourable times or fitting conditions for combining them that are known to them? And if anyone perhaps wonders at the swiftness of the growth, that those animals were made so quickly, let him consider how these things are procured by men according to the measure of human ability. But these things are applied by men with all the more difficulty, the more they lack subtlety of the senses and nimbleness of body in their earthly limbs. Hence, the easier it is for angels, even wicked ones, to draw the inmost causes out of the elements, the more wonderful is the swiftness found in such works of theirs.

paras.t: His quoque Augustini verbis addenda sunt, quæ in Summa contra gentiles libro tertio scribit Thomas : Considerandum est, inquiens, quod dum angeli vel dæmones adhibent res naturales ad determinatos effectus, utuntur eis ut instrumentis, sicut medicus utitur herbis ad curandum. Ex instrumento autem procedit non solum effectus suæ virtuti correspondens, sed etiam effectus ultra propriam virtutem, in quantum agit virtute principalis agentis. Serra namque et securis non possent facere lectum, nisi in quantum agunt ut motæ ab arte ad talem effectum. Nec calor naturalis posset generare carnem, nisi virtute animæ vegetabilis, quæ utitur eo ut instrumento. Conveniens ergo est, quod ex ipsis naturalibus proveniant aliqui altiores effectus, ex hoc quod spirituales substantiæ eis utuntur, ut instrumentis. Sicque, quamvis tales effectus non sint absolute miracula, quia ex naturalibus causis proveniunt, mirabiles tamen nobis redduntur dupliciter : Uno modo ex hoc, quod per spirituales substantias tales causæ modo nobis insolito applicantur ad certos effectus. Unde et ingeniosorum artificum opera mirabilia his videntur, qui non percipiunt qualiter illi operantur. Alio modo ex hoc, quod causæ naturales appositæ ad aliquos effectus producendos, aliquid sortiuntur virtutis ex hoc, quod sunt instrumenta spiritualium substantiarum, et hoc magis accedit ad rationem miraculi.
paras.en: To these words of Augustine must be added what Thomas writes in the Summa contra Gentiles, book three. It is to be considered, he says, that when angels or demons apply natural things to determinate effects, they use them as instruments, as a physician uses herbs for healing. Now from an instrument there proceeds not only an effect corresponding to its own power, but also an effect beyond its proper power, inasmuch as it acts by the power of the principal agent. For a saw and an axe could not make a bed, except inasmuch as they act as moved by the craft towards such an effect. Nor could natural heat generate flesh except by the power of the vegetative soul, which uses it as an instrument. It is fitting, therefore, that certain higher effects should come from natural things themselves, from the fact that spiritual substances use them as instruments. And so, although such effects are not miracles absolutely, since they come from natural causes, yet they are made wonderful to us in two ways. In one way, from the fact that such causes are applied by spiritual substances to certain effects in a manner unusual to us; hence the works of skilful craftsmen too seem wonderful to those who do not perceive how they work. In another way, from the fact that natural causes applied to produce certain effects acquire some power from being instruments of spiritual substances; and this comes nearer to the nature of a miracle.

paras.t: Ex his patet plena objectionis præfatæ solutio. Ad id autem quod objectum est, opera Dei debere distingui a factis magorum, et quod conversio virgæ Aaron in serpentem, non fuisset sufficiens argumentum suæ legationis, quod esset a Deo, patet responsio ex verbis Thomæ super secundum Sententiarum, distinctione 7, asserentis : Signa facta per bonos, distingui possunt ab his quæ fiunt per malos, tripliciter. Primo, ex efficacia virtutis agentis : quoniam signa facta per bonos, fiunt virtute divina, et in his ad quæ se virtus activa naturæ nullo modo extendit : quæ dæmones nequaquam facere possunt, nisi in præstigiis tantum, quæ diu durare non valent. Secundo, ex utilitate, quoniam signa facta per bonos, sunt de rebus utilibus, ut in curationibus infirmitatum : signa autem facta per malos, sunt de rebus nocivis aut vanis, ut quod volant in aere, vel membra hominum efficiunt stupida. Et hanc differentiam assignat S. Petrus in Itinerario S. Clementis. Tertia differentia est, quantum ad finem : quoniam signa bonorum, ordinantur ad ædificationem fidei et morum bonorum : signa autem malorum, sunt in manifestum nocumentum fidei, bonorumque morum. Differunt quoque in modo agendi, quoniam boni faciunt ea per invocationem Dei pie ac reverenter ; sed mali quibusdam deliramentis, incantationibus, abusionibusque utuntur.
paras.en: From this the full answer to the objection mentioned above is plain. As to the other objection, that the works of God ought to be distinguished from the deeds of magicians, and that the turning of Aaron's rod into a serpent would not have been a sufficient proof that his embassy was from God, the answer is plain from the words of Thomas on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 7, who asserts: Signs done by the good can be distinguished from those done by the wicked in three ways. First, by the efficacy of the power acting: for signs done by the good are done by divine power, and in things to which the active power of nature in no way extends; and these demons can by no means do, except in illusions [*præstigia*: conjuring tricks that deceive the senses] only, which cannot last long. Secondly, by their usefulness: for signs done by the good concern useful things, as in the healing of sicknesses, while signs done by the wicked concern harmful or vain things, such as flying in the air or making men's limbs numb. And St Peter gives this difference in the Itinerary of St Clement [the work also known as the Clementine Recognitions]. The third difference concerns the end: for the signs of the good are ordered to the building up of faith and of good morals, while the signs of the wicked tend to the manifest harm of faith and of good morals. They differ also in the manner of acting: for the good do them by calling upon God devoutly and reverently, but the wicked use certain ravings, incantations and abuses.

paras.t: Denique, quod Strabus et Magister in historiis dicunt virgas magorum non realiter, sed ludificatorie versas in dracones, non dicunt assertive, sed opinative vel inquisitive. Nam disjunctive loquuntur, dicendo quod factum sit illud vel per illusionem sensuum, vel per virtutes naturalium rerum. Similiter intelligendum est quod loquitur Augustinus de figmentis illis phantasticis. Insuper dici potest, quod conversio virgarum magorum in dracones, non sit facta tam subito ut apparebat. Quum enim versa fuisset virga Aaron in serpentem, videntes dæmones Pharaonem vocare maleficos suos ad similia perpetranda, potuerunt mox in virgis magorum facere alterationes et dispositiones notabiles, ad convertendum eas in dracones. Et fuit notabile tempus inter illam vocationem, et virgarum projectionem. Hæc circa præsentem passum tam prolixe induxi, quoniam ad sequentium capitulorum expositionem, intelligentiamque proficiunt.
paras.en: Lastly, when Strabo and the Master in the Histories say that the magicians' rods were turned into serpents not really but by way of illusion, they do not say it as an assertion but as an opinion or an inquiry. For they speak disjunctively, saying that it was done either by an illusion of the senses or by the powers of natural things. In the same way is to be understood what Augustine says of those imaginary fictions. Further, it can be said that the turning of the magicians' rods into serpents was not done as suddenly as it seemed. For when Aaron's rod had been turned into a serpent, the demons, seeing Pharao call his sorcerers to do the like, could at once make notable alterations and dispositions in the magicians' rods so as to turn them into serpents; and there was a notable space of time between that calling and the casting down of the rods. I have brought in these things on the present passage at such length because they help towards the exposition and understanding of the following chapters.

paras.t: Postremo, ex dictis potest dari solutio, qualiter multa per magicam artem, sic et sic fieri vel potius apparere potuerunt : sicut quod legitur in Itinerario B. Clementis, quod Simon Magus similitudinem vultus sui impressit Faustiniano patri S. Clementis, ita quod solus beatissimus Petrus apostolus in hoc falli nequivit. Similiter in Vitis Patrum narratur de quodam, cujus uxor videbatur conversa in equam : adduxit eam ad sanctissimum virum Macarium, qui solus vidit in femina illa formam humanam. Nam et Fratribus eremitis videbatur quod esset equa. Interdum quoque apparet hominibus, quod gallus trahat maximam trabem, quum non trahat nisi festucam aut stramen. Denique, de sanctis viris leguntur mira, quæ nequaquam facta sunt magica arte, sed divina virtute : sicut quod S. Fronto episcopus apud Petragoricas celebrans, quum redisset ad se, dixit se sanctam Martham sepelivisse. Beatus quoque Ambrosius in Mediolano celebrans, atque in Missa obdormiens, excitatus a clericis, dixit se obsequium præbuisse funeri sanctissimi præsulis Martini. Præterea B. Augustinus octavodecimo de Civitate Dei velle videtur, quod homine dormiente et vivo manente, phantasticum ejus velut incorporatum in alicujus animalis aut hominis effigie, apparet quandoque sensibus alienis. Unde et de sancto patre Bernardo legitur, quod interdum quando infirmus corporaliter in infirmaria jacebat, videbatur ire per chorum in Matutinis, et monachos intueri, somnolentosque suscitare.
paras.en: Finally, from what has been said an answer can be given as to how many things could be done, or rather could appear, by magic art in this way or that: as we read in the Itinerary of Bl. Clement that Simon Magus impressed the likeness of his own face on Faustinian, the father of St Clement, so that only the most blessed apostle Peter could not be deceived in this. Likewise in the Lives of the Fathers it is told of a certain man whose wife seemed to have been turned into a mare: he brought her to the most holy man Macarius, who alone saw in that woman a human form; for to the brother hermits too she seemed to be a mare. Sometimes also it appears to men that a cock is dragging a very great beam, when it is dragging nothing but a straw or a stalk. Lastly, wonderful things are read of holy men which were in no way done by magic art but by divine power: as that St Fronto, bishop among the Petragorici [the people of Périgueux], while celebrating Mass, said when he came to himself that he had buried St Martha. Blessed Ambrose too, celebrating in Milan and falling asleep at Mass, said when roused by the clerics that he had attended the funeral of the most holy bishop Martin. Moreover, Bl. Augustine in the eighteenth book of the City of God seems to hold that while a man is asleep and remains alive, his phantasm [*phantasticum*: the likeness of a man formed in the imagination], as though embodied in the likeness of some animal or man, sometimes appears to the senses of others. Hence it is also read of our holy father Bernard that sometimes, when he lay sick in body in the infirmary, he was seen to go through the choir at Matins, looking at the monks and rousing the drowsy.

paras.t: Circa hæc scribit Richardus de Mediavilla, super primum Sententiarum, distinctione 37 : Dici potest, quod in veritate nec corpus, nec anima Ambrosii interfuit sepulturæ sancti Martini, sed forte angelus in specie Ambrosii apparens. Quod dum fieret, videbatur Ambrosio soporato, quod interesset illi sepulturæ. Nec est putandum, quod phantasticum hominis realiter exeat de homine dormiente; sed quandoque contingit, quod homo somniat se esse præsentem alieno conspectui : et quando hoc somniat, tunc spiritus in specie illius hominis apparet illi, in cujus conspectu ille dormiens somniat se esse præsentem. Verum de hac materia scribit B. Augustinus diffuse de Civitate Dei libro octavodecimo, capitulis 17 et 18, in quibus de quibusdam transformationibus et apparitionibus satis miranda refert.
paras.en: On these things Richard of Middleton writes, on the first book of the Sentences, distinction 37: It can be said that in truth neither the body nor the soul of Ambrose was present at the burial of St Martin, but perhaps an angel appearing in the form of Ambrose; and while this was being done, it seemed to Ambrose, as he slept, that he was present at that burial. Nor is it to be thought that a man's phantasm really goes out of the sleeping man; but it sometimes happens that a man dreams that he is present before another's eyes, and when he dreams this, a spirit in the form of that man then appears to him before whose eyes the sleeper dreams that he is present. But Bl. Augustine writes on this matter at length in the eighteenth book of the City of God, chapters 17 and 18, where he relates quite wonderful things of certain transformations and apparitions.

paras.t: Induratumque est cor Pharaonis, et non audivit eos, id est, verbis et signis Moysis ac Aaron non obtemperavit, sicut præceperat Dominus Pharaoni per Moysen, ut obtemperaret. Cur autem hac vice non acquievit, dici potest, quia reputavit facta magorum ac deorum suorum in hoc signo esse parificata, quod Deus Israel per Aaron fecit ; vel quia signum istud magicis artibus adscripsit. Potius tamen, quia non reputavit signum istud tale ac tantum, ut propter ipsum dignum duceret dimittere Israelitas.
paras.en: [[7:13|And Pharao's heart was hardened|Induratumque est cor Pharaonis]], [[7:13|and he did not hearken to them|et non audivit eos]], that is, he did not obey the words and signs of Moses and Aaron, [[7:13|as the Lord had commanded|sicut præceperat Dominus]] Pharao through Moses, that he should obey. As to why he did not give way this time, it can be said that he reckoned the deeds of the magicians and of his gods to have been made equal, in this sign, to what the God of Israel did through Aaron; or that he ascribed this sign to magic arts. But rather, because he did not reckon this sign to be such and so great that he should think fit to let the Israelites go on account of it.

paras.t: Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen : Ingravatum est cor Pharaonis, et non vult dimittere populum Hebræorum. Vade ad eum mane : quatenus, dum adhuc jejunus et sobrius est, aptior sit ad considerandum quæ dices ad eum, et inexcusabilior, si non obtemperaverit ; ecce enim egredietur ad aquas : forte ad deambulandum pro sanitate circa fluenta Nili ; et stabis in occursum ejus super ripam fluminis, id est, in ripa Nili stabis intrepidus ad occurrendum regi : et virgam quæ conversa est in draconem, id est virgam tuam, quæ fuit versa in colubrum, et in naturam rediit virgæ, tolles in manu tua.
paras.en: [[7:14|And the Lord said to Moses|Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen]]: [[7:14|Pharao's heart is hardened|Ingravatum est cor Pharaonis]], [[7:14|he will not let the people go|et non vult dimittere populum]] of the Hebrews. [[7:15|Go to him in the morning|Vade ad eum mane]]: so that, while he is still fasting and sober, he may be the fitter to consider what thou shalt say to him, and the more inexcusable if he does not obey; [[7:15|behold he will go out to the waters|ecce enim egredietur ad aquas]], perhaps to walk for his health along the streams of the Nile; [[7:15|and thou shalt stand to meet him on the ' bank of the river|et stabis in occursum ejus super ripam fluminis]], that is, thou shalt stand fearless on the bank of the Nile to meet the king; and [[7:15|the rod that was turned into a serpent|virgam quæ conversa est in draconem]], that is, thy rod, which was turned into a serpent and went back to the nature of a rod, [[7:15|thou shalt take in thy hand|tolles in manu tua]].

paras.t: Dicesque ad eum : Dominus Deus Hebræorum misit me ad te, dicens : Dimitte populum meum, ut sacrificet mihi in deserto, et usque ad præsens audire noluisti. Hæc igitur dicit Dominus : In hoc scies per evidentiam facti, et per experientiam pœnæ tibi nunc infligendæ, quod sim Dominus, id est Dominus universorum per universalem auctoritatem et potestatem plenariam, qua et his qui meum dominium recognoscere nolunt, ad libitum infero pœnas, et eos vinco ac mihi subjicio. Ecce percutiam virga quæ in manu mea est, aquam fluminis, id est, ego Dominus jubebo fluvium percuti cum hac virga, quæ in mea est potestate : vel ego Moyses ex parte Dei præcipiam, ut Aaron cum hac virga percutiat flumen; et vertetur in sanguinem. Hoc loco ponitur singulare pro plurali, quia non solum in sanguinem versus est unus fluvius Nili, per diversa loca Ægypti currentis, sed multi aut omnes fluvii ejus, ut paulo post habetur in textu.
paras.en: [[7:16|And thou shalt say to him|Dicesque ad eum]]: [[7:16|The Lord God of the Hebrews sent me to thee, saying: Let my people go to sacrifice to me in the desert|Dominus Deus Hebræorum misit me ad te, dicens : Dimitte populum meum, ut sacrificet mihi in deserto]], [[7:16|and hitherto thou wouldst not hear|et usque ad præsens audire noluisti]]. [[7:17|Thus therefore saith the Lord|Hæc igitur dicit Dominus]]: [[7:17|In this thou shalt know|In hoc scies]], by the evidence of the deed and by experience of the punishment now to be inflicted on thee, [[7:17|that I am the Lord|quod sim Dominus]], that is, the Lord of all things by universal authority and full power, by which I inflict punishments at my pleasure even on those who will not acknowledge my lordship, and overcome them and subject them to myself: [[7:17|behold I will strike with the rod, that is in my hand, the water of the river|Ecce percutiam virga quæ in manu mea est, aquam fluminis]], that is, I the Lord will command the river to be struck with this rod, which is in my power; or: I, Moses, on God's behalf will command Aaron to strike the river with this rod; [[7:17|and it shall be turned into blood|et vertetur in sanguinem]]. Here the singular is put for the plural, for not only was the one river of the Nile, which runs through various places of Egypt, turned into blood, but many or all of its rivers, as is related a little later in the text.

paras.t: Pisces quoque qui sunt in fluvio, id est diversis fluviis, morientur : quia in sanguine non poterunt vivere diu. Sicque Deus punivit Ægyptios in eorum substantiis et animalibus. Nec hoc fuit contra Dei justitiam, quod propter peccata hominum innoxia bruta occidit, quum propter homines facta sint irrationalia universa : idcirco utendum est eis secundum exigentiam finis institutionis eorum, hoc est secundum merita ac demerita hominum, prout super Genesim plenius dictum est. Et computrescent aquæ, id est, corrumpentur. Vel sensus est, quod etiam sanguis in quem conversa est aqua, in se ipso computruit. Et affligentur Ægyptii bibentes aquam fluminis. Si tota aqua Nili fuit versa in sanguinem, quomodo Ægyptii biberunt aquam fluminis? Est itaque sensus : Affligentur Ægyptii habentes aquam fluminis, id est, quam tentaverint bibere de fluvio converso ex aqua in sanguinem : quia sanguis ille fuit Ægyptiis non solum rubei coloris, sed et amari saporis, quod Ægyptii ignorabant quousque de illo gustare cœperunt; atque ut Josephus loquitur, intulit eis gemitus et dolores. Hebræis vero fuit dulcis atque potabilis.
paras.en: [[7:18|And the fishes that are in the river|Pisces quoque qui sunt in fluvio]], that is, in the various rivers, [[7:18|shall die|morientur]], because they will not be able to live long in blood. And so God punished the Egyptians in their goods and their animals. Nor was it against God's justice that he slew harmless brute beasts for the sins of men, since all irrational things were made for the sake of men; therefore they are to be used as the end for which they were established requires, that is, according to the merits and demerits of men, as was said more fully on Genesis. [[7:18|and the waters shall be corrupted|Et computrescent aquæ]], that is, shall be spoiled [the Latin *computrescent* is literally "shall rot"]. Or the sense is that even the blood into which the water was turned rotted in itself. [[7:18|and the Egyptians shall be afflicted when they drink the water of the river|Et affligentur Ægyptii bibentes aquam fluminis]]. If the whole water of the Nile was turned into blood, how did the Egyptians drink the water of the river? The sense, then, is this: The Egyptians shall be afflicted, having the water of the river [Denis here writes *habentes*, "having", for the text's *bibentes*, "drinking"], that is, the water which they tried to drink from the river turned from water into blood; for that blood was to the Egyptians not only red in colour but bitter in taste, which the Egyptians did not know until they began to taste it; and, as Josephus says, it brought them groans and pains. But to the Hebrews it was sweet and drinkable.

paras.t: Dixit quoque Dominus ad Moysen. Istud fuit quando Moyses stetit in præsentia Pharaonis : idcirco allocutio ista fuit forsitan solum interior sine visibili apparitione et exteriore allocutione angelica. Poterat tamen angelus apparere et loqui Moysi in præsentia aliorum, absque scitu, adspectu, ac auditione illorum. Dic ad Aaron : Tolle virgam tuam, id est, virgam quam semel projecisti in terram, ut converteretur in colubrum, sume de manu mea, et extende manum tuam, id est, manum tuam eleva, super aquas Ægypti, et super fluvios eorum, et rivos, et paludes, et omnes lacus aquarum, ut vertantur in sanguinem. Aaron una elevatione manus suæ in aere super aquas Ægypti, designavit quod omnipotentia Dei per suum obsequium operatura esset in aquis illis supernaturalem earum conversionem in cruorem. Et sit cruor in omni terra Ægypti, tam in ligneis vasis quam in saxeis.
paras.en: [[7:19|The Lord also said to Moses|Dixit quoque Dominus ad Moysen]]. This was when Moses stood in Pharao's presence; therefore this speaking was perhaps only inward, without any visible apparition or outward speech of an angel. Yet an angel could appear and speak to Moses in the presence of others without their knowing, seeing or hearing it. [[7:19|Say to Aaron|Dic ad Aaron]]: [[7:19|Take thy rod|Tolle virgam tuam]], that is, the rod which thou didst once cast down on the ground that it might be turned into a serpent, take it from my hand; [[7:19|and stretch forth thy hand|et extende manum tuam]], that is, lift up thy hand, [[7:19|upon the waters of Egypt, and upon their rivers, and streams and pools, and all the ponds of waters, that they may be turned into blood|super aquas Ægypti, et super fluvios eorum, et rivos, et paludes, et omnes lacus aquarum, ut vertantur in sanguinem]]. By one lifting of his hand in the air over the waters of Egypt, Aaron signified that the almighty power of God, through his service, would work in those waters their supernatural change into blood. [[7:19|and let blood be in all the land of Egypt, both in vessels of wood and of stone|Et sit cruor in omni terra Ægypti, tam in ligneis vasis quam in saxeis]].

paras.t: Feceruntque Moyses et Aaron sicut præceperat Dominus. Et elevans Aaron virgam, percussit, id est, cum virga sua tetigit, aquam fluminis circa quod stetit, coram Pharaone et servis ejus. Sicque tangendo unum flumen, designavit quod virtus divina spiritualiter tangeret cuncta flumina Ægypti modo præfato. Quæ versa est in sanguinem. Et pisces qui erant in flumine, mortui sunt. Et eadem hora ceteræ aquæ Ægypti in sanguinem sunt conversæ in instanti : quoniam virtus divina, quum sit infinita, instantanee operatur dum vult. Denique sicut in libro Sapientiæ scriptum est, Per quæ quis peccat, per hæc et punitur : ideo juste puniti sunt Ægyptii in ista conversione aquarum, qui tam graviter peccaverunt, submergendo in eis infantulos Hebræorum. Computruitque fluvius; non unus dumtaxat, sed omnes fluvii in Ægypto sic versi, quoniam grandis fœtor inde erupit, qui et de cadaveribus piscium partim poterat exhalare, sicque fœtore illo cruciabantur Ægyptii. Et quoniam vita animalium præsertim in sanguine est, recte per sanguinem sunt puniti, qui infantium vitam exstinxerunt in aqua. Cur autem Aaron, et non Moyses, aquam percussit, eadem ratio assignatur, quæ de hoc quod virgam projecit. Et fuit sanguis in tota terra Ægypti. Etiam in vasis ligneis atque in lapideis, in quibus haustæ fuerunt aquæ, et in eisdem vasis seu urnis vertebantur in sanguinem.
paras.en: [[7:20|And Moses and Aaron did as the Lord had commanded|Feceruntque Moyses et Aaron sicut præceperat Dominus]]: [[7:20|and lifting up|Et elevans]] Aaron [[7:20|the rod|virgam]], [[7:20|he struck|percussit]], that is, touched with his rod, [[7:20|the water of the river|aquam fluminis]] by which he stood, [[7:20|before Pharao and his servants|coram Pharaone et servis ejus]]. And so, by touching one river, he signified that the divine power would touch spiritually all the rivers of Egypt in the manner described above. [[7:20|and it was turned into blood|Quæ versa est in sanguinem]]. [[7:21|And the fishes that were in the river died|Et pisces qui erant in flumine, mortui sunt]]. And in the same hour the other waters of Egypt were turned into blood in an instant: for the divine power, being infinite, works instantaneously when it wills. Lastly, as it is written in the book of Wisdom, [[Wis 11:17|by what things a man sinneth, by the same also he is tormented|Per quæ quis peccat, per hæc et punitur]]: therefore the Egyptians, who had sinned so grievously by drowning the little children of the Hebrews in these waters, were justly punished in this turning of the waters. [[7:21|and the river corrupted|Computruitque fluvius]]; not one only, but all the rivers in Egypt that were so turned, since a great stench broke out from them, which could also come in part from the carcasses of the fish; and so the Egyptians were tormented by that stench. And since the life of animals is above all in the blood, those who had put out the life of infants in water were rightly punished by blood. As to why Aaron, and not Moses, struck the water, the same reason is given as for his casting down the rod. [[7:21|and there was blood in all the land of Egypt|Et fuit sanguis in tota terra Ægypti]]: even in the vessels of wood and of stone in which water had been drawn; in those very vessels or jars it was turned into blood.

paras.t: Feceruntque similiter malefici Ægyptiorum incantationibus suis : hoc est, per magicas artes et diabolicas opes, per applicationem occultam naturalium causarum, verterunt aquam in sanguinem, sicut de conversione virgarum in dracones præhabitum est.
paras.en: [[7:22|And the magicians of the Egyptians with their enchantments did in like manner|Feceruntque similiter malefici Ægyptiorum incantationibus suis]]: that is, by magic arts and the help of devils, through the hidden application of natural causes, they turned water into blood, as was set out above on the turning of the rods into serpents.

paras.t: Quæritur, unde habuerint hanc aquam, præsertim si omnes Ægypti aquæ in sanguinem sunt conversæ. Circa hoc recitat Lyra : Dicunt Hebræi, quod non omnes aquæ Ægypti erant in sanguinem versæ, sed solum aquæ Nili, et quæ fluebant ex Nilo, non autem fontes. Contra quod objicitur, quia jam dictum est, quod Moyses dixit ad Aaron : Extende manum tuam super aquas Ægypti. Ex quo apparet, quod omnis aqua Ægypti fuit in sanguinem versa. Rursus paulo post dicitur : Foderunt omnes Ægyptii per circuitum fluminis, aquam ut biberent : quod non fecissent, si habuissent fontes aquarum potabiles. Doctores autem catholici dicunt communiter, quod aqua fuit magis allata ex terra Gessen, ubi habitabant Hebræi, et quod plaga ista non exstitit ibi. Contra quod objicitur, quia secundum Josephum, etiam plaga hæc fuit ibi. Imo nisi et in terra Gessen fuisset, non fuissent Ægyptii habitantes ibidem, pariter cum Hebræis hac plaga percussi. Verumtamen Josephus non dicit hoc evidenter. Hinc Lyra probabilius reputat, quod ministerio dæmonum fuit ab extra Ægyptum, magis allata. Asserit quoque, quod fluvius fuit in terra Gessen Hebræis potabilis, quoniam statim revertebatur ad aquæ naturam, quando Hebræi hauserunt ex eo. Verumtamen Josephus dicit, quod fluvius fuit Hebræis potabilis, quamvis mutatus. Magister quoque in historiis dicit : Videtur quod alibi quam in Nilo, aqua fuerit in Ægypto. Per quod innuere perhibetur, quod aqua fuit ex Ægypti fontibus non conversis deducta ad magos, ut dicunt Hebræi. Augustinus vero sentit aquam terræ Gessen, in qua manebant Hebræi, non fuisse versam in sanguinem. Ad objectum autem dici posset, quod omnes Ægyptii longe a fontibus habitantes, foderunt pro aqua, ut dictum est.
paras.en: It is asked where they got this water, especially if all the waters of Egypt were turned into blood. On this Lyra relates: The Hebrews say that not all the waters of Egypt were turned into blood, but only the waters of the Nile and those that flowed from the Nile, and not the springs. Against which it is objected that it has already been said that Moses said to Aaron: [[7:19|stretch forth thy hand upon the waters of Egypt|Extende manum tuam super aquas Ægypti]]; from which it appears that all the water of Egypt was turned into blood. Again, a little later it is said: [[7:24|And all the Egyptians dug round about the river for water to drink|Foderunt omnes Ægyptii per circuitum fluminis, aquam ut biberent]]; which they would not have done had they had springs of drinkable water. But the Catholic doctors commonly say that the water was brought to the magicians [*magis*, "to the magicians"] from the land of Gessen, where the Hebrews dwelt, and that this plague was not there. Against which it is objected that, according to Josephus, this plague was there too; indeed, unless it had been in the land of Gessen as well, the Egyptians dwelling there together with the Hebrews would not have been struck by this plague. Yet Josephus does not say this clearly. Hence Lyra reckons it more probable that it was brought to the magicians from outside Egypt by the ministry of demons. He asserts also that in the land of Gessen the river was drinkable for the Hebrews, since it at once returned to the nature of water when the Hebrews drew from it. Yet Josephus says that the river was drinkable for the Hebrews though it was changed. The Master in the Histories also says: It seems that there was water in Egypt elsewhere than in the Nile; by which he is taken to hint that the water was brought to the magicians from springs of Egypt that had not been changed, as the Hebrews say. But Augustine holds that the water of the land of Gessen, in which the Hebrews lived, was not turned into blood. To the objection, however, it could be said that all the Egyptians who lived far from springs dug for water, as was said.

paras.t: Et induratum est cor Pharaonis, nec audivit eos, etc. Avertitque se, et ingressus est domum suam, nec apposuit cor suum etiam hac vice : præsertim quia malefici sui videbantur comparati Moysi et Aaron in hoc signo.
paras.en: [[7:22|and Pharao's heart was hardened, neither did he hear them|Et induratum est cor Pharaonis, nec audivit eos]], etc. [[7:23|And he turned himself away, and went into his house|Avertitque se, et ingressus est domum suam]], [[7:23|neither did he set his heart to it|nec apposuit cor suum]] [[7:23|this time also|etiam hac vice]]: especially because his sorcerers seemed to be a match for Moses and Aaron in this sign.

paras.t: Foderunt itaque omnes Ægyptii per circuitum fluminis, aquam ut biberent, hoc est, ad hoc ut aquam potui aptam invenirent, foderunt puteos profunde in terra. Verumtamen secundum Josephum, non aquam, sed sanguinem repererunt. Non enim poterant bibere aquam fluminis, hoc est de cruore qui fuit in loco, in quo antea fuit aqua. Impletique sunt septem dies postquam percussit Dominus fluvium : id est, septem diebus duravit hæc plaga, scilicet sanguis in omni terra Ægypti, in qua omnes fluvii erant in sanguinem versi. Unus tamen fluvius fuit specialiter percussus a Deo, per virgam et obsequium Aaron. Evolutisque septem diebus, redierunt aquæ ad suam naturam. Circa quod Josephus scribit, quod Pharao timens et hæsitans ex hac plaga, licentiavit Hebræos ad exeundum : sed sublata plaga, revocavit sententiam suam. Hæc autem conversio aquarum in sanguinem, fuit non primum signum, sed prima plaga Ægypto inflicta.
paras.en: [[7:24|And all the Egyptians dug round about the river for water to drink|Foderunt itaque omnes Ægyptii per circuitum fluminis, aquam ut biberent]], that is, they dug wells deep in the ground so as to find water fit to drink. Yet according to Josephus they found not water but blood. [[7:24|for they could not drink of the water of the river|Non enim poterant bibere aquam fluminis]], that is, of the gore that was in the place where the water had been before. [[7:25|And seven days were fully ended, after that the Lord struck the river|Impletique sunt septem dies postquam percussit Dominus fluvium]]: that is, this plague lasted seven days, namely the blood in all the land of Egypt, in which all the rivers had been turned into blood. Yet one river was struck by God in a special way, by the rod and the service of Aaron. And when the seven days had passed, the waters returned to their own nature. On this Josephus writes that Pharao, afraid and wavering because of this plague, gave the Hebrews leave to go out; but when the plague was taken away, he revoked his decision. Now this turning of the waters into blood was not the first sign, but the first plague inflicted on Egypt.

20.title: Expositio capituli vicesimi: Locutusque est Dominus cunctos sermones hos
20.title_en: Exposition of the twentieth chapter: “And the Lord spoke all these words”

paras.t: Jam datio legis describitur. Locutusque est Dominus cunctos sermones hos. In fine præcedentis capituli scriptum est, qualiter Moyses de celsitudine montis descendens, recitavit populo ea quæ ibi sunt scripta. Moyse itaque inferius exsistente cum populo, locutus est Dominus verba nunc exponenda, tam Moyse quam populo audiente, dicens : EEgo sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui eduxi te de terra Ægypti, de domo servitutis. Quemadmodum refert Lyra, Hebræi dicunt, quod istud sit unum et primum præceptum Decalogi, per quod affirmative præcipit Deus, ut ipse solus habeatur et colatur pro vero Deo, qui tam potenter et miraculose eduxit Israel de Ægypto. Quocirca Rabbi Paulus reprehendit Lyram, eo quod simpliciter narret prætactam Hebræorum opinionem, quasi probabiliter possit teneri, et non reprobet eam : quia si posset teneri, sequeretur secundum Rabbi Paulum, quod doctores catholici in enumeratione Decalogi deviassent a ratione. Verum hæc reprehensio est inepta, nec tenet consequentia illa : quia (ut infra patebit) etiam nostri doctores in modo numerandi, distinguendi, ac situandi decem præcepta, variis modis senserunt ; nec tamen hine sequitur, quod in hoc deviaverunt a ratione. Frequenter enim circa eamdem materiam diversæ opiniones possunt probabiliter teneri, absque errore et deviatione a ratione, quando non defenduntur cum incauta et temeraria assertione, ut patuit plenius in expositione exordii Geneseos, quod sancti doctores diversimode exposuerunt.
paras.en: Now the giving of the Law is described. [[20:1|And the Lord spoke all these words|Locutusque est Dominus cunctos sermones hos]]. At the end of the preceding chapter it is written how Moses, coming down from the height of the mountain, recited to the people what is written there. So, while Moses was below with the people, the Lord spoke the words now to be expounded, in the hearing of both Moses and the people, saying: [[20:2|I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.|Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui eduxi te de terra Ægypti, de domo servitutis.]] As Lyra reports, the Hebrews say that this is one commandment, the first of the Decalogue, by which God commands affirmatively that He alone be held and worshipped as the true God, He who so mightily and miraculously brought Israel out of Egypt. For this reason Rabbi Paul censures Lyra for simply relating this opinion of the Hebrews as though it could be held as probable, without rejecting it: for if it could be held, it would follow, according to Rabbi Paul, that the Catholic doctors had departed from reason in their numbering of the Decalogue. But this censure is beside the point, and the consequence does not hold: for (as will appear below) our own doctors too have held various views on the way of numbering, dividing and ordering the ten commandments, and yet it does not follow that they departed from reason in this. For often several opinions about the same matter can be held as probable, without error or departure from reason, so long as they are not defended with incautious and rash assertion, as was shown more fully in the exposition of the opening of Genesis, which the holy doctors have expounded in different ways.

paras.t: Deinde Rabbi Paulus reprobat præfatam Hebræorum opinionem, quia in verbis his, Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, non ponitur aliquod verbum imperativum aut præceptivum; sed est ibi solum denuntiatio quædam, qua Deus annuntiat populo quod ipse qui loquitur, sit Deus qui eos de Ægypto eduxit. Et in isto Rabbi Paulus catholice sentit, quia et Glossa ait: Non est istud mandatum, sed significatio cujus sit mandatum. Hoc idem asserit Augustinus et alii expositores communiter. Deinceps Rabbi Paulus tangit motiva Hebræorum, dicentium verba prehabita esse primum mandatum. Primum est, quia ad omnium divinorum observantiam præceptorum, necesse est præsupponere quod ille qui jussit ea, sit Deus qui Israel transtulit ex Ægypto : quoniam fides seu præsuppositio illa, est ratio obligandi ad servandum ipsius præcepta. Idcirco per verba hæc. EEgo sum Dominus Deus tuus, dicunt affirmative juberi, quod hoc firmiter credatur. Secundum eorum motivum est, quoniam antequam aliquis possit præcipere aliis, oportet ut recipiatur ab eis pro superiore. Ideo dicunt Deum primo jussisse per verba inducta, quod ipse haberetur ab Hebræis in Deum. Sed ista motiva quamvis aliquid contineant veritatis, non tamen concludunt propositumquia jam ante horum prolationem verborum filii Israel crediderunt, quod ille qui eos eduxit, esset verus Deus, et specialiter Deus eorum. Unde submersis Ægyptiis, cecinerunt : Cantemus Domino, gloriose enim magnificatus est. Quartodecimo quoque capitulo scriptum est, quod eis per maris fundum transductis, Ægyptiisque submersis, crediderunt Domino et Moysi servo ejus. Denique, præcedenti capitulo fassi sunt se velle esse subjectos imperio Dei, dicentes : Cuncta quæ locutus est Dominus, faciemus. Itaque Deus tanquam præambulum quoddam pramittens, locutus est populo Israel : EEgo sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui licet sim universorum Dominus atque Deus per creationem et gubernationem, conservationem et judiciariam potestatem, tamen sum specialiter Dominus Deus tuus, quem elegi mihi in populum peculiarem, et cui nunc legem et præcepta hæc tribuo.
paras.en: Next, Rabbi Paul rejects this opinion of the Hebrews, because in the words [[20:2|I am the Lord thy God|Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus]] no verb of command or precept is used; there is only a kind of declaration, by which God announces to the people that He who speaks is the God who brought them out of Egypt. And in this Rabbi Paul thinks as a Catholic, for the Gloss too says: This is not a commandment, but a statement of whose commandment it is. Augustine and the other expositors commonly assert the same. Rabbi Paul then touches on the reasons of the Hebrews who say that these words are the first commandment. The first is that, for the keeping of all the divine precepts, it must be presupposed that He who commanded them is the God who brought Israel out of Egypt; for that belief, or presupposition, is the ground of the obligation to keep His precepts. Therefore, they say, by the words [[20:2|I am the Lord thy God|Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus]] it is affirmatively commanded that this be firmly believed. Their second reason is that before anyone can command others, he must be accepted by them as their superior; so they say that God first commanded, by these introductory words, that He be held by the Hebrews as God. But these reasons, though they contain some truth, do not prove the point, because even before these words were spoken the children of Israel believed that He who brought them out was the true God, and in a special way their God. Hence, when the Egyptians had been drowned, they sang: [[15:1|Let us sing to the Lord: for he is gloriously magnified|Cantemus Domino: gloriose enim magnificatus est]]. And in the fourteenth chapter it is written that, when they had been led across the bed of the sea and the Egyptians drowned, [[14:31|they believed the Lord, and Moses his servant|crediderunt Domino, et Moysi servo ejus]]. Finally, in the preceding chapter they professed that they were willing to be subject to God's rule, saying: [[19:8|All that the Lord hath spoken, we will do|Cuncta quæ locutus est Dominus, faciemus]]. So God, setting this down first as a kind of preamble, spoke to the people of Israel: [[20:2|I am the Lord thy God|Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus]]; that is, though I am Lord and God of all things by creation and governance, by preservation and by power of judgment, yet I am in a special way the Lord thy God, thine whom I have chosen for myself as a peculiar people, and to whom I now give this law and these precepts.

paras.t: Consequenter exprimitur primum præceptum : Non habebis deos alienos coram me. Quasi dicat : Me solum pro vero Deo habebis, adorabis et coles ; omnes ceteros qui dii vocantur, refutabis adorare et colere per latriæ cultum, ita quod nec eos qui mendaciter dii vocantur, ut Jupiter, Mars, Saturnus, qui scelerati fuerunt, nec illos qui in Scripturis dii vocantur per participationem et gratiam, ut angeli et homines sancti, adorabis et coles latriæ cultu. Dæmones quoque a gentilibus dii mendaciter vocabantur. Corpora autem cælestia animata ponebant, sicque cælos, stellas, planetas, vocabant deos per quamdam participationem. De quibus in primo Timæi loquitur in persona Dei Plato philosophus : 0 dii deorum, quorum idem paer opifexque ego. Omnes hi possunt dii alieni vocari, in quantum per vitiosum cultum eorum homines alienantur, avertuntur et reprobantur a vero Deo: et item, quoniam Deus jussit, ut fideles sui ab illorum cultu se alienarent: rursumque, quia a vera deitate sunt alieni. Itaque ait : Non habebis deos alienos coram me, id est nullibi, quoniam ego ubique sum præsens, et cuncta intueor.
paras.en: Next the first commandment is stated: [[20:3|Thou shalt not have strange gods before me.|Non habebis deos alienos coram me.]] As if to say: Me alone shalt thou hold, adore and worship as the true God; all the others who are called gods thou shalt refuse to adore and worship with the worship of latria [the worship due to God alone]. So thou shalt adore and worship with latria neither those who are falsely called gods, such as Jupiter, Mars and Saturn, who were wicked men, nor those who in the Scriptures are called gods by participation and grace, such as the angels and holy men. The demons too were falsely called gods by the gentiles. And the gentiles held the heavenly bodies to be living things, and so called the heavens, the stars and the planets gods by a kind of participation; of these Plato the philosopher speaks in the person of God in the first book of the Timaeus: 'O gods of gods, whose father and maker I am.' All these can be called strange gods [dii alieni, literally 'alien gods'], inasmuch as by the sinful worship of them men are estranged, turned away and cast off from the true God; and again, because God commanded His faithful to estrange themselves from their worship; and again, because they are strangers to true divinity. Therefore He says: [[20:3|Thou shalt not have strange gods before me|Non habebis deos alienos coram me]], that is, nowhere, for I am present everywhere and behold all things.

paras.t: Non facies tibi sculptile, id est idolum aliquod ex quacumque materia, in qua sculpi potest. Et specialiter potest per idolum designari imago rei confictæ, quæ nullam exsistentiam habet, nec esse potest, quum dicat Apostolus : Idolum nihil est. Neque omnem similitudinem quæ est in cælo desuper, et quæ in terra deorsum, nec eorum quæ sunt in aquis sub terra : id est, nullam tibi formabis similitudinem per fusuram sive picturam cujuscumque rei creatæ, videlicet ad colendum aliquid tale, ita ut nec cælestium neque terrestrium neque aquaticorum imaginem tibi formes, aut fieri facias. Hinc subditur: Non adorabis ea neque coles, quia nec ipsam rem creatam, nec ejus imaginem. Aliqui namque putaverunt aliquid numinis esse in ipsis idolis, statuis seu imaginibus, ut Trismegistus, qui dixit : Statuas dico animatas sensu et spiritu plenas, imbecillitatem et sanitatem hominibus facientes. Aliqui vero hoc non credentes, coluerunt deos absque imagine eorumdem. Unde Varro, Valeriusque testantur, quod antiqui Romani deos diu absque imaginibus coluerunt.
paras.en: [[20:4|Thou shalt not make to thyself a graven thing|Non facies tibi sculptile]]: that is, any idol, of whatever material can be carved. And by 'idol' may especially be meant the image of a made-up thing, which has no existence and cannot exist, since the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 8:4|an idol is nothing|nihil est idolum]]. [[20:4|nor the likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or in the earth beneath, nor of those things that are in the waters under the earth|neque omnem similitudinem quæ est in cælo desuper, et quæ in terra deorsum, nec eorum quæ sunt in aquis sub terra]]: that is, thou shalt form for thyself no likeness of any created thing, by casting or by painting, for the purpose of worshipping any such thing; so that thou shalt neither form nor have made for thyself an image of things in the heavens, on the earth, or in the waters. Hence it is added: [[20:5|Thou shalt not adore them, nor serve them|Non adorabis ea, neque coles]]: neither the created thing itself nor its image. For some thought that there was something of divinity in the idols themselves, the statues or images; such was Trismegistus, who said: 'I speak of statues ensouled, full of sense and spirit, which bring sickness and health to men.' Others, not believing this, worshipped the gods without images of them; hence Varro and Valerius testify that the ancient Romans long worshipped their gods without images.

paras.t: Ego enim sum Dominus Deus tuus fortis, zelotes, id est, instar amatoris seu mariti aut sponsi zelotypi, volens solus amari et coli ut Deus et sponsus a fidelibus animabus : idcirco prohibeo eis fornicari cum diis alienis, quemadmodum sponsus non vult sponsam suam alteri commisceri. Qui autem accedit meretricem, non indignatur si et alter eam accedat, quia non habet ad illam amorem zelotypum qui socium et communicatorem excludit. Unde zelotes seu zelator nunc appellatur, qui sic vult solus amari, ita ut nihil secum ametur, in derogationem aut minorationem sui amoris. Sic igitur præcipit Deus se coli et honorari, ut ei dumtaxat tota mente adhæreamus, serviamus, atque vacemus, et non sit anima nostra dæmonum aut idolorum, alienorumve deorum adultera, sed Dei solummodo sponsa.
paras.en: [[20:5|I am the Lord thy God, mighty, jealous|ego sum Dominus Deus tuus fortis, zelotes]]: that is, like a jealous lover, husband or bridegroom, who wishes to be loved and cherished alone, as God and Bridegroom, by faithful souls. Therefore I forbid them to commit fornication with strange gods, just as a bridegroom will not have his bride joined to another. A man who goes in to a harlot is not indignant if another goes in to her too, because he has no jealous love for her, the kind that shuts out a companion and sharer. So He is here called jealous (zelotes, or zealous) who wishes to be loved alone in such a way that nothing be loved along with Him to the detriment or lessening of love for Him. Thus God commands that He be worshipped and honoured in such a way that we cleave to Him alone with our whole mind, serve Him and give ourselves to Him, and that our soul be no adulteress with demons, idols or strange gods, but the bride of God alone.

paras.t: Visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios, in tertiam et quartam generationem, eorum qui oderunt me. Non absolute ait, in tertiam et quartam generationem ; sed addit, Eorum qui oderunt me. Verumtamen additio ista, Eorum qui oderunt me, potest referri ad id quod dixit, Iniquitatem patrum, et etiam ad filios. Sed istud bonitati et æquitati Dei derogare videtur, ut iniquitatem parentum ulciscatur in sobolem, præsertim quum per Ezechielem locutus sit : Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris. Et per eumdem Prophetam ac Jeremiam : Omnis, inquit, qui comederit uvam acerbam, obstupescent dentes ejus. Nihilo minus idem Jeremias fatetur in Threnis : Patres nostri peccaverunt, et non sunt; et nos iniquitates eorum portavimus. Et in Josue leguntur filii Israel fugati, et quidam eorum occisi sunt propter peccatum Achan. Itaque circa materiam istam inveniuntur variæ auctoritates Scripturæ, quæ sibi invicem contrariari videntur. Nam et infra legitur, quod nunc in textu asseritur.
paras.en: [[20:5|visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me|visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios, in tertiam et quartam generationem eorum qui oderunt me]]. He does not say simply, 'unto the third and fourth generation,' but adds, 'of them that hate me.' Yet this addition, 'of them that hate me,' can be referred to what He said, 'the iniquity of the fathers,' and also to the children. But it seems to detract from God's goodness and fairness that He should avenge the iniquity of parents upon their offspring, especially since He has said through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 18:20|the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father|filius non portabit iniquitatem patris]]. And through the same Prophet, and through Jeremias: [[Jer 31:30|every man that shall eat the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge|omnis homo qui comederit uvam acerbam, obstupescent dentes ejus]]. Yet the same Jeremias confesses in the Lamentations: [[Lam 5:7|Our fathers have sinned, and are not: and we have borne their iniquities.|Patres nostri peccaverunt, et non sunt: et nos iniquitates eorum portavimus.]] And in Josue we read that the children of Israel were put to flight, and some of them slain, for the sin of Achan. So on this matter we find various authorities of Scripture which seem to contradict one another; and indeed what the text asserts here is read again below.

paras.t: Sed omnium horum solutio et concordantia ex dictis patet doctorum. Nempe, ut scribit S. Thomas in secunda secundæ, quod et ex dictis Alexandri de Hales habetur : Pœna potest considerari dupliciter : Primo, in quantum pœna, et prout per eam reparatur æqualitas justitiæ, dum peccator qui peceando nimis acquievit propriæ voluntati in derogationem justitiæ, aliquid patitur contra suam voluntatem, in ipsius justitiæ recompensam : sicque pœna pro proprio peccato infligitur. Secundo, consideratur pœna, ut medicina peccati, non solum curativa præteriti, sed etiam præservativa futuri, conservativaque boni : et sic aliqui puniuntur sine propria culpa, sed non sine causa. Per medicinam autem non est subtrahendum majus bonum, ut minus bonum obtineatur, sed econverso. Hinc aliqui absque propria culpa in temporalibus puniuntur per damna aut infirmitates, ut probentur, humilientur, aut alio modo gratiam sortiantur, sicque in spiritualibus bonis crescant, aut aliquo modo misericordiam consequantur. Nunquam tamen aliquis per spiritualium subtractionem bonorum punitur, nec in vita præsenti, neque futura, sine propria culpa. Sic ergo servi et filii in corporalibus aliquando puniuntur propter parentum aut dominorum suorum peccata, in quantum secundum corpus sunt aliquid seu res quædam illorum, ita quod parentes ac domini puniuntur in illis : unde in auctoritatibus dicitur, usque ad tertiam et quartam generationem, quia usque ad tot generationes vivere possunt parentes. Nec istud repugnat divine justitiæ, quoniam Deus hoc ipsum ordinat in ipsorum, sic patientium, bonum. Auctoritates autem contra hæc allegate, intelliguntur de pœnis spiritualibus et æternis.
paras.en: But the solution and harmonizing of all these is clear from what the doctors say. For, as St. Thomas writes in the Secunda Secundae [of the Summa], and as is also found in the words of Alexander of Hales, punishment can be considered in two ways. First, as punishment, inasmuch as by it the equality of justice is restored: the sinner who in sinning indulged his own will too far, to the detriment of justice, suffers something against his will in repayment to justice; and in this way punishment is inflicted for one's own sin. Secondly, punishment is considered as a medicine for sin, not only healing past sin but also guarding against future sin and preserving what is good; and in this way some are punished without fault of their own, though not without cause. But by medicine a greater good is not to be taken away to obtain a lesser, but the reverse. Hence some, without fault of their own, are punished in temporal things by losses or sicknesses, so that they may be tried, humbled or in some other way obtain grace, and so grow in spiritual goods, or in some way obtain mercy. Yet no one is ever punished by the withdrawal of spiritual goods, either in the present life or in the life to come, without fault of his own. So servants and children are sometimes punished in bodily things for the sins of their parents or masters, inasmuch as in the body they are something belonging to them, a kind of possession of theirs, so that the parents and masters are punished in them. Hence the authorities say 'unto the third and fourth generation,' because parents can live to see that many generations. Nor is this contrary to divine justice, since God ordains it for the good of those who suffer in this way. The authorities alleged against this are to be understood of spiritual and eternal punishments.

paras.t: Præterea Origenes solvit quæstionem hanc aliter, per patres peccantium, intelligens dæmones tentatores; per generationes, primam, secundam, tertiam et quartam, eos qui peccanti cooperantur, consentiunt, aut alio modo communicant.
paras.en: Origen, moreover, solves this question differently, understanding by the fathers of sinners the demons who tempt them, and by the first, second, third and fourth generations those who cooperate with the sinner, consent to him, or share in his sin in some other way.

paras.t: Et faciens misericordiam in millia his qui diligunt me, et custodiunt præcepta mea : id est, multo copiosius et protensius misereor posteris amantium me, et obedientium mihi, præsertim posteris prædestinatis. Nam ut ait Jacobus apostolus, Superexaltat misericordia judicium. Et Psalmista : Miserationes ejus super omnia opera ejus. Verumtamen in hac re attendere possumus, quam mirabilia et incomprehensibilia sint judicia Dei, quia interdum immediati filii justissimorum patrum sunt pessimi, et econverso. Ecce quam sanctus vir fuit Josias, et tamen filii ejus pessimi erant. Sic et Ezechias rex sanctus, filius fuit vitiosissimi Achaz. Denique, infra discutietur de ordinatione, enumeratione et situatione Decalogi ; et utrum dicta hucusque, sint ad unum præceptum spectantia, an potius sint duo præcepta.
paras.en: [[20:6|And shewing mercy unto thousands to them that love me, and keep my commandments.|et faciens misericordiam in millia his qui diligunt me, et custodiunt præcepta mea.]] That is, I show mercy far more abundantly and far longer to the descendants of those who love me and obey me, especially to descendants who are predestined. For as the apostle James says: [[Jas 2:13|mercy exalteth itself above judgment|superexaltat autem misericordia judicium]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 144:9|his tender mercies are over all his works|miserationes ejus super omnia opera ejus]]. Yet in this matter we may observe how wonderful and incomprehensible are the judgments of God: for sometimes the immediate sons of most just fathers are very wicked, and the reverse. See how holy a man Josias was, and yet his sons were very wicked; so too Ezechias, a holy king, was the son of the most vicious Achaz. Finally, below we shall discuss the order, numbering and arrangement of the Decalogue, and whether what has been said so far belongs to one commandment, or rather makes two.

paras.t: Sequitur aliud præceptum, et ut patebit, secundum in ordine. Non assumes nomen Dei tui in vanum : id est, nec falsum, nec sine rationabili causa jurabis per Deum. Nec enim insontem habebit Dominus eum, qui assumpserit nomen Domini Dei sui frustra : id est, talem tam inaniter jurantem, Deus non reputabit innoxium, sed transgressorem, damnationeque dignum ; imo decet ut nunquam sine reverentia et cordis attentione Deum nominemus, aut etiam nominari audiamus. Judæi vero affirmant hoc præcepto etiam prohiberi prolationem indebitam nominis Domini tetragrammaton, quod non licuit nominari nisi sacerdotibus, quando populum benedixerunt in templo.
paras.en: Another commandment follows, the second in order, as will appear. [[20:7|Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain|Non assumes nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum]]: that is, thou shalt not swear by God either falsely or without reasonable cause. [[20:7|for the Lord will not hold him guiltless that shall take the name of the Lord his God in vain|nec enim habebit insontem Dominus eum qui assumpserit nomen Domini Dei sui frustra]]: that is, God will not count one who swears so idly as innocent, but as a transgressor and worthy of damnation. Indeed, it is fitting that we should never name God, or even hear Him named, without reverence and attention of heart. The Jews, moreover, affirm that this commandment also forbids the improper utterance of the Lord's four-lettered name [the Tetragrammaton], which none but the priests were permitted to pronounce, when they blessed the people in the temple.

paras.t: Sequitur præceptum tertium : Memento ut diem sabbati sanctifices : id est, in sanctis operibus diem illum expendas, et divino cultui applices illum. Per quod aliorum dierum solennium, et nunc dominicæ diei jubetur celebritas. Instituit autem Dominus sabbatum, id est diem septimum, celebrari, in signum quod ipse die septimo requievit a cunctis operibus suis, et in commemorationem beneficii creationis, imo et aliorum Dei beneficiorum, quorum jugiter memores debemus esse. Propter quod præcepto huic præmittitur, Memento : quod verbum etiam ideo præmittitur, quoniam cum summa diligentia cultui est insistendum divino. Vel, ut asserit Rabbi Paulus, ideo verbum istud præmittitur, quia jam ante in descensu manna datum fuit istud præceptum, ut supra patuit. Recitat quoque Rabbi Paulus : Hebræi credunt quod sanctificatio sabbati præcipua consistat in corporalibus delectationibus ; traduntque quod quilibet tenetur in illo die ter manducare, videlicet semel prandere, et bis cœnare, atque quod omnes hoc facientes, sint securi a judicio gehennæ, ut in libro eorum de sabbato, expresse habetur. Ecce quam ridiculosum et stultum est hoc.
paras.en: The third commandment follows: [[20:8|Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day.|Memento ut diem sabbati sanctifices.]] That is, spend that day in holy works and give it to divine worship. By this the keeping of the other feast days is commanded too, and now of the Lord's Day. The Lord instituted the sabbath, that is, the seventh day, to be kept as a sign that He Himself rested on the seventh day from all His works, and in remembrance of the benefit of creation, and indeed of God's other benefits, which we ought to remember continually. That is why the word 'Remember' is set before this commandment; it is set there also because divine worship must be attended to with the greatest diligence. Or, as Rabbi Paul asserts, this word is set before it because this commandment had already been given when the manna came down, as was seen above. Rabbi Paul also relates that the Hebrews believe the chief sanctification of the sabbath to consist in bodily pleasures, and teach that everyone is bound to eat three times on that day, namely to dine once and sup twice, and that all who do this are safe from the judgment of Gehenna, as is expressly stated in their book on the sabbath. See how ridiculous and foolish this is!

paras.t: Sex diebus operaberis, nisi in eorum aliquo aliqua solennitas occurrat, et facies omnia opera tua : unumquodque loco et tempore opportuno. Septimo autem die sabbatum Domini Dei tui est, id est, qui deputatus est cultui veri Dei. Non facies omne opus tu : id est, nullum servile aut mechanicum, præsertim nullum opus iniquum facies tu, id est facere tibi licet, et filius tuus et filia tua, servus tuus et ancilla tua, jumentum tuum, quia et pecora quæ laborant hominibus, voluit Deus tunc quiescere, convenienterque refici ; et advena qui est intra portas tuas, id est tibi cohabitat in villis, urbibus, aut domibus tuis. Et potest, per advenam intelligi quicumque ad Judaismum conversus. Deinde subjungitur ratio institutionis solennitatis sabbativæ : Sex enim diebus fecit Deus cælum et terram, mare et omnia quæ in eis sunt. Et requievit die septimo. Quod qualiter multipliciter possit intelligi, in expositione primi capituli Genesis diffuse expositum est. Idcirco benedixit Dominus diei sabbati, privilegiando eum præ ceteris diebus, et sanctificavit eum, id est divino eultui consecravit. Porro de expositione multiplici et plena intelligentia hujus præcepti et ceterorum præceptorum Decalogi, tot et tanta in aliis scripsi opusculis, imo et tanta inde habentur ubique, quod nequaquam stare intendo nunc in horum expositione hoc loco.
paras.en: [[20:9|Six days shalt thou labour|Sex diebus operaberis]], unless some feast falls on one of them, [[20:9|and shalt do all thy works|et facies omnia opera tua]], each in its proper place and time. [[20:10|But on the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord thy God|Septimo autem die sabbatum Domini Dei tui est]], that is, the day set apart for the worship of the true God. [[20:10|thou shalt do no work on it, thou|non facies omne opus in eo, tu]]: that is, no servile or mechanical work, and above all no wicked work, shalt thou do; [[20:10|nor thy son, nor thy daughter, nor thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy beast|et filius tuus et filia tua, servus tuus et ancilla tua, jumentum tuum]], for God willed that even the beasts that labour for men should then rest and be suitably refreshed; [[20:10|nor the stranger that is within thy gates|et advena qui est intra portas tuas]], that is, who lives with thee in thy villages, cities or houses. By the stranger may also be understood anyone converted to Judaism. Then the reason for instituting the solemnity of the sabbath is added: [[20:11|For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them, and rested on the seventh day|Sex enim diebus fecit Dominus cælum et terram, et mare, et omnia quæ in eis sunt, et requievit in die septimo]]. The many ways in which this can be understood were set out at length in the exposition of the first chapter of Genesis. [[20:11|therefore the Lord blessed the seventh day|idcirco benedixit Dominus diei sabbati]], privileging it above the other days, [[20:11|and sanctified it|et sanctificavit eum]], that is, consecrated it to divine worship. As for the manifold exposition and full understanding of this commandment and of the other commandments of the Decalogue, I have written so much in other works, and so much on the subject is found everywhere, that I do not at all intend to dwell on their exposition in this place.

paras.t: Honora patrem tuum et matrem tuam, imo et ceteros progenitores, spiritualesque patres ac seniores, et benefactores ac magistros, cordiali affectu, decenti affatu, reali obtemperatione atque obsequio, et si opus fuerit, etiam sustentatione. De hac re infinita quodammodo dici possent. Subditur autem merces seu ratio hujus præcepti, ut sis longevus super terram, id est diu ac prospere vivas in terra. Non quod istud sit finale, principaleque premium observationis hujus præcepti, sed aliquantula retributio recte correspondens eidem : quoniam eum qui debite honorat principia suæ vitæ, puta parentes, decuit in ipsa sua vita prosperitatem et diuturnitatem sortiri, quemadmodum eum qui facit misericordiam, decet misericordiam consequi. Deus autem rudi populo veteris Testamenti temporalem promisit mercedem, ut vel sic ad obediendum alliceretur; tamen sub illa mercede subintellexit æternam ac spiritualem, quæ sola est premium condignum actuum virtuosorum, ex caritate Dei manantium, imo et ex actuali motione Spiritus Sancti. Unde quod ait, Ut sis longævus super terram quam Dominus Deus tuus dabit tibi,rite exponitur de regione cælestis patrie. De qua fertur : Credo videre bona Domini in terra viventium. Itemque : Beati mites, quoniam ipsi possidebunt terram : in qua justi sunt longævi, quia in æternum vivent in ea. Et quamvis prædicta secundum communem legem ita se habeant, quandoque tamen contingit occulto Dei judicio, quod honoratores parentum brevis et ærumnosæ sint vite, inhonoratores vero eorum, longeva ac prosperæ. Quod Deus sic ordinat ad majorem obedientium felicitatem, atque ad graviorem inobedientium damnationem. Vel ex aliis abditis causis id accidit.
paras.en: [[20:12|Honour thy father and thy mother|Honora patrem tuum et matrem tuam]], and indeed thy other forebears, thy spiritual fathers and elders, thy benefactors and teachers: with heartfelt affection, with fitting speech, with real obedience and service, and, if need be, with support as well. Endless things, in a way, could be said on this. Then the reward, or reason, of this commandment is added: [[20:12|that thou mayst be longlived upon the land|ut sis longævus super terram]], that is, that thou mayst live long and prosperously in the land. Not that this is the final and principal reward for keeping this commandment, but a modest recompense rightly answering to it: for it was fitting that he who duly honours the sources of his life, namely his parents, should obtain prosperity and length in that very life, just as it is fitting that he who shows mercy should obtain mercy.
